REAL-TIME WAREHOUSE DETECTION ON JETSON AGX ORIN:
YOLOv8 VS. EFFICIENTDET-D4 VS. NVIDIA TAO DETECTNET_V2

Executive conclusion

YOLOv8m exported to TensorRT INT8 is the best overall starting point for this deployment. It offers the strongest combination of single-frame latency, a compact OTA artifact, practical retraining ergonomics, and sufficient model capacity for small pallet labels and visually heterogeneous package damage. On Jetson AGX Orin 64GB, published TensorRT measurements report approximately 248 FPS for YOLOv8m INT8 at 640×640, equivalent to 4.03 ms of amortized inference time per frame, versus 171 FPS or 5.85 ms in FP16. That is a 1.45× INT8-over-FP16 throughput gain (https://edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin/yolov8/m/). A separate Jetson benchmark on AGX Orin 32GB reports 145 FPS INT8 and 105 FPS FP16 for YOLOv8m, or approximately 6.90 ms and 9.52 ms per frame, respectively (https://www.jetson-ai-lab.com/archive/tutorial_ultralytics.html).

For a 200-camera, 30-FPS deployment, however, no single Jetson AGX Orin can process all feeds. The aggregate requirement is:

200 cameras × 30 frames/s = 6,000 frames/s.

At the published 248-FPS YOLOv8m INT8 inference rate, the theoretical inference-only requirement is:

6,000 / 248 = 24.2, rounded up to 25 AGX Orin 64GB modules.

After accounting for decode, resize, batching inefficiency, tracking, post-processing, networking, thermal headroom, and tail latency, a realistic initial sizing is approximately 32–40 modules if every frame must be inferred. This is roughly five to seven cameras per module. If inference is reduced to 10–15 FPS per camera while a tracker propagates detections between inference frames, the required module count can be cut substantially without reducing the source-camera rate.

TAO DetectNet_v2 is the strongest of the three for an NVIDIA-native deployment pipeline: it has first-class pruning, retraining, QAT, TensorRT engine generation, DeepStream integration, calibration-cache handling, and DLA support. A pruned DetectNet_v2/ResNet18 can deliver much greater batched throughput than YOLOv8m. NVIDIA reports 1,116 FPS for PeopleNet DetectNet_v2/ResNet18 INT8 at 960×544 on AGX Orin 64GB, and 890 FPS for ResNet34, although these figures use large GPU batches and therefore do not represent batch-one end-to-end camera latency (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/model_zoo/overview.html). DeepStream 6.4 reports 993 FPS for PeopleNet/ResNet34 and 1,103 FPS for TrafficCamNet/ResNet18 under its Jetson performance configurations (https://archive.docs.nvidia.com/metropolis/deepstream/6.4/dev-guide/text/DS_Performance.html).

DetectNet_v2 nevertheless has two strategic drawbacks: it is a legacy TensorFlow 1 pipeline now listed under TAO deprecations, and adding new SKU classes still requires representative replay data for old classes. It is not a native, guarantee-bearing continual-learning system. YOLOv8 is therefore the better maintainability choice for monthly SKU updates, while TAO DetectNet_v2 is preferable if NVIDIA-supported deployment automation, QAT, pruning, DeepStream, and DLA utilization outweigh long-term framework flexibility.

EfficientDet-D4 is not recommended for this use case. It is accurate and compact—20.7 million parameters, 55.2 billion FLOPs, 1024×1024 native input, and 49.7 COCO mAP—but its BiFPN and high input resolution make it materially slower and more difficult to export and quantize reliably than YOLOv8 (https://github.com/google/automl/blob/master/efficientdet/README.md; https://arxiv.org/html/1911.09070v7). The official Google implementation reports 42.8 ms batch-one latency on a T4 for D4, or only 23 FPS, although that is not an Orin measurement (https://github.com/google/automl/blob/master/efficientdet/README.md). There is no authoritative, directly comparable AGX Orin D4 INT8 benchmark in the gathered evidence, so any precise Orin D4 latency claim would be speculative. EfficientDet’s TensorRT conversion history also includes ONNX operator and INT8 calibration failures, making it the highest integration-risk option.

Most importantly, the requested mAP degradation and sustained power for the organization’s custom 50,000-image warehouse dataset cannot be established from public benchmarks. Those values depend on the exact train/validation split, image resolution, label taxonomy, frequency and size of damaged regions, calibration images, power mode, cooling solution, JetPack/TensorRT version, and preprocessing. The figures below are therefore separated into published measurements, defensible planning ranges, and required acceptance tests. They should not be presented as measurements of the custom dataset until the proposed benchmark is run.

1. Workload and system implications

1.1 Throughput target

The raw workload is 6,000 frames per second. The corresponding frame deadline for each camera is:

1 / 30 FPS = 33.33 ms per frame.

Meeting a 33.33-ms per-camera deadline does not mean one module can support an arbitrary number of cameras. Aggregate throughput and video decoding also matter.

Published AGX Orin video capability is finite. An earlier AGX Orin technical description lists up to 24 simultaneous 1080p30 H.265 decode streams (https://www.miivii.com/pdf/nvidia-jetson-agx-orin-technical-brief.pdf). NVIDIA’s DeepStream 6.4 reference pipeline used 37 H.265 or 15 H.264 1080p30 streams on AGX Orin with inference, tracking, two secondary classifiers, and display disabled (https://archive.docs.nvidia.com/metropolis/deepstream/6.4/dev-guide/text/DS_Performance.html). NVIDIA has also stated that an AGX Orin cannot meet a 30-stream 1080p30 H.264 decode requirement under the discussed configuration because decode becomes the bottleneck; pipeline performance is governed by the slowest stage (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/jetson-agx-orin-64-gb-source30-1080p-dec-infer-resnet-tiled-display-int8-deepstream-expected-fps/294215).

The deployment must consequently be sharded across modules even if the detector’s synthetic inference throughput appears sufficient.

1.2 Inference-only module counts

Using published or derived detector throughput:

YOLOv8m, AGX Orin 64GB, 640×640, TensorRT INT8:

248 FPS → 1,000 / 248 = 4.03 ms/frame.
6,000 / 248 = 24.19 → at least 25 modules.

YOLOv8l, AGX Orin 64GB, 640×640, TensorRT INT8:

163 FPS → 6.13 ms/frame.
6,000 / 163 = 36.81 → at least 37 modules.

YOLOv8n, AGX Orin 64GB, 640×640, TensorRT INT8:

504 FPS → 1.98 ms/frame.
6,000 / 504 = 11.90 → at least 12 modules.

These AGX Orin 64GB YOLO figures are reported as measured TensorRT results: YOLOv8n 504 FPS INT8 and 371 FPS FP16; YOLOv8m 248 and 171; YOLOv8l 163 and 108 (https://edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin/yolov8/n/; https://edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin/yolov8/m/; https://edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin/yolov8/l/).

TAO DetectNet_v2/ResNet34 PeopleNet, published batched throughput:

890 FPS → 1.12 ms of amortized GPU time/frame.
6,000 / 890 = 6.74 → at least 7 modules for inference alone.

TAO DetectNet_v2/ResNet18 PeopleNet:

1,116 FPS → 0.896 ms amortized/frame.
6,000 / 1,116 = 5.38 → at least 6 modules.

Those TAO numbers use GPU batches of 32 on AGX Orin 64GB and 960×544 input (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/model_zoo/overview.html). They are throughput figures, not batch-one latency. A camera frame may wait while a batch is assembled, and preprocessing, clustering/NMS, transfer, and decoder time are excluded. At 200 synchronized cameras, batching is feasible, but tail latency must be measured.

There is insufficient direct evidence to compute a trustworthy EfficientDet-D4 AGX Orin module count. The official D4 model has 55.2 billion FLOPs at 1024×1024 and reports 42.8-ms batch-one T4 latency; a fixed 640×640 D4 variant reports 21.7 ms and lower COCO mAP of 45.7 (https://github.com/google/automl/blob/master/efficientdet/README.md). Neither figure is an Orin INT8 result. A production decision should not extrapolate D0 or D1 Orin performance to D4 because resolution, BiFPN width/depth, memory traffic, and post-processing do not scale linearly.

1.3 Recommended topology

For full 30-FPS inference with YOLOv8m:

• Engineering minimum: 25 AGX Orin 64GB modules based only on 248-FPS inference throughput.
• Recommended pilot design: 32 modules, approximately six or seven cameras per module.
• Conservative production design: 36–40 modules if the same module performs network ingest, hardware decode, image transforms, tracking, event rules, and local active-learning selection.
• Power provisioning at a 50-W module power mode: 32 modules × 50 W = 1.6 kW of module-budget power, or 40 × 50 W = 2.0 kW. Carrier boards, storage, networking and cooling increase wall power beyond this.
• Keep 20–30% throughput reserve for new models, hotter ambient conditions, camera bursts, and p99 latency.

An alternative is to decode cameras continuously at 30 FPS but infer every second or third frame. At 15 inference FPS per camera:

200 × 15 = 3,000 inferences/s.
3,000 / 248 = 12.1 → at least 13 modules inference-only.

At 10 inference FPS per camera:

200 × 10 = 2,000 inferences/s.
2,000 / 248 = 8.06 → at least 9 modules inference-only.

A DeepStream tracker can bridge frames between detector invocations. This is often preferable for inventory counting, but short-duration package-damage views must not be skipped. Labels and damage should therefore use different policies: tracking and lower detector frequency may be acceptable for pallets, while high-resolution damage crops may require event-triggered secondary inference.

2. Model comparison

2.1 Summary table

The table distinguishes published evidence from deployment planning estimates.

YOLOv8m, TensorRT INT8

• Representative input: 640×640.
• Parameters: 25.9 million.
• Published COCO FP model accuracy: 50.2 mAP50–95.
• Approximate raw INT8 weight payload: 25.9 MB before engine metadata/plugins.
• AGX Orin 64GB measured throughput: 248 FPS INT8, 171 FPS FP16.
• Derived latency: 4.03 ms INT8, 5.85 ms FP16.
• INT8 speedup over FP16: 248 / 171 = 1.45×.
• Expected custom-data mAP loss: approximately 0.5–2.0 absolute points with representative calibration and mixed precision or QAT; 3–7% relative degradation is possible with ordinary static PTQ, especially under blur/noise. This is a planning range, not a measurement.
• Recommended sustained module mode: 30–50 W, with 50 W preferred for stable multi-stream production.
• Main strengths: fast, compact, straightforward custom training and checkpoint warm-starting, extensive community and deployment support.
• Main weaknesses: no built-in solution to catastrophic forgetting; commercial closed-source use may require an Ultralytics Enterprise license.

YOLOv8 specifications are published at https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/yolov8. Ultralytics reports 3.2M/37.3 mAP for v8n, 11.2M/44.9 for v8s, 25.9M/50.2 for v8m, 43.7M/52.9 for v8l, and 68.2M/53.9 for v8x, all at 640 pixels. Licensing terms state that embedded, proprietary, internal-business and commercial deployment without releasing the project under AGPL requires an enterprise license (https://www.ultralytics.com/license/).

EfficientDet-D4, TensorRT INT8

• Native input: 1024×1024.
• Parameters: 20.7 million.
• FLOPs: 55.2 billion.
• Published COCO mAP: 49.7.
• Approximate raw INT8 weight payload: 20.7 MB.
• Official T4 batch-one latency: 42.8 ms in the reported optimized benchmark, or 23 FPS; not an Orin INT8 result.
• Fixed 640×640 variant: 45.7 COCO mAP and 21.7-ms reported latency, demonstrating the accuracy cost of reducing resolution.
• AGX Orin INT8 latency: not established by the available evidence. A planning assumption should be validated with the exact exported graph; approximately 10–25 ms inference-only is a reasonable engineering hypothesis but must not be treated as a measured result.
• Expected custom-data mAP loss: approximately 1–3 absolute points with good QAT; potentially much worse with PTQ or an incorrect export/calibration path.
• Recommended sustained module mode: 40–50 W because of the 1024-pixel input and BiFPN workload.
• Main strengths: strong multi-scale accuracy, relatively few parameters, potentially good sensitivity to small damage regions.
• Main weaknesses: slow relative to current YOLO implementations; more fragile ONNX/TensorRT path; older ecosystem; difficult INT8 calibration; native D4 resolution consumes substantial compute and memory bandwidth.

The original EfficientDet work defines D4 as a 1024-pixel input model using EfficientNet-B4, 224 BiFPN channels, seven BiFPN layers and four box/class layers (https://arxiv.org/html/1911.09070v7). The same work reports approximately 49.7 COCO mAP, 20.7M parameters and 55B FLOPs (https://github.com/google/automl/blob/master/efficientdet/README.md). Public TensorRT issues document cases where EfficientDet INT8 produced no boxes or junk output and where PTQ accuracy was poor enough to require QAT or a newer TensorRT version (https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/issues/3415). Older attempts to convert official D4 through ONNX also encountered unsupported or problematic graph operations around post-processing (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/running-trtexec-on-googles-efficientdet-d4-in-onnx-format/173615/1).

TAO DetectNet_v2, preferably pruned ResNet18 or ResNet34, TensorRT INT8

• Representative published input: 960×544.
• Published AGX Orin 64GB throughput:
  – ResNet18 PeopleNet: 1,116 FPS at GPU batch 32.
  – ResNet34 PeopleNet v2.3: 890 FPS at batch 32.
  – Unpruned ResNet34 PeopleNet v2.5: 421 FPS at batch 16.
• Derived amortized GPU times:
  – ResNet18: 1,000 / 1,116 = 0.896 ms/frame.
  – Pruned ResNet34: 1.124 ms/frame.
  – Unpruned ResNet34: 2.375 ms/frame.
• These are not batch-one end-to-end latency measurements.
• Expected custom-data mAP loss after QAT: less than approximately one absolute mAP point is an appropriate target based on NVIDIA’s PeopleNet QAT example, but it is not guaranteed on pallet labels or damage.
• Recommended sustained module mode: 30–50 W on GPU; DLA can improve system efficiency and free GPU capacity, although DLA QAT deployment has caveats.
• Main strengths: highest batched throughput; integrated pruning/QAT/retraining; DeepStream and DLA deployment; reproducible calibration and engine-generation workflow.
• Main weaknesses: legacy/deprecated TensorFlow 1 model family; grid-based design may require careful tuning for very small labels and irregular damage; less flexible than YOLO for rapid architectural iteration.

NVIDIA’s model-zoo measurements were made with `trtexec` and list GPU and DLA throughput by precision and batch size (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/model_zoo/overview.html). NVIDIA’s QAT example reports that QAT-trained PeopleNet maintained mAP within 1% of its floating-point baseline while INT8 nearly doubled FPS versus FP16 on a T4 (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/improving-int8-accuracy-using-quantization-aware-training-and-tao-toolkit/). That is evidence that DetectNet_v2 can quantize well, not proof that it will do so on this custom warehouse taxonomy.

3. INT8 latency and TensorRT optimization

3.1 YOLOv8 optimization gains

For YOLOv8m on AGX Orin 64GB:

FP16 throughput = 171 FPS.
INT8 throughput = 248 FPS.
Throughput gain = 248 / 171 = 1.450, or 45.0%.

FP16 reciprocal latency = 1,000 / 171 = 5.85 ms.
INT8 reciprocal latency = 1,000 / 248 = 4.03 ms.
Latency reduction = (5.85 − 4.03) / 5.85 = 31.1%.

For YOLOv8l:

FP16 = 108 FPS, or 9.26 ms.
INT8 = 163 FPS, or 6.13 ms.
Speedup = 163 / 108 = 1.51×.
Latency reduction = 33.8%.

For YOLOv8n:

FP16 = 371 FPS, or 2.70 ms.
INT8 = 504 FPS, or 1.98 ms.
Speedup = 1.36×.
Latency reduction = 26.4%.

The figures are reciprocal throughput rather than observed p50 or p99 application latency. Camera-to-result latency will be larger.

An AGX Orin 32GB benchmark reports the following TensorRT FPS at 640×640:

• YOLOv8n: FP16 323, INT8 385.
• YOLOv8s: FP16 213, INT8 303.
• YOLOv8m: FP16 105, INT8 145.
• YOLOv8l: FP16 73.5, INT8 114.

These correspond to YOLOv8m reciprocal latencies of 9.52 ms FP16 and 6.90 ms INT8, and an INT8 speedup of 1.38× (https://www.jetson-ai-lab.com/archive/tutorial_ultralytics.html). Differences from the 64GB measurements reinforce the need to specify module SKU, power mode, JetPack, TensorRT, clocks and cooling.

3.2 What TensorRT contributes

TensorRT optimization is more than datatype conversion. Its builder performs layer and pointwise fusion, chooses hardware-specific tactics, targets Tensor Cores, and can exploit batching, CUDA graphs and multiple execution streams (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/performance/best-practices.html).

For example, TensorRT can fuse convolution plus activation or chains of pointwise operators into one kernel. NVIDIA states that fusion avoids host kernel-launch overhead—typically 5–15 microseconds per absorbed launch—and avoids materializing intermediate tensors in DRAM (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/performance/optimization.html). This is particularly valuable in feature-pyramid detectors with many short convolution and elementwise operations.

INT8 also reduces model-weight and activation bandwidth and uses Orin’s INT8 Tensor Core capability. The AGX Orin 64GB is rated for up to 275 INT8 TOPS, has 204 GB/s memory bandwidth, and supports power configurations from 15 W to 60 W; the 32GB version is rated at 200 INT8 TOPS and 15–40 W (https://www.nvidia.com/content/dam/en-zz/Solutions/gtcf21/jetson-orin/nvidia-jetson-agx-orin-technical-brief.pdf).

TensorRT engines are target-specific. NVIDIA’s DetectNet_v2 DeepStream documentation warns that an engine must be regenerated when the target hardware, TensorRT, or CUDA version changes; using an engine built for a different environment can cause degraded accuracy or refusal to load (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/ds_tao/detectnet_v2_ds.html). OTA distribution should therefore normally ship ONNX plus calibration/QDQ information and build the engine on-device, or ship separate signed engines for every exact JetPack/module combination.

3.3 Calibration and mixed precision

TensorRT supports both post-training quantization and quantization-aware training. PTQ requires representative calibration data and may degrade sensitive models; explicit Q/DQ quantization provides direct control over which tensors and operations are quantized (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/10.x.x/inference-library/work-quantized-types.html; https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/inference-library/quantized-types-workflows.html).

Quantization error comes from rounding and clamping. A scale wide enough to avoid clipping increases rounding error; a narrow scale reduces rounding resolution but clips outliers (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/inference-library/accuracy-considerations.html). Damage detection is vulnerable because subtle scratches, crushed corners, tears and punctures can be represented by low-amplitude feature responses.

Recommended calibration set:

• At least 1,000–2,500 images sampled from the 50,000-image training corpus.
• Stratify by camera, aisle, lighting, motion blur, pallet type, packaging material, label size, damage type, SKU frequency, daytime, and exposure.
• Include difficult negatives such as tape seams, printed graphics, shadows, reflections, stretch wrap and partially hidden labels.
• Do not use validation or test images for calibration selection if those sets are intended to estimate generalization.
• Recalibrate whenever the network structure or input distribution changes. NVIDIA’s TensorRT API documentation explicitly says recalibration is required when model structure or input data changes (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/10.x.x/_static/python-api/infer/Int8/Calibrator.html).

If full INT8 exceeds the accepted mAP loss, retain sensitive detection-head, box-decoding, normalization, resize or output layers in FP16. NVIDIA recommends mixed precision for layers where reduced precision damages accuracy (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/inference-library/accuracy-considerations.html).

4. Expected mAP degradation on the custom 50K-image dataset

4.1 What can and cannot be claimed

No public source can determine the INT8 mAP loss on an unseen proprietary dataset. It would be incorrect to report, for example, that YOLOv8 loses exactly 1.2 mAP or that EfficientDet loses 2.0 mAP on these 50,000 warehouse images without running both engines on a locked test set.

Public evidence gives only priors:

• NVIDIA reports DetectNet_v2 PeopleNet QAT within 1% of the floating-point baseline (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/improving-int8-accuracy-using-quantization-aware-training-and-tao-toolkit/).
• One small YOLOv8n experiment reported a 1.16-point mAP50 loss and a 1.49-point mAP50–95 loss after INT8 quantization, but it used only 94 evaluation images for the reported comparison, CPU ONNX Runtime rather than Jetson TensorRT, and overlapping bootstrap intervals. It is not production-grade evidence for this warehouse system (https://github.com/malcomzww/edge-detection-tracking-jetson-notes).
• A broader quantization study reports static TensorRT INT8 speedups of approximately 1.5–3.3× with roughly 3–7% mAP50–95 degradation on clean data, while blur, noise and compression can worsen robustness (https://arxiv.org/html/2508.19600).
• A YOLOv8s TFLite report observed a much larger drop from 0.449 to 0.382 mAP50–95, a 6.7-point absolute or 14.9% relative loss, showing that full INT8 can fail badly when the backend/calibration path is not appropriate (https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/9473).
• NVIDIA documents an EfficientDet INT8 failure case that produced no boxes or junk results, emphasizing that successful engine construction does not demonstrate retained accuracy (https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/issues/3415).

4.2 Planning ranges

For budgeting and experiment design—not final acceptance—the following ranges are reasonable:

YOLOv8m:
• Representative PTQ: 1–3 absolute mAP50–95 points of loss.
• QAT or well-tuned mixed precision: 0.5–1.5 points.
• Poor calibration or full quantization of sensitive outputs: potentially 5–7 points or complete failure.

EfficientDet-D4:
• Representative PTQ: 2–5 points, with unusually high failure risk.
• QAT/mixed precision: target 1–3 points.
• Poor export/calibration: potentially unusable output.

TAO DetectNet_v2:
• TAO QAT after prune/retrain: target less than 1 point.
• PTQ with a representative set: approximately 1–3 points.
• PTQ without representative small-label and damage examples: potentially larger losses or spurious boxes.

These are hypotheses to test. They are not observed results from the 50K-image dataset.

4.3 Required dataset evaluation

Freeze a camera-disjoint test set before optimization. A suitable split is:

• 40,000 training images.
• 5,000 validation images.
• 5,000 test images.

The exact allocation can change, but test cameras, SKU introduction dates, aisles and recording sessions should be separated from training to prevent frame-neighbor leakage.

Report at minimum:

• mAP50–95 and mAP50.
• Per-class AP for pallet label, intact package, crushed corner, tear, puncture, water damage, stretch-wrap damage and any other operational classes.
• Precision and recall at the production confidence threshold.
• AP by object-size bucket, especially labels below 32×32 pixels in the model input.
• False positives per camera-hour.
• Missed damage per 1,000 damaged packages.
• Count error per pallet.
• Performance by camera, aisle, lighting condition and SKU age.
• FP16 versus INT8 paired bootstrap confidence intervals.
• p50, p95 and p99 camera-to-result latency, not only `trtexec` throughput.

For a 92% precision requirement, select the confidence threshold on validation data, then report precision once on the locked test set. Do not infer “precision above 92%” from mAP; they are different metrics.

5. Power draw under sustained load

5.1 Supported power envelope

NVIDIA specifies the AGX Orin 64GB at 15–60 W, with optimized 15-W, 30-W and 50-W modes and a MAXN mode that can enable up to 60 W. The AGX Orin 32GB supports 15–40 W (https://www.nvidia.com/content/dam/en-zz/Solutions/gtcf21/jetson-orin/nvidia-jetson-agx-orin-technical-brief.pdf).

NVIDIA cautions that MAXN is unconstrained and may engage hardware throttling when total module power exceeds its TDP budget; it does not guarantee the best performance for every workload and is not the preferred heavy-load production mode without appropriate thermal configuration (https://docs.nvidia.com/jetson/archives/r36.5.2/DeveloperGuide/SD/PlatformPowerAndPerformance/JetsonOrinNanoSeriesJetsonOrinNxSeriesAndJetsonAgxOrinSeries.html).

The evidence gathered does not include controlled, model-specific rail-power measurements for all three detectors. Therefore exact claims such as “YOLOv8m draws 42 W” or “EfficientDet-D4 draws 47 W” would be unsupported.

5.2 Defensible planning estimates

At a fixed 50-W nvpmodel setting, all three models can drive the module close to its configured sustained envelope when continuously queued. The difference will appear more reliably in energy per inference and achieved throughput than in the configured wattage ceiling.

Planning expectations:

• YOLOv8m INT8: approximately 35–50 W module power under continuously saturated multi-stream GPU inference in a 50-W profile.
• EfficientDet-D4 INT8: approximately 40–50 W because its 1024×1024 input and BiFPN should keep GPU and memory heavily occupied.
• DetectNet_v2 INT8 GPU: approximately 30–50 W depending on backbone, batch size and whether the workload saturates the GPU.
• DetectNet_v2 on DLA: potentially lower GPU utilization and better system efficiency, but overall power must still be measured; DLA does not automatically minimize single-stream latency.

These are power-envelope planning ranges, not empirical measurements.

A useful inference-only efficiency estimate for YOLOv8m, assuming the module actually averages 45 W at 248 FPS, would be:

45 J/s / 248 frames/s = 0.181 J/frame.

At exactly 50 W:

50 / 248 = 0.202 J/frame.

For YOLOv8l at 163 FPS and 50 W:

50 / 163 = 0.307 J/frame.

These figures illustrate why YOLOv8m is preferable to v8l unless the larger model produces a material warehouse-accuracy gain.

5.3 Measurement procedure

Use `tegrastats` or direct INA rail telemetry and log:

• VDD_IN or total module input power.
• GPU, CPU, SOC and memory rail power if exposed.
• GPU and DLA utilization.
• Temperature and clock throttling.
• Average and 95th-percentile power after at least 30 minutes.
• Energy/frame = average watts / sustained end-to-end FPS.

Run each detector with identical camera recordings, decode settings, input resolution policy, batch size and power mode. Include a decode-only baseline and subtract it only if reporting detector incremental power; retain full module power for facility planning.

A two-hour thermal soak is preferable to a short `trtexec` run. The fan, carrier board, NVMe device and network interfaces should be included in separate wall-power reporting.

6. Model size and the practical sub-100-MB accuracy floor

6.1 Model-size calculation

For weights alone:

Model size ≈ parameter count × bytes per parameter.

YOLOv8m:
• FP16: 25.9M × 2 = 51.8 MB.
• INT8: 25.9M × 1 = 25.9 MB.

YOLOv8l:
• FP16: 43.7M × 2 = 87.4 MB.
• INT8: 43.7 MB.

YOLOv8x:
• FP16: 68.2M × 2 = 136.4 MB.
• INT8: 68.2 MB.

EfficientDet-D4:
• FP16: 20.7M × 2 = 41.4 MB.
• INT8: 20.7 MB.

Actual TensorRT engines are larger than raw weights because they include graph metadata, tactic information and possibly plugin state. Nonetheless, the 100-MB limit is not intrinsically restrictive for YOLOv8m, YOLOv8l or EfficientDet-D4 at INT8. Even YOLOv8x’s raw INT8 weights fit below 100 MB. Size must be checked on the serialized engine produced by the exact TensorRT version.

Consequently, “below 100 MB” should not force a nano-class model. The organization can deploy YOLOv8m or likely YOLOv8l under that cap and preserve substantially more accuracy than YOLOv8n. Ultralytics’ published COCO results illustrate the capacity gap: 37.3 mAP50–95 for v8n, 44.9 for v8s, 50.2 for v8m and 52.9 for v8l (https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/yolov8).

6.2 Practical accuracy floor

There is no universal mAP floor associated with 100 MB. Model size alone does not determine accuracy; input resolution, annotation quality, class balance, object size, quantization strategy and domain shift matter more.

For this project, the practical deployment floor should be defined operationally as:

• Overall precision at the selected threshold: at least 92%.
• Damage-class recall: preferably at least 90%, because high precision alone can hide unacceptable missed damage.
• INT8 mAP50–95: no more than two absolute points below the accepted FP16 baseline.
• Per-critical-class AP: no more than three points below FP16.
• No camera or major SKU family below 90% precision without a documented exception.
• False alarms and misses expressed in warehouse operational units, not only mAP.

If a concise planning estimate is required, a sub-100-MB YOLOv8m or YOLOv8l TensorRT INT8 artifact should target approximately 97–99% of its FP16 mAP after QAT or carefully calibrated mixed precision. For example, if the custom FP16 YOLOv8m reaches 0.60 mAP50–95, the practical release floor should be approximately 0.58–0.59, not a generic value copied from COCO.

For production precision, the floor is 92% because that is the stated operational requirement. It must be validated separately for pallet labels and package damage. A model with 92% overall precision but 75% precision on rare puncture damage does not satisfy the business objective.

7. Incremental learning and monthly SKU updates

7.1 None of the three provides “no-retraining” class addition

New SKUs create at least three forms of drift:

• Appearance drift: new package artwork, colors, label layouts and materials.
• Class drift: genuinely new detector categories.
• Frequency drift: old SKUs becoming rare.
• Environmental drift: new aisles, cameras, lighting and seasonal packaging.

Fine-tuning only on the newest SKU images causes catastrophic forgetting. NVIDIA’s TAO guidance explicitly says that adding a new class requires representative data for both old and new classes; supplying only the new class causes performance on old classes to deteriorate (https://developer.nvidia.com/tao-toolkit-usecases-whitepaper/4-add-new-classes-objects-existing-ai-model).

Thus monthly updates should be incremental fine-tuning with replay—not training from scratch, but also not a weight patch trained exclusively on new SKUs.

7.2 YOLOv8 pipeline

Ultralytics supports training from a custom checkpoint, resuming interrupted training, and exporting to ONNX or TensorRT. Resume restores model weights, optimizer, learning-rate scheduler, epoch and dataset state; a new dataset can also be supplied when continuing from prior weights (https://docs.ultralytics.com/modes/train). For monthly updates, the correct pattern is normally a fresh fine-tuning run warm-started from the last approved `best.pt`, not an exact interrupted-run resume.

Advantages:

• Simple Python and CLI workflow.
• Easy warm-start from the current production model.
• Straightforward dataset YAML changes.
• Broad support for data augmentation, export and benchmarking.
• Easier integration of rehearsal, distillation or custom continual-learning losses than in a closed model recipe.
• Compact checkpoints and engines.

Limitations:

• Native resume is not continual learning.
• Changing class count modifies the head and still requires replay of old classes.
• QAT and mixed-precision TensorRT workflows may require more custom engineering than TAO’s recipe.
• Ultralytics’ stated license requires an Enterprise license for proprietary embedded deployment unless the complete project is released under AGPL (https://www.ultralytics.com/license/).

7.3 TAO DetectNet_v2 pipeline

TAO offers a highly integrated sequence:

1. Start from trainable pretrained weights.
2. Fine-tune on the custom dataset.
3. Apply L1 regularization in preparation for pruning.
4. Prune.
5. Retrain the pruned model, with regularization disabled.
6. Enable QAT.
7. Evaluate.
8. Export ONNX and calibration information.
9. Generate a target-specific TensorRT engine.
10. Deploy through DeepStream.

NVIDIA’s documentation states that pruning removes parameters and requires retraining to recover the slight accuracy loss (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/7.0.1/text/cv_finetuning/tensorflow_1/object_detection/detectnet_v2.html). TAO’s DetectNet_v2 deploy workflow samples calibration batches across the training dataset and applies the same preprocessing as training (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/tao_deploy/detectnet_v2.html).

Transfer learning is supported by loading matching pretrained layer weights and randomly initializing absent layers, enabling changes in domain and resolution (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/7.0.1/text/cv_finetuning/tensorflow_1/object_detection/detectnet_v2.html).

This is the most robust packaged optimization/deployment pipeline of the three. However:

• DetectNet_v2 appears under TAO’s TensorFlow 1 deprecation area (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/deprecations/tensorflow_1/object_detection/detectnet_v2.html).
• It does not automatically solve catastrophic forgetting.
• Adding classes still requires old-class replay.
• Its configuration and container stack are more rigid.
• QAT INT8 deployment on Jetson DLA has a caveat: the current workflow does not natively support QAT scale deployment to DLA in the cited configuration; TAO instructs users to force PTQ to create a DLA-compatible calibration cache (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/tao_deploy/detectnet_v2.html).

7.4 EfficientDet pipeline

EfficientDet can be fine-tuned, but compared with the other two it has:

• A less active reference ecosystem.
• A TensorFlow/ONNX/TensorRT path that has historically needed custom plugins or graph surgery.
• Greater PTQ sensitivity.
• No compelling built-in continual-learning or edge-fleet deployment advantage.

It is therefore the weakest monthly-update option unless the organization already has a mature TensorFlow EfficientDet pipeline.

7.5 Overall update-pipeline judgment

Best NVIDIA-native packaged deployment pipeline: TAO DetectNet_v2.

Best long-term, developer-friendly monthly model lifecycle: YOLOv8.

Best overall recommendation for this project: YOLOv8m plus a disciplined MLOps layer for replay, active learning, QAT, regression testing and TensorRT engine generation.

If the team is small, strongly standardized on DeepStream, and does not want to maintain quantization/export code, TAO DetectNet_v2 may be operationally safer in the short term. If the deployment is expected to evolve for several years, the legacy TensorFlow 1 status makes YOLOv8 the safer model-development foundation.

8. Edge active learning and the 92% precision target

8.1 Can edge active learning maintain more than 92% precision?

It can substantially reduce annotation and training cost, but it cannot guarantee precision above 92% without validation and periodic replay-based fine-tuning. Active learning selects the most useful examples; it does not update detector weights by itself.

Research on incremental one-stage detection shows that knowledge distillation over classification, box regression and feature representations can add new classes while reducing catastrophic forgetting. RILOD reported learning a new class in minutes in edge/cloud and edge-only experiments, compared with hours for conventional fine-tuning (https://arxiv.org/html/1904.00781v2). This demonstrates feasibility, not a guarantee for this warehouse dataset.

Industrial active-learning work reports that uncertainty-guided, class-balanced sampling can approach full-data accuracy with fewer labeled examples (https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/275137160/Winands-2025-Adaptive-Retraining-Techniques-for-Foreign.pdf). Continual workspace-monitoring research found replay-based strategies to be the best-performing baselines and zero-shot detection materially weaker (https://www.esann.org/sites/default/files/proceedings/2024/ES2024-128.pdf).

The correct answer is therefore conditional:

• Yes, an edge-assisted active-learning loop can plausibly maintain greater than 92% precision between major retraining cycles if drift is gradual, confidence is calibrated, old-class replay is retained, human review covers uncertain and novel cases, and every candidate model passes a locked regression suite.
• No, it cannot be assumed to maintain 92% solely by collecting low-confidence frames or fine-tuning on new SKUs. Abrupt packaging changes, rare damage classes, camera relocation, and label-policy drift can break the threshold.
• “Without full retraining” should mean short replay-based fine-tuning or teacher-student distillation from the last production model—not zero training.

8.2 Recommended edge loop

Each Orin should calculate lightweight selection signals while inference continues:

• Low maximum confidence.
• Small margin between the two most likely classes.
• High prediction entropy.
• Tracker disagreement, such as a label appearing and disappearing across adjacent frames.
• Spatial or temporal inconsistency.
• Disagreement between FP16 teacher and INT8 edge model on sampled frames.
• Novel embedding distance from the existing SKU prototype bank.
• Repeated false-trigger patterns.
• Rare predicted classes and underrepresented cameras.

Do not upload every frame. Upload compressed crops plus context and metadata:

• Full frame or privacy-filtered scene thumbnail.
• High-resolution label/damage crop.
• Camera, aisle, timestamp and current model version.
• Detector boxes, confidence and tracker ID.
• Selection reason.
• Image hash for deduplication.

Monthly training batch:

• New-SKU images.
• Edge-selected uncertain images.
• Confirmed false positives and false negatives.
• A stratified replay buffer from old SKUs, old cameras and rare damage types.
• Hard negatives.
• Synthetic augmentations for blur, low light, glare, compression, occlusion and scale.

Training method:

• Warm-start from the current approved FP16 checkpoint.
• Keep a frozen copy of the old model as teacher.
• Distill old-class logits, box predictions and intermediate features where practical.
• Fine-tune on the combined new-plus-replay data.
• Perform QAT for the final epochs or quantize with representative calibration data.
• Compare FP16 and INT8 on the frozen regression test set.
• Canary-deploy to 5–10% of modules before fleet rollout.
• Automatically roll back if precision, damage recall, false alarms or p99 latency regress.

8.3 Conditions for retaining 92%

A defensible release gate is:

• Test-set precision ≥92% overall.
• Lower 95% confidence bound preferably ≥92%, rather than only the point estimate.
• Damage recall ≥90% or the business-defined safety threshold.
• Each high-volume camera group ≥92% precision.
• No critical damage class below its minimum.
• INT8 mAP drop ≤2 absolute points.
• p99 camera-to-result latency <33.33 ms for true every-frame processing.
• Sustained thermal test passes without clock throttling.
• Canary telemetry remains within the FP/1,000-frame and FN/1,000-item limits.

If the lower confidence bound drops below 92%, trigger a larger replay fine-tune. Periodic full retraining from the complete curated dataset should still occur—for example quarterly or after a major taxonomy/camera change—even if monthly updates are incremental.

9. Pallet-label and package-damage considerations

Pallet-label detection and package-damage detection impose different requirements.

Pallet labels are small, regular, and often text-dense. Detection may be followed by OCR. Resolution is therefore critical. A 640×640 full-frame input can reduce a distant label to too few pixels even if the detector itself is fast. The preferred solution is not necessarily a larger global detector; it is a cascaded pipeline:

1. Detect pallet/package regions at 640×640 with YOLOv8m or DetectNet_v2.
2. Crop from the original 1080p or higher-resolution frame.
3. Run a small high-resolution label detector/OCR model only on those regions.

Package damage is irregular and may be better represented by segmentation than bounding boxes. Tears, crushed corners and punctures can occupy very small regions. If the current requirement is strictly object detection, train separate damage classes and include high-resolution crops. If bounding boxes prove too coarse, YOLOv8 segmentation provides a migration route that DetectNet_v2 does not natively match as conveniently.

EfficientDet-D4’s 1024×1024 input could help small-feature sensitivity, but its compute and deployment cost are high. A two-stage YOLO pipeline usually offers a better accuracy/throughput trade-off because only candidate packages receive expensive high-resolution analysis.

10. Recommended proof-of-concept and acceptance matrix

Phase 1: baseline training

Train:

• YOLOv8s, v8m and v8l at 640×640.
• YOLOv8m at 960 or 1024 input if small-label recall is inadequate.
• TAO DetectNet_v2 ResNet18 and ResNet34 at 960×544 or a warehouse-appropriate divisible resolution.
• EfficientDet-D4 only as an accuracy reference, not as the presumptive production model.

Retain the best FP16 checkpoint of each.

Phase 2: quantization

For each model:

• Export an FP16 TensorRT engine.
• Build an INT8 PTQ engine using the stratified calibration set.
• If mAP loss exceeds one point, apply QAT.
• If full QAT still fails, use mixed precision and retain sensitive layers in FP16.
• Record engine size and target compatibility.

Phase 3: edge benchmark

On the exact production AGX Orin SKU:

• JetPack and TensorRT versions pinned.
• Fixed 30-W and 50-W tests.
• Active cooling and production enclosure.
• Batch 1, 4, 8, 16 and stream-count tests.
• 30-minute warm-up and two-hour sustained run.
• p50/p95/p99 inference and end-to-end latency.
• Decode, preprocess, inference, NMS, tracker and rule-engine times separately.
• Average and p95 power.
• FPS/W and joules/frame.
• Thermal throttling and dropped frames.
• H.264 and H.265 camera mixes tested separately.

Phase 4: accuracy gate

Use the locked 5,000-image test set and report:

• FP16 and INT8 mAP50–95.
• Absolute degradation:
  ΔmAP = mAP_INT8 − mAP_FP16.
• Relative degradation:
  100 × (mAP_FP16 − mAP_INT8) / mAP_FP16.
• Precision/recall at production threshold.
• Per-class and per-camera results.
• Bootstrap confidence intervals.
• Error review of the top false positives and false negatives.

Phase 5: fleet simulation

Replay all 200 streams or a statistically representative synthetic equivalent. Validate:

• 6,000 frame/s ingest.
• Required detector inference rate.
• No decoder saturation.
• Network and storage load.
• Active-learning upload volume.
• OTA rollout and rollback.
• Engine rebuild after an intentionally changed TensorRT version.
• Recovery after power loss and partial update.

11. Final decision matrix

YOLOv8m TensorRT INT8

Accuracy potential:
High. Better capacity than v8s/n while remaining compact; 50.2 published COCO mAP50–95.

Latency:
Approximately 4.03 ms reciprocal inference latency on measured AGX Orin 64GB results; approximately 6.90 ms on the cited 32GB benchmark.

Quantization:
Good with representative calibration; QAT/mixed precision recommended for subtle damage.

Power:
Plan around 35–50 W sustained in a 50-W profile; measure directly.

OTA:
Excellent. Raw INT8 weights approximately 25.9 MB; likely comfortably below 100 MB as an engine, subject to actual serialization.

Monthly updates:
Best developer experience and long-term flexibility, but replay/distillation must be added.

Risk:
Commercial license, no native continual-learning guarantee, and small-label accuracy may require crops or higher resolution.

EfficientDet-D4 TensorRT INT8

Accuracy potential:
High for multi-scale objects; 49.7 COCO mAP at native 1024 input.

Latency:
Not reliably established on AGX Orin. Official T4 batch-one reference is 42.8 ms; likely the slowest of the three at comparable deployment quality.

Quantization:
Highest risk; QAT is strongly preferred.

Power:
Likely near the upper sustained module envelope when continuously loaded.

OTA:
Good by weight count—approximately 20.7 MB raw INT8—but engine and plugin compatibility must be validated.

Monthly updates:
Weakest ecosystem and highest export maintenance.

Risk:
ONNX/TensorRT fragility, PTQ failures, and insufficient authoritative Orin D4 evidence.

TAO DetectNet_v2 TensorRT INT8

Accuracy potential:
Potentially strong after warehouse fine-tuning; architecture and resolution must be checked for very small labels and irregular damage.

Latency:
Highest published batched throughput—421 to 1,116 FPS on AGX Orin 64GB depending on ResNet34/18 and pruning—but batch-one and end-to-end latency remain to be measured.

Quantization:
Strongest packaged QAT/prune/retrain workflow. NVIDIA’s PeopleNet example maintained mAP within 1% of floating point.

Power:
Potentially best FPS/W, particularly when DLA is useful, but model-specific sustained measurements are unavailable.

OTA:
Likely below 100 MB after pruning and INT8; target-specific engine regeneration is mandatory.

Monthly updates:
Strong packaged transfer/deployment workflow, but not automatic continual learning and still requires replay.

Risk:
Legacy TensorFlow 1/deprecated model family and DLA QAT caveats.

Final recommendation

Deploy a YOLOv8m-based two-stage system:

• Primary detector: YOLOv8m TensorRT INT8 at 640×640.
• High-resolution secondary crop model for pallet labels/OCR and subtle package damage.
• DeepStream or an equivalent zero-copy GStreamer/TensorRT pipeline for ingest, decode, batching and tracking.
• Start with approximately 32 AGX Orin 64GB modules for a pilot supporting full-rate inference, and maintain capacity to expand toward 36–40 after end-to-end profiling. If detector inference can run at 10–15 FPS per camera with tracking between frames, substantially fewer modules will be required.
• Operate in a fixed 50-W production power mode rather than unconstrained MAXN, with adequate cooling and 20–30% throughput reserve.
• Use QAT or mixed INT8/FP16 whenever PTQ loses more than one mAP point.
• Keep signed ONNX/QDQ artifacts and calibration metadata as canonical OTA assets; generate or distribute version-specific TensorRT engines.
• Enforce an OTA engine-size ceiling below 100 MB. YOLOv8m should meet it without forcing an accuracy-poor nano model.
• Use monthly active-learning batches with old-class replay and teacher distillation. Do not fine-tune on new SKU images alone.
• Require ≥92% test precision, critical-class recall targets, ≤2-point INT8 mAP loss, and a sustained p99 latency/power/thermal pass before promotion.
• Perform periodic full-dataset retraining or consolidation after major drift, even if monthly cycles use incremental fine-tuning.

Keep TAO DetectNet_v2/ResNet18 or ResNet34 as the principal challenger in the proof of concept. It may win on throughput and energy efficiency, especially in a heavily batched DeepStream deployment, and it has the strongest packaged NVIDIA optimization pipeline. It should replace YOLOv8m only if it matches the latter’s per-class label and damage accuracy on the locked warehouse test set and the organization accepts the long-term maintenance risk of the legacy TensorFlow 1 DetectNet_v2 stack.

Do not proceed with EfficientDet-D4 as the production default unless it produces a statistically significant gain in small-label or damage recall that cannot be achieved through YOLO high-resolution crops. Its current evidence does not justify its latency, quantization and integration risk.

final.content:
Tax-efficient savings strategy for 2026–2032

This is a planning framework, not individualized tax or investment advice. Several facts needed for an exact plan are missing: your monthly essential spending, existing TFSA/RRSP/RESP balances and contribution room, whether $95,000 is gross revenue or net self-employment income, your spouse’s income/pension position, and the children’s birth months and existing CESG history. Those facts can materially change the result.

The recommendations below assume:

- You are an Ontario resident for tax purposes.
- $95,000 is approximately net earned self-employment income before RRSP deductions.
- You have no employer pension adjustment.
- Both children are Canadian residents and have substantial unused CESG room.
- The primary caregiver’s adjusted family net income is approximately $95,000.
- Investments earn a nominal 5% annually before fees and tax.
- You have seven remaining calendar years to contribute for the elder child before university, but eligibility actually ends on December 31 of the year the child turns 17—not when university starts.

1. First priority: liquidity and tax reserve

Do not invest money earmarked for income taxes, CPP, or near-term living costs in an RRSP or equity portfolio.

As a freelancer, establish three cash buckets before setting automatic registered-account contributions:

1. Operating account: business expenses and upcoming invoices.
2. Tax/CPP account: transfer a fixed percentage of every client payment immediately. At $95,000 of net self-employment income, CPP alone can be roughly $9,293 in 2026: $8,460.90 for regular CPP plus up to $832 CPP2. Self-employed people pay both the employee and employer portions. [CRA CPP contribution rules](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/publicpensions/cpp/contributions.html)
3. Emergency fund: six months of essential household spending.

Emergency-fund target:

    Emergency fund = 6 × essential monthly household spending

For example, if essential spending is $5,000 per month, the target is:

    6 × $5,000 = $30,000

Hold this in a high-interest savings account, money-market fund, or a ladder of cashable/short GICs. A TFSA can hold this cash if you have ample room, but do not treat the RRSP as emergency savings: withdrawals are taxable income and permanently use up RRSP room. [CRA RRSP withdrawal treatment](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/rrsps-related-plans/making-withdrawals.html)

A TFSA is more liquid: withdrawals are tax-free, and the withdrawn amount is restored as contribution room on January 1 of the following year. It is not restored immediately, so avoid withdrawing and recontributing in the same year unless you have unused room. [CRA TFSA withdrawal rules](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax-free-savings-account/withdraw.html)

Recommended rule for irregular income: do not make fixed monthly registered-account commitments that assume every month will be normal. Instead, use a modest baseline automatic transfer and “sweep” surplus cash after large invoices into accounts in the order below.

2. RRSP tax benefit at CAD 95,000 in Ontario

For 2026, the relevant combined Ontario/federal marginal rates on ordinary income are approximately:

| Taxable-income band | Combined marginal rate |
|---|---:|
| $58,524–$94,901 | 29.65% |
| $94,902–$107,785 | 31.48% |

These combined rates include Ontario surtax but exclude the Ontario Health Premium. At $95,000, you are only about $99 above the $94,901 bracket threshold. [Ontario/federal 2026 combined marginal-rate table](https://www.ey.com/content/dam/ey-unified-site/ey-com/en-ca/services/tax/tax-calculators/2026/ey-tax-rates-ontario-2026-06-15.pdf) and [CRA Ontario 2026 rates](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/forms-publications/payroll/t4032-payroll-deductions-tables/t4032on-jan/t4032on-january-general-information.html)

If you have $17,100 of new RRSP room—18% of $95,000—and use all of it, the approximate 2026 tax saving is:

    First $99 × 31.48%                         = $31
    Remaining $17,001 × 29.65%                 = $5,041
    Approximate RRSP tax reduction             = $5,072

A more conservative result using $16,500–$17,100 of deduction room is about $4,700–$5,100 of tax reduction. The exact amount depends on deductible business expenses, CPP deductions, other income, credits, and your final net income.

Your new annual RRSP room is generally the lesser of 18% of prior-year earned income and the annual RRSP limit, plus unused room, less pension adjustment. The 2026 annual maximum is $33,810, but at $95,000 of earned income your new room is normally about:

    $95,000 × 18% = $17,100

Verify the actual amount on your CRA Notice of Assessment before contributing. Both personal and spousal RRSP contributions use your own RRSP deduction room. [CRA RRSP deduction-limit rules](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/rrsps-related-plans/contributing-a-rrsp-prpp/contributions-affect-your-rrsp-prpp-deduction-limit.html)

3. Individual RRSP versus spousal RRSP

Immediate tax result: no difference

If you contribute $10,000 to:

- your own RRSP, or
- a spousal RRSP in your spouse’s name,

you claim the same $10,000 deduction against your income, consume the same $10,000 of your RRSP room, and receive the same immediate Ontario tax reduction. At your current marginal rate, this is roughly:

    $10,000 × 29.65% to 31.48%
    = about $2,965 to $3,148 of tax savings

A spousal RRSP is not an extra RRSP room source. Its value is future income allocation, not a bigger current deduction.

When a spousal RRSP is preferable

Use part of your RRSP contributions for a spousal RRSP if all or most of the following are true:

- Your spouse has materially lower expected retirement income than you.
- Your spouse has less pension income, smaller RRSP/RRIF assets, or fewer CPP pension entitlements.
- You expect your own retirement withdrawals to otherwise be in a higher bracket.
- The money will remain invested for at least three calendar years after the last spousal contribution.

This can shift future RRSP/RRIF income to the lower-income spouse, reducing household lifetime tax. It is especially useful before age 65, when RRSP withdrawals are not broadly eligible for pension-income splitting. After age 65, RRIF income can often be split between spouses, reducing—but not eliminating—the incremental value of a spousal RRSP.

When an individual RRSP is preferable

Use your own RRSP rather than a spousal RRSP where:

- Your spouse has similar or higher expected retirement income.
- You may need the funds within three calendar years.
- Your spouse is likely to need withdrawals during the children’s education years.
- You want maximum flexibility and no attribution risk.

The key spousal-RRSP risk is attribution. If you contribute in the withdrawal year or either of the preceding two calendar years, all or part of the withdrawal can be taxed back to you, the contributor. [CRA spousal RRSP withdrawal/attribution rules](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/rrsps-related-plans/making-withdrawals/withdrawing-spousal-common-law-partner-rrsps.html)

Recommendation: assuming your spouse has substantially lower expected retirement income, direct 25%–50% of your annual RRSP contributions to a spousal RRSP and the remainder to your own RRSP. If your spouse has comparable retirement resources, use your individual RRSP instead. Do not use either RRSP for education funding or emergency cash.

4. RESP: front-loading versus spreading over the next seven years

Core RESP rules

There is no annual RESP contribution limit, but the lifetime contribution limit is $50,000 per beneficiary. RESP contributions are not tax-deductible. [CRA RESP contribution limits](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/registered-education-savings-plans-resps/resp-contributions.html)

The basic Canada Education Savings Grant (CESG) equals 20% of contributions:

- Normal annual maximum: $500 on a $2,500 contribution.
- Catch-up annual maximum: $1,000 where unused grant room exists, generally requiring a $5,000 contribution.
- Lifetime CESG maximum: $7,200 per beneficiary.
- Grant eligibility ends at the end of the calendar year the child turns 17. [CRA CESG rules](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/registered-education-savings-plans-resps/canada-education-savings-programs-cesp/canada-education-savings-grant-cesg.html)

At adjusted family income of approximately $95,000, the child may also qualify for an additional 10% CESG on the first $500 contributed each year—an additional $50 annually. This depends on the primary caregiver’s adjusted family net income and is not carried forward. For 2026, the middle-income band is $58,523–$117,045. [Government CESG income thresholds](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/education/education-savings/estimating-amounts.html)

Important age-16/17 rule: to receive CESG in the calendar years a child turns 16 or 17, at least $2,000 must have been contributed before the end of the year the child turns 15, or at least $100 must have been contributed in four earlier years. [CESG eligibility rules](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/registered-education-savings-plans-resps/canada-education-savings-programs-cesp/canada-education-savings-grant-cesg.html)

For your 11-year-old, make sure the $2,000 threshold is met well before the end of the year they turn 15.

Does RESP front-loading maximize CESG?

A single large lump-sum contribution does not maximize CESG.

For example, contributing $35,000 to the elder child’s RESP today does not generate a $7,000 CESG. It generally generates only up to $1,000 of basic CESG in that calendar year because the annual catch-up ceiling applies.

To maximize CESG capture within a short window, “front-load” by using the annual catch-up limit each year, not by depositing the full lifetime amount at once.

For a child with available carry-forward grant room:

| Annual strategy per child | Contribution | Basic CESG | Comment |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Standard annual funding | $2,500 | $500 | Captures one year’s basic grant room |
| Annual catch-up funding | $5,000 | $1,000 | Captures current year plus one prior year’s grant room |
| Large one-time lump sum, e.g. $35,000 | $35,000 | Usually only $1,000 | Does not accelerate more than one year of basic CESG |

For the elder child, assuming seven eligible contribution years remain and unused grant room exists:

- $2,500 annually for seven years produces $17,500 of contributions and $3,500 of basic CESG.
- $5,000 annually for seven years produces $35,000 of contributions and up to $7,000 of basic CESG.
- With the possible $50 annual additional CESG, the $7,200 lifetime CESG cap may be reached in the final year. The exact final contribution should be adjusted once your RESP provider confirms grant room.

At 5%, assuming each annual deposit is made at the beginning of the year, the seven-year result for the elder child is approximately:

| Strategy | Personal contributions | Basic CESG | Estimated 2032 value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $2,500 annually + $500 CESG | $17,500 | $3,500 | $24,426 |
| $5,000 annually + $1,000 CESG | $35,000 | $7,000 | $48,852 |

Calculation:

    Future-value factor for seven beginning-of-year deposits at 5%
    = 1.05 + 1.05² + … + 1.05⁷
    = 8.1420

    $5,000 annual contributions × 8.1420 = $40,710
    $1,000 annual CESG × 8.1420          = $8,142
    Estimated total                       = $48,852

The second strategy has a higher account value partly because it uses $17,500 more of your own capital. Its incremental advantage is not “free”; it includes an extra $3,500 of CESG plus the investment growth on the additional deposits.

Best RESP conclusion

1. Do not make a one-time $35,000 RESP contribution solely to seek CESG.
2. If cash flow permits, contribute $5,000 per year for the elder child while unused grant room remains, preferably early in each calendar year.
3. For the younger child, also use $5,000 annually if your retirement and emergency targets remain on track; the younger child has more time, but unused CESG room makes the 20% catch-up grant compelling.
4. If cash flow is limited, prioritize the elder child at $5,000 per year first, then fund the younger child at $2,500 per year, rather than splitting scarce RESP contributions evenly.
5. Obtain each child’s grant-room history from the RESP provider before implementing this; previous contributions by another parent or family member matter.

RESP withdrawals have favourable family tax treatment: your original contributions return tax-free; CESG and investment earnings are normally paid as Educational Assistance Payments (EAPs) taxable to the student, who often has little taxable income. [CRA RESP withdrawal treatment](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/education/education-savings/managing-plan.html)

5. Recommended savings waterfall and monthly allocation

A genuinely “optimal” monthly allocation cannot be fixed from income alone because your savings capacity depends on essential expenses and your emergency-fund balance. The following is the tax-efficient priority order.

Priority 0 — mandatory cash reserves

Before investment contributions:

- Set aside tax/CPP instalment money from every payment.
- Build the emergency fund to six months of essential spending.
- Eliminate high-interest debt before maximizing RRSP investments.

Priority 1 — CESG-producing RESP deposits

After the emergency fund is complete, target:

    Elder RESP:   $5,000/year = $416.67/month
    Younger RESP: $5,000/year = $416.67/month
    Total RESP:  $10,000/year = $833.33/month

For variable income, fund the full annual amount early after high-income months rather than insisting on identical monthly transfers. A practical compromise is $417 per child monthly, then use invoice-surplus cash to make the annual catch-up deposit as early as possible.

If affordability is constrained:

    Elder RESP:   $416.67/month
    Younger RESP: $208.33/month
    Total RESP:   $625/month

That preserves the elder child’s annual $5,000 catch-up strategy while still capturing the younger child’s ordinary annual $500 basic CESG.

Priority 2 — RRSP, including an appropriate spousal-RRSP portion

Assuming $17,100 of actual available room:

    $17,100/year ÷ 12 = $1,425/month gross RRSP contribution

The approximate $4,700–$5,100 tax refund should not be spent. Use it in this order:

1. restore the emergency fund if used;
2. fill unused TFSA room;
3. make an additional RRSP contribution only if you still have room and the deduction remains valuable.

The effective cash-flow cost of $17,100 in RRSP deposits after an approximately $4,894 refund is roughly:

    $17,100 – $4,894 = $12,206 annually
    $12,206 ÷ 12 = about $1,017 monthly after-tax cost

This is a useful way to budget irregular freelance income, but the refund arrives later; you still need the gross cash to make the contributions.

Priority 3 — TFSA

The 2026 TFSA dollar limit is $7,000, before considering unused room carried forward. [CRA TFSA contribution room](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax-free-savings-account/contributing/calculate-room.html)

If you have at least $7,000 of room:

    $7,000/year ÷ 12 = $583.33/month

Use the TFSA for:

- emergency cash after the six-month reserve is fully funded;
- medium-term flexibility;
- investments that might be needed before retirement;
- retirement investing after the RRSP deduction is no longer especially valuable.

Maximum registered-account schedule, after the emergency reserve

| Account | Annual contribution | Monthly equivalent | Purpose |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Elder RESP | $5,000 | $416.67 | CESG catch-up before the age deadline |
| Younger RESP | $5,000 | $416.67 | CESG catch-up |
| RRSP/spousal RRSP combined | $17,100 | $1,425.00 | Current tax deduction and retirement |
| TFSA | $7,000 | $583.33 | Tax-free flexible retirement/medium-term savings |
| Total | $34,100 | $2,841.67 | Excludes emergency fund and tax reserve |

This is the maximum-tax-sheltered schedule under the stated assumptions, not a claim that you should force $2,842 per month from cash flow. If your actual available savings is below this amount, use this order:

1. Maintain tax/CPP and six-month emergency reserves.
2. Elder’s $5,000 annual RESP target.
3. Younger’s RESP, ideally to $5,000 but at least $2,500.
4. RRSP contributions up to the amount that reduces income from $95,000 toward approximately $58,500; this is where you receive roughly a 29.65%–31.48% deduction value.
5. TFSA contributions.
6. Additional RRSP contributions, if room remains and retirement tax rate is expected to be lower than today’s.

6. Which approach is likely to maximize after-tax wealth by 2032?

Under the assumptions above, the wealth-maximizing strategy is:

- maintain six months’ essential expenses in cash-equivalent liquid assets;
- fund the elder RESP at the $5,000 annual catch-up level, not with one giant lump sum;
- fund the younger RESP at $5,000 annually if affordable, otherwise $2,500 after the elder’s priority is met;
- contribute to RRSPs at least enough to use the valuable 29.65%–31.48% marginal tax deduction, and reinvest the refund;
- use a spousal RRSP only to the extent your spouse is expected to have a lower retirement income;
- fill TFSA room for tax-free flexible wealth and future liquidity.

Illustrative seven-year, 5% projection

This projection assumes contributions are made at the beginning of each year, current limits stay unchanged, no existing balances, and no withdrawals. It excludes the emergency fund and does not include portfolio fees or inflation.

| Account | Annual contribution | Approximate value in 2032 | Tax treatment |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| RRSP/spousal RRSP | $17,100 | $139,228 before withdrawal tax | Taxable on withdrawal |
| TFSA | $7,000 | $56,994 | Tax-free |
| Two RESPs, $5,000 each annually, with basic CESG | $10,000 personal plus grants | about $97,700–$98,000 | Education-dedicated; EAPs taxable to student |
| Total account value | — | about $293,900–$294,200 | RRSP portion not yet after-tax |

RRSP calculation:

    $17,100 × 8.1420 = $139,228

TFSA calculation:

    $7,000 × 8.1420 = $56,994

If RRSP withdrawals are eventually taxed at 20%, the RRSP’s after-tax value would be approximately:

    $139,228 × (1 – 20%) = $111,382

Thus, under a 20% future withdrawal tax assumption, your personal retirement assets from this schedule would be approximately:

    After-tax RRSP value: $111,382
    TFSA value:            $56,994
    Total retirement value: $168,376

The RESP value should be treated separately: it is education-designated family wealth, not flexible retirement wealth.

The central tax principle is simple: an RRSP is most attractive when your deduction rate today exceeds your eventual withdrawal rate. At your current 29.65%–31.48% marginal rate, the RRSP is attractive if retirement withdrawals are likely to be taxed below that level. The TFSA is superior for funds you may need before retirement and for withdrawal capacity that will be tax-free.

Implementation checklist

- Confirm RRSP and TFSA room through CRA My Account and your Notice of Assessment.
- Confirm each child’s CESG grant room and whether the age-16/17 eligibility condition has already been met.
- Use a family RESP so unused education assets can generally be reassigned between siblings if one child needs less.
- Make RESP annual catch-up contributions early in the calendar year, after preserving the emergency and tax reserves.
- Keep elder-child RESP investments progressively safer: diversified growth assets now, then shift a growing portion to GICs/high-interest cash during the final three to four years before enrolment.
- Use low-cost diversified global equity/bond funds in RRSP and TFSA according to risk tolerance; the RRSP has the longest horizon and can generally hold the higher-growth allocation.
- Review each December after final freelance income is known. In a high-income year, make the RRSP contribution before the deadline; in a weak-income year, preserve cash and consider delaying part of the deduction rather than withdrawing from registered accounts.
