## 5. Ecological validity: NEPSY-II compared with WISC-V

## 5.1 Definitional problem

“Ecological validity” is used inconsistently. A 2024 systematic review of executive-function assessment found that the term can refer variously to face validity, task naturalism, construct validity, criterion validity, sensitivity, specificity, or prediction of real-world functioning. Only 28 reviewed articles—31%—provided a formal definition. The authors recommended defining the term explicitly or replacing it with concrete labels such as criterion validity (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/conceptualization-of-the-term-ecological-validity-in-neuropsychological-research-on-executive-function-assessment-a-systematic-review-and-call-to-action/01C595F6F8931798F9053A0628260BA0).

Two components should be separated:

- **Verisimilitude:** how much a task resembles everyday activities.
- **Veridicality:** how strongly performance predicts or corresponds to functioning outside the test room.

NEPSY-II can appear more ecologically representative because it samples stories, inhibition, switching, attention, memory for designs, social perception, and complex instructions. That may improve face validity or content breadth. It does **not**, by itself, establish veridicality.

## 5.2 Pediatric neuropsychologists’ review position

A pediatric neuropsychology review emphasized that clinicians are increasingly expected not only to identify cognitive deficits but also to explain their implications for everyday functioning. It concluded that most ecological-validity knowledge comes from adult and older-adult samples and that the relation between test performance and everyday functioning is less examined and less understood in children (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21622965.2012.686330).

This review does not establish that NEPSY-II is more ecologically valid than WISC. Rather, it places both within a pediatric evidence base that is underdeveloped.

An older ADHD-focused ecological review concluded that laboratory measures of inattention, impulsivity, and overactivity generally showed low-to-moderate ecological validity, with some traditional tasks performing unsatisfactorily. It recommended greater reliance on natural-setting assessment and repeated multimethod measurement over longer periods (https://articles.researchsolutions.com/the-ecological-validity-of-laboratory-and-analogue-assessment-methods-of-adhd-symptoms/doi/10.1007/bf00909976).

## 5.3 Performance tests versus real-world ratings

Toplak et al.’s practitioner review is highly influential because it directly examined whether structured performance measures and ratings of everyday executive functioning assess the same thing. Across 20 studies—13 child and 7 adult samples—only 68 of 286 correlations were statistically significant, and the median correlation was **r = .19** (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23057693/).

The proportion significant was:

\[
68/286 = 23.8\%.
\]

The variance shared by two measures correlated at .19 is:

\[
r^2 = .19^2 = .0361,
\]

or only **3.6% shared variance**.

The authors did not conclude that one measure type was valid and the other invalid. Rather:

- performance tasks index the **efficiency of cognitive abilities under structured conditions**;
- ratings index **success in goal pursuit over time in ordinary settings**.

That distinction applies to both WISC-V and NEPSY-II. A child can perform adequately in a quiet, novel, one-to-one session with repeated examiner prompts and still struggle in an unstructured classroom requiring self-initiation, time management, persistence, and resistance to distraction.

## 5.4 WISC-V ecological-validity evidence

Pearson’s WISC-V technical supplement explicitly describes correlations with academic performance, adaptive functioning, behavioral regulation, and related clinical measures as evidence relevant to construct and ecological validity. It also acknowledges that the primary technical manual’s studies in typically developing children did not establish how cognitive impairment affects broader psychosocial functioning; the supplement was intended to provide additional information in special groups, including ADHD (https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/wisc-v/wisc-v-tech-manual-supplement.pdf).

This is evidence that ecological validity was considered, but it should not be confused with strong longitudinal prediction of everyday ADHD impairment. Correlation with a rating scale or achievement test is only one form of criterion-related evidence, and shared method, range restriction, informant effects, and comorbidity can influence results.

## 5.5 NEPSY-II ecological-validity evidence

NEPSY-II’s publisher states that results can inform diagnoses and interventions related to academic, social, and behavioral difficulties and may guide educational planning (https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-introduction.pdf). These are intended uses, not direct proof that its subtests predict functioning better than WISC-V.

The independent Child Neuropsychology review describes NEPSY-II’s broad content, clinical-group studies, and psychometric evidence, while also noting limitations and gaps in supporting evidence for some interpretive positions (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09297040903146966). No accessible comparative review identified here showed that NEPSY-II outperforms WISC-V in predicting teacher-rated classroom behavior, homework completion, peer function, adaptive independence, or long-term academic outcome.

## 5.6 Ecological-validity conclusion

The most defensible synthesis is:

- **NEPSY-II has greater neuropsychological content breadth and may have greater face validity for certain executive-control problems.**
- **WISC-V provides stronger standardized composite interpretation and some documented relations with academic, adaptive, and behavioral measures.**
- **Neither has demonstrated strong ecological validity for ADHD by itself.**
- **No direct pediatric evidence supports a general claim that NEPSY-II is ecologically superior to WISC-V.**
- Ecological assessment should incorporate parent and teacher ratings, schoolwork and academic records, behavioral observations, and information about functioning across time and settings.

## 6. Psychometric and structural evidence

### 6.1 WISC-V

WISC-V’s composite framework is an advantage, but its narrower factors should not be overinterpreted. The ADHD measurement-invariance study found:

- adequate model fit in ADHD and control groups;
- configural and metric invariance;
- failure of full scalar invariance;
- partial scalar invariance only after freeing several subtest and factor intercepts;
- greater measurement precision for FSIQ than for cognitive subdomains (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38248904/).

Implications:

1. The same broad configuration and factor-loading pattern may apply across groups.
2. Mean comparisons can nevertheless be biased if intercepts differ.
3. A low WMI should be interpreted in the context of confidence intervals, other indices, behavioral observations, language and learning data, and symptom history.
4. Within-person index discrepancies are not automatically disorder-specific.

The WISC-V special-group supplement supplies evidence linking test scores with other measures in clinical groups, but publisher studies should ideally be supplemented by independent replication (https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/wisc-v/wisc-v-tech-manual-supplement.pdf).

### 6.2 NEPSY-II

The NEPSY-II normative sample consisted of approximately 1,200 children aged 3–16, collected in 2005–2006, according to the independent review (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233025061_NEPSY-II_A_Developmental_Neuropsychological_Assessment_Second_Edition). For the present age band, recent analyses used 600 children aged 7–12 from the norming sample.

A 2024 exploratory factor analysis found that a six-factor solution offered the best fit for ages 7–12 and that most subtests contained sufficient specificity to permit individual interpretation, although caution was advised for Social Perception. It also highlighted reliability variation, with stability coefficients ranging from 0.21 to 0.91 (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8).

A related confirmatory structural analysis of 23 scores from 600 children aged 7–12 found:

- support for multidimensionality;
- a best-fitting model with a general factor and four first-order factors;
- general-factor loadings for subtests ranging from .21 to .69, mean .44;
- domain-specific effects ranging from .00 to .45;
- strong subtest-specific effects whose constructs were unclear.

The authors concluded that findings supported subtest-level rather than composite-level interpretation, but that scores still require caution (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09297049.2024.2357376).

The apparent discrepancy between a six-factor exploratory solution and a general-plus-four-factor confirmatory solution is not necessarily contradictory. Exploratory and confirmatory analyses answer different questions and impose different constraints. Both studies converge on three clinically important points:

1. NEPSY-II is multidimensional.
2. Its originally labeled domains are not simple homogeneous scales.
3. Individual subtests contain substantial specific variance, which may be clinically informative but is not always constructually clear.

### 6.3 Normative obsolescence and cultural validity

NEPSY-II’s U.S. norms were collected in 2005–2006, and WISC-V was introduced substantially later. Changes in educational exposure, technology use, population demographics, and secular score trends may affect current interpretation. Neither instrument should be assumed culturally or linguistically invariant across all populations. The WISC-V invariance study’s need to match migration background and education illustrates the importance of demographic context (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38248904/). Contemporary cross-cultural validation is a major gap for both batteries.

## 7. Theoretical frameworks shaping interpretation

### 7.1 Lurian developmental neuropsychology

NEPSY was developed within a Lurian tradition emphasizing functional systems and patterns of primary and secondary deficits rather than one-to-one localization. Its broad battery and process-oriented interpretation reflect the idea that complex behavior emerges from interacting cognitive systems. Earlier validation literature describes NEPSY as resting on Lurian theory (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0887617704000472).

Clinical implication: a poor score should not automatically be assigned to a single isolated faculty. The examiner should determine whether the failure originated in attention, language comprehension, memory encoding, inhibition, motor execution, or another interacting process.

### 7.2 Hierarchical intelligence and CHC models

WISC-V is structured around a hierarchy of general and broad cognitive abilities, including working memory and processing speed. This supports composite-score interpretation and comparisons among broad abilities. It also raises the question of whether lower WMI reflects a specific working-memory deficit or general cognitive variance.

### 7.3 Baddeley’s working-memory model

The ADHD working-memory literature frequently uses Baddeley’s distinction among:

- phonological storage/rehearsal;
- visuospatial storage/rehearsal;
- central-executive control.

The Rapport et al. experiment explicitly used this model and found the largest deficit in central-executive functioning (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18317920/). Martinussen et al.’s modality-by-process meta-analysis similarly distinguished verbal versus spatial and storage versus manipulation (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/15782085).

This framework explains why one broad WMI may conceal clinically important heterogeneity.

### 7.4 Executive-function deficit models of ADHD

Classical EF theories predict deficits in inhibition, vigilance, working memory, and planning. Willcutt et al.’s meta-analysis supported medium group effects across these domains but rejected a universal single-deficit account (https://www.biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com/article/S0006-3223(05)00171-X/abstract).

### 7.5 Multiple-deficit and shared-vulnerability models

Current evidence favors heterogeneous, multiple-pathway accounts. Not every child with ADHD has measurable working-memory impairment; similar weaknesses occur in learning disorder, autism, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and other conditions. Comorbid ADHD-SLD groups may display broad cognitive inefficiency rather than a disorder-specific profile (https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/17/9948).

### 7.6 Processing-speed and time-based resource-sharing accounts

Experimental work suggests that working-memory demands and processing speed interact. One study found that increasing working-memory demands markedly reduced information-processing speed, whereas experimentally slowing processing did not significantly change working-memory performance; ADHD and non-ADHD groups differed particularly under high working-memory demand (https://psy.fsu.edu/clc/Publications/nihms-1047828.pdf). Other experimental work has proposed the reverse causal route under some task conditions: slow processing may increase cognitive load and reduce working-memory capacity, consistent with time-based resource-sharing theory (https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/clinical/2167702616668320/).

These apparently conflicting findings likely reflect different manipulations, task architectures, and definitions of speed. Clinically, they argue against interpreting WMI and PSI as independent, process-pure markers.

### 7.7 Performance efficiency versus goal attainment

Toplak et al.’s framework distinguishes optimal-condition task efficiency from everyday success in pursuing goals (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23057693/). This provides the clearest theoretical account of why structured tests may correlate weakly with parent and teacher reports without either being invalid.

## 8. Methodological appraisal of key evidence

### 8.1 Meta-analyses

**Willcutt et al. (2005)**  
Strengths:
- 83 studies;
- 3,734 ADHD and 2,969 comparison participants;
- multiple EF domains;
- examination of intelligence, achievement, referral status, and comorbidity.

Limitations:
- predates WISC-V and NEPSY-II;
- heterogeneous ADHD definitions and tasks;
- group effect sizes do not provide individual diagnostic accuracy;
- publication bias and task impurity remain possible.

Contribution: established that EF weakness is important but neither necessary nor sufficient for ADHD.

**Martinussen et al. (2005)**  
Strengths:
- 26 studies;
- explicit modality and storage/manipulation distinctions;
- confidence intervals;
- consideration of comorbid language/learning problems and intelligence.

Limitations:
- predates the current test editions;
- “exploratory” meta-analysis;
- heterogeneous task classifications;
- does not compare WISC-V with NEPSY-II.

Contribution: established the especially large spatial and spatial-central-executive effects that should guide test selection.

**Recent WAIS-IV/WISC-V meta-analysis**  
Strengths:
- searched PsycINFO, Embase, and MEDLINE;
- more than 1,800 neurodivergent participants;
- directly addressed current Wechsler editions.

Limitations:
- combined child/adult and WAIS/WISC evidence in the broader synthesis;
- relatively small number of independent data sources;
- test profiles are not diagnostic-accuracy studies;
- medication, comorbidity, and referral pathways may vary.

Contribution: strongest current synthesis cautioning against ADHD diagnosis from Wechsler profiles (https://academic.oup.com/acn/article/39/4/498/7286382).

### 8.2 WISC-V clinical studies

Matched case-control studies improve control of demographic confounding but can exaggerate diagnostic performance relative to real clinics if controls are healthy rather than clinically similar. Studies of already diagnosed cases can characterize profiles but cannot establish prospective diagnostic utility unless the index test is interpreted blind to diagnosis and prespecified thresholds are tested.

The 2021 ADHD-plus-SLD study used clinically relevant groups but could not isolate ADHD from comorbidity because the main ADHD group also had SLD (https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/17/9948).

The invariance study used strong matching and modern latent-variable methods but had 91 participants per group, which is modest for complex multigroup factor modeling, and it concerned the German adaptation rather than all language versions (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38248904/).

### 8.3 NEPSY-II studies

Manual special-group studies provide preliminary known-groups validity but are vulnerable to:

- selective subtest administration;
- healthy-control contrasts;
- small or poorly representative diagnostic groups;
- multiple outcomes;
- lack of prespecified cutoffs;
- absence of blinded classification;
- publisher involvement.

The 2025 ADHD/anxiety study addressed a clinically difficult differential diagnosis but included only 48 participants distributed across three groups, producing limited power and unstable effect estimates (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12191324/).

Recent structural studies are methodologically important because they use the large norming sample and modern factor analysis. Their limitation is that norming data do not establish diagnostic or ecological validity in ADHD.

### 8.4 Ecological-validity studies

The strongest conclusion is negative but informative: ecological validity is often undefined, and direct pediatric evidence is sparse. Correlations between task and rating measures are typically small. Cross-sectional correlation also does not establish prediction, causal relevance, or intervention responsiveness.

Future work should distinguish:

- concurrent criterion validity;
- predictive validity;
- incremental validity over symptoms and IQ;
- naturalistic performance;
- face validity;
- treatment sensitivity.

## 9. Conflicting evidence and synthesis

### Conflict 1: ADHD has robust working-memory deficits, yet WISC-V WMI is often normal

Resolution: Meta-analytic deficits are group averages and are especially large on spatial, high-load, and central-executive tasks. Standard WISC-V WMI tasks may be less demanding, more structured, and partly compensated by attention from the examiner. ADHD is heterogeneous; not all affected children have WM impairment.

### Conflict 2: Some WISC-V studies find strong WMI differences, while meta-analysis finds only slight reductions

Resolution: Effect size depends on sample ascertainment, clinical severity, medication, comorbidity, control-group type, language adaptation, and whether analyses use raw group differences, index discrepancies, or norm-referenced impairment rates. ADHD-plus-SLD samples predictably show broader and larger deficits than uncomplicated community ADHD.

### Conflict 3: NEPSY-II is described as clinically sensitive, but its reliability and structure are variable

Resolution: A task can be sensitive to a process at the group level while still having insufficient reliability for confident individual classification. NEPSY-II’s value is often qualitative and hypothesis-driven, but this makes disciplined base-rate interpretation essential.

### Conflict 4: NEPSY-II appears more “real-world” than WISC-V, yet ecological correlations are weak

Resolution: Realistic task content is verisimilitude, not demonstrated real-world prediction. Both tests remain short, structured, examiner-supported samples under optimal conditions.

### Conflict 5: Executive tests and behavioral ratings disagree

Resolution: They measure partly different levels—maximum cognitive efficiency versus everyday goal attainment. The low median correlation of .19 is therefore not merely noise; it signals that both forms of information are needed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23057693/).

### Conflict 6: Processing speed versus working memory as the stronger ADHD marker

Resolution: Some WISC-V studies identify WMI differences; others find PSI more discriminative. Speed and working-memory load interact, and neither is ADHD-specific. The clinically relevant question is not which index “proves” ADHD but which mechanism best explains the child’s observed impairment.

## 10. Citation and influence map

Formal citation counts vary by database and date and were not independently standardized here; therefore, exact citation rankings would be misleading. Influence is better identified through repeated appearance in meta-analyses, reviews, theoretical discussions, and clinical guidance.

### Foundational and highly influential works

1. **Willcutt et al. (2005), “Validity of the Executive Function Theory of ADHD”**  
   Its 83-study synthesis established the medium magnitude and nonuniversality of executive deficits and remains foundational for multiple-deficit interpretations (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15950006/).

2. **Martinussen et al. (2005), “A Meta-Analysis of Working Memory Impairments…”**  
   Seminal for distinguishing spatial from verbal and storage from central-executive deficits (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/15782085).

3. **Rapport et al. (2008)**  
   Influential in applying Baddeley’s model and latent process decomposition to 8–12-year-old boys with ADHD (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18317920/).

4. **Toplak, West, and Stanovich (2013)**  
   Central to the distinction between performance-based executive efficiency and ratings of real-world goal attainment (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23057693/).

5. **Korkman, Kirk, and Kemp’s NEPSY/NEPSY-II manuals and developmental framework**  
   Foundational to the broad pediatric neuropsychological approach embodied in NEPSY-II.

6. **AAP clinical guidelines and 2024 diagnostic systematic review**  
   Most consequential for clinical policy: neuropsychological tests can characterize function but generally do not improve ADHD diagnostic accuracy enough to replace standard clinical assessment (https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/85858/cdc_85858_DS1.pdf; https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/153/4/e2024065854/196923/Tools-for-the-Diagnosis-of-ADHD-in-Children-and).

### Current state-of-the-art contributions

- Modern WISC-V meta-analysis showing limited ADHD profile specificity (https://academic.oup.com/acn/article/39/4/498/7286382).
- WISC-V ADHD measurement-invariance analysis (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38248904/).
- Modern NEPSY-II exploratory and confirmatory structural studies in ages 7–12 (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8; https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09297049.2024.2357376).
- Systematic critique of the inconsistent use of “ecological validity” (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/conceptualization-of-the-term-ecological-validity-in-neuropsychological-research-on-executive-function-assessment-a-systematic-review-and-call-to-action/01C595F6F8931798F9053A0628260BA0).

## 11. Recommended assessment strategy for children aged 8–12

### 11.1 If the referral question is ADHD diagnosis only

Do not routinely administer either full battery solely to confirm ADHD. Prioritize:

- developmentally appropriate clinical interview;
- developmental, medical, sleep, medication, psychosocial, and educational history;
- evidence of onset and impairment;
- parent and teacher symptom ratings;
- impairment across at least two settings;
- screening for learning disorder, anxiety, mood disorder, autism, language disorder, trauma, and sensory or medical causes.

This follows the AAP conclusion that neuropsychological testing generally does not improve diagnostic accuracy in otherwise straightforward cases (https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/85858/cdc_85858_DS1.pdf).

### 11.2 If intellectual or learning ability is in question

Use **WISC-V** as the principal cognitive instrument. Examine:

- WMI and its Digit Span/Picture Span composition;
- PSI;
- GAI versus CPI only as descriptive, not diagnostic;
- confidence intervals and base rates of discrepancies;
- performance across auditory-verbal and visual conditions;
- academic achievement testing.

A low WMI supports a working-memory weakness but not an ADHD diagnosis.

### 11.3 If executive-process differentiation is required

Add selected **NEPSY-II** tasks based on a priori hypotheses:

- Auditory Attention and Response Set for selective/sustained attention and set switching;
- Inhibition for automatic-response suppression and speed-accuracy tradeoff;
- Word List Interference for verbal working memory under interference;
- Memory for Designs for visual-spatial memory;
- Animal Sorting or Design Fluency where concept formation, flexibility, or generation is relevant.

Avoid “fishing expeditions” across many subtests and interpreting every low score as pathology. Report base rates and measurement uncertainty.

### 11.4 If visual-spatial working memory is the central question

Because meta-analytic effects are largest for spatial working memory, consider:

- WISC-V Picture Span;
- WISC-V Integrated Spatial Span and VWMI if available;
- NEPSY-II Memory for Designs;
- a validated high-load spatial working-memory task if the research or clinical setting permits.

These should be treated as complementary because they place different demands on recognition, recall, spatial location, sequencing, manipulation, and executive control.

### 11.5 If ecological function is central

Add:

- parent and teacher executive-function ratings;
- school observations or structured teacher reports;
- records of assignment completion, organization, and classroom independence;
- academic fluency and sustained work samples;
- direct questions about routines, transitions, multistep instructions, homework, and peer functioning.

Do not use a laboratory test score as a proxy for functioning across a full day or week.

## 12. Priority research gaps

1. **Direct head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy research.**  
   Studies should administer WISC-V and prespecified NEPSY-II subtests to the same 8–12-year-olds and use an independent, blinded, multidisciplinary ADHD reference diagnosis.

2. **Criterion definition for “working-memory deficit.”**  
   Research must prespecify whether impairment means a score below a norm cutoff, latent-factor deficit, reliable within-person weakness, experimental high-load failure, or real-world functional impairment.

3. **Sensitivity and specificity with external validation.**  
   Models should report sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, predictive values at realistic prevalence, ROC AUC with confidence intervals, calibration, and external replication. Data-derived composites should not be evaluated only in the sample used to create them.

4. **Clinically relevant controls.**  
   Healthy-control contrasts are insufficient. Comparison groups should include SLD, anxiety, autism, sleep disorders, language disorder, depression, and mixed referrals.

5. **Modality and process decomposition.**  
   Future studies should separate verbal versus visual-spatial, storage versus manipulation, and low versus high load rather than relying only on global WMI.

6. **Medication and state effects.**  
   Studies should standardize and report stimulant status, time since dose, sleep, fatigue, motivation, anxiety, and testing time.

7. **Sex and presentation differences.**  
   Many foundational studies overrepresented boys and combined ADHD presentations. Evidence suggests inattentive presentation may show distinctive manipulation deficits, but replication is needed.

8. **Incremental validity.**  
   The key question is not whether a test differs between groups but whether it adds prediction beyond history, symptom ratings, IQ, achievement, and comorbidity.

9. **Ecological and predictive validity.**  
   Studies should test whether WISC-V or NEPSY-II predicts teacher-rated impairment, assignment completion, independent task persistence, academic growth, and adaptive functioning over time.

10. **Intervention relevance.**  
    Research should determine whether test-defined deficits identify children who benefit from specific accommodations or interventions and whether score changes track meaningful functional improvement.

11. **Reliability and base rates.**  
    NEPSY-II subtest reliability and the base rate of low-score scatter require further study in clinical samples. WISC-V discrepancy interpretations also need disorder-specific base rates and replication.

12. **Cross-cultural and linguistic validation.**  
    Measurement invariance should be tested across language, race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, migration background, and educational context.

13. **Norm updates.**  
    The field needs contemporary norms, especially for NEPSY-II, whose U.S. standardization data were collected in 2005–2006.

14. **Open and reproducible methods.**  
    Preregistration, published analysis plans, shared deidentified data where lawful, independent replication, and clear reporting of all administered outcomes would reduce selective reporting.

---

## Final answer

For children aged 8–12, **WISC-V is the better-supported instrument for detecting and quantifying a broad norm-referenced working-memory weakness**, because it provides an explicit WMI with auditory-verbal and visual components and optional expanded visual-spatial assessment. **NEPSY-II is better viewed as a complementary, process-oriented battery** that can reveal inhibition, sustained attention, response-set, interference, and memory-process problems that WISC-V may not isolate.

However, **there is no adequate head-to-head evidence showing that WISC-V or NEPSY-II has superior sensitivity for ADHD diagnosis or even superior sensitivity to independently defined ADHD-related working-memory impairment**. WISC-V WMI weaknesses are neither universal nor specific to ADHD, while NEPSY-II’s relevant findings are distributed across heterogeneous subtests rather than a single validated working-memory composite.

The proposition that **NEPSY-II is more ecologically valid than WISC-V is not established**. NEPSY-II has broader and sometimes more naturalistic content, but pediatric neuropsychologists emphasize that prediction of everyday childhood functioning remains understudied. Performance tests and everyday executive ratings correlate only weakly—median r = .19, approximately 3.6% shared variance—so neither battery should substitute for parent and teacher reports, school data, and direct evidence of functional impairment.

The strongest scholarly and clinical position is therefore multimethod and hypothesis driven: use WISC-V when broad cognitive and working-memory measurement is required; add carefully selected NEPSY-II subtests for executive-process differentiation; and diagnose ADHD from clinical, developmental, multi-informant, cross-setting evidence rather than from either cognitive profile.

Title tag: How to Become a Nail Tech in PA: License Guide Meta description: Learn how to become a nail tech in PA, complete 200 training hours, pass the state exam, budget for costs, and start your salon career. URL slug: /how-to-become-a-nail-tech-pa # How to Become a Nail Tech in PA If you enjoy detailed artwork, beauty trends, and working with people, nail technology can offer a practical path into the beauty industry. Better yet, Pennsylvania does not require a college degree or years of schooling. Learning how to become a nail tech in PA starts with three main tasks: complete an approved 200-hour program, apply through the state licensing system, and pass the required examination. Applicants must generally be at least 16 and have completed the 10th grade or its equivalent. The education rule is waived for veterans and people age 35 or older. Your license will let you provide manicures, pedicures, artificial nails, sculptured nails, and related nail services. It does not cover unrelated hair or skin services. This guide explains the training, application, costs, and job outlook so you can move forward with fewer surprises. ## Training and Education Requirements The first step in how to become a nail tech in PA is enrolling in a nail tech training Pennsylvania program. The school must be licensed by the Pennsylvania State Board of Cosmetology. Do not rely only on a school’s advertising. Verify its license through Pennsylvania’s PALS license search before paying tuition. Pennsylvania requires at least **200 hours of nail technology instruction**. The state’s recommended course outline divides those hours this way: - Professional practice: 25 hours - Sciences: 75 hours - Nail treatments: 75 hours - Pedicuring: 25 hours That adds up to 200 hours: 25 + 75 + 75 + 25 = 200. The official curriculum appears in [49 Pa. Code § 7.129](https://www.pacodeandbulletin.gov/secure/pacode/data/049/chapter7/s7.129.html). Expect to study sanitation, infection control, nail structure, client safety, manicures, pedicures, gels, acrylics, nail tips, product handling, and Pennsylvania law. Choose a program that offers plenty of hands-on practice, not just test preparation. State rules allow nail technology students to begin supervised work on members of the public after completing 50 instructional hours. When comparing schools, ask about schedules, completion rates, kits, books, payment plans, and whether exam preparation is included. If you are learning how to become a nail tech in PA while working, an evening or part-time course may be easier to manage. ## Pennsylvania Nail Technician Licensing Steps Understanding how to become a nail tech in PA also means following the application process in the right order. The main PA cosmetology board requirements are straightforward. ### 1. Confirm That You Qualify You must be at least 16 years old and normally need a 10th-grade education or equivalent. The education requirement does not apply if you are a veteran or at least 35 years old. These rules appear in the state regulations and the [Pennsylvania examination handbook](https://www.pearsonvue.com/content/dam/VUE/vue/en/documents/clients/pa-cosmetology-and-barber/203900.pdf). ### 2. Finish Your Approved Training Complete all 200 hours and obtain your school transcript and completed affidavit. Early testing is available after 150 hours, but Pennsylvania will not issue your final nail technician license PA until the school submits proof that you completed the full program. ### 3. Apply Through PALS Create an account at [PALS](https://www.pals.pa.gov/) and select the State Board of Cosmetology application. Be ready to provide proof of age, education, training, and criminal-history checks. Current state guidance says applicants may need a recent check from each state where they lived, worked, or trained during the previous five years. Follow the checklist shown in your application because document-age rules can change. ### 4. Pass the State Examination After approval, Pearson VUE sends an authorization-to-test email. The nail examination is a computer-based, multiple-choice theory and procedural-skills test. There is no hands-on practical examination. Topics include safety, sanitation, nail analysis, manicures, pedicures, enhancements, and state rules. The exam has 60 scored questions plus 15 unscored pretest questions. You may attempt it again within your authorization period, but each retake costs another examination fee. ### 5. Verify Your License After you pass and satisfy every document requirement, the state issues the license. Check PALS before accepting paid clients. For the latest rules, use the Board’s official [Nail Technician Licensure Requirements Snapshot](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dos/department-and-offices/bpoa/boards-commissions/cosmetology/nail-technician-licensure-snapshot). ## Costs and Timeline The state lists an initial cost of **$119**, calculated as a $26 application fee plus a $93 testing fee. The nail technician license PA renewal fee is currently $97 every two years. Pennsylvania lists no continuing-education requirement for renewal. Training is the larger expense. Published examples range from $2,668 in billed tuition and lab fees at one career center to $5,554.11 for a private-school package that includes tuition, kits, digital materials, and the $93 exam. Using those examples, an estimated starting range is: - Lower example: $2,668 + $119 = **$2,787** - Higher example: $5,554.11 + $26 application fee = **$5,580.11** Background checks, transportation, extra supplies, and retesting can raise the total. Request a written, all-inclusive price from each school. At 40 training hours per week, 200 ÷ 40 equals five weeks. At 20 hours per week, it equals ten weeks. Add time for documents, application review, exam scheduling, and license issuance. In practice, how to become a nail tech in PA may take two to four months, but part-time study or application problems can extend that estimate. ## Career Outlook for Pennsylvania Nail Technicians The career outlook is encouraging. Pennsylvania projects employment for manicurists and pedicurists to rise from 8,880 jobs in 2022 to 9,730 in 2032. That is an increase of 850 jobs, or **850 ÷ 8,880 × 100 = 9.6%**, with about 1,162 openings per year. The state lists 2025 annual wages of $20,830 at entry level, $29,550 on average, and $33,840 at the experienced level ([Pennsylvania In-Demand Occupations List](https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/dli/documents/cwia/products/pa%20idol.pdf)). Nationally, the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 7% growth from 2024 to 2034 and reports 2024 median pay of $34,660, or $16.66 per hour ([BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/manicurists-and-pedicurists.htm)). Income varies by location, hours, tips, services, and client loyalty. Build clean work habits, strong rebooking skills, and a photo portfolio. You can also explore broader [career resources](https://insightcortex.com/) while planning your goals. ## Frequently Asked Questions

How many hours are required to become a nail tech in Pennsylvania?

Pennsylvania requires 200 hours of nail technology instruction at a licensed cosmetology school. The curriculum must cover professional practice, science, nail treatments, and pedicuring. Although students may qualify for early testing after 150 hours, they must complete all 200 hours before the state issues a permanent license.

Can I become a nail technician online in Pennsylvania?

You should not assume that a fully online course will satisfy Pennsylvania licensing rules. The required training must come from a licensed school and includes practical skills. A school may deliver some theory in a flexible format, but confirm that the Board will accept every hour before enrolling or paying tuition.

Do I need a high school diploma for a Pennsylvania nail license?

A diploma is not always required, but most applicants must show that they completed the 10th grade or an equivalent level of education. The education requirement is waived for veterans and applicants who are 35 or older. You must still meet the training, examination, application, and age requirements.

How much is the Pennsylvania nail technician exam?

The Pearson VUE theory and procedural-skills examination currently costs $93. Pennsylvania also charges a $26 state application fee, making the official initial licensing total $119. Fees can change, and a failed or missed examination may require another payment, so confirm the amount before scheduling.

Does Pennsylvania require a practical nail exam?

No hands-on practical examination is currently required. Candidates take one computer-based, multiple-choice test covering both theory and procedural knowledge. You should still practice real services during school because safe filing, product application, sanitation, and client care are essential once you begin working with paying customers.

How often must I renew my nail technician license PA?

Pennsylvania nail technician licenses renew every two years. The current renewal fee is $97, and nail technician licenses expire on January 31 of even-numbered years. The Board lists no continuing-education requirement, but you must renew on time and keep your contact details current in PALS.

Can an out-of-state nail technician get licensed in Pennsylvania?

Possibly. Pennsylvania offers reciprocity or license portability in qualifying cases. The state snapshot says reciprocity applicants must document at least two years of licensed work experience where they hold a current license. Agreements and equivalent-requirement decisions can change, so contact the Board before submitting fees or documents.

## Start Your Pennsylvania Nail Career Now that you know how to become a nail tech in PA, your next move is simple: compare licensed schools, tour your top choices, and request complete cost details in writing. Then finish the 200 hours, submit a careful PALS application, and prepare for the state test. Keep copies of every transcript, receipt, background check, and email. A little organization can prevent long delays. With focused training and consistent client care, you can turn your interest in nails into a licensed Pennsylvania career.

final.content:
DIAMONDROCK HOSPITALITY: FINANCING STRATEGY, HEDGING EFFECTIVENESS, AND CAPITAL-ALLOCATION FLEXIBILITY

Executive conclusion

DiamondRock Hospitality’s financing strategy has generally balanced interest-rate protection with capital-allocation flexibility effectively, although it deliberately retains meaningful exposure to floating rates.

The evidence is:

• Interest expense remained relatively stable while the company transformed its balance sheet. It increased only $0.635 million, or 4.1%, from Q2 2023 to Q2 2024 and only $0.125 million, or 0.7%, from Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. The latter period included the replacement of all remaining mortgage debt with unsecured term loans.

• In the more directly relevant Q3 2024-to-Q3 2025 comparison, unsecured term-loan interest rose $1.558 million, but mortgage interest fell $2.113 million. Thus, the combined recurring interest cost of those two debt categories declined by $0.555 million, or 3.4%, despite the migration to unsecured debt.

• Swap cash settlements continued to reduce interest expense, but the quarterly benefit fell from $1.155 million in Q3 2024 to $0.847 million in Q3 2025. Consequently, the underlying improvement in term-loan-plus-mortgage interest before swap settlements was approximately $0.863 million; a $0.308 million reduction in the swap benefit narrowed the reported improvement to $0.555 million.

• The transformation was not costless. Q3 2025 total interest expense rose $0.125 million, and DiamondRock recognized a $5.850 million loss on debt extinguishment. Including that one-time refinancing charge, quarterly financing-related expense increased by $5.975 million. Over the first nine months of 2025, interest expense declined $2.297 million, but interest expense plus the extinguishment loss increased $3.553 million.

• The strategy materially increased flexibility: by September 30, 2025, DiamondRock had no secured mortgage debt, an entirely unencumbered hotel portfolio, debt that was fully prepayable without penalty, no maturities until January 2028, $400 million available under an undrawn revolver, and $145.3 million of unrestricted cash. Total debt was approximately $1.1 billion, essentially unchanged from year-end 2024 despite the refinancing. (DiamondRock Q3 2025 results: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000083/exhibit9913q2025.htm)

• The company retained only partial rate protection. Management stated that, including swaps, approximately 30% of debt was fixed and 70% remained floating. That creates exposure if SOFR rises, but it also preserves the ability to benefit from falling rates and to prepay or reallocate capital without mortgage prepayment penalties. The swap portfolio’s active notional amount at September 30, 2025 was approximately $325 million, almost exactly 30% of $1.1 billion of debt.

• Free cash flow for the nine months ended September 30, 2025 was $114.789 million, calculated as $175.730 million of operating cash flow less $60.941 million of capital expenditures. This was sufficient to fund the approximately $71.1 million Worthington mortgage repayment made from cash on hand, but it covered only 38.8% of the full $295.808 million of mortgage principal repaid during the nine-month period. Accordingly, operations supported a meaningful part of the refinancing, but the complete mortgage exit also depended on the new $300 million unsecured term loan, temporary revolver usage, and balance-sheet cash.

Overall, the strategy has been effective: DiamondRock accepted moderate short-term refinancing and transaction costs in exchange for an unencumbered portfolio, longer maturities, penalty-free prepayment, and greater capital-allocation optionality. The principal residual risk is that 70% floating-rate exposure leaves financing costs sensitive to SOFR if interest rates do not decline as management anticipates.

1. Change in interest-rate swap fair values: December 2023 to June 2024

DiamondRock reported four interest-rate swaps at both December 31, 2023 and June 30, 2024. The fair values were assets in both periods, in thousands of dollars:

| Swap | Notional | Fixed rate | Maturity | Dec. 31, 2023 fair value | June 30, 2024 fair value | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Swap 1 | $87.5m | 1.63% | July 25, 2024 | $1.660m | $0.216m | $(1.444)m |
| Swap 2 | $87.5m | 1.63% | July 25, 2024 | $1.658m | $0.216m | $(1.442)m |
| Swap 3 | $75.0m | 3.36% | January 1, 2028 | $0.554m | $1.958m | $1.404m |
| Swap 4 | $75.0m | 3.50% | January 1, 2027 | $0.449m | $1.537m | $1.088m |
| Total | $325.0m | — | — | $4.321m | $3.927m | $(0.394)m |

Source: DiamondRock’s June 30, 2024 Form 10-Q, including the detailed swap table: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000095/drh-20240630.htm

Calculation:

$3.927 million − $4.321 million = −$0.394 million

Percentage change:

−$0.394 million ÷ $4.321 million = −9.12%

Therefore, the total positive fair value of the swap portfolio declined by $394,000, or approximately 9.1%, between December 31, 2023 and June 30, 2024.

The aggregate movement masks substantially different changes by maturity:

• The two short-dated 1.63% swaps, which expired in July 2024, declined by a combined $2.886 million:

($0.216m − $1.660m) + ($0.216m − $1.658m)
= −$1.444m − $1.442m
= −$2.886m

• The two longer-dated swaps increased by a combined $2.492 million:

($1.958m − $0.554m) + ($1.537m − $0.449m)
= $1.404m + $1.088m
= $2.492m

• Net movement:

−$2.886m + $2.492m = −$0.394m

This pattern is consistent with the approaching expiration of the short-dated swaps reducing their remaining economic value, while movements in the yield curve increased the value of the longer-dated fixed-pay swaps.

The $394,000 decline should not be interpreted as a $394,000 increase in cash financing cost. Swap fair value is a mark-to-market balance-sheet measurement based on the interest-rate yield curve, implied volatility, and counterparty credit risk. DiamondRock classifies the measurements as Level 2. The economic effect on current financing cost is better assessed through the swap settlements recorded in interest expense and through the company’s effective interest rates. (DiamondRock Q2 2024 Form 10-Q: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000095/drh-20240630.htm)

2. Q2 2023 to Q2 2024 interest-expense analysis

DiamondRock’s total interest expense increased from $15.567 million in Q2 2023 to $16.202 million in Q2 2024. The company reported the following components, in thousands:

| Interest-expense component | Q2 2023 | Q2 2024 | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Mortgage debt interest | $4.111m | $4.009m | $(0.102)m |
| Unsecured term-loan interest | $10.608m | $11.368m | $0.760m |
| Credit-facility interest and unused fees | $0.317m | $0.312m | $(0.005)m |
| Debt-cost and debt-premium amortization | $0.512m | $0.513m | $0.001m |
| Swap mark-to-market expense | $0.019m | $0.000m | $(0.019)m |
| Total | $15.567m | $16.202m | $0.635m |

Source: DiamondRock Q2 2024 Form 10-Q: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000095/drh-20240630.htm

Total change:

$16.202m − $15.567m = $0.635m

Percentage increase:

$0.635m ÷ $15.567m = 4.08%

Excluding the noncash swap mark-to-market item from Q2 2023, recurring interest expense increased from $15.548 million to $16.202 million:

Q2 2023 excluding mark-to-market:
$15.567m − $0.019m = $15.548m

Change:
$16.202m − $15.548m = $0.654m

Percentage:
$0.654m ÷ $15.548m = 4.21%

Interpretation

The increase was driven almost entirely by unsecured term-loan interest, which rose $760,000, or 7.2%:

$0.760m ÷ $10.608m = 7.16%

Mortgage interest fell $102,000, while credit-facility expense and swap mark-to-market expense fell by $5,000 and $19,000, respectively.

The modest 4.1% rise in total interest expense indicates that the swap strategy mitigated, but did not eliminate, the impact of higher floating-rate costs. At June 30, 2024:

• DiamondRock had approximately $800 million of unsecured term loans and $373.3 million of property-specific mortgage debt.

• Total debt was approximately $1.2 billion.

• The total weighted-average interest rate, including swaps, was 5.22%.

• The disclosed rate on the relevant floating-rate term loan was 6.80% before the effect of swaps.

These figures show the practical protection provided by the swaps: the swapped portions of the term loans materially reduced the company’s effective borrowing rate below the otherwise applicable floating rate. (DiamondRock Q2 2024 results and balance-sheet discussion: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/diamondrock-hospitality-company-reports-second-quarter-2024-results-302212778.html)

Nevertheless, the company did not fully fix the debt portfolio. That was a deliberate trade-off: partial swaps reduced the immediate rate burden while leaving debt sufficiently floating and prepayable to preserve future refinancing and capital-allocation flexibility.

3. Q3 2024 to Q3 2025 interest-expense analysis

The Q3 comparison captures the actual transition from mortgage financing to an all-unsecured balance sheet.

DiamondRock’s total interest expense increased only $125,000, from $16.986 million in Q3 2024 to $17.111 million in Q3 2025:

$17.111m − $16.986m = $0.125m

Percentage change:

$0.125m ÷ $16.986m = 0.736%, or approximately 0.7%

The components were:

| Interest-expense component | Q3 2024 | Q3 2025 | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Unsecured term-loan interest | $12.665m | $14.223m | $1.558m |
| Mortgage debt interest | $3.527m | $1.414m | $(2.113)m |
| Credit-facility interest and unused fees | $0.315m | $0.504m | $0.189m |
| Debt-issuance-cost amortization | $0.479m | $0.494m | $0.015m |
| Finance-lease interest | $0.000m | $0.476m | $0.476m |
| Total | $16.986m | $17.111m | $0.125m |

Source: DiamondRock Q3 2025 Form 10-Q and interest-expense discussion: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm

The $476,000 finance-lease amount is the reconciling difference:

Q3 2025 known components before finance-lease expense:
$14.223m + $1.414m + $0.504m + $0.494m = $16.635m

Finance-lease expense:
$17.111m − $16.635m = $0.476m

DiamondRock explained that the finance-lease interest arose after an October 2024 ground-lease extension changed that lease’s classification from operating to finance lease. Thus, it is not a direct cost of replacing mortgage debt with term loans.

3.1 Debt-interest cost directly attributable to mortgage-to-term-loan transition

To isolate the core debt-composition effect, combine unsecured term-loan and mortgage interest.

Q3 2024:

$12.665m + $3.527m = $16.192m

Q3 2025:

$14.223m + $1.414m = $15.637m

Net change:

$15.637m − $16.192m = −$0.555m

Percentage change:

−$0.555m ÷ $16.192m = −3.43%

Therefore, the recurring interest cost associated with term loans plus mortgages declined by $555,000, or 3.4%, even though term-loan interest increased materially. The $2.113 million decline in mortgage interest more than offset the $1.558 million increase in term-loan interest:

−$2.113m + $1.558m = −$0.555m

This is the clearest evidence that the debt-composition shift itself did not materially increase recurring financing cost in Q3 2025.

3.2 Effect of swap settlements on the comparison

DiamondRock’s derivative disclosure shows that interest-rate swaps reduced interest expense by:

• Q3 2024: $1.155 million
• Q3 2025: $0.847 million

Source: DiamondRock’s September 30, 2025 derivative schedule: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/R13.htm

The swap benefit therefore declined by:

$0.847m − $1.155m = −$0.308m

In other words, swaps still reduced Q3 2025 interest expense, but by $308,000 less than in Q3 2024.

Because the reported term-loan and mortgage interest figures reflect the swap effect recognized in interest expense, an approximate pre-swap comparison can be constructed by adding the swap benefit back:

Q3 2024 pre-swap term-loan-plus-mortgage interest:
$16.192m + $1.155m = $17.347m

Q3 2025 pre-swap term-loan-plus-mortgage interest:
$15.637m + $0.847m = $16.484m

Pre-swap decline:
$16.484m − $17.347m = −$0.863m

Thus:

• Underlying pre-swap term-loan-plus-mortgage cost improved by approximately $863,000.

• The reduction in swap benefit worsened the year-over-year comparison by $308,000.

• The resulting reported improvement was $555,000:

−$0.863m + $0.308m = −$0.555m

This means the favorable Q3 2025 debt-interest result did not arise solely from larger hedge settlements. In fact, hedge income declined. The improvement instead came from the changing debt composition, lower outstanding mortgage balances during the quarter, and the pricing of the refinanced unsecured debt.

4. Net change in financing costs during the mortgage-to-unsecured transition

There are three useful ways to measure the net change, depending on whether “financing costs” means recurring debt interest, total reported quarterly interest expense, or total financing-related expense including the one-time extinguishment charge.

4.1 Recurring mortgage plus unsecured term-loan interest

As calculated above:

Q3 2024: $16.192 million  
Q3 2025: $15.637 million  
Net change: −$0.555 million, or −3.4%

This measure indicates that the central mortgage-to-term-loan transition lowered recurring debt interest during the comparison period.

4.2 Total quarterly interest expense

Q3 2024: $16.986 million  
Q3 2025: $17.111 million  
Net change: +$0.125 million, or +0.7%

The reason total interest expense rose despite the $555,000 decline in mortgage-plus-term-loan interest was the combination of:

• $189,000 more credit-facility interest and unused fees;
• $15,000 more debt-cost amortization;
• $476,000 of new finance-lease interest.

Reconciliation:

−$0.555m + $0.189m + $0.015m + $0.476m = $0.125m

Therefore, the debt refinancing itself reduced recurring mortgage-plus-term interest, while other financing and lease-related costs produced the small increase in reported total interest expense.

4.3 Total quarterly financing-related expense including debt extinguishment

DiamondRock recognized a $5.850 million loss on debt extinguishment in Q3 2025, compared with no such loss in Q3 2024. (DiamondRock Q3 2025 Form 10-Q: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm)

Q3 2024:
Interest expense = $16.986m  
Debt-extinguishment loss = $0  
Total = $16.986m

Q3 2025:
Interest expense = $17.111m  
Debt-extinguishment loss = $5.850m  
Total = $22.961m

Net increase:

$22.961m − $16.986m = $5.975m

Thus, the all-in quarterly accounting cost of financing increased $5.975 million because of the one-time refinancing charge. This should be separated from recurring interest cost: the extinguishment loss represents the cost of accelerating the financing transformation, not a permanent increase in the run-rate cost of debt.

4.4 Nine-month perspective

For the nine months ended September 30:

• 2024 interest expense: $49.434 million
• 2025 interest expense: $47.137 million

Source: DiamondRock Q3 2025 Form 10-Q: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm

Change:

$47.137m − $49.434m = −$2.297m

Percentage:

−$2.297m ÷ $49.434m = −4.65%

Therefore, reported interest expense declined $2.297 million, or 4.7%, over the first nine months of 2025.

Including the $5.850 million debt-extinguishment loss:

2025:
$47.137m + $5.850m = $52.987m

2024:
$49.434m + $0 = $49.434m

Net change:
$52.987m − $49.434m = $3.553m

Accordingly, recurring interest cost improved, but total financing-related accounting expense increased by $3.553 million when the refinancing charge is included.

Cash interest paid provides additional evidence of lower recurring cash financing costs:

• Nine months ended September 30, 2024: $48.646 million
• Nine months ended September 30, 2025: $43.972 million

Change:

$43.972m − $48.646m = −$4.674m

Percentage:

−$4.674m ÷ $48.646m = −9.61%

Cash interest paid therefore declined by $4.674 million, or 9.6%. (Cash-flow information from the September 2025 filing: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm)

DiamondRock also paid $11.574 million of financing costs during the first nine months of 2025. These payments are financing cash outflows rather than recurring interest, but they are part of the economic cost of establishing the new capital structure.

5. Evolution of the hedge portfolio and remaining rate exposure

5.1 Hedge coverage in 2024

At June 30, 2024, DiamondRock’s four swaps had $325 million of aggregate notional value against approximately $800 million of unsecured term loans and approximately $1.173 billion of total debt.

Swap coverage as a percentage of term loans:

$325m ÷ $800m = 40.6%

Swap coverage as a percentage of total debt:

$325m ÷ $1,173.3m = 27.7%

The swaps therefore fixed a meaningful but minority portion of total debt. This was sufficient to reduce the effective weighted-average rate but left substantial exposure to floating SOFR.

The weighted-average rate on total debt was 5.22% including swaps at June 30, 2024, while the disclosed rate on the relevant floating term loan was 6.80% before swaps. This large difference demonstrates that the swaps were economically valuable during a period of elevated short-term rates. (DiamondRock Q2 2024 release: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/diamondrock-hospitality-company-reports-second-quarter-2024-results-302212778.html)

5.2 Hedge coverage at September 2025

At September 30, 2025, DiamondRock’s swap portfolio consisted of:

| Notional | Fixed rate | Effective date | Maturity | Sept. 30, 2025 fair value |
|---:|---:|---|---|---:|
| $75.0m | 3.36% | March 1, 2023 | January 1, 2028 | $(0.061)m |
| $75.0m | 3.50% | March 1, 2023 | January 1, 2027 | $0.004m |
| $37.5m | 3.27% | October 1, 2024 | January 1, 2028 | $0.042m |
| $37.5m | 3.27% | October 1, 2024 | January 1, 2028 | $0.042m |
| $25.0m | 3.07% | January 2, 2025 | January 1, 2027 | $0.134m |
| $75.0m | 3.25% | January 2, 2025 | January 1, 2026 | $0.140m |
| $75.0m forward swap | 3.23% | January 2, 2026 | January 1, 2029 | $(0.133)m |
| Total fair value | — | — | — | $0.168m |

Source: DiamondRock’s September 2025 derivative schedule: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/R13.htm and https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/R40.htm

The swaps active as of September 30, 2025 had $325 million of notional amount:

$75m + $75m + $37.5m + $37.5m + $25m + $75m = $325m

Against $1.1 billion of total debt:

$325m ÷ $1.1bn = 29.5%

That reconciles closely to management’s statement that approximately 30% of debt was fixed, including swaps, and 70% was floating.

The forward-starting $75 million swap effective January 2, 2026 replaces some protection as existing swaps mature. DiamondRock also entered into another $50 million swap on October 15, 2025, effective January 4, 2027. This staggered approach reduces “cliff” exposure from all swaps expiring simultaneously. (Derivative disclosure: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/R13.htm)

5.3 Declining swap values do not mean the hedges failed

The aggregate swap fair value fell to only $0.168 million by September 30, 2025, from $4.674 million at December 31, 2024:

$0.168m − $4.674m = −$4.506m

The decline mainly reflects changes in the forward interest-rate curve and the shortening remaining terms. It does not mean the swaps ceased to provide cash-flow protection. The swaps still reduced Q3 2025 interest expense by $847,000 and nine-month 2025 interest expense by $2.485 million.

However, the benefit was diminishing:

• Nine-month 2024 swap reduction to interest expense: $5.863 million
• Nine-month 2025 swap reduction: $2.485 million
• Decline in hedge benefit: $3.378 million

Calculation:

$2.485m − $5.863m = −$3.378m

Source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/R13.htm

This is consistent with maturing low-fixed-rate swaps and lower market rates. DiamondRock’s decision not to hedge all debt allows it to benefit if SOFR falls, but it also means the company remains exposed if rates rise again.

6. Mortgage repayment and unsecured refinancing strategy

6.1 Starting position

At June 30, 2024, DiamondRock had:

• Approximately $1.2 billion of total debt;
• $800 million of unsecured term loans;
• $373.3 million of property-specific, non-recourse mortgage debt;
• $400 million of unused revolving-credit capacity;
• $125.2 million of unrestricted corporate cash.

Source: DiamondRock Q2 2024 results: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/diamondrock-hospitality-company-reports-second-quarter-2024-results-302212778.html

The property mortgages carried relatively low fixed rates but restricted individual hotel assets and could limit portfolio-level financing and disposition flexibility.

6.2 2025 mortgage repayments

DiamondRock repaid all three remaining mortgages in 2025:

1. Worthington Renaissance Fort Worth Hotel

• December 2024 principal balance: approximately $71.8 million.
• Contract rate: 3.66%.
• The mortgage was repaid on May 6, 2025 using cash on hand.

2. Hotel Clio

• December 2024 principal balance: approximately $54.7 million.
• Contract rate: 4.33%.
• DiamondRock drew $60 million on the revolver on July 2, 2025 and used the proceeds to repay the mortgage at its July 3 maturity.
• The $60 million revolver draw was repaid on July 22 after completion of the amended credit facility.

3. Westin Boston Seaport District

• December 2024 principal balance: approximately $169.4 million.
• Contract rate: 4.36%.
• The loan was repaid on September 5, 2025 using proceeds from the amended unsecured credit facility.

Source: DiamondRock Q3 2025 Form 10-Q: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm

Total mortgage principal payments during the nine months were $295.808 million. DiamondRock simultaneously received $300 million of proceeds from a new senior unsecured term loan. The near one-for-one relationship shows that the company largely recapitalized the same amount of debt rather than materially increasing leverage:

New unsecured term-loan proceeds: $300.000m  
Mortgage principal payments: $295.808m  
Difference: $4.192m

At September 30, 2025, total debt was $1.100 billion versus $1.0958 billion at December 31, 2024, a gross increase of only approximately $4.2 million. Net debt remained conservative because unrestricted cash increased to $145.336 million.

6.3 New unsecured structure

On July 22, 2025, DiamondRock refinanced, upsized and extended its senior unsecured facility from $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion. The new structure consisted of:

• $400 million revolving credit facility maturing January 2030, with two six-month extension options;
• $500 million term loan maturing January 2028, with two six-month extension options;
• $300 million term loan maturing January 2029, with two six-month extension options;
• $300 million term loan maturing January 2030.

The facility uses a leverage-based pricing grid ranging from SOFR plus 1.35% to SOFR plus 2.25%. At the company’s then-current leverage, pricing was at the lowest end of the grid. (DiamondRock Q3 2025 results: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000083/exhibit9913q2025.htm)

By September 30, 2025:

• Total debt was approximately $1.1 billion.
• The weighted-average interest rate was approximately 5.3%.
• The entire hotel portfolio was unencumbered.
• All debt was prepayable without penalty.
• There were no maturities until January 2028.
• The $400 million revolver was undrawn.
• Unrestricted cash was $145.3 million.

These characteristics materially improve capital-allocation flexibility. DiamondRock can now sell, renovate, refinance or reposition hotels without negotiating individual mortgage releases, and it can reduce debt or reborrow without property-specific prepayment penalties.

7. Free cash flow for the nine months ended September 30, 2025

Using the conventional definition of free cash flow as operating cash flow less capital expenditures:

Net cash provided by operating activities: $175.730 million  
Less capital expenditures: $60.941 million  
Free cash flow: $114.789 million

Calculation:

$175.730m − $60.941m = $114.789m

Source figures: DiamondRock Q3 2025 Form 10-Q: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm; capital expenditure discussion: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000083/exhibit9913q2025.htm

Free-cash-flow margin against reported revenue of $845.957 million was:

$114.789m ÷ $845.957m = 13.57%

This is an analyst-calculated measure rather than a company-defined GAAP metric. It excludes:

• $89.023 million of proceeds from the hotel sale;
• debt issuance and repayment proceeds;
• common and preferred distributions;
• share repurchases;
• proceeds and repayments under the credit facilities.

That makes it suitable for assessing the amount of internally generated cash available after maintaining and improving the hotel portfolio.

8. Could operations fund the debt refinancing?

The answer is “partly, and sufficiently for the cash-funded mortgage repayment, but not for the entire $295.8 million mortgage exit.”

8.1 Coverage of the Worthington cash repayment

DiamondRock’s reported mortgage repayment excluding scheduled amortization through June 30, 2025 was approximately $71.089 million. Free cash flow of $114.789 million covered that amount by:

$114.789m ÷ $71.089m = 1.615 times, or 161.5%

Excess free cash flow after that repayment:

$114.789m − $71.089m = $43.700m

Thus, nine-month operational free cash flow was more than sufficient to fund the Worthington mortgage repayment that DiamondRock made with cash on hand.

8.2 Coverage of all mortgage principal payments

Total nine-month mortgage principal payments were $295.808 million.

Free-cash-flow coverage:

$114.789m ÷ $295.808m = 38.80%

Operating-cash-flow coverage before capital expenditures:

$175.730m ÷ $295.808m = 59.41%

Therefore, operations alone did not fund the complete exit from mortgage debt during the nine-month period. The complete transaction required:

• Cash generated by operations and existing cash for Worthington;
• A temporary $60 million revolver draw for Hotel Clio;
• The new $300 million unsecured term loan to repay the revolver and fund the Westin Boston mortgage;
• Balance-sheet liquidity, supplemented by $89.023 million of hotel-sale proceeds during the period.

This distinction is important. DiamondRock had enough recurring cash generation to contribute substantially and to repay the cash-funded mortgage without stressing liquidity, but the company sensibly used long-term unsecured financing rather than consume nearly $300 million of cash to extinguish all mortgages.

8.3 Financing-cost coverage

Free cash flow also comfortably covered nine-month cash interest:

$114.789m ÷ $43.972m = 2.61 times

However, because operating cash flow is measured after cash interest, this ratio should be read as an indication of residual cash-generating capacity rather than a formal interest-coverage ratio.

Free cash flow also exceeded the $11.574 million of financing costs paid by approximately:

$114.789m − $11.574m = $103.215m

The company therefore had ample operational cash generation to absorb the transaction costs associated with the refinancing.

9. Capital-allocation priorities and their role in the financing transformation

DiamondRock allocated capital to four principal uses during the first nine months of 2025:

| Use of capital | Nine months ended Sept. 30, 2025 |
|---|---:|
| Hotel capital expenditures | $60.941m |
| Common-stock and unit distributions | $81.868m |
| Preferred-stock distributions | $7.362m |
| Common-stock repurchases | $35.519m |
| Mortgage principal payments | $295.808m |
| Financing costs paid | $11.574m |

Source: DiamondRock Q3 2025 Form 10-Q: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm

9.1 Hotel reinvestment remained funded

The company invested $60.9 million in capital improvements during the first nine months and expected full-year 2025 capital spending of $85 million to $90 million. Projects included:

• Renovation of guestrooms at Hilton Garden Inn New York/Times Square Central;
• Repositioning of Orchards Inn as The Cliffs at L’Auberge in Sedona, including a new pool, property connection, guestrooms, arrival experience and event space;
• Guestroom renovation at Kimpton Hotel Palomar Phoenix.

Source: DiamondRock Q3 2025 results: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000083/exhibit9913q2025.htm

The company therefore did not achieve the financing transformation by starving the hotel portfolio of capital. Operational cash generation funded $60.9 million of property investment and still left $114.8 million of free cash flow.

9.2 Distributions and repurchases remained priorities

Common and preferred distributions totaled:

$81.868m + $7.362m = $89.230m

Free cash flow after those distributions:

$114.789m − $89.230m = $25.559m

DiamondRock also repurchased $35.519 million of stock during the nine months. Free cash flow after capital expenditures, common and preferred distributions, and repurchases was therefore:

$114.789m − $89.230m − $35.519m = −$9.960m

This calculation shows that operating free cash flow covered capital expenditures and all distributions, and covered most—but not all—of the share repurchases. The remaining uses were supported by existing cash and asset-sale proceeds.

Management reported that through November 6, 2025 it had repurchased 4.8 million shares for approximately $37.1 million at a weighted-average price of $7.72 and retained $137 million of authorization under the $200 million repurchase program. During Q3 alone it repurchased 1.5 million shares for $11.8 million, or $7.87 per share. (DiamondRock Q3 2025 results: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000083/exhibit9913q2025.htm)

The new unsecured, prepayable debt structure supports this priority because management can direct excess cash among debt reduction, hotel investment and share repurchases without mortgage-specific restrictions.

9.3 Liquidity remained strong after refinancing and capital returns

At September 30, 2025, DiamondRock had:

• $145.336 million of unrestricted cash;
• $400 million of undrawn revolver capacity;
• Approximately $545 million of immediately identifiable corporate liquidity before hotel-level restricted cash;
• No secured debt;
• No debt maturity until January 2028.

These resources indicate that the company did not sacrifice liquidity to complete the mortgage exit or fund shareholder returns.

10. Overall assessment: does the strategy balance risk and flexibility?

10.1 Evidence that the strategy is working

Interest expense has been stable

• Q2 2023 to Q2 2024: +$0.635 million, or +4.1%.
• Q3 2024 to Q3 2025: +$0.125 million, or +0.7%.
• Nine months 2024 to nine months 2025: −$2.297 million, or −4.7%.
• Nine-month cash interest paid: −$4.674 million, or −9.6%.

The mortgage-to-term-loan shift did not increase core recurring debt interest

• Combined term-loan and mortgage interest declined $555,000 in Q3 2025 versus Q3 2024.
• On a pre-swap basis, the decline was approximately $863,000.
• The lower swap benefit reduced, rather than created, the reported improvement.

The swap program has provided meaningful protection

• The June 2024 weighted-average debt rate was 5.22% including swaps, materially below the 6.80% pre-swap rate disclosed for the relevant floating-rate term loan.
• Swaps reduced interest expense by $5.863 million in the first nine months of 2024 and by $2.485 million in the first nine months of 2025.
• Staggered maturities and forward-starting swaps reduce the risk that all hedge protection expires at once.

The unsecured refinancing greatly increased flexibility

• The entire portfolio became unencumbered.
• Debt became fully prepayable without penalty.
• Maturities were extended to 2028-2030.
• A $400 million revolver remained undrawn.
• The company retained $145.3 million of cash.
• Total debt remained approximately $1.1 billion rather than increasing materially.

Operational cash generation supported the transformation

• Nine-month free cash flow was $114.789 million.
• That was sufficient to cover the cash-funded Worthington repayment.
• It funded property capital expenditures and all common and preferred distributions.
• It absorbed refinancing costs while the company retained substantial liquidity.

10.2 Costs and residual risks

The refinancing imposed meaningful one-time costs

• Q3 2025 included a $5.850 million extinguishment loss.
• Interest expense plus the extinguishment charge rose by $5.975 million year over year in Q3.
• Nine-month interest expense plus extinguishment loss rose $3.553 million.
• Cash financing costs paid were $11.574 million.

Floating-rate exposure remains substantial

Management indicated that approximately 70% of debt remained floating after swaps. This positioning is advantageous if short-term rates decline, but it creates a clear downside risk if SOFR rises or remains elevated.

A rough sensitivity illustrates the exposure. Applying a hypothetical 1 percentage-point increase to approximately 70% of $1.1 billion of debt:

Floating debt:
$1.1bn × 70% = $770m

Approximate annual incremental interest:
$770m × 1% = $7.7m

This is a simplified sensitivity that ignores timing, floors, changing debt balances, pricing-grid movements and future swaps, but it shows that the residual floating exposure is economically material.

Lower-rate mortgages were replaced with market-rate unsecured debt

The three retired mortgages bore fixed rates of approximately 3.66%, 4.33% and 4.36%, below the approximately 5.3% weighted-average rate on DiamondRock’s unsecured debt at September 30, 2025. Therefore, the refinancing traded some low-cost secured funding for flexibility, longer maturities, and an unencumbered portfolio. The short-term interest cost was controlled because the mortgages were repaid at different times, swaps offset part of floating-rate expense, and lower SOFR expectations supported the unsecured structure. But the replacement debt is not inherently cheaper than the retired mortgages on a coupon basis.

Operational cash did not fund the entire mortgage exit

Free cash flow covered 38.8% of total mortgage principal repayments. The strategy therefore relied on capital-market access and the new unsecured term loan as well as internal cash generation. This is not a weakness by itself—matching long-lived hotel assets with long-term financing is appropriate—but it means continued access to bank markets remains important.

Final judgment

DiamondRock’s evolving financing strategy has achieved a reasonable and generally effective balance.

The interest-rate swaps reduced cash interest during a high-rate period without locking the entire balance sheet into fixed-rate debt. As the company transitioned from mortgages to unsecured term loans, total quarterly interest expense remained almost flat, combined mortgage-plus-term-loan interest actually declined, and nine-month cash interest paid fell materially. At the same time, DiamondRock eliminated secured debt, released every hotel from mortgage encumbrances, extended maturities, maintained an undrawn $400 million revolver, and made all debt prepayable without penalty.

The price of that flexibility was a $5.850 million extinguishment loss, $11.574 million of cash financing costs, and continued exposure on approximately 70% of debt to floating rates. The strategy will look particularly favorable if SOFR declines, because DiamondRock retains substantial floating exposure while its limited swaps protect a core portion of debt. It will look less favorable if short-term rates rise sharply, because the hedge ratio is only about 30%.

Operationally, the transformation appears supportable. Free cash flow of $114.789 million funded the cash-based mortgage repayment, hotel reinvestment and distributions while preserving liquidity. Nevertheless, the complete $295.808 million mortgage repayment program was financed through a combination of operational cash, existing liquidity, temporary revolver usage and the new $300 million unsecured term loan—not through free cash flow alone.

On balance, DiamondRock has prioritized flexibility over maximum near-term fixed-rate protection, but it has done so without causing a material increase in recurring interest expense or leverage. That makes the financing strategy effective, provided management continues to manage the 70% floating-rate exposure through staggered swaps, disciplined leverage, and sufficient operating liquidity.
