final.content:
EDGE COMPUTING’S TRANSFORMATION OF INDUSTRIAL IoT ARCHITECTURES AS OF 2024

Executive summary

By 2024, industrial IoT had largely moved beyond the simple model of “connect every sensor to a distant public cloud.” The emerging architecture is hierarchical:

1. Sensors, actuators, cameras, relays, robots, and PLCs generate data.
2. Device-level or site-level edge systems perform filtering, feature extraction, inference, coordination, and safety-critical control.
3. Only alarms, derived features, state changes, summaries, selected raw evidence, and model-training data go to a regional or public cloud.
4. The cloud remains responsible for fleet-wide analytics, long-term storage, model training, cross-site optimization, business integration, and centralized governance.

This is not the elimination of cloud computing. It is a redistribution of functions according to timing, bandwidth, resilience, privacy, and compute requirements.

The three use cases show different versions of that transformation:

| Use case | Functions moving to the edge | Functions remaining in cloud | Practical latency target | WAN/cloud data-reduction target | Availability objective |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Manufacturing predictive maintenance | Signal conditioning, FFT/features, anomaly detection, local alarms and interlocks, outage buffering | Long-horizon failure prediction, model training, fleet benchmarking, CMMS/ERP integration | Approximately 10–50 ms for immediate anomaly/trip logic; under 100 ms for monitoring alerts | Commonly 60–90%; approximately 90% is a reasonable project target | Continue monitoring and alarming through WAN outages; reduce equipment downtime rather than merely improve IT uptime |
| Autonomous mobile robots | Localization or selected perception, fleet orchestration, path conflict resolution, safety-zone analytics, local digital twins | Global optimization, historical analytics, simulation and model training | Approximately 1–10 ms network target for tightly coupled control; tens of milliseconds for perception/fleet decisions | Approximately 80–95% reduction in traffic sent beyond the site if video/LiDAR stay on premises; robot-to-local-edge traffic itself may increase | Five-nines-class communications is the design aspiration; robot must retain an onboard safe-stop/fallback mode |
| Energy distribution | Relay/protection logic, state-change detection, waveform/event filtering, DER and microgrid control, local operation during backhaul failure | System-wide ADMS, planning, asset analytics, model training, regulatory history | No more than 3 ms for IEC 61850 fast protection messaging; tens of milliseconds to seconds for less critical analytics | Approximately 90–99.9% for event-driven or feature-only export, depending on sampling and retention policy | Protection messaging can require 99.9999% timely delivery in engineered schemes; redundant paths and autonomous local operation are essential |

The percentages for manufacturing are supported by documented deployment guidance. The AMR and grid percentages are best treated as engineering targets derived from keeping high-volume sensor streams local, because the cited real-world case studies generally report stability and operational outcomes rather than publishing raw before-and-after byte counts.

A critical distinction is therefore required:

- “Latency target” is not always the same as measured application latency.
- “Bandwidth reduction” may refer to WAN/cloud traffic, not traffic between devices and a local edge server.
- “Availability improvement” may mean continued local control during cloud or WAN failure, not that the edge server itself has a higher standalone hardware SLA.
- Vendor case studies demonstrate feasibility and operational value, but seldom disclose enough baseline data for an independently audited end-to-end SLA comparison.

1. The cross-industry architectural change

1.1 Cloud-centric industrial IoT

A typical first-generation cloud-centric architecture was:

Sensor/PLC/camera/robot/meter  
→ gateway or protocol converter  
→ plant or carrier network  
→ internet/WAN  
→ public-cloud ingestion  
→ cloud database/data lake  
→ cloud analytics or inference  
→ alert or command returned over the WAN  
→ operator, PLC, robot, relay, or maintenance system

Its advantages were centralized administration, elastic compute, consolidated data, and relatively easy integration with enterprise applications. Its limitations were equally important:

- Every raw sample competed for scarce upstream bandwidth.
- Response time included access-network, WAN, cloud-queue, cloud-processing, and return-path delay.
- A WAN or cloud outage could interrupt analytics or decision-making.
- Sending raw production, video, or grid data off site increased privacy and attack-surface concerns.
- Cloud ingestion, egress, compute, and long-term storage costs increased with sensor frequency.
- Remote cloud control could not provide deterministic timing for safety or protection functions.

AWS’s industrial architecture guidance explicitly calls sending all sensor data unfiltered to the cloud a common anti-pattern. It also identifies cloud-only analysis, lack of edge buffering, fixed sampling rates, and assuming unlimited connectivity as industrial anti-patterns (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/modern-industrial-data-technology-lens/midaperf05-bp01.html).

1.2 Edge-distributed industrial IoT

The 2024 pattern is a three-tier system:

Field/device edge  
- Embedded controllers, intelligent sensors, relays, robot computers
- Hard real-time loops, emergency stop, basic filtering, compression, immediate inference

Site or network edge  
- Industrial gateways, edge servers, local Kubernetes clusters, on-premises MEC
- Data normalization, aggregation, digital twins, fleet coordination, local databases, more capable AI inference
- Temporary storage and store-and-forward operation

Cloud  
- Cross-site data lake and dashboards
- Model training and deployment management
- Fleet benchmarking and long-term optimization
- Enterprise applications, regulatory records, and historical retention

AWS describes the intended manufacturing outcome as distributing processing between edge and cloud, performing reduction, summarization, and filtering locally while preserving information required for cloud analytics and storage. Its guidance says edge preprocessing typically reduces manufacturing bandwidth requirements by 60–90%, lowers cloud storage and ingestion costs proportionally, minimizes local decision latency, and enables continued operation during connectivity disruption (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/modern-industrial-data-technology-lens/midaperf05-bp01.html).

The architecture’s central principle is therefore not “edge instead of cloud,” but “put each function at the lowest-latency, most failure-tolerant tier that can execute it safely.”

2. Manufacturing predictive maintenance

2.1 Before-and-after architecture

Before: cloud-centric condition monitoring

Machine vibration, temperature, acoustic, pressure, and electrical sensors  
→ PLC/historian/gateway  
→ raw or lightly processed time series uploaded over the WAN  
→ cloud stream processor and database  
→ cloud anomaly or remaining-useful-life model  
→ alert returned to maintenance personnel or CMMS

Typical limitations included:

- High-frequency, multi-axis vibration produces far more data than temperature monitoring.
- Limited factory links delayed bulk transfers.
- A disconnected plant lost cloud inference or had to queue raw data.
- Cloud round trips were unsuitable for an immediate trip or machine-protection decision.
- Cloud storage and ingestion costs grew approximately in proportion to raw data volume.

After: edge-distributed predictive maintenance

Machine sensors  
→ PLC or ruggedized edge gateway  
→ local resampling, filtering, synchronization and FFT/feature extraction  
→ local anomaly classifier and alarm/interlock  
→ local time-series buffer  
→ selected features, anomalies, health scores, and short raw event windows sent to cloud  
→ cloud retraining, long-horizon prediction, fleet comparison and CMMS/ERP integration  
→ signed model/configuration updates returned to edge

This division is appropriate because anomaly detection and emergency response are latency-sensitive, while model training and comparison across many machines benefit from cloud scale.

AWS recommends local stream averaging, delta-based transmission, KPI calculation, adaptive sampling, local ML inference, and prioritizing alarms over historical data during constrained connectivity. It also recommends temporary edge persistence and automatic retry so data are not permanently lost in an outage (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/modern-industrial-data-technology-lens/midaperf05-bp01.html).

2.2 Quantified impact

Latency

A practical 2024 target is:

- 10–50 ms for a local anomaly decision or protective response
- Under 100 ms for a maintenance alert that is not part of a hard safety loop
- Seconds to minutes for cloud synchronization and long-horizon prognosis

A 2024 electronic-assembly predictive-maintenance study reported an average edge-processing latency of 12 ms. It also reported 94.3% failure-prediction success, an average 72-hour warning horizon, a 37% reduction in unplanned downtime, a 37% reduction in maintenance cost, and a 15% improvement in overall equipment effectiveness. These figures are experimental results rather than a universal manufacturing SLA and should not be assumed to transfer unchanged to every plant (https://journal.esrgroups.org/jes/article/view/9347).

A separate hybrid edge-cloud predictive-maintenance experiment published in late 2024 reported:

- 35% lower latency than cloud-only processing
- 60% lower bandwidth usage
- 28% lower energy consumption

Its edge tier used K-nearest-neighbor inference for immediate anomaly detection, while an LSTM in the cloud performed deeper time-series prediction (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39771653/).

If a cloud-only workflow takes 40 ms from sample to anomaly decision, a 35% reduction gives:

Edge-cloud latency  
= 40 ms × (1 − 0.35)  
= 26 ms

The cited study gives a relative reduction, not a universal absolute baseline; the resulting 26 ms is an illustration of the arithmetic, not its reported measured latency.

The 3M case provides a different latency measure: data movement and preparation that had taken weeks through manual export, SharePoint upload, VM startup, and database restoration was reduced to minutes with Azure SQL Edge and Azure IoT Edge. The model was cloud-trained but executed locally where manufacturing-line data resided. 3M also reported that the design kept operating when the plant was offline and was fault-tolerant under almost any network condition (https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/844496-3m-manufacturing-azure-sql-edge).

Bandwidth

AWS’s documented range for typical manufacturing edge preprocessing is 60–90% lower network bandwidth (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/modern-industrial-data-technology-lens/midaperf05-bp01.html). The 2024 hybrid predictive-maintenance experiment reported 60% lower bandwidth than cloud-only processing (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39771653/).

Illustrative volume calculation:

Assume raw machine telemetry is 100 GB/day.

At 60% reduction:

Cloud-bound volume  
= 100 GB × (1 − 0.60)  
= 40 GB/day

At 90% reduction:

Cloud-bound volume  
= 100 GB × (1 − 0.90)  
= 10 GB/day

Avoided WAN and cloud ingestion is therefore 60–90 GB/day per 100 GB/day of raw data.

The correct target depends on whether raw waveforms must be retained for forensic analysis. A responsible design keeps continuous features and health scores, but uploads short pre-event and post-event raw windows so aggressive compression does not erase evidence of emerging failure modes.

Availability and operational SLA

The strongest availability gain is architectural: anomaly detection and local alarms continue during internet or cloud outages. AWS explicitly identifies resilience and continued local operation as benefits of edge preprocessing, while 3M states its plant could continue operating while offline (AWS: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/modern-industrial-data-technology-lens/midaperf05-bp01.html; 3M: https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/844496-3m-manufacturing-azure-sql-edge).

Predictive-maintenance systems more often report reduced machine downtime than IT-service availability. The 2024 assembly-line study’s 37% reduction in unplanned downtime can be translated into availability only if a baseline is supplied.

For example, if a line previously suffered 87.6 hours of unplanned downtime per year:

Baseline unplanned-downtime fraction  
= 87.6 / 8,760  
= 1.0%

Baseline availability  
= 99.0%

After a 37% reduction:

New downtime  
= 87.6 × (1 − 0.37)  
= 55.188 hours/year

New availability  
= 1 − 55.188 / 8,760  
= 99.37%

Availability gain  
= 99.37% − 99.00%  
= 0.37 percentage points

This is a scenario calculation applying the reported 37% downtime reduction, not the study’s reported baseline availability.

2.3 Real-world example: 3M

At a US 3M plant, two production-line streams arrived at different times, and plant connectivity was limited. 3M deployed a custom module using Azure SQL Edge through Azure IoT Edge. The system correlated equipment sensor data with product data, executed a cloud-trained prediction algorithm locally, and synchronized results to the cloud. The algorithm could predict manufacturing-line problems hours before they appeared (https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/844496-3m-manufacturing-azure-sql-edge).

Operational and maintainability details included:

- One engineer reportedly took an average of six hours to add Azure SQL Edge to existing business processes.
- Data-processing steps that previously took weeks were reduced to minutes.
- A consistent SQL codebase reduced the need for custom code, monitoring, amendments, and support.
- The local edge tier addressed limited network capacity and supported offline operation.
- Cloud services remained available for visualization, Databricks, HDInsight, and Azure Machine Learning work after synchronization.

The case is strong evidence for architectural feasibility and maintainability, but it does not publish a millisecond inference result, byte-count reduction, final downtime percentage, or contractual SLA.

2.4 Trade-offs

Cost

Benefits:

- 60–90% lower WAN demand can reduce network, cloud-ingestion, processing, and storage costs.
- Early failure warning reduces emergency repairs and lost production.
- Existing cloud-trained models can be reused locally.
- A standard runtime and codebase can reduce integration effort, as demonstrated at 3M.

Costs:

- Industrial gateways require rugged hardware, local storage, power conditioning, and sometimes redundant servers.
- Accelerators may be required for acoustic or high-frequency vibration inference.
- Every plant becomes a small distributed-computing environment needing monitoring and lifecycle support.
- Savings can be offset by overprovisioned gateways or excessive retention of both raw and transformed data.

Security

Benefits:

- Sensitive raw production data can remain in the plant.
- Reduced data export lowers exposure on WAN paths.
- Local operation reduces dependence on internet availability.

Risks:

- The attack surface expands from a few cloud services to many gateways.
- Gateways bridge IT and OT networks and can become high-value pivot points.
- A compromised model or preprocessing rule can suppress legitimate alarms.
- Local physical access creates tampering and credential-extraction risks.

Required controls include secure boot, signed models and containers, hardware-rooted identity, certificate rotation, least-privilege protocol access, OT/IT segmentation, encrypted store-and-forward queues, and centralized vulnerability and configuration management.

Maintainability

Benefits:

- Containerized runtimes and a common cloud-edge codebase can simplify deployment.
- Remote fleet management can standardize model and configuration updates.
- Local databases allow existing engineering tools to continue working.

Risks:

- Models can drift differently by machine, product, tooling, and plant.
- Edge resource constraints can make cloud models too large to deploy unchanged.
- Hundreds of edge nodes create version skew and observability gaps.
- Filtering can remove information later needed to identify a new failure mode.

The preferred approach is to retain model and data-lineage records, use staged/canary deployment, monitor drift, preserve raw event windows, and provide a remotely enforceable rollback path.

3. Autonomous mobile robots

3.1 Before-and-after architecture

Before: cloud-centric or fragmented onboard architecture

AMR cameras/LiDAR/encoders  
→ onboard computer or Wi-Fi access point  
→ remote or regional server/cloud  
→ navigation, work assignment, or fleet-management service  
→ commands returned through Wi-Fi  
→ robot drive controller

Two problematic extremes existed:

- Fully onboard robots duplicated expensive compute and maps across every robot and had limited fleet-wide coordination.
- Remote-cloud robots depended on WAN and Wi-Fi handoffs for functions that could not tolerate unpredictable delay.

After: edge-distributed AMR architecture

Robot safety controller and minimum viable localization remain onboard  
↔ private 5G/Wi-Fi 6/industrial wireless  
↔ on-premises or carrier MEC edge

The local edge runs:

- Shared map and digital twin
- Multi-robot fleet orchestration
- Route and intersection conflict resolution
- Selected vision/LiDAR inference
- Task manager and warehouse/manufacturing integration
- Local session state and fast failover

The regional/public cloud runs:

- Historical analysis
- Simulation and digital-twin training
- Model training
- Multi-site optimization
- Software artifact repository and business integration

Safety-critical stopping must not rely solely on a remote server. Even when route planning or perception is offloaded, the robot needs onboard collision avoidance or a certified safe-stop mode if connectivity or edge compute fails.

3.2 Quantified impact

Latency

AMRs contain several latency classes:

- Motor and emergency-stop loops: local, typically not remotely closed
- Tightly coupled edge control: approximately 1–10 ms network objective
- Perception and route replanning: often tens of milliseconds
- Fleet scheduling and work assignment: tens to hundreds of milliseconds may be acceptable

A 5G-TSN mobile-robot prototype tested 100,000 packets in an industrial shop-floor environment and reported that latency was bounded to 1 ms at the 99.9th-percentile level. This was a pre-commercial URLLC prototype and therefore demonstrates technical feasibility rather than the performance of every production private-5G deployment (https://publications.rwth-aachen.de/record/848246/files/848246.pdf).

For strict offloaded motion control, a sensible requirement is therefore:

- Network one-way or bounded transport target: approximately 1 ms where supported
- End-to-end perception/decision/control target: under 10 ms for the most demanding edge-controlled functions
- Less critical fleet decisions: under approximately 50 ms

A 2024 field-robotics study of a 5G edge-server harvesting robot reported peak processing performance more than 18 times that of a standalone NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX configuration. The result concerns processing speed, not an 18-fold reduction in every end-to-end control loop, because camera capture, radio transmission, serialization, queueing, and actuator response remain in the path (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/rob.22384).

Illustratively, if a standalone perception task requires 180 ms and the compute portion receives an 18-fold speedup:

Accelerated compute time  
= 180 / 18  
= 10 ms

If network and serialization add 8 ms, end-to-end time is approximately:

10 + 8 = 18 ms

This example shows why compute speedup and total control latency must be measured separately.

Bandwidth

Edge computing changes where AMR bandwidth is consumed.

Robot-to-local-edge traffic may remain high or increase because cameras and LiDAR are offloaded. The major reduction is in traffic crossing the enterprise WAN or reaching the public cloud. If local edge services consume raw sensor streams and send only metadata, event clips, maps, and health summaries to the cloud, a target of 80–95% lower off-site traffic is reasonable.

Illustrative calculation:

Assume an AMR produces 100 Mb/s of aggregate camera and LiDAR traffic during operation. A local edge server consumes it and exports:

- 4 Mb/s of selected event video and diagnostics
- 1 Mb/s of maps, task status, health data, and summaries

WAN traffic after edge placement  
= 4 + 1  
= 5 Mb/s

WAN reduction  
= (100 − 5) / 100  
= 95%

For 20 robots:

Cloud-centric raw export  
= 20 × 100 Mb/s  
= 2,000 Mb/s, or 2 Gb/s

Edge-distributed export  
= 20 × 5 Mb/s  
= 100 Mb/s

Avoided WAN traffic  
= 1.9 Gb/s, or 95%

This is a design example, not a published measurement from Makino or Nokia. It also does not represent a reduction in the private radio access network between robots and the edge.

Availability and SLA

AMRs require both communication availability and safe degraded behavior.

A five-nines service objective means:

Allowed annual downtime  
= 8,760 hours × (1 − 0.99999)  
= 0.0876 hours  
= 5.256 minutes/year

A 99.9% service permits:

8,760 × 0.001  
= 8.76 hours/year

Thus moving from 99.9% to 99.999% reduces the nominal annual outage budget by:

8.76 hours − 0.0876 hours  
= 8.6724 hours

However, an AMR cannot equate network SLA with safety. The robot must stop safely or continue a restricted onboard function when connectivity is lost.

The cited 5G-TSN prototype’s 1 ms bound at the 99.9th percentile is a latency distribution, not a five-nines service-availability result. Conversely, “five nines” does not prove that every delivered packet meets a 1 ms deadline. Both timing and availability must be specified.

3.3 Real-world example: Makino, public 5G, and AWS Wavelength

Makino Milling Machine previously connected AMRs to a control server over Wi-Fi using protocols including HTTPS and WebRTC. As robots moved between access points, delayed handoffs caused communication instability. Makino adopted public 5G and moved relevant server functions closer through AWS Wavelength. The company reported improved communication stability and real-time operability and launched the system in less than five months (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/industries/makino-improves-performance-of-autonomous-mobile-robots-with-aws-wavelength-and-5g-network/).

Makino selected public 5G rather than constructing a private-5G environment, producing cost savings according to the AWS account. The example illustrates a middle option between on-premises private infrastructure and a distant regional cloud: carrier MEC can place compute near the radio network while allowing the enterprise to avoid owning the complete 5G stack.

The case does not disclose exact round-trip latency, handoff-interruption time, byte reduction, or a contractual availability figure. Its quantitative claims should therefore be limited to the under-five-month launch timeline; latency and SLA figures elsewhere in this report are engineering targets or results from separate prototypes.

3.4 Real-world example: Nokia headless AMR and on-premises orchestration

Nokia and Aalborg University demonstrated a “headless” AMR whose navigation was offloaded over 5G to an edge cloud. LiDAR and other sensory information were streamed to edge-based navigation and route planning, and drive-control information was returned to the robot. Benefits identified by Nokia included shared access to fleet sensor information, easier compute upgrades for AI, and reduced robot power drain (https://www.nokia.com/bell-labs/collaboration-opportunities/d-a-p/5g-and-edge-cloud-for-enabling-the-industrial-applications/).

Nokia separately described an on-premises edge orchestration prototype designed to coordinate hundreds or potentially thousands of robots from multiple vendors. Sensor data were processed on Nokia’s MX Industrial Edge, using local ML and AI to manage interactions while retaining data privacy and taking advantage of predictable local connectivity (https://www.nokia.com/blog/commanding-robots-from-the-edge/).

These cases demonstrate the architectural shift but do not publish enough data for independent before-and-after bandwidth or availability calculations.

3.5 Trade-offs

Cost

Benefits:

- GPU and map services can be pooled instead of duplicated on every robot.
- Lighter onboard computing can reduce robot power consumption, heat, and potentially capital cost.
- Centralized local orchestration can improve utilization and reduce traffic conflicts.
- Makino avoided the capital and operating cost of owning a private-5G system by using public 5G and carrier edge infrastructure.

Costs:

- Private 5G, MEC servers, GPU accelerators, redundant networking, spectrum, and integration can be expensive.
- Carrier MEC introduces recurring service charges and provider dependency.
- High-rate wireless uplinks must be engineered for aggregate camera/LiDAR loads.
- Edge failure can affect many robots simultaneously, increasing correlated-failure risk.

The cost choice is workload-dependent:

- Heavy onboard compute favors autonomous operation but duplicates hardware.
- On-premises edge pools resources and preserves data locality but has high initial cost.
- Carrier MEC reduces ownership burden but can increase recurring cost and lock-in.
- Regional public cloud is easiest to scale but least suitable for tightly bounded control.

Security

Benefits:

- Video and facility maps can remain on site.
- Private SIM-based cellular identity provides stronger device admission control than poorly managed shared Wi-Fi.
- A local edge allows segmentation from the public internet.

Risks:

- A compromised fleet orchestrator can disrupt many robots.
- Spoofed localization, task, or map data can cause unsafe movement.
- Robot-edge APIs and over-the-air update systems become critical trust paths.
- Multi-vendor orchestration expands software-supply-chain risk.
- Public 5G/MEC adds carrier and cloud-provider trust dependencies.

Controls should include mutual authentication, per-robot identity, encrypted transport, signed maps and commands, safety-controller separation, rate limits, anomaly detection, software bills of materials, signed updates, and independent onboard safe-stop logic.

Maintainability

Benefits:

- Updating one shared perception or planning service is easier than touching every robot.
- Shared maps and digital twins reduce inconsistent fleet state.
- Centralized telemetry improves diagnosis and capacity planning.

Risks:

- Edge and robot software versions must remain compatible.
- Network jitter or congestion can produce faults that resemble robot defects.
- A central update can create fleet-wide regression.
- Multiple robot vendors use different control and automation interfaces.
- Local-edge orchestration itself must be made highly available.

A maintainable design uses standardized interfaces, staged rollout, simulation before deployment, dual edge instances, capacity headroom, per-robot rollback, and clear partitioning between uncertified optimization software and certified safety functions.

4. Energy distribution

4.1 Before-and-after architecture

Before: centralized SCADA/cloud-oriented architecture

Meters, intelligent electronic devices, PMUs, power-quality monitors, DER controllers, and substation sensors  
→ field network  
→ control center or public-cloud platform  
→ centralized state estimation, anomaly detection, and optimization  
→ command returned to feeder, inverter, switch, or substation

This remains suitable for planning, billing, broad supervisory control, and nonurgent asset analysis. It is unsuitable as the sole architecture for protection or local stability because:

- Backhaul failure can isolate a substation or feeder.
- A distant cloud cannot guarantee millisecond deadlines.
- High-frequency waveform and video data can saturate constrained field links.
- Distributed energy resources create rapid local changes that may require autonomous response.

After: hierarchical grid-edge architecture

IEDs, relays, meters, PMUs, cameras, and DERs  
→ substation/feeder/transformer edge gateway  
→ local protection, event detection, aggregation, state estimation, DER coordination, and buffering  
→ selected events, features, health scores and summaries sent to regional or cloud platform  
→ ADMS, cross-region optimization, model training, planning and long-term records  
→ policies and models distributed back to grid-edge systems

For the fastest protection path, processing may reside directly in the relay or substation LAN rather than in a general-purpose edge server. “Edge” in a grid therefore includes intelligent relays and substation automation, not merely a small cloud appliance.

A 2024 distribution-network study describes a device-edge-cloud system in which high-frequency acquisition devices send data over 5G to edge servers for low-delay processing; edge servers split selected workloads to a cloud server over optical fiber to manage growth and exploit cloud capacity. The optimization jointly selects transmission power, edge server, and edge-cloud data-splitting ratio (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/energy-research/articles/10.3389/fenrg.2024.1440487/full).

4.2 Quantified impact

Latency

Power distribution contains much stricter deadlines than ordinary IoT monitoring.

IEC 61850-5 identifies Type 1A fast messages for high-speed automation, protection, and interlocking with a 3 ms transmission requirement. Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories’ discussion of the standard states that engineered Ethernet systems routinely meet this requirement in normal operation and that complete transfer time must be verified during site acceptance using the physical devices and network (https://selinc.com/api/download/104190/?lang=en).

The same source reports:

- Modern protection Ethernet switches normally deliver packets in well under 1 ms.
- A calculated 20-switch path for a 100-byte message, including two 100 Mb/s links and nineteen 1 Gb/s links, had a best-case network latency of approximately 0.11 ms.
- Typical measured total signal-application time in its test arrangement was under 14 ms, including device inputs, processing, messaging, and output action.
- The test design sought 3 ms transmission 99.9999% of the time and no more than 18 ms for the remainder.
- Network reconfiguration around path failure had to remain within the 18 ms maximum; otherwise redundant networks and protocols were required.

The 0.11 ms calculation can be restated from the source:

- Two 100 Mb/s links
- Nineteen 1 Gb/s links
- Twenty switches, each adding approximately 4 microseconds
- 112 effective bytes per frame after overhead

Total  
≈ 17,920 ns + 17,024 ns + 80,000 ns  
= 114,944 ns  
≈ 0.115 ms

This is a best-case packet-path calculation, not end-to-end relay action.

Accordingly, useful 2024 design targets are:

- Protection/interlocking message: no more than 3 ms
- Local fault classification and control: single-digit to low tens of milliseconds, depending on application
- Feeder optimization and DER coordination: tens of milliseconds to seconds
- Asset-health analytics: seconds to minutes
- Planning and long-term optimization: cloud timescales

Bandwidth

Grid-edge systems reduce WAN traffic by publishing state changes, events, features, and summaries instead of continuous raw waveform streams.

Illustrative high-frequency example:

Suppose one device produces a 10 kHz measurement stream and the edge exports a 10 Hz summary during normal operation.

Reduction based only on sample count:

Reduction  
= 1 − 10 / 10,000  
= 1 − 0.001  
= 0.999  
= 99.9%

If event logic also uploads raw fault windows, the annual reduction will be somewhat less than 99.9%, depending on event frequency and window duration.

A less aggressive scheme that forwards one out of every ten equivalent records reduces data by:

1 − 1/10 = 90%

A reasonable target range is therefore:

- Approximately 90% for conservative filtering with substantial diagnostic export
- 99% or more for normal-state summaries plus event-triggered waveform upload
- Approximately 99.9% in a 10 kHz-to-10 Hz normal-state summarization example

These are architectural calculations, not measured byte reductions from the Iberdrola case.

IEC 61850 GOOSE itself illustrates event-driven communication. The SEL source explains that a GOOSE message is published immediately after a state change and retransmitted in a short burst, followed by lower-frequency heartbeat messages. It is not normally published continuously at a high fixed rate because doing so would consume excessive shared Ethernet bandwidth (https://selinc.com/api/download/104190/?lang=en).

That same source shows why edge traffic engineering matters: messages from only three IEDs could aggregate to more than 10 Mb/s during a change of state and saturate a 10 Mb/s port. Prioritization, VLANs, multicast filtering, faster perimeter links, and high-capacity backbones are therefore necessary even when average traffic appears low.

Availability and SLA

Protection and direct-control availability requirements are much stricter than ordinary cloud IoT SLAs.

The SEL engineering paper assumes:

- 99.99% successful timely receipt for control-blocking schemes
- 99.999999% for direct-control schemes under IEC 60834-1 assumptions
- A test objective of meeting the 3 ms transmission time 99.9999% of the time, with no delay above 18 ms for the remainder

Source: https://selinc.com/api/download/104190/?lang=en.

Annual failure-budget equivalents illustrate the scale:

For 99.99% availability:

8,760 × (1 − 0.9999)  
= 0.876 hours  
= 52.56 minutes/year

For 99.9999%:

8,760 × 0.000001  
= 0.00876 hours  
= 31.536 seconds/year

For 99.999999%:

8,760 × 0.00000001  
= 0.0000876 hours  
= 0.31536 seconds/year

These annualized calculations are intuitive comparisons; message-delivery dependability is not necessarily contracted or measured as continuous service uptime. A system may be available but violate a deadline, so grid protection must monitor both packet delivery and bounded latency.

The availability improvement from edge distribution comes from:

- Local operation when backhaul or public cloud fails
- Redundant Ethernet paths
- Rapid failover or parallel redundancy
- Local buffering and later synchronization
- Eliminating the WAN from the critical protection loop

The edge does not make failures disappear. It changes a cloud or WAN outage from a potential loss of local control into a temporary loss of central visibility, provided that the local edge has sufficient autonomy and redundancy.

4.3 Real-world example: Iberdrola i-DE SmartPoint

In 2024, AWS described SmartPoint, developed by Iberdrola’s i-DE distribution business in Spain and Portugal. i-DE manages millions of heterogeneous operational assets, including poles, transformation centers, substations, and lines. The system connects legacy and modern IoT sensors and uses video-derived insights to detect anomalies. Operators receive substation event alerts and correlate data so incidents can be assigned to field personnel (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/industries/iberdrola-reduces-incidents-at-power-distribution-facilities-using-aws-iot-and-edge-services/).

The architecture used AWS IoT and edge services alongside serverless cloud components. The account emphasizes:

- Compatibility with legacy and modern sensors
- Local/edge processing for video and IoT data
- Event and anomaly reporting rather than indiscriminate raw-data handling
- Serverless cloud services to reduce infrastructure-management burden and scale during critical periods
- Lower platform operational load and faster time to market

The source reports that the platform reduced incidents but does not provide a precise latency, data-reduction percentage, or before-and-after availability figure. It should therefore be treated as a real deployment example supporting the architecture and operational model, not as the source of the numerical targets above.

4.4 2024 research example: Guangdong distribution cloud-edge collaboration

A 2024 Frontiers in Energy Research paper from Guangdong Power Grid researchers addresses high-frequency data acquisition in low-voltage distribution systems with photovoltaic generation, storage, and controllable loads. Its architecture contains:

- Device layer: acquisition systems on distributed electrical equipment
- Edge layer: multiple edge servers reached over 5G
- Cloud layer: a cloud server reached from the edge over optical fiber

The edge handles latency-sensitive work; the cloud relieves edge processing pressure and supplies greater computing capacity. The proposed algorithm dynamically optimizes device transmission power, edge-server selection, and edge-cloud data split while considering both delay and device energy consumption. Simulations outperformed comparison algorithms on total processing delay and energy use, although the fetched publication text does not expose a simple universal percentage that can responsibly be quoted here (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/energy-research/articles/10.3389/fenrg.2024.1440487/full).

This example is useful because it shows that edge placement is not binary. Grid data can be split dynamically according to channel quality, acquisition frequency, edge load, and cloud capacity.

4.5 Trade-offs

Cost

Benefits:

- Avoiding continuous waveform or video backhaul reduces telecom and cloud-storage cost.
- Local fault identification can reduce outage duration and field inspection effort.
- Virtualized functions can consolidate multiple applications on common substation hardware.
- Existing cloud systems remain useful for system-wide optimization and long-term records.

Costs:

- Utilities need hardened, long-lived computers that meet temperature, electromagnetic, power, and lifecycle requirements.
- Redundant networks, precision timing, backup power, and parallel edge nodes add significant capital cost.
- Integration with legacy relays, SCADA, and proprietary protocols is difficult.
- Utility assets may remain in service much longer than ordinary IT hardware or software support cycles.

Security

Benefits:

- Sensitive waveform, customer, facility, and video data can remain local.
- Protection can continue if external connections are intentionally isolated.
- Segmentation limits dependence on public-cloud access.

Risks:

- Thousands of substations, feeders, and transformer sites create a large physical and cyber attack surface.
- A compromised edge controller could manipulate DERs, suppress alarms, or issue switching commands.
- Virtualizing several grid functions on one platform can turn it into a common-mode failure point.
- Remote management creates a path from enterprise or cloud systems into critical OT.
- False data injection and time-synchronization attacks can invalidate otherwise correct algorithms.

Required measures include hardware roots of trust, signed firmware and workloads, strict separation of protection from analytics, authenticated time synchronization, allow-listed protocols, one-way or tightly controlled data flows where appropriate, redundant communications, continuous integrity monitoring, and physical tamper controls.

Maintainability

Benefits:

- Centralized software distribution can update analytics across many substations.
- Standard edge platforms can replace isolated appliances.
- Local buffering improves diagnostics after communication outages.

Risks:

- Utility equipment has multi-decade lifecycles, while containers, operating systems, and AI frameworks change rapidly.
- A single model may not generalize across feeder topology, DER mix, weather, or equipment type.
- Remote sites are expensive to visit if an update fails.
- Deterministic protection requires extensive factory and site acceptance testing.

IEC 61850 engineering guidance, as summarized by SEL, requires complete transfer-time testing with physical devices and networks and recommends verification during design, factory acceptance, site acceptance, and operation (https://selinc.com/api/download/104190/?lang=en). This is more demanding than ordinary cloud DevOps and is a major maintainability cost of grid-edge computing.

5. Comparative implications

5.1 Latency transformation

Cloud-centric latency is approximately:

Device acquisition  
+ local network  
+ WAN/carrier path  
+ cloud queue  
+ cloud computation  
+ return path  
+ actuator processing

Edge-distributed latency removes the regional WAN and cloud queue from the immediate loop:

Device acquisition  
+ local/private network  
+ edge computation  
+ local return path  
+ actuator processing

The resulting target depends on physical consequence:

- Predictive-maintenance alarm: approximately 10–100 ms
- AMR edge control: approximately 1–10 ms network objective and tens of milliseconds for many perception tasks
- Grid protection message: no more than 3 ms

The edge is most transformative where the required deadline is shorter than normal WAN variability, not merely where average cloud latency is inconvenient.

5.2 Bandwidth transformation

Cloud-centric systems send data first and decide its value later. Edge-distributed systems decide value near the source.

Representative reduction mechanisms include:

- Manufacturing: FFT and condition features instead of continuous raw vibration
- AMRs: detections, maps, and event clips instead of public-cloud export of every camera/LiDAR frame
- Distribution grids: state changes, phasors, event windows, and health scores instead of all waveform samples

Quantitatively:

- Manufacturing: documented typical reduction of 60–90%
- AMR off-site WAN: design target of 80–95%, although local wireless traffic may remain high
- Distribution: design target of 90–99.9%, depending on sample summarization and event retention

The percentage should always specify the measurement boundary. An AMR project may reduce public-cloud traffic 95% while increasing private-5G uplink traffic because perception is being offloaded from the robot.

5.3 Availability transformation

Cloud-centric availability is multiplicative across dependencies:

Application availability  
≈ device × access network × WAN × cloud service × return path

Edge distribution removes WAN and public cloud from local critical operation, but adds local edge hardware and software. The new dependency chain is:

Local operation  
≈ device × local network × edge service

Central visibility and fleet analytics may still depend on WAN and cloud, but their failure no longer has to halt the local process.

The architecture improves resilience only if:

- The edge is redundant where required.
- Devices fail safely.
- State is buffered and reconciled after reconnection.
- Updates do not create correlated fleet-wide failures.
- Local operation has been tested during actual disconnection, not merely assumed.

6. Overall cost, security, and maintainability balance

Cost conclusion

Edge computing trades variable cloud and network costs for distributed capital and operating expense.

It is economically strongest when:

- Raw data rates are high.
- Connectivity is constrained or costly.
- Downtime has high economic consequences.
- Many devices can share one site-edge platform.
- Local decisions prevent damage or lost production.

It is weaker when:

- Sensors produce only small, infrequent messages.
- Deadlines are measured in seconds or minutes.
- Sites lack personnel or systems to maintain distributed infrastructure.
- Cloud connectivity is already highly reliable and inexpensive.

Security conclusion

Edge computing can improve privacy and reduce data movement, but it does not automatically improve security. It relocates risk:

- Less raw data is exposed in transit.
- More privileged compute nodes exist in physically accessible locations.
- Edge gateways often connect previously separated OT and IT environments.
- Centralized orchestration can produce larger correlated consequences if compromised.

Security must therefore be designed as a fleet lifecycle: identity, secure boot, signed workloads, encrypted communication and storage, segmentation, attestation, inventory, patching, rollback, and physical protection.

Maintainability conclusion

The edge’s largest hidden cost is fleet operations. A proof of concept with one gateway is not representative of production across hundreds of machines, robots, or substations.

The maintainable 2024 pattern is:

- Common cloud-edge development and packaging
- Declarative configuration
- Remote health and version inventory
- Canary rollout and automatic rollback
- Local fallback during failed updates
- Data/model lineage
- Capacity and thermal monitoring
- Long-term compatibility with industrial protocols

The 3M case demonstrates how a consistent SQL codebase can reduce custom integration and support effort (https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/844496-3m-manufacturing-azure-sql-edge). ABB similarly described using AKS Edge Essentials to maintain one application version across Windows, Linux, edge, and cloud, reducing development, deployment, and administration burdens as the edge estate expanded (https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/1705722215075384871-abb-aks-edge-essentials-discrete-manufacturing-switzerland-en).

7. Final assessment

As of 2024, edge computing was transforming industrial IoT from a telemetry pipeline into a distributed control-and-intelligence system.

In predictive maintenance, the important shift is from uploading all condition data for remote interpretation to extracting features, detecting anomalies, buffering evidence, and issuing immediate alerts at the plant. Documented bandwidth reductions are commonly 60–90%, while local decision targets are approximately 10–50 ms. The availability gain is continued monitoring and alarming during WAN failure and lower machine downtime.

For autonomous mobile robots, the edge creates a shared local brain for fleet coordination, perception, maps, and digital twins while preserving onboard safety. Approximately 1–10 ms network targets support tightly coupled functions, and local processing can avoid 80–95% of off-site raw sensor traffic. The main caveat is that robot-to-edge traffic remains substantial and no communications SLA can replace onboard safe-stop logic.

For electricity distribution, edge computing is becoming part of the protection and resilience architecture. Fast IEC 61850 messaging targets no more than 3 ms, engineered schemes can target 99.9999% timely delivery, and event-based filtering can avoid 90–99.9% of normal raw-data export. The trade-off is the need to operate secure, deterministic, redundant computing infrastructure across geographically dispersed and long-lived utility assets.

The enduring architecture is therefore hybrid: immediate, safety-relevant, bandwidth-intensive and outage-sensitive functions execute locally; compute-intensive training, historical analysis, cross-site learning, and enterprise coordination remain in the cloud.

The race was **Bubba Gump Shrimp Company’s “Run Forrest Run 5K”**—also advertised as the **Bubba Gump Shrimp Company’s 7th Annual Run Forrest Run 5K**.

A 2008 event listing places the race at **California’s Great America in Santa Clara** and identifies it as a 5K fun run presented by Bubba Gump Shrimp Company: https://www.sanjose.com/run-forrest-run-5k-e330431.
