# 7. PE investment thesis

## Investment case

FutureMeds is an attractive PE-quality asset if diligence validates sustained cash conversion and disciplined debt capacity. The thesis rests on five pillars:

1. **Rapid scale with evidence of profitability.** Revenue grew 116% in FY2023 and 73% in FY2024, while operating margin held around 12.4%–12.5%. The business crossed from a FY2022 operating loss to £3.347m FY2024 operating profit. [Pomanda](https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd); [The Accounts](https://theaccounts.uk/company/12521988/futuremeds-ltd/)

2. **Defensible strategic position in a fragmented clinical-site market.** A wholly owned 29-site European network, 220+ investigator base, 1,400+ provider partnerships, DCT reach in 18 countries and 70m+ prospective-patient-access claim create a differentiated platform versus single-site operators and pure-play recruitment vendors. [FutureMeds](https://www.futuremeds.com/); [SCRS page](https://www.futuremeds.com/meet-futuremeds); [FutureMeds DCT page](https://www.futuremeds.com/dct-overview)

3. **High-value customer proposition.** Faster enrolment, stronger retention, hybrid access and reliable data directly address significant sponsor/CRO pain points—late enrolment and site underperformance—where operational performance can support pricing power and repeat business. [FutureMeds](https://www.futuremeds.com/); [FutureMeds purpose page](https://www.futuremeds.com/about-us/our-purpose)

4. **Proven buy-and-build platform.** The acquisitions of emovis and CPS added DCT/homecare capability and UK site presence. Phoenix can repeat this playbook in fragmented local European site markets, provided integration and compliance processes scale. [FutureMeds emovis announcement](https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-acquires-emovis-marking-a-new-era-in-european-dct-solutions); [FutureMeds CPS announcement](https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-acquires-the-glasgow-based-renowned-clinical-research-site-cps-research)

5. **External proof of sponsor appeal.** HGL’s reported 10x exit multiple and Phoenix’s decision to become a strategic shareholder after a multi-year relationship indicate meaningful investor confidence. This is qualitative validation, not a substitute for valuation underwriting. [HGL exit announcement](https://hglcapital.co.uk/2025/10/06/hgl-private-capital-announces-successful-exit-from-futuremeds/); [Fairmount](https://fairmountpress.wordpress.com/2025/07/29/futuremeds/)

## Principal value-creation levers

### 1. Drive organic growth and site utilisation
Increase trial volume, enrolled patients and studies per site by using central business development, cross-selling DCT services, systematic sponsor key-account management and better matching of studies to investigator/site capabilities. The current network’s cumulative 2,320+ studies and 32,000+ patients demonstrates operational experience, but public data do not reveal current utilisation or capacity. [FutureMeds](https://www.futuremeds.com/)

### 2. Improve gross margin and standardise operations
FY2024 gross margin was 42.4%, down from 44.3% in FY2023. Potential levers include central procurement, standardised site SOPs, shared technology, nursing-provider purchasing, harmonised regulatory/quality processes and improved staffing utilisation. Any initiative must preserve patient experience and GCP-quality outcomes. [Pomanda](https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd)

### 3. Expand DCT and hybrid penetration
emovis brought a mature homecare/DCT platform, and FutureMeds claims 330+ DCT trials across 18 countries. Increasing DCT attach rates to traditional site studies can increase share of trial spend per sponsor relationship and potentially smooth capacity constraints. [FutureMeds DCT overview](https://www.futuremeds.com/dct-overview); [FutureMeds emovis announcement](https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-acquires-emovis-marking-a-new-era-in-european-dct-solutions)

### 4. Continue selective buy-and-build
Target local dedicated research sites, patient-recruitment specialists and homecare providers in countries where FutureMeds can leverage central sales, quality systems and sponsor access. HGL’s funding history explicitly supported this strategy, and two acquisitions in 2023 establish a precedent. [HGL portfolio](https://hglcapital.co.uk/portfolio/futuremeds/); [FutureMeds CPS announcement](https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-acquires-the-glasgow-based-renowned-clinical-research-site-cps-research)

### 5. Increase revenue quality and cash conversion
The highest-value operational lever may be reducing debtors and improving contract terms. Public data indicate FY2024 debtors of £4.606m, equivalent to approximately 17.1% of annual revenue. This is only a point-in-time measure, not DSO, but warrants focus given rapid growth and financing costs. [Pomanda](https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd)

### 6. Build data and commercial moat
Use patient-engagement data, site-performance benchmarking, protocol-feasibility services and repeat sponsor/CRO relationships to improve win rates and pricing. This lever is plausible given the network model but requires validation that the company owns or can lawfully use the relevant data and is compliant with GDPR, clinical-research ethics and country-level regulations.

## Valuation considerations

### Appropriate valuation framework
Because valuation was not disclosed, valuation should be based on a normalised EBITDA framework, triangulated with revenue multiples and strategic value of the network/DCT platform.

A buyer should first establish:
1. audited / quality-of-earnings EBITDA;
2. acquisition and integration adjustments;
3. maintenance versus growth capex;
4. working-capital normalisation;
5. debt-like items, earn-outs, leases, tax liabilities and pension exposure;
6. sponsor/CRO concentration and backlog;
7. country/site profitability and utilisation;
8. regulatory-compliance record and audit history.

### Illustrative—not market-derived—valuation sensitivity
Using the calculated FY2024 **indicative EBITDA proxy of £5.159m**, illustrative enterprise values would be:

| Illustrative EV / EBITDA multiple | Indicative EV |
|---:|---:|
| 8.0x | £41.3m |
| 10.0x | £51.6m |
| 12.0x | £61.9m |
| 14.0x | £72.2m |

Calculation: £5.159m × selected multiple.

These are mathematical scenarios only, **not valuation estimates or evidence of comparable-market trading multiples**. They exclude net debt, contingent consideration and transaction costs. A premium multiple would require proof of repeatable organic growth, contracted/repeat revenue, low concentration, clean compliance history, attractive cash conversion and scalable DCT/IP differentiation. A discount would be justified by sponsor concentration, debt, inconsistent organic growth, site underutilisation, country/regulatory complexity or dependence on management/founders.

### Revenue-based perspective
On FY2024 revenue of £26.967m:
* 1.5x revenue = £40.5m EV;
* 2.0x revenue = £53.9m EV;
* 2.5x revenue = £67.4m EV.

Again, these are sensitivity calculations, not observed transaction multiples. Revenue multiples are less appropriate than EBITDA/cash-flow multiples where gross margin, working capital, funding needs and patient-enrolment risk vary materially among clinical-services providers.

## Likely exit routes and timeline

### Likely exit routes
1. **Secondary sale to a larger PE sponsor.** Most likely if Phoenix can demonstrate several years of organic growth, integration success, higher EBITDA, deleveraging and stronger contracted/repeat sponsor revenue.
2. **Strategic sale to a global CRO, clinical-services platform, patient-recruitment business, site-network consolidator, laboratory/technology-enabled clinical-services group or pharma-services provider.** Strategic buyers may value geographic site access, investigator relationships, patient-engagement capability and DCT/homecare infrastructure.
3. **Merger with another European or global site-management platform.** This could create country density and sponsor-scale advantages.
4. **IPO:** possible only after substantially larger scale, more predictable earnings and a proven multi-country governance model; materially less likely than a strategic or secondary PE exit.

### Likely timeline
A typical Phoenix-era hold would be **approximately four to six years from the July 2025 investment**, suggesting a likely exit window of **2029–2031**. This is an inference based on conventional PE holding periods, not a disclosed Phoenix plan. Earlier exit could occur if strategic demand for European site-network assets is strong and the company delivers accelerated consolidation; later exit could result from debt deleveraging requirements, integration complexity or a weak M&A market.

---

# 8. Top five risks

## 1. Leverage, interest burden and refinancing risk
FY2024 interest payable of £1.583m consumed nearly half of operating profit, leaving EBIT/interest coverage of only c. 2.1x. Four Ares Management security charges were registered in November 2025, while the prior Barclays charge was satisfied. The amounts and terms are undisclosed. Higher rates, weak cash conversion, covenant pressure or an acquisition-financing burden could constrain growth and equity value. [Pomanda](https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd); [Companies House charges](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/12521988/charges)

## 2. Customer/programme concentration and clinical-development cyclicality
FutureMeds does not disclose customer concentration, backlog or renewal/retention. Revenue can be exposed to cancellations, sponsor budget cuts, drug-programme failures, protocol amendments, CRO vendor rationalisation and enrolment delays. The broad network is a possible mitigant, but not proof of diversified revenue. [Fairmount](https://fairmountpress.wordpress.com/2025/07/29/futuremeds/); [FutureMeds](https://www.futuremeds.com/)

## 3. Acquisition integration and execution risk
Growth has included the acquisitions of emovis and CPS. Further M&A could create systems, culture, clinical-quality, data-privacy, local-regulatory and investigator-retention risks. Historic headline growth cannot be assumed to be fully organic. [FutureMeds emovis announcement](https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-acquires-emovis-marking-a-new-era-in-european-dct-solutions); [FutureMeds CPS announcement](https://www.futuremeds.com/post/futuremeds-acquires-the-glasgow-based-renowned-clinical-research-site-cps-research)

## 4. Regulatory, quality, patient-safety and data-privacy risk
Clinical research is highly regulated. Deficiencies in GCP compliance, investigator oversight, informed consent, pharmacovigilance, home-visit protocols, data integrity, GDPR or country-specific trial rules could result in audit findings, exclusion from sponsor panels, reputational damage, delays or liability. DCT expansion increases the number of operational interfaces that must be consistently controlled. The company emphasises quality systems and PI oversight, but public evidence does not provide audit-finding history, litigation record or compliance KPIs. [SCRS page](https://www.futuremeds.com/meet-futuremeds); [FutureMeds DCT page](https://www.futuremeds.com/dct-overview)

## 5. Working-capital and labour-capacity risk
The company has scaled headcount sharply, with 397 FY2024 average employees and a 287-to-397 year-on-year increase reported in public coverage. Debtors of £4.606m in FY2024 indicate potentially meaningful collection and funding needs. Clinical research delivery relies on scarce investigators, nurses and experienced site staff; wage inflation, turnover or inability to staff studies could pressure margins and service quality. [The Accounts](https://theaccounts.uk/company/12521988/futuremeds-ltd/); [Business Mondays](https://businessmondays.co.uk/private-equity-specialist-hgl-private-capital-announces-successful-exit-from-futuremeds/); [Pomanda](https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd)

---

# 9. Bottom-line conclusion

FutureMeds is a credible, attractive outsourced-pharma-services platform: it has grown revenue from £7.2m in FY2022 to £27.0m in FY2024, achieved a 42.4% gross margin and £3.35m operating profit, built a 29-site/7-country European footprint, and established DCT reach across 18 countries. The operational model has strategic value because sponsors and CROs need reliable patient access, site performance and hybrid trial execution. The July 2025 Phoenix investment and HGL’s reported 10x exit outcome reinforce the asset’s market attractiveness. [Pomanda](https://pomanda.com/company/12521988/Futuremeds-Ltd); [FutureMeds](https://www.futuremeds.com/); [HGL exit announcement](https://hglcapital.co.uk/2025/10/06/hgl-private-capital-announces-successful-exit-from-futuremeds/)

For a private-equity investor, the central underwriting question is not whether FutureMeds can grow—it has already done so—but whether its operating-profit growth translates consistently into free cash flow after working capital, capex, acquisition integration and debt service. The c. £1.58m FY2024 interest cost, 2.1x EBIT interest coverage and new Ares security package make capital-structure diligence essential. Before assigning a premium valuation, an investor should obtain a quality-of-earnings review, full debt documents, customer- and study-level concentration analysis, backlog and repeat-business data, DSO/cash-conversion reporting, site-level profitability and utilisation, compliance/audit history, and a detailed organic-versus-acquired growth bridge.

final.content:
# Career transition into AI safety research from backend engineering: realistic routes and Europe–US comparison

## Bottom line

A 28-year-old backend engineer in Berlin has several credible routes into AI safety research without immediately doing a PhD. The highest-probability route is usually **research engineering for evaluations, AI control, red-teaming, safety infrastructure, or interpretability tooling**, rather than attempting to enter directly as a theory-focused research scientist.

Your current backend experience is directly useful in a field that needs people who can build reliable experiment platforms, secure model-access systems, data pipelines, evaluation harnesses, observability, distributed compute tooling, and reproducible infrastructure. That is not peripheral work: frontier safety research increasingly depends on software systems capable of running structured evaluations against powerful models.

A practical strategy is:

1. retain your Berlin job initially;
2. spend 6–12 months becoming demonstrably competent in ML experimentation and AI-safety evaluation;
3. produce public technical artifacts;
4. enter through a structured fellowship, independent-research programme, safety-oriented research-engineering role, or an adjacent ML/security role;
5. decide later whether a funded MSc/PhD is necessary for the research questions you want to pursue.

Europe—especially Berlin, London, and parts of Germany—is a realistic place to begin. The US has a denser concentration of frontier labs, funding, compute, and influential independent evaluation organizations, but relocation creates a materially higher immigration burden and a more competitive, often more commercially intertwined research environment.

---

# 1. What “AI safety research” can mean for a backend engineer

“AI safety” is not one occupation. It covers at least four overlapping tracks, with very different entry requirements.

| Track | Typical work | Fit from backend development | Need for PhD |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Empirical technical safety | Model evaluations, red-teaming, robustness, scalable oversight, control, interpretability experiments | High after ML upskilling | Usually no for research engineering; sometimes for scientist roles |
| Safety/security engineering | Evaluation platforms, sandboxing, secure access, monitoring, experiment infrastructure, model-hosting systems | Very high | No |
| AI governance / technical policy | Evaluation standards, AI Act compliance, frontier-risk policy, institutional design | Moderate; high if you can translate technical systems into policy evidence | No, though advanced degree can help |
| Theory / agent foundations | Formal alignment, decision theory, mathematical foundations, proofs | Low-to-moderate unless you already enjoy serious mathematics/theory | Often helpful, though not universally mandatory |

The most natural initial specialization is **empirical safety plus research infrastructure**. MATS describes its empirical track as hands-on ML research in “AI control, interpretability, scalable oversight, evaluations, red-teaming, and robustness,” and explicitly says the primary tool is ML engineering: designing and running experiments on language models, working in Python, operating moderate-scale model infrastructure, and selecting useful experiments. It also notes that educational background and seniority are weighted relatively lightly compared with demonstrated ability and mission fit.  
Source: [MATS Empirical Track](https://www.matsprogram.org/tracks/empirical)

This route is especially suitable if your backend experience includes some combination of:

- production Python, Go, Java, Rust, TypeScript, or C++;
- distributed systems and queues;
- databases, logging, observability, and incident response;
- cloud infrastructure, CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes, IaC;
- security engineering, authentication/authorization, audit trails, secrets management;
- performance profiling, reliability, APIs, test frameworks, or developer tooling;
- data pipelines and experiment tracking.

Those capabilities map well to safety work that must be rigorous, repeatable, secure, and scalable.

---

# 2. The most realistic pathways

## Pathway A: Move into AI-safety research engineering or evaluation engineering

### Why it is the strongest first option

This is the most direct way to convert backend skills into safety impact without pretending that a few online courses make someone a senior ML researcher.

Frontier organizations need systems that can:

- run thousands of model-evaluation tasks;
- isolate tool-using agents safely;
- collect, normalize, and analyze experiment traces;
- run red-team exercises and adversarial tests;
- provide researchers secure access to sensitive models and data;
- monitor research workloads;
- manage compute, model versions, datasets, permissions, and reproducibility;
- turn prototype research code into reliable internal systems.

The UK AI Security Institute (AISI) illustrates this bridge clearly. Its Core Technology Team builds tools and infrastructure for research work, including Inspect plugins, systems for evaluations at scale, hosting frontier open-weight models for evaluations, researcher platforms, and tooling for human studies. Its example responsibilities include scaling proxy infrastructure for secure model access, supporting custom project infrastructure, hosting models, implementing open-source plugins, and ensuring that an evaluation testing exercise has robust and secure infrastructure and monitoring.  
Source: [UK AISI Core Technology Team expression of interest](https://job-boards.eu.greenhouse.io/aisi/jobs/5000476101)

AISI is especially relevant because it recruits “researchers, engineers, policy analysts and operators from a wide range of backgrounds,” and its technical hiring process includes a CV and statement, one or two assessments such as technical interviews or take-home coding tests, and two to four interviews.  
Source: [UK AISI careers](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/careers)

Anthropic provides another concrete example. Its safeguards-evaluation engineering work combines applied ML research and production engineering: design experiments; improve evaluation quality; build representative datasets; simulate realistic user behavior; validate grader accuracy; study safety behavior across multi-turn conversations, tools, long contexts, and diverse users; and ship evaluation methods into pipelines that gate training and launch decisions.  
Source: [Anthropic, Staff+ Software Engineer—Safeguards Evals](https://job-boards.greenhouse.io/anthropic/jobs/5251671008)

Its interpretability work also requires infrastructure familiar to experienced backend engineers: stable, performant training jobs across thousands of chips; customized inference systems; activation editing; model-serving systems; performance optimization; and production-grade developer infrastructure.  
Source: [Anthropic, Research Engineer—Interpretability](https://job-boards.greenhouse.io/anthropic/jobs/4980430008)

### What you must add

You do not need to become a world-class ML theorist before applying, but you do need evidence that you can operate in an ML research setting:

1. **Python fluency for ML**, especially PyTorch.
2. **Deep-learning fundamentals**: transformers, attention, optimization, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, evaluation methodology.
3. **Experimental discipline**: baselines, ablations, dataset contamination concerns, validity/reliability, uncertainty, reproducibility.
4. **Practical LLM systems work**: APIs, open-weight models, inference, fine-tuning, eval harnesses, tool-using agents.
5. **Safety-specific literacy**: misuse evaluations, cyber/CBRN evaluations, deception or scheming, model control, interpretability, monitoring, adversarial testing.

### Portfolio projects that signal competence

Avoid generic “chatbot” projects. Build work that looks like safety research infrastructure or evaluation science.

Good projects include:

- **An evaluation harness for tool-using coding agents**: sandbox tasks, define success metrics, record trajectories, compare models and prompting strategies, and document failure modes.
- **A reproducible red-team platform**: task generation, structured attack taxonomies, trace capture, scoring, human-review interface, and dashboards.
- **An LLM-agent containment sandbox**: restricted filesystem/network access, policy enforcement, logging, and attack-surface analysis.
- **A model-behavior regression suite**: test whether safety behavior changes across prompts, languages, tool availability, long contexts, or model versions.
- **An open-source Inspect plugin or related evaluation tooling**: relevant because AISI and METR use Inspect-related infrastructure. AISI explicitly references Inspect plugins, while METR runs an open-source platform for AI-agent evaluations at scale built on Inspect AI.  
  Sources: [AISI Core Technology Team](https://job-boards.eu.greenhouse.io/aisi/jobs/5000476101); [METR](https://metr.org/)
- **An interpretability pipeline for small open models**: activation collection, sparse autoencoder feature visualization, steering-vector experiments, intervention tracking, and statistical reporting.
- **An incident/observability layer for agentic systems**: audit logs, data lineage, permissions, anomaly detection, model/tool call traces, and reproducible replay.

The goal is not necessarily publication. It is to demonstrate that you can identify a concrete safety question, build the apparatus to test it, interpret results cautiously, and communicate limitations.

---

## Pathway B: Structured transition programmes and fellowships

Fellowships can give you mentorship, time, peers, research direction, and a credible signal. They are competitive and should not be treated as the only path, but they can accelerate a transition much more effectively than isolated self-study.

### Berlin and Germany options

#### SAIGE Incubator

Safe AI Germany’s SAIGE Incubator is particularly suitable for someone keeping a full-time job during a transition. It is a three-month, part-time programme designed to run alongside study or employment, with a stated commitment of **10–20 hours per week**. Participants work in teams of one to five on an expert-mentor project and can choose Technical AI Safety, AI Governance and Policy, Technical AI Governance, or Communications and Field-Building. It includes research-skills workshops, global speakers, career advice, local and national networking, and a possible three-month extension.  
Sources: [Safe AI Germany](https://safeaigermany.org/); [SAIGE Incubator](https://safeaigermany.org/incubator)

For a backend engineer, prioritize the **Technical AI Safety** or **Technical AI Governance** tracks and seek projects involving evaluations, safety cases, monitoring, security, or infrastructure rather than a vague reading-group project.

#### AI Safety Saarland Advanced Fellowship

AI Safety Saarland offers a **10-week Advanced Fellowship** focused on technical approaches to understanding highly capable models and addressing problems including misalignment and misuse.  
Source: [AI Safety Saarland Advanced Fellowship](https://www.ais-saarland.org/ai-security-1)

This could work as an intensive test of whether you enjoy technical safety research rather than just its mission.

#### AI Safety Berlin community

AI Safety Berlin runs a coworking hub at CIC Berlin, co-located with the Foresight AI Node. Its public description says it has around 10 daily coworking members and averages 20–25 participants at twice-monthly open coworking days. Its visiting-researcher pilot aims to bring experienced researchers to Berlin for two-to-four-week residencies, creating opportunities for presentations, feedback, collaboration, and local skill-building. The pilot pays travel, local transport, accommodation, and coworking but not salaries or stipends.  
Source: [AI Safety Berlin Visiting Researcher Pilot](https://grantmaking.aisafety.com/projects/da4a2baf-9681-4bf7-bf50-5ca9c21d8e6e)

This is not itself a salaried transition route, but it is useful for finding collaborators, receiving feedback on a portfolio project, meeting visiting researchers, and learning which organizations actually hire.

#### German funding and applied-safe-AI research

Germany has meaningful “safe and trustworthy AI” activity even when it is not branded as frontier alignment:

- The DFG established the six-year **LaSTing** priority programme in March 2025: “Robust Assessment & Safe Applicability of Language Modelling,” with an initial three-year funding period. It spans computational linguistics, AI, computer science, psychology, neuroscience, philosophy, and related fields.  
  Source: [DFG LaSTing Priority Programme](https://www.dfg.de/en/news/news-topics/announcements-proposals/2025/ifr-25-32)
- Hasso Plattner Institute received an ARIA Safeguarded AI grant for formal methods to elicit and aggregate safety specifications and risk thresholds, with a listed 12-month postdoctoral role.  
  Source: [HPI ARIA Safeguarded AI grant](https://hpi.de/en/article/aria-safeguarded-ai-grant/)
- The federally funded **Safe AI Engineering** project began in March 2025, involves 24 industry and research partners, has a three-year duration, and reports €34.5 million in funding. Partners include TU Berlin, DLR, Fraunhofer, KIT, Bosch, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, Continental, Intel Deutschland, TÜV AI.Lab, and others. Its focus is lifecycle methods for safety of AI-enabled automated driving.  
  Source: [Safe AI Engineering project](https://safe-ai-engineering.de/en/new-safe-ai-engineering-research-project-launched/)

These are viable avenues if you are open to **applied safety, robustness, certification, testing, or security** rather than exclusively long-term loss-of-control research.

### UK and European options

#### ARENA

The Alignment Research Engineer Accelerator (ARENA) is a four-to-five-week ML bootcamp focused on AI safety. It has been run in person at the London Initiative for Safe AI (LISA). The programme’s stated purpose is to give people ML engineering skills, community, and confidence to contribute to technical AI safety. Its published alumni examples include later work at Apollo Research, Anthropic, METR, MATS, and LASR.  
Source: [ARENA announcement](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/zWZ3iF95B7WaDyhv3/arena-5-0-call-for-applicants)

This is likely more useful than a generic ML bootcamp because it connects ML learning to alignment-relevant problems and a concentrated safety network.

#### LASR Labs

London AI Safety Research Labs runs a **13-week full-time** research programme. The cited 2025 cohort offered an **£11,000 stipend**, food, office space, and travel, and placed participants into supervised teams of three to four working toward an academic-style paper. Published alumni outcomes include roles at UK AISI, Apollo, OpenAI’s dangerous-capabilities evaluations team, Open Philanthropy, and PhD programmes; all five 2024 papers were accepted to NeurIPS workshops, and four of five 2023 teams had papers accepted to NeurIPS workshops or ICLR.  
Source: [LASR Labs programme announcement](https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/odZGKykSrDGva9sJ6/lasr-labs-summer-2025-applications-are-open-1)

LASR is a strong option once you can credibly propose or contribute to an empirical research project. It is less compatible with maintaining a normal full-time job because it is full-time.

#### MATS

The Mentorship for Alignment Research Students programme is one of the most established transitions into technical AI safety. It connects fellows with mentors from organizations including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Redwood Research, and ARC. The programme operates in Berkeley and London; its research phase is listed as 12 weeks, with possible six-to-12-month funded extensions.  
Source: [MATS programme](https://www.matsprogram.org/)

Its current application information lists:

- **$19,200 stipend**;
- **$24,000 compute**;
- free housing and food;
- travel coverage;
- J-1 visa coverage if needed;
- tracks in empirical research, theory, strategy and forecasting, policy and governance, systems security, founding and field-building, and biosecurity.  
Source: [MATS application page](https://www.matsprogram.org/apply)

Quantitative conversion:

- The general MATS stipend is stated as **$1,250/week**.  
  Source: [MATS programme](https://www.matsprogram.org/)
- For a 12-week research period:  
  **$1,250 × 12 = $15,000** in weekly stipend.
- The application page’s **$19,200** package is therefore consistent with funding that covers more than the 12 research weeks, or a cohort-specific structure; applicants should treat the live application page as controlling.
- Compute support at **$2,000/week × 12 weeks = $24,000**, matching the application page.

MATS’s summer 2025 cohort supported **98 fellows and 57 mentors** over a 10-week research phase; its winter 2025 cohort supported roughly **80 fellows and 40 mentors**.  
Sources: [MATS Summer 2025](https://www.matsprogram.org/program/summer-2025); [MATS Winter 2025](https://www.matsprogram.org/program/winter-2025)

The programme reports that 10% of alumni have co-founded safety organizations or research teams and lists alumni hires at Anthropic, Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Meta AI, UK AISI, Redwood Research, METR, RAND CAST, ARC, FAR.AI, Apollo Research, academia, and other organizations. This is self-reported programme outcome information, not an independently audited placement rate, but it indicates the programme’s importance as a network and signaling mechanism.  
Source: [MATS programme](https://www.matsprogram.org/)

#### PIBBSS and Dovetail

PIBBSS is an approximately three-month interdisciplinary programme matching researchers with AI-safety mentors. It explicitly lists software engineering, machine learning, mathematics, theoretical computer science, and related fields as relevant backgrounds. Its technical AIXI track includes topics that mix theory and implementation, such as in-context reinforcement learning and measuring LLM latent knowledge of harmful datasets.  
Source: [PIBBSS Fellowship](https://princint.ai/programs/fellowship/)

Dovetail’s 2025 fellowship was a 10-week graduate-level mathematics programme, with possible extension to a year full-time, focused on agent foundations. It welcomed people outside academia but is a much better fit if you genuinely enjoy rigorous mathematical work.  
Source: [Dovetail fellowship announcement](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/5XAB9rS8KdLhagwzR/apply-for-the-2025-dovetail-fellowship)

#### Cambridge AI Safety Hub Alignment Fellowship

This five-week programme is open to professionals considering an AI-safety career. Its technical track is intended for people with computer-science, mathematics, physics, or other quantitative backgrounds, covering LLM training, interpretability, behavioral evaluations, oversight, monitoring, and safe deployment.  
Source: [Cambridge AI Safety Hub Alignment Fellowship](https://caish.org/fellowship)

It is a useful low-cost first filter: after five weeks, you should know whether you are more motivated by technical evaluations, interpretability, control, governance, or another area.

---

## Pathway C: Apply to adjacent safety, security, and trustworthy-AI roles before “AI safety researcher” roles

A title such as “research engineer” is not always required at the first move. You can build relevant experience in roles such as:

- ML platform engineer;
- LLM evaluation engineer;
- AI red-team engineer;
- AI security engineer;
- trust-and-safety engineer;
- ML infrastructure engineer;
- applied scientist for robustness or verification;
- safety case / model-risk engineer;
- AI audit or assurance engineer;
- responsible-AI engineer;
- cybersecurity engineer working on AI-enabled systems;
- reliability or observability engineer supporting AI products.

This is particularly rational if you need income continuity. A first move into an AI-focused engineering job can provide model exposure and ML credibility; then a second move can target specialized safety research.

The field increasingly treats evaluation systems as core safety work. Under the EU AI Act, providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must evaluate models using standardized protocols and tools; document adversarial testing; assess and mitigate systemic risks; report serious incidents; and provide cybersecurity protections.  
Source: [EU AI Act, Article 55](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-55)

The Commission presumes systemic-risk status for models trained using cumulative compute above **10^25 FLOP**, subject to other criteria and designation mechanisms.  
Source: [European Commission GPAI provider guidelines](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/guidelines-obligations-general-purpose-ai-providers)

This creates durable demand in Europe for people who can make evaluations, evidence collection, security, monitoring, and documentation operational.

---

## Pathway D: Do a funded MSc or PhD—but only if it is strategically necessary

A graduate degree is most justified if you want to work on:

- mechanistic interpretability at a highly theoretical level;
- alignment theory or agent foundations;
- formal verification, formal methods, or mathematically rigorous control;
- novel ML methods where independent research leadership is expected;
- academic careers;
- research-scientist roles at frontier labs that prefer publication records.

It is less necessary if your target is safety research engineering, evaluation infrastructure, model auditing, red teaming, or empirical experimentation.

A good decision rule:

- **Do not do a degree merely to “get into AI safety.”**
- Do pursue one if, after substantial hands-on study and a project/fellowship, you discover that your comparative advantage and motivation are in questions that require sustained academic mentorship, research depth, and mathematical training.

European doctoral routes may be financially more accessible than US ones because they are often employment contracts or funded positions, but availability varies greatly by group and project. The EU’s Horizon Europe programme has a 2021–27 budget reported as €95.5 billion in current prices, including €5.4 billion from NextGenerationEU, although only part of this supports AI-related research and only a smaller subset is directly relevant to frontier safety.  
Source: [EUR-Lex Horizon Europe summary](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=LEGISSUM:horizon_europe)

# 3. A concrete 12-month transition plan while living in Berlin

## Months 0–2: choose a tractable target and establish foundations

Choose one of two targets:

1. **Evals / AI control / safety infrastructure** — recommended default for a backend engineer.
2. **Interpretability / empirical alignment** — appropriate if you enjoy ML experimentation and model internals.

Learn enough to build rather than merely read:

- Python, NumPy, PyTorch;
- transformer internals;
- training vs inference;
- fine-tuning, prompting, tool use, and agent architectures;
- experimental design, statistical uncertainty, evaluation validity;
- model risk domains: cyber, CBRN, harmful manipulation, autonomous capability, loss of control.

Use the Cambridge Alignment Fellowship or comparable foundational programme to map the field.  
Source: [Cambridge AI Safety Hub](https://caish.org/fellowship)

Join AI Safety Berlin events and seek feedback early.  
Source: [AI Safety Berlin Visiting Researcher Pilot](https://grantmaking.aisafety.com/projects/da4a2baf-9681-4bf7-bf50-5ca9c21d8e6e)

## Months 2–5: build one substantial public artifact

Allocate a realistic **8–15 hours per week** if employed full time. This is less than a fellowship but enough to produce a credible repository in a few months.

An example project:

### “Agentic coding-system safety evaluation harness”

Build:

- a task suite with benign and adversarial tasks;
- containerized, permission-limited execution;
- explicit threat models;
- structured event logs for prompts, tool calls, files, network requests, and outcomes;
- scoring methodology with automated and human-review components;
- model comparisons across different tool-access configurations;
- reproducible experiment configurations and a results report;
- a clear statement of what your tests do **not** establish.

This maps to the actual work of organizations studying autonomous capability, cybersecurity, model control, and evaluation integrity. METR, for example, evaluates frontier systems’ ability to carry out substantial tasks, including research and app development, cyberattacks, and behaviors that make systems hard to shut down; it also studies behavior that threatens the integrity of evaluations and mitigations.  
Source: [METR About](https://metr.org/about)

## Months 5–8: obtain external feedback and contribute upstream

- Apply to SAIGE, ARENA, AI Safety Saarland, LASR, MATS, PIBBSS, or similar programmes depending on timing and eligibility.
- Make a small contribution to an evaluation framework or a safety-oriented open-source project.
- Write a concise technical report, not just code.
- Attend Berlin and European safety events; ask researchers for feedback on a specific artifact, not generic career advice.
- Consider a part-time research collaboration if a credible mentor has a concrete project.

## Months 8–12: apply in parallel

Apply to:

1. European/UK fellowships;
2. evaluation and research-engineering roles;
3. ML infrastructure roles at organizations with safety-relevant work;
4. relevant academic research-assistant or engineer roles;
5. safety/security roles in German and European institutions;
6. US opportunities only where a sponsor clearly supports the needed visa route.

A good application package contains:

- a one-page safety-focused CV;
- a GitHub repository with unusually good documentation;
- a 2–5 page technical report;
- a short statement identifying a safety question you care about and why your project is a useful contribution;
- evidence of ML competence;
- a concise description of your systems engineering strengths.

# 4. Europe versus US: opportunity comparison

## A. Concentration of opportunity

### United States

The US has the greatest concentration of frontier AI companies, capital, advanced compute, and independent safety/evaluation organizations. It offers opportunities at labs such as Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind’s US operations, Meta AI, and a dense Bay Area ecosystem of independent and nonprofit organizations.

METR is a prominent US-based independent evaluator. It says its mission is to develop scientific methods for assessing catastrophic risks from autonomous AI capabilities, and it emphasizes transparency and publishing research and risk assessments where possible. It has worked with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, and Amazon; is part of the NIST AI Safety Institute Consortium; partners with the UK AI Security Institute; and provides technical assistance to the European AI Office.  
Source: [METR About](https://metr.org/about)

MATS has a Berkeley presence and can serve as a high-value US entry point, particularly because its current application information states that it covers J-1 visas when needed.  
Source: [MATS application](https://www.matsprogram.org/apply)

The main advantage of the US is therefore **density**: more frontier models, more compute, more funding, more peers, more jobs, and more direct proximity to high-impact model-development decisions.

The main disadvantage is that most direct roles are exceptionally competitive, often located in expensive cities, and can require a difficult immigration path.

### Europe and UK

Europe is less dense in private frontier labs but has meaningful advantages:

- Berlin offers a relatively low-friction base for community-building and independent work.
- London is one of the strongest global safety hubs because of the UK AI Security Institute, LISA, Apollo Research, MATS London, LASR, and a wider safety community.
- The EU’s regulatory environment creates demand for evaluations, documentation, risk mitigation, cybersecurity, and technical assurance.
- Germany and Europe have strong research institutions, security expertise, automotive/robotics safety, formal methods, privacy, and trustworthy-AI research.
- Existing EU residency or work rights remove a major barrier that would exist in the US.

Apollo Research, with London and San Francisco presence, is a concrete example of a Europe-linked frontier-safety organization. It studies scheming, strategic deception, evaluation awareness, and misaligned behavior; runs pre-deployment evaluations; develops monitoring research; and works with governments and frontier labs. Its evaluations researcher/engineer role describes work in efficient automated-analysis pipelines, LLM post-training knowledge, evaluation frameworks such as Inspect, and interaction with models before public release. It states that it can sponsor visas in the UK and US, though sponsorship is not guaranteed for every role or candidate.  
Sources: [Apollo Research](https://apolloresearch.ai/); [Apollo science](https://apolloresearch.ai/science); [Apollo Research Scientist/Engineer—Evaluations](https://jobs.lever.co/apolloresearch/4a65c6e1-785a-4f88-8998-a97574afb7ee)

The UK AISI is another major European opportunity. It says it has **more than 100 technical staff**, including alumni of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Oxford; substantial funding and computing; priority access to top models; and a close relationship to UK government policymaking. It focuses on advanced-AI capabilities and impacts, risk evaluations, and mitigations including safeguards, alignment, and control.  
Source: [UK AI Security Institute](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/)

### Practical implication

For a Berlin-based engineer, Europe/UK should be the **default first geography**, with US applications pursued selectively through programmes or employers that explicitly handle immigration. London is probably the most attractive nearby hub if you want frontier-evaluation work without immediately confronting US immigration.

---

## B. Funding

### Europe

European funding is more fragmented. It comes through:

- national research funders;
- EU research programmes;
- government institutes;
- universities;
- philanthropic or community-supported fellowships;
- industry collaborations;
- regulatory compliance and assurance demand.

The overall Horizon Europe programme has a €95.5 billion 2021–27 budget in current prices, but this must not be misread as a €95.5 billion AI-safety budget. It covers all EU research and innovation.  
Source: [EUR-Lex Horizon Europe](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=LEGISSUM:horizon_europe)

Concrete European examples include:

- £11,000 plus food, office space, and travel for the 13-week LASR programme.  
  Source: [LASR](https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/odZGKykSrDGva9sJ6/lasr-labs-summer-2025-applications-are-open-1)
- Talos Network’s European-policy fellowship offers possible funding of up to **€3,000/month for up to six months** for selected incubation projects, plus a two-month transition stipend for incubation-track fellows; this is not guaranteed simply by acceptance. It also offers paid four-to-six-month placements at European governance organizations.  
  Source: [Talos Fellowship](https://www.talosnetwork.org/talos-fellowship)
- Germany’s Safe AI Engineering programme reports **€34.5 million** over three years with 24 partners, showing that sizable applied-safe-AI funding exists.  
  Source: [Safe AI Engineering](https://safe-ai-engineering.de/en/new-safe-ai-engineering-research-project-launched/)
- A German 2025 generative-AI verification project, GENS(AI)FE, received a grant of up to **€771,453.99**, another example of federal funding directed at verifying and securing generative AI.  
  Source: [GENS(AI)FE grant notice](https://www.forschung-it-sicherheit-kommunikationssysteme.de/dateien/projekte/zuwendungsbescheid_gens-ai-fe_validaitor-gmbh.pdf)

The main European funding limitation is not a total absence of money; it is that the money is often routed through academic consortia, public programmes, applied domains, and compliance-oriented work rather than through many highly capitalized independent frontier labs.

### United States

The US has far more private capital concentrated in frontier model development, which translates into higher compensation, larger compute budgets, and more roles around model training, post-training, safeguards, evaluation, and research infrastructure.

MATS is unusually generous for a transition fellowship: $19,200 stipend, $24,000 compute, housing and food, travel, and J-1 visa support where needed.  
Source: [MATS application](https://www.matsprogram.org/apply)

Public funding for US safety institutions has been less certain. A coalition letter noted that NIST could use up to $10 million annually under existing law to establish and operate the US AI Safety Institute, while NIST had requested an additional $47.7 million for AI research, standards, and testing; the letter also described a more than 10% overall NIST budget cut in FY2024 that was extended through FY2025. This is advocacy material rather than a final appropriations report, but it indicates funding uncertainty in the public-sector safety ecosystem.  
Source: [FY26 NIST funding coalition letter](https://publicknowledge.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/FY26-NIST-Funding-Coalition-Letter-House.pdf)

The US AI Safety Institute’s stated mission is to advance understanding and mitigation of risks from advanced AI, housed within NIST, with research, testing, and guidance aimed at AI-risk assessment and safeguards.  
Source: [NIST AISI vision](https://www.nist.gov/system/files/documents/2024/05/21/AISI-vision-21May2024.pdf)

### Funding conclusion

- **US:** more money and compute concentrated in industry; higher salaries and more frontier access; more dependence on private labs and volatile policy conditions.
- **Europe:** less concentrated private funding, but stable public research infrastructure, EU/national programmes, a growing regulatory market, and lower immigration friction for someone already in Berlin.

For a career transitioner, the key question is not “where is total funding higher?” The answer is plainly the US. The useful question is “where can I credibly get funded time and mentorship in the next 12–24 months?” For a Berlin resident, Europe and the UK may be more accessible initially.

## C. Visa and work authorization

Your exact situation depends on nationality and current German residence status. The comparison below therefore distinguishes EU/EEA/Swiss citizens from third-country nationals.

### Europe and Germany

If you are an EU/EEA/Swiss national, moving within much of Europe is generally far simpler than moving to the US. If you are a third-country national already resident in Germany, your status and future eligibility matter; obtain personalized immigration advice before changing employment, enrolling in a programme, or spending extended time outside Germany.

For highly qualified employment in Germany, the EU Blue Card requires a job offer or binding contract for at least six months, qualification requirements, insurance, and a salary threshold. The European Commission’s Germany page stated a **€45,300** 2024 threshold, while the German Federal Foreign Office listed 2026 thresholds of **€50,700** generally and **€45,934.20** for bottleneck occupations. These figures change annually, so use the current official threshold rather than relying on historic numbers.  
Sources: [European Commission, EU Blue Card Germany](https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/eu-immigration-portal/eu-blue-card/eu-blue-card-germany_en); [German Federal Foreign Office Blue Card guidance](https://uk.diplo.de/uk-en/02/2449360-2449360)

For a 2026 benchmark:

- General threshold: **€50,700/year**, or **€4,225/month** gross.
- Bottleneck threshold: **€45,934.20/year**, or **€3,827.85/month** gross.

Arithmetic check:

- €50,700 ÷ 12 = **€4,225/month**.
- €45,934.20 ÷ 12 = **€3,827.85/month**.

Germany also provides routes for IT professionals without formal academic qualifications. The official “Make it in Germany” guidance says an EU Blue Card may be possible for IT professionals without a formal qualification if they have at least **three years of similar professional experience within the previous seven years**; other professional-experience visa routes may also apply.  
Source: [Make it in Germany—IT professionals](https://www.make-it-in-germany.com/en/visa-residence/types/it-professionals)

For research specifically, a non-EU researcher can use a research residence route if they have a hosting agreement with a recognized research body. The agreement must state the research purpose, duration, funding, and qualifications.  
Source: [European Commission—Researcher in Germany](https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/eu-immigration-portal/researcher-germany_en)

This makes German/European university, institute, and qualifying employer positions more administratively feasible than a US move for many people.

### United States

The main routes relevant to an employed researcher or engineer are generally H-1B, O-1, and J-1 for eligible temporary research/fellowship arrangements.

#### H-1B

H-1B specialty-occupation eligibility requires a role involving theoretical and practical application of specialized knowledge, normally requiring a directly related bachelor’s degree or equivalent; the applicant must meet applicable degree/equivalency requirements.  
Source: [USCIS H-1B specialty occupations](https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/h-1b-specialty-occupations)

For many private-sector hires, H-1B selection and timing are constraints. This makes it a poor plan to assume that a US employer will simply solve immigration for an early-career transitioner, even if you are technically strong.

#### O-1A

O-1A is for individuals with extraordinary ability in science, education, business, or athletics, demonstrated by sustained national or international acclaim. USCIS says it requires extensive documentation and normally either a qualifying major award or at least three alternative forms of evidence; satisfying three categories alone does not automatically establish eligibility because USCIS assesses the totality of evidence.  
Sources: [USCIS O-1 overview](https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/temporary-workers/o-1-visa-individuals-with-extraordinary-ability-or-achievement); [USCIS policy manual](https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-2-part-m-chapter-4)

An O-1 is not a realistic first-step plan for someone newly entering safety research. It can become plausible later after meaningful publications, prominent open-source work, field recognition, critical-role evidence, major awards, invited speaking, high compensation, or documented original contributions.

#### J-1 research scholar

The J-1 research-scholar category is for foreign nationals conducting research, observing, or consulting in connection with research projects at research institutions, corporate research facilities, museums, libraries, and post-secondary institutions. It is temporary, sponsor-based, and has program-specific restrictions.  
Source: [US State Department BridgeUSA—Research Scholar](https://j1visa.state.gov/programs/research-scholar)

MATS explicitly says it covers J-1 visas if needed, making it a practical exception to the broader US visa problem.  
Source: [MATS application](https://www.matsprogram.org/apply)

### Visa conclusion

- If you already have secure German/EU work rights, **Europe/UK offers lower administrative friction**.
- If you are a third-country national in Germany, preserve your German status carefully and check whether a change of employer, self-funded fellowship, remote work, or UK placement affects it.
- In the US, target opportunities that **explicitly sponsor or organize the visa**, such as MATS’s J-1 support or roles like Apollo’s that state potential sponsorship.
- Do not build a plan around O-1 until you have a much stronger public record.

# 5. Research culture: Europe versus US

These are tendencies, not universal rules. Individual labs differ more than countries in many respects.

## United States: frontier-lab proximity, pace, resources, and commercialization

The US ecosystem is characterized by:

- close proximity to frontier model development;
- high compensation and large private compute budgets;
- rapid iteration and deployment pressure;
- a dense informal network, especially in the Bay Area;
- more opportunities to move between startups, labs, nonprofits, and investors;
- a blend of open research with proprietary work, embargoes, and security restrictions.

Anthropic’s open roles alone show the breadth of safety-adjacent technical work in a frontier lab: interpretability, safeguards research, ML/research engineering, cybersecurity RL, post-training model evaluation, distributed RL systems, research infrastructure, cyber-evaluations engineering, red teaming, biological safety, and AI reliability.  
Source: [Anthropic jobs](https://www.anthropic.com/careers/jobs)

This is a major advantage for an engineer: there are many ways to become safety-relevant without having the title “alignment researcher” on day one.

But the downsides are real:

- direct research access may be proprietary;
- the work may be shaped by product deadlines, legal constraints, security concerns, and corporate incentives;
- Bay Area cost of living is high;
- immigration dependence can reduce freedom to take risks or switch jobs;
- roles may change rapidly as models and company priorities change.

Independent organizations partly counterbalance this. METR says it seeks transparency and openness where possible and publishes research and risk assessments; it does not accept compensation for its risk-assessment work, although companies may provide access and tokens.  
Source: [METR](https://metr.org/)

## Europe and UK: regulation, public institutions, independent research, and distributed communities

Europe has a stronger institutional emphasis on:

- public-interest research;
- standards, assurance, auditing, and formal accountability;
- privacy, security, human rights, and product safety;
- government capacity;
- technical governance;
- cross-border collaboration and public funding.

The EU AI Act is a major cultural and economic force: systemic-risk GPAI providers are expected to perform model evaluation, adversarial testing, systemic-risk mitigation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity protections.  
Source: [EU AI Act Article 55](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-55)

This makes Europe especially attractive if you are interested in turning safety principles into reliable evaluation processes, policy evidence, auditing, compliance tooling, model documentation, secure infrastructure, and governance mechanisms.

The UK occupies a distinctive middle position: it is geographically close to Europe but has an unusually strong frontier-risk institution in AISI and a concentrated London research community. AISI describes itself as operating within government while functioning with a startup-like structure, with over 100 technical staff, substantial funding/compute, model access, and partnerships.  
Source: [UK AISI](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/)

Apollo Research demonstrates that European organizations can also conduct highly frontier-relevant work: fundamental research on scheming, pre-deployment evaluations, monitoring, and collaboration with labs and governments.  
Sources: [Apollo Research](https://apolloresearch.ai/); [Apollo science](https://apolloresearch.ai/science)

### Cultural comparison in practical terms

| Dimension | Europe / UK | US |
|---|---|---|
| Frontier-lab density | Lower in continental Europe; strong in London | Highest, especially Bay Area |
| Public-sector safety capacity | Strong and growing; EU AI Act creates operational demand | Present but public funding/policy can be less stable |
| Independent evaluation ecosystem | Strong in UK; growing across Europe | Very strong, especially Bay Area |
| Compute and salary | Generally lower | Generally higher |
| Visa burden for Berlin resident | Often lower, especially with EU rights | Substantially higher unless sponsored |
| Research openness | More public, regulatory, academic, and standards-oriented on average | Mixed: major open/nonprofit work alongside highly proprietary frontier labs |
| Research tempo | Often slower and more institutional; UK safety hub can be fast | Often faster, startup/lab-driven, product-linked |
| Good initial niche for backend engineer | Evaluation infrastructure, assurance, AI security, standards, technical governance, applied safety | Frontier evals, model infrastructure, safeguards, interpretability systems, agent security |

# 6. Where Berlin specifically fits

Berlin is a credible base for the first phase, even if it is not the global center of frontier-model training.

Advantages:

- AI Safety Berlin community and coworking access;
- proximity to German policy, civil society, startups, universities, and EU-facing work;
- the Foresight AI Node co-location described by AI Safety Berlin;
- reasonable access to London and other European hubs;
- ability to build a portfolio while maintaining current employment;
- German research and public-interest technology ecosystem;
- future opportunities from Germany’s growing AI-safety/security institutional capacity.

AI Safety Berlin’s stated purpose in its visiting-researcher pilot is explicitly to connect experienced researchers with local researchers and career transitioners and seed a European relocation pipeline.  
Source: [AI Safety Berlin Visiting Researcher Pilot](https://grantmaking.aisafety.com/projects/da4a2baf-9681-4bf7-bf50-5ca9c21d8e6e)

Germany’s AI Safety and Security Institute (AISI Deutschland) is currently being established. The Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) and Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) form an initial “virtual nucleus”; responsibilities are split between cybersecurity/security and safety, with later expansion planned. The institute is described as an analytical-operational competence center rather than a regulator.  
Source: [BSI—AISI Deutschland](https://www.bsi.bund.de/DE/Themen/Unternehmen-und-Organisationen/Informationen-und-Empfehlungen/AISI/aisi_node.html)

This is forward-looking rather than an immediate large hiring market. It should be monitored, not treated as the sole plan.

# 7. What not to do

1. **Do not quit a stable backend job before testing your fit.**  
   Start with structured study and a serious project. Use an incubator or fellowship to validate your interest before sacrificing income.

2. **Do not over-index on theoretical alignment if you dislike mathematics.**  
   Evaluations, model control, agent security, and research systems are intellectually serious, high-impact safety areas where your current skills are unusually relevant.

3. **Do not collect certificates instead of producing evidence.**  
   One well-designed, well-documented safety evaluation project is more useful than many generic course completions.

4. **Do not describe generic responsible-AI work as frontier safety without being precise.**  
   Bias, fairness, privacy, robustness, misuse, cybersecurity, model autonomy, control, interpretability, and long-term alignment overlap but are not interchangeable. Be honest about the risk domain you are addressing.

5. **Do not assume all fellowships lead to jobs.**  
   They offer mentorship and signal, not guaranteed employment. MATS, LASR, and other programmes have impressive published alumni outcomes, but selection is competitive and individual outcomes vary.

6. **Do not treat US relocation as necessary for impact.**  
   It may later be valuable, but London, Berlin, and Europe offer real routes—especially in evaluations, policy, security, assurance, and public institutions.

7. **Do not make immigration an afterthought.**  
   If non-EU, verify German residence rules before a fellowship or employment change; if targeting the US, apply preferentially to programmes and employers with explicit visa support.

# 8. Recommended decision framework

## Stay in Berlin and build toward Europe/UK first if:

- you need income stability;
- you already have German/EU work authorization;
- you enjoy backend/infrastructure more than pure theory;
- you are interested in evaluations, monitoring, AI security, robust deployment, policy, or regulatory assurance;
- you want to test the field before taking a high-risk relocation step.

This is the recommended default.

## Target London after initial portfolio-building if:

- you want a dense safety community without US visa complexity;
- you are drawn to AISI, Apollo, LASR, MATS, ARENA, or policy-facing technical work;
- you can secure UK work authorization or employer sponsorship;
- you want more frontier-risk focus than is currently concentrated in Germany.

## Target the US if:

- you have a clear sponsor-backed opportunity;
- you want maximum proximity to frontier labs and compute;
- you have already built a strong research-engineering record;
- you can tolerate immigration, cost-of-living, and market volatility;
- the particular role provides unique model access or mentorship unavailable in Europe.

## Consider a PhD if:

- your demonstrated preference is for theory, formal methods, or independent research leadership;
- you have found a supervisor and project genuinely aligned with safety;
- the opportunity is funded;
- the expected research skill gain outweighs several years of foregone industry earnings and practical engineering experience.

---

# Final recommendation

For this profile, the most realistic and strategically sound route is:

1. **Aim for empirical AI safety research engineering, evaluations, AI control, or safety infrastructure.**
2. **Use Berlin for a low-risk 6–12 month runway**: join the local community, use SAIGE or a similar programme, study ML systematically, and build a serious public evaluation/infrastructure project.
3. **Apply to UK/European transition programmes**—especially ARENA, LASR, MATS London, AI Safety Saarland, PIBBSS, and relevant German safe-AI research projects—while also applying to adjacent research-engineering roles.
4. **Treat London as the most practical next hub** if you want frontier-oriented work and can solve UK work authorization.
5. **Treat the US as a second-stage option**, best pursued through a clearly funded fellowship or an employer that explicitly sponsors the necessary visa.
6. **Delay a PhD decision** until you have real experience of research work and know whether your durable comparative advantage is research engineering, empirical ML research, technical governance, or theory.

Your backend background is not a detour from AI safety. It is a credible entry asset—provided you translate it into ML fluency, safety-specific judgment, and demonstrable research or evaluation work.
