# 4. Carrier Transicold assessment

## 4.1 Reliability on a 12-hour off-grid journey

Carrier’s Supra HE line is a self-powered truck refrigeration range intended for controlled-temperature transport. It combines mechanical and electric subsystems, and relevant variants support diesel road operation and optional electric standby.

For the Supra HE 8, Carrier publishes:

- diesel high-speed capacity at 0°C/30°C: 7,710 W;
- diesel low-speed capacity at 0°C/30°C: 6,300 W;
- capacity at -20°C/30°C: 3,950 W high speed and 3,730 W low speed;
- standby capacity at 0°C/30°C: 6,250 W;
- airflow: 2,577 m³/hour;
- weight: 440 kg;
- three-cylinder, 719 cc engine;
- high-ambient capability up to +55°C;
- 26.5% lower fuel consumption than the legacy Supra comparison model.

Source: https://www.carrier.com/truck-trailer/en/uk/products/eu-truck-trailer/truck/Supra-HE-8/.

Across the Supra HE range, Carrier states fuel-consumption reduction of up to **29%** compared with the legacy Supra 1050, extended maintenance intervals, lower weight and fewer moving parts (https://www.carrier.com/truck-trailer/en/eu/products/eu-truck-trailer/truck/supra-he-series/ and https://www.shareddocs.com/hvac/docs/2000/Public/08/Supra-HE_ENG.pdf).

### Reliability advantages

- Independent diesel operation is suitable for 12+ hours without grid power.
- Carrier states that the direct-coupled architecture has fewer moving parts, supporting reliability and reduced maintenance.
- Published +55°C ambient capability is suitable for West African operating conditions.
- Variable fans and the semi-electric architecture should reduce energy use relative to the older platform.
- Multiple capacities and multi-temperature options are available.

### Reliability limitations

- The reviewed Carrier sources give percentage fuel savings but not an absolute litres-per-hour figure for the Supra HE. A direct fuel comparison with Thermo King cannot therefore be made responsibly from the published evidence alone.
- Percentage savings against a legacy Carrier model do not establish a 29% saving against a current Thermo King unit.
- As with Thermo King, compliance depends on the complete insulated body, air distribution, load plan, fuel quality and preventive maintenance.
- The semi-electric design still has a diesel engine and refrigeration circuit; it is not mechanically maintenance-free.

Carrier should be required to run a loaded 12- to 24-hour demonstration at +2°C to +8°C, including a simulated traffic stop, door opening and cellular outage. Measure actual fuel consumption rather than applying the marketing percentage to a Thermo King figure.

## 4.2 Monitoring

Carrier’s Lynx Fleet platform is described as providing:

- real-time operational visibility;
- decision support;
- cargo-safety information;
- temperature accuracy support;
- fleet-management information;
- reports and analytics;
- integration/API capabilities in the container implementation.

Carrier has supplied Lynx Fleet devices with Supra and Citimax refrigeration equipment for training at the Africa Centre of Excellence for Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain in Kigali (https://www.carrier.com/truck-trailer/en/eu/news/news-article/carrier-transicold-enhances-cold-chain-training-with-advanced-refrigeration-solutions-at-the-africa-centre-of-excellence-for-sustainable-cooling-and-cold-chain.html). Carrier also describes Lynx as providing end-to-end visibility and real-time monitoring in its BluEdge telematics program (https://www.carrier.com/container-refrigeration/en/worldwide/news/news-article/carrier-transicold-container-refrigeration-launches-bluedge-partner-program-for-lynx-and-telematics-solutions.html).

### Connectivity conclusion

The reviewed evidence establishes real-time connected monitoring but does not specify native satellite communications for the truck platform. The procurement specification should therefore treat Lynx Fleet as cellular unless Carrier documents otherwise.

As with Thermo King, require:

- dual-SIM/multi-network service;
- offline storage and automatic data backfill;
- at least two calibrated cargo probes;
- door and reefer-status inputs;
- SMS, email and operations-center alarms;
- a separate satellite path on critical corridors.

A Nigerian monitoring provider reports compatibility with both Carrier and Thermo King, up to eight calibrated probes per vehicle, ±0.3°C accuracy, GPS, door events and alerts by SMS, WhatsApp and email, with a claimed average detection time of three to four minutes. These are supplier claims, not independently verified performance, but they illustrate the type of third-party monitoring specification available in the market (https://tranzit.ng/services/cold-chain/).

## 4.3 Maintenance

Carrier states that it has more than 900 service locations across Europe, the Middle East and Africa (https://www.carrier.com/truck-trailer/en/eu/contact-us/service-center-locator/).

Local evidence is stronger than for Thermo King, although authorization and parts capability still require due diligence:

- **Accra/Tema:** Continental Reefers and Refrigeration Services states that its team is trained and certified by reefer manufacturers including Carrier and Daikin (https://continentalreefers.com/). A separate business reference identifies Addfra Limited as a Ghana-based Carrier transport-refrigeration distributor, but the gathered evidence for this was a LinkedIn result rather than an official Carrier page, so formal status should be confirmed.
- **Lagos:** Mandilas markets Carrier Transicold equipment and publishes several Lagos service locations, including Lekki-Epe Expressway, Ogba and Lagos Island (https://www.mandilasng.com/2023/10/16/unlocking-the-power-of-the-cold-chain-with-carrier-transicold-from-mandilas/). Confirm that the listed automotive centers have Carrier transport-refrigeration technicians, diagnostic tools and reefer parts rather than only general vehicle-service capability.
- **Dakar:** Carrier’s official contact page lists a Carrier Transicold contact at SICAP Foire No. 245, Dakar, telephone +221 77 099 8521 (https://www.carrier.com/truck-trailer/en/eu/contact-us/).
- **Abidjan:** no specific Carrier Transicold truck/trailer workshop was conclusively verified in the evidence reviewed.

On present evidence, Carrier has the better documented support position in **Accra/Tema, Lagos and Dakar**, but both brands have an evidence gap in **Abidjan**.

# 5. Innovative off-grid alternatives

## 5.1 WHO-prequalified long-range passive cold boxes

Passive cold boxes are the most mature off-grid transport alternative. They maintain temperature through insulation and conditioned coolant packs, requiring no grid supply, fuel, compressor or vehicle alternator during transit.

WHO’s freeze-free cold-box specification defines:

- short range: minimum cold life of 48 hours at +43°C;
- long range: minimum cold life of 96 hours at +43°C.

The boxes are intended for moving vaccines from one fixed store to another and have a maximum loaded weight normally no greater than 50 kg (WHO/PQS/E004/CB05.4: https://extranet.who.int/prequal/sites/default/files/document_files/WHO_PQS_E004_CB05.4.pdf).

For a 12-hour trip, the minimum long-range design margin is:

**96 hours ÷ 12 hours = 8 times the planned journey duration**

Actual field margin is lower if boxes are repeatedly opened, coolant packs are incorrectly prepared, the lid seal is damaged, or the equipment is exposed to conditions outside its qualified use.

### Product examples

**AOV ACB-264SL**

- WHO PQS reference: E004/023;
- storage capacity: 6 litres;
- cold life at +43°C: 132 hours 18 minutes;
- indicative UNICEF price: $102.21.

Source: https://supply.unicef.org/s0002344.html.

**B Medical RCW25/CF**

- WHO PQS reference: E004/005;
- storage capacity: 20 litres;
- cold life at +43°C: 134.6 hours;
- fully loaded weight: 38.9 kg;
- supplied with 24 × 0.6-litre ice packs;
- three-year replacement warranty;
- indicative UNICEF price: $646.71.

Source: https://supply.unicef.org/s0002235.html.

**AOV ACB 316 L**

- storage capacity: 18 litres;
- cold life at +43°C: 145 hours 51 minutes;
- listed price: $115 per unit.

Source: https://extranet.who.int/prequal/sites/default/files/imd_products/83d134ad-ba58-4819-9be1-c68807e430f1_0.pdf.

Price and freight should be checked at tender date. The wide difference between the cited 18-litre and 20-litre box prices also shows that indicative catalogue prices cannot substitute for a landed-cost quotation and verification that the exact current model remains prequalified.

### Dose capacity

Dose capacity depends on vaccine presentation. WHO defines packed volume per dose as the space occupied by the dose, primary container and packaging. Published examples vary widely: BCG in a 20-dose vial may require 1.2 cm³ per dose, while some single-dose presentations require 15–45 cm³ per dose (WHO packaging guidance: https://extranet.who.int/prequal/sites/default/files/document_files/WHO_IVB_05.23_eng.pdf).

For planning, using **3.3 cm³ per dose**:

- 20 litres = 20,000 cm³;
- 20,000 ÷ 3.3 = **6,061 doses**, rounded down to approximately 6,000 doses per box.

MSF guidance gives a similar practical value for a roughly 20.7-litre RCW25:

- 9,400 doses at 2.2 cm³/dose;
- 6,200 doses at 3.3 cm³/dose;
- 4,900 doses at 4.3 cm³/dose.

Source: https://medicalguidelines.msf.org/en/viewport/mme/english/appendix-19-cold-chain-equipment-32408362.html.

Therefore, capacity must be calculated against the actual presentation mix. A 20-litre box is not inherently a 6,000-dose box for all vaccines.

### Advantages

- Highest off-grid resilience for 12-hour movements.
- Minimal field repair requirement.
- Direct WHO-PQS product options.
- Easy to use as emergency rescue capacity.
- Low capital cost compared with a dedicated reefer vehicle.
- Can travel in an ordinary van, boat or other available vehicle.

### Limitations

- Coolant packs must first be frozen or otherwise conditioned at a functioning cold-chain facility.
- Incorrect frozen packs can freeze adsorbed vaccines.
- Passive equipment does not actively correct a developing excursion.
- Frequent opening sharply reduces performance.
- Large campaigns need many boxes, coolant packs and trained handlers.
- Loaded box weight and coolant mass reduce transport efficiency.

WHO’s vaccine-management guidance specifically emphasizes correct passive-container and coolant-pack use to minimize freezing risk (https://www.who.int/publications-detail-redirect/WHO-IVB-15.03).

## 5.2 Solar direct-drive and PCM systems

Solar direct-drive systems are best regarded as **nodes that support transport**, not replacements for vehicle refrigeration during all journeys.

The WHO-prequalified ARKTEK YBC-10 SDD is a 10-litre solar direct-drive refrigerator with:

- WHO code E003-118e;
- 200 W photovoltaic modules;
- 3.5 kWh/m²/day solar reference condition;
- 51–100 hours of holdover;
- more than three days of protection during inadequate sunlight;
- an integrated 30-day temperature logger;
- energy-harvesting outputs including 5 V USB.

Source: https://extranet.who.int/prequal/immunization-devices/e003-118e.

This equipment can maintain vaccines at an off-grid health post and prepare PCM packs for outreach. It is not, by itself, evidence that the installed refrigerator can safely operate inside a moving vehicle under vibration, changing solar exposure and repeated door opening.

Field-test evidence from western Senegal reported that an Arktek SDD/PCM prototype maintained vaccine temperature at approximately 3°C–5°C, achieved an eight-day holdover in testing and could freeze removable PCM packs for standard vaccine carriers. A 100 W solar panel was reported as sufficient in that trial. Because the evidence is a prototype/field-study summary rather than the current WHO product data sheet, it should support a pilot, not an automatic procurement assumption.

Solar/PCM is most useful for:

- off-grid staging points;
- freezing or conditioning packs for passive delivery;
- reducing generator dependence;
- maintaining contingency stock while a vehicle is delayed;
- charging phones and monitoring gateways.

## 5.3 Transport loggers for passive systems

WHO’s listing for ColdTrace Transport, E006-102, describes:

- Bluetooth Low Energy transmission from a sensor in the vaccine carrier to a smartphone;
- cloud upload;
- one- to 60-minute logging intervals;
- up to 125 days of stored records at the stated configuration;
- immediate excursion alerts;
- GPS-tagged trip summaries;
- ±0.5°C accuracy;
- a lithium battery intended to last up to five years under typical use.

Source: https://extranet.who.int/prequal/immunization-devices/e006-102.

The listing reports an acceptance date of 5 August 2025. Procurement should verify that the product is currently listed at the time of award.

ColdTrace is cellular only when paired with a smartphone that has data connectivity. During a coverage gap it can continue to log locally, but “real-time” remote visibility is unavailable unless the phone or gateway has a satellite connection. This distinction should be explicit in service-level agreements.

## 6.2 Contract requirements

For each active-refrigeration award, require the bidder to provide:

1. workshop name, address and authorization letter in each city;
2. number of certified truck/trailer refrigeration technicians;
3. 24/7 mobile-response telephone number;
4. normal and emergency response times;
5. stocked quantities of belts, filters, sensors, controllers, starter components, refrigerant and compressor-related parts;

# 7. Total cost per vaccine dose

## 7.1 Why a universal cost figure is not possible

No public evidence gathered provides comparable, delivered West African prices for complete Thermo King and Carrier pharmaceutical vehicles, local maintenance contracts, insurance, driver costs or telecom subscriptions. A defensible procurement comparison therefore requires a common cost model populated by vendor bids.

Cost per successfully delivered dose should be calculated as:

**Cost per successfully delivered dose = total annualized transport-system cost ÷ doses delivered within specification**

The denominator must exclude:

- broken or missing doses;
- doses quarantined after unresolved excursions;
- doses rejected because a trip record is missing;
- doses damaged by freezing;
- undelivered doses caused by vehicle failure.

The figures below are an **illustrative planning model**, not supplier quotations.

## 7.2 Common assumptions

Illustrative route and utilization:

- journey duration: 12 hours;
- 250 journeys per year;
- evaluation life: five years;
- total lifetime journeys: 250 × 5 = **1,250**;
- active-vehicle shipment: 100,000 doses;
- low-volume shipment: 6,000 doses;
- packed-volume assumption: 3.3 cm³/dose;
- refrigeration diesel: $1.25/litre;
- common truck/driver/insurance/toll allocation: $250 per large trip;
- costs exclude vaccine acquisition, taxes and financing;
- active-system capex represents an assumed incremental insulated-body/refrigeration/telematics package, not a documented OEM price.

Because these are assumptions, bids should replace every line before award.

## 7.3 Thermo King illustrative high-volume cost

Assumptions:

- incremental refrigeration/body/telematics capital: $85,000;
- annual maintenance and parts: $6,000;
- telematics subscription: $600/year;
- independent trip logger/documentation: $2/trip;
- refrigeration fuel: published 3.6 L/hour;
- successful dose rate: 98%, allowing 2% for illustrative wastage/rejection.

### Calculation

Capital per trip:

**$85,000 ÷ 1,250 trips = $68.00**

Maintenance per trip:

**$6,000 ÷ 250 = $24.00**

Telematics per trip:

**$600 ÷ 250 = $2.40**

Reefer fuel:

**3.6 L/hour × 12 hours = 43.2 L**

**43.2 L × $1.25 = $54.00**

Total trip cost:

- common vehicle/driver cost: $250.00
- capital: $68.00
- maintenance: $24.00
- reefer fuel: $54.00
- telematics: $2.40
- logger/documentation: $2.00

**Total = $400.40 per trip**

Successfully delivered doses:

**100,000 × 98% = 98,000 doses**

Cost per successful dose:

**$400.40 ÷ 98,000 = $0.004086**

Rounded result: **$0.0041 per dose**, or **0.41 US cents per dose**.

## 7.4 Carrier illustrative high-volume cost

Because Carrier did not publish an absolute Supra HE fuel rate in the evidence reviewed, the model uses an explicit assumption of **2.8 L/hour** for planning only. This must be replaced by trial data.

Assumptions:

- incremental package capital: $88,000;
- annual maintenance: $5,500;
- telematics: $600/year;
- logger/documentation: $2/trip;
- illustrative reefer fuel: 2.8 L/hour;
- successful dose rate: 98.5%.

### Calculation

Capital per trip:

**$88,000 ÷ 1,250 = $70.40**

Maintenance per trip:

**$5,500 ÷ 250 = $22.00**

Telematics per trip:

**$600 ÷ 250 = $2.40**

Reefer fuel:

**2.8 L/hour × 12 hours = 33.6 L**

**33.6 L × $1.25 = $42.00**

Total trip cost:

- common vehicle/driver cost: $250.00
- capital: $70.40
- maintenance: $22.00
- reefer fuel: $42.00
- telematics: $2.40
- logger/documentation: $2.00

**Total = $388.80 per trip**

Successfully delivered doses:

**100,000 × 98.5% = 98,500**

Cost per successful dose:

**$388.80 ÷ 98,500 = $0.003947**

Rounded result: **$0.0039 per dose**, or **0.39 US cents per dose**.

### Interpretation

The modeled Carrier advantage is only:

**$0.004086 − $0.003947 = $0.000139 per dose**

That is approximately **0.014 cents per dose**. This difference is smaller than the uncertainty in capital price, real fuel use, maintenance and wastage. No procurement decision should be based on this modeled difference without local bid and trial data.

## 7.5 Passive long-range boxes for a 100,000-dose movement

Using the 20-litre RCW25 at 3.3 cm³/dose:

**20,000 cm³ ÷ 3.3 cm³/dose = 6,061 doses/box**

Boxes needed:

**100,000 ÷ 6,061 = 16.5**, rounded up to **17 boxes**

Loaded box mass:

**17 × 38.9 kg = 661.3 kg**

Box capital:

**17 × $646.71 = $10,994.07**

Assuming 250 uses across the planning horizon:

**$10,994.07 ÷ 250 uses = $43.98 per shipment**

Illustrative additional assumptions:

- ordinary vehicle/driver cost: $250;
- coolant conditioning and energy: $20;
- handling and inspection: $60;
- logger/connectivity allocation: $20;
- successful dose rate: 99%.

Total:

**$250 + $43.98 + $20 + $60 + $20 = $393.98**

Successfully delivered doses:

**100,000 × 99% = 99,000**

Cost per successful dose:

**$393.98 ÷ 99,000 = $0.00398**

Rounded result: **$0.0040 per dose**, or **0.40 cents per dose**.

This result is close to the active-vehicle figures, but it hides a substantial operational burden: 17 heavy boxes, 408 coolant packs if each RCW25 uses 24 packs, more handling events and lower cargo-volume efficiency. Passive transport is therefore not automatically preferable for 100,000-dose trunk movements even where its direct cost is competitive.

## 7.6 Low-volume 6,000-dose comparison

### Thermo King active vehicle

Using the same $400.40 trip cost and a 98% successful rate:

**6,000 × 98% = 5,880 delivered doses**

**$400.40 ÷ 5,880 = $0.0681 per dose**

Result: **6.81 cents per delivered dose**.

### Carrier active vehicle

**6,000 × 98.5% = 5,910 delivered doses**

**$388.80 ÷ 5,910 = $0.0658 per dose**

Result: **6.58 cents per delivered dose**.

### One RCW25 passive box

Illustrative small-vehicle case:

- small vehicle/driver: $150;
- box capital per use: $646.71 ÷ 250 = $2.59;
- coolant conditioning: $10;
- handling: $10;
- monitoring allocation: $2;
- total: **$174.59**;
- successful rate: 99%;
- delivered doses: **6,000 × 99% = 5,940**.

Cost:

**$174.59 ÷ 5,940 = $0.0294 per dose**

Result: **2.94 cents per delivered dose**.

If the same $250 transport allocation is used rather than a small vehicle:

**($250 + $2.59 + $10 + $10 + $2) ÷ 5,940**

**$274.59 ÷ 5,940 = $0.0462**

Result: **4.62 cents per delivered dose**.

Thus passive transport remains cheaper for the small consignment under either transport-cost assumption.

## 7.7 Break-even insight

The dominant active-vehicle cost is the trip itself, not the refrigeration brand. At an approximately $400 trip cost:

- 100,000 delivered doses: about $0.004/dose;
- 20,000 doses: about $0.020/dose before adjusting for losses;
- 6,000 doses: about $0.067/dose;
- 1,000 doses: about $0.40/dose.

Fleet scheduling and load consolidation will therefore produce larger savings than selecting one active brand based on a small modeled fuel difference.

## 7.8 Costs omitted from the illustration

Tender evaluation must add:

- complete chassis cost or lease;
- import duty, VAT and port charges;
- body certification and thermal mapping;
- validation after major repairs;
- finance cost and residual value;
- insurance;
- road tolls and border charges;
- driver and security costs;
- satellite airtime;
- calibration;
- spare reefer or contingency rental;
- depot electricity and pre-cooling;
- generators or solar equipment for coolant-pack preparation;
- vaccine wastage and emergency replacement;
- carbon or emissions costs, if applicable;
- inventory carrying cost caused by slower or smaller passive movements.

---

# 8. Monitoring architecture recommended for all three options

## 8.1 Minimum architecture

Every shipment should have three distinct data layers:

1. **Refrigeration-control data**
   - set point;
   - supply and return air;
   - engine status;
   - alarm code;
   - fuel level if available.

2. **Independent product-space data**
   - at least two calibrated probes in an active body;
   - at least one calibrated logger in every passive box;
   - accuracy appropriate to vaccine transport;
   - tamper-evident assignment to the shipment.

3. **Location and communication**
   - GPS location;
   - cellular upload using at least two networks where commercially possible;
   - offline data retention;
   - satellite position/alarm messaging for critical remote routes.

The independent logger is essential. A reefer controller showing normal air temperature does not prove that every pallet or box remained within range.

## 8.2 Alarm escalation

Suggested escalation:

- warning alarm before reaching the release limit;
- driver alert immediately;
- operations-center SMS/email/app alert;
- quality-assurance alert if not acknowledged within five minutes;
- route to nearest approved cold store or transfer vehicle;
- quarantine on arrival after any unresolved excursion;
- no automatic disposal without vaccine-specific stability assessment.

## 8.3 Communications uncertainty

“Real-time” should be contractually defined. A logger that records every minute but uploads only when a phone reconnects is continuous monitoring, but not continuous remote visibility. Specify:

- maximum permitted alert latency where coverage exists;
- required memory during outages;
- reconnection/backfill behavior;
- satellite availability requirement by route class;
- ownership and exportability of raw data;
- minimum data-retention period;
- API access and cybersecurity controls.

---

# 9. Procurement decision

## 9.1 Recommended route segmentation

### Tier 1: high-volume trunk routes

Use an active, self-powered reefer when:

- the load is large enough to utilize the vehicle efficiently;
- multiple pallets or tens of thousands of doses move on a fixed schedule;
- door openings can be controlled;
- a qualified maintenance network and rescue plan exist.

Select between Thermo King and Carrier through a loaded operational trial and a five-year bid, not brochure claims alone.

### Tier 2: regional and last-mile routes

Use WHO-prequalified passive boxes when:

- the shipment is below approximately one active-vehicle economic load;
- the route has weak cellular or maintenance coverage;
- arrival delays are likely;
- delivery is to an off-grid facility;
- the shipment may transfer between vehicle, boat or motorcycle.

The precise threshold should be derived from local vehicle prices, but the illustrative 6,000-dose case strongly favors passive transport.

### Tier 3: off-grid facilities

Install solar direct-drive refrigerators or PCM-conditioning equipment at selected remote hubs. Use those hubs to:

- maintain buffer stock;
- condition packs;
- support outreach carriers;
- provide rescue storage during breakdowns.

### Tier 4: contingency

Carry or stage long-range passive boxes along active routes. A contingency plan should identify how many doses can be transferred, where conditioned packs are held, and how quickly another vehicle can arrive.

## 9.2 Preferred active supplier by criterion

- **Pharmaceutical validation and documented telematics:** Thermo King advantage.
- **Published platform fuel-efficiency improvement and reduced mechanical complexity:** Carrier advantage.
- **Evidence of support in the named West African cities:** Carrier advantage in Accra/Tema, Lagos and Dakar; both uncertain in Abidjan.
- **Published absolute fuel figure:** Thermo King advantage.
- **Native satellite:** no demonstrated advantage; specify third-party integration.
- **WHO prequalification:** neither refrigeration-unit brand should be assumed compliant by itself; evaluate the completed vehicle against E002.

## 9.3 Suggested award structure

A prudent award would avoid single-supplier dependence:

- one framework lot for WHO-qualified active refrigerated vehicles;
- one lot for five-year maintenance and emergency recovery by city;
- one lot for telematics, independent loggers and satellite integration;
- one lot for WHO-PQS passive boxes and coolant packs;
- one lot for solar direct-drive/PCM hubs;
- optional second-source active equipment where fleet size justifies it.

Splitting refrigeration hardware and monitoring into interoperable lots also prevents lock-in, provided system responsibilities are clearly assigned.

---

# 10. Required acceptance tests

Before final selection, run both active finalists on the same test route and payload.

## Active vehicle test

1. Pre-cool to the approved loading temperature.
2. Load representative thermal mass using the proposed pallet arrangement.
3. Place calibrated probes at mapped hot and cold points.
4. Run at least 12 hours, preferably 24.
5. Include midday stationary operation.
6. Open the door for a controlled interval.
7. Simulate cellular loss and verify local recording/backfill.
8. Record fuel consumed by the reefer separately from the truck.
9. Confirm alarm transmission and escalation.
10. Shut down the unit briefly under an approved protocol to test recovery.
11. Review all data as a GDP/quality release exercise.
12. Repeat at the highest practicable ambient condition.

## Passive-box test

1. Condition coolant packs exactly according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
2. Load the actual vaccine packaging or representative thermal mass.
3. Place calibrated loggers at expected hot and cold points.
4. Test at least the longest route plus a 100% delay margin.
5. Test freeze risk as well as heat exposure.
6. Include realistic handling and one controlled opening if the route requires it.
7. Verify smartphone upload, offline recording and backfill.
8. Repeat after boxes have undergone field handling to detect seal or insulation degradation.

---

# Final conclusion

For 12-hour journeys with no electricity, all three solution classes can be technically suitable, but their risk profiles differ:

- **Thermo King** offers a robust independent diesel platform, an explicit fuel-consumption figure, a 2,000-hour maintenance interval and the strongest pharmaceutical-specific telematics documentation. Its weakness for this procurement is the lack of conclusively verified authorized maintenance coverage in Accra, Lagos and Abidjan from the available evidence.

- **Carrier Transicold** offers comparable self-powered capability, published +55°C performance, a newer high-efficiency architecture and the strongest currently identifiable service presence in Accra/Tema, Lagos and Dakar. Its claimed fuel savings are against legacy Carrier equipment, and an absolute local fuel rate must be established by trial.

- **WHO-prequalified passive cold boxes** offer the highest inherent off-grid reliability and directly documented cold lives of roughly 132–146 hours in the cited products. They are the preferred economic and technical solution for small shipments and difficult last-mile routes, but require rigorous coolant-pack preparation, freeze prevention and box-level monitoring.

The recommended procurement is therefore a **hybrid network**: qualified active reefers for consolidated trunk transport; long-range freeze-free passive boxes for regional, last-mile and emergency use; solar direct-drive/PCM equipment at selected off-grid nodes; and dual-path monitoring combining cellular data with local storage and satellite capability on critical routes. Final supplier selection should be driven by loaded route trials, completed-vehicle WHO qualification, named four-city maintenance commitments and bid-based cost per successfully delivered—not merely dispatched—dose.

final.content:
COMMERCIAL KITCHEN SOLUTIONS FOR SINGAPORE, BANGKOK, MANILA, AND JAKARTA

Executive conclusion

The chain should standardize a regional kitchen architecture and performance specification rather than force every cooking process onto one manufacturer.

The strongest practical configuration is:

1. Core programmable cooking: RATIONAL iCombi Pro or an equivalent high-volume combi platform for roasting, steaming, baking, regeneration, batch grilling, and production scheduling.
2. Modular cookline and induction: Electrolux Professional therma line for boiling, sautéing, griddling, and lower-heat-load induction work.
3. High-output Asian cooking: Nayati gas or induction wok stations, particularly in Jakarta and where authentic “wok hei” is required.
4. Tandoor: a separately approved gas or electric commercial tandoor, installed as a specialist module with local spare clay liners and burner/electrical support. The evidence does not show one tandoor manufacturer with a verified service network in all four cities.
5. Ventilation: engineered Type I grease exhaust with demand-controlled kitchen ventilation, variable-speed exhaust and make-up air, grease filtration, and conditioned/dehumidified replacement air. Halton M.A.R.V.E.L. is the best-documented regional-design candidate in the evidence, but installation and statutory sign-off should be performed by licensed local contractors.
6. Warewashing: Hobart where local service is contractually confirmed; its own Singapore operation and Bangkok office/spares center are verified.
7. Regional fabrication and value option: Nayati for stainless-steel fabrication and selected cooking/refrigeration/washing equipment, with especially strong logistics in Indonesia.

No supplier examined has sufficiently documented, city-level coverage for every category in all four markets. A dual-source strategy is therefore safer than a single-OEM award:

- Regional premium platform: Electrolux Professional plus RATIONAL.
- Regional Asian/value platform: Nayati.
- Specialist systems: Halton/local ventilation integrator, Hobart warewashing, and an approved tandoor vendor.

The electricity-cost hierarchy supports the strongest efficiency measures in Singapore, Manila, and Bangkok, while Jakarta’s lower electricity tariff and Nayati’s domestic manufacturing/service position make it the best market for a more capital-efficient Nayati-led package. A cross-country 2025 comparison cited effective commercial/industrial rates of approximately US$0.238/kWh in Singapore, US$0.128 in Thailand, US$0.1215 for the standard Meralco case in the Philippines, and US$0.077 in Indonesia. These are useful directional comparisons but are not restaurant quotations and may differ in tax, voltage, demand-charge, and procurement treatment (https://meralcomain.s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/2026-02/positioning_the_philippines_for_hyperscale_data_center_growth.pdf).

1. Recommended regional equipment standard

1.1 Standard production backbone

Use programmable combi ovens as the common production backbone in all four cities. They are suited to high-volume, multi-cuisine production because one platform can handle steaming, roasting, baking, regeneration, and many grill-like batch processes while storing standardized cooking programs.

RATIONAL states that its iCombi Pro can save “up to 70%” of energy against the comparison used in its own example, reducing monthly consumption from 5,000 kWh to 1,500 kWh. It also claims up to 50% less time, more than 30% less space, up to 20% more raw-ingredient yield, and up to 95% less fat and oil. These are manufacturer claims rather than independently verified restaurant results and should be validated in a menu-specific trial (https://www.rational-online.com/en_us/icombi-pro/cost-savings/index.php).

Its cleaning system is a material operational advantage for a chain. RATIONAL’s iCareSystem recognizes the degree of soiling, proposes a cleaning program and chemical quantity, and offers light, medium, strong, fast, water-only, and rinse programs. Eco mode uses less water and care chemical but takes longer than normal mode (https://www.rational-online.com/media/downloads/anwendungshinweise/autodose/rational-anwendungshinweise-icombi-pro-wa62-en-gb.pdf).

Recommended deployment per major production kitchen:

- At least two combi units rather than one oversized unit, to provide redundancy and separate allergen or production streams.
- Standardized program library controlled by corporate culinary operations.
- Water treatment sized to local water quality.
- Automatic cleaning, error reporting, and preventive-maintenance logs.
- Separate dedicated high-heat modules for wok, tandoor, and open-flame grilling; a combi oven should not be treated as a complete substitute for those techniques.

1.2 Modular European/international cookline

Electrolux Professional therma line is suitable as the common modular range where the chain prioritizes precise control, lower kitchen heat, and ease of cleaning.

Its free-zone induction system offers adaptive power and temperature management, 16 displayed temperature or power settings, and up to three stored settings per zone. The range is available in modular 800, 850, and 900 mm formats for heavy-duty kitchens (https://www.electroluxprofessional.com/commercial-kitchen-equipment/cooking-ranges/thermaline-modular-80-85-90/).

A documented therma line induction wok is rated at 5 kW, 400 V three-phase, with a 300 mm zone in a 500-by-900 mm module (https://tools.electroluxprofessional.com/Mirror/Doc/MAD3/Food/Electrolux%20Professional/English/589034_thermaline_90_1_zone_induction_wok_1_side.pdf?version=1781726866). Electrolux describes the smooth glass-ceramic surface as not directly heated, reducing food burn-on; it also cites immediate full power, low heat dissipation to the kitchen, overheat protection, and front access to major components (https://www.electroluxprofessional.com/gb/commercial-kitchen-equipment/cooking-ranges/thermaline-cooking-ranges/modular-cooking-range-line-thermaline-90-2-zone-induction-wok-and-plate-1-side-589038/).

These characteristics are attractive in tropical, air-conditioned kitchens because less appliance heat enters the room and less grease burns onto the surface. However, the documented 5 kW induction wok should be chef-tested against the chain’s required pan size, batch weight, recovery time, and “wok hei.” It is not directly equivalent to a 28 kW gas wok.

1.3 High-output wok stations

Nayati has the strongest documented Asian cooking range among the reviewed suppliers. Its lineup includes single- and double-burner gas woks, turbo woks, induction woks, soup-boiler combinations, premix-engine burners, deep-drawn wok decks, wall-mounted water faucets, and knee-operated controls (https://www.nayati.com/product/asian-cooking/).

The documented NGTL 6-65 SO is a 28 kW LPG/LNG single-burner tabletop wok, compared with 5 kW for the documented Electrolux induction wok. It uses an AISI 304 stainless-steel top panel and cast-iron wok ring (https://www.nayati.com/product/ngtl-6-65-so/).

This is not an efficiency comparison—gas input and electric input cannot be compared one-for-one without measured pan efficiency—but it does demonstrate the very different heat-intensity categories:

- Electrolux induction wok: 5 kW electrical input.
- Nayati gas wok: 28 kW fuel input.
- Input ratio: 28 ÷ 5 = 5.6.

The gas unit’s much higher input makes it the safer starting point for high-throughput Cantonese, Thai, Indonesian, or other flame-intensive stir-frying. The induction unit is better where lower room heat, cleanability, precision, and avoiding combustion products are more important.

Recommended standard:

- Specify gas turbo/high-output woks only for menu stations that pass a chef-defined high-flame requirement.
- Use induction woks for sauces, lower-volume stir-fry, finishing, vegetarian/allergen stations, and locations where gas or exhaust capacity is constrained.
- Require flame-failure protection, accessible shutoff, removable drip trays, deep-drawn decks, and water-saving faucets.
- Place gas wok banks under independently controlled heavy-duty hood zones.
- Avoid continuously running deck-water cooling unless the appliance specifically requires it; water and drainage cost should be measured during trials.

1.4 Grills, griddles, and teppanyaki

For flat-top and teppanyaki production, Nayati offers gas- and electric-powered units in 1.2 m and 1.5 m widths. Its documented design has a 20 mm ferritic-steel plate, independent heating zones, and surface temperatures up to 250°C (https://www.nayati.com/the-new-teppanyaki-series/).

For standardization:

- Electric griddles or induction planchas are preferable for breakfast, sandwiches, seafood, and moderate-volume meat production because they simplify cleaning and reduce combustion heat.
- Gas charbroilers remain appropriate where live-flame flavor is a core product attribute.
- Heavy grease-producing charbroilers should receive the highest exhaust allocation and a dedicated grease-management plan.
- Combi ovens can absorb batch roasting and some grill-mark production, reducing the number of open grills operating during off-peak periods.

1.5 Tandoor ovens

Tandoor is the weakest category for a single regional service contract. The evidence shows manufacturers exporting clay, stainless-steel, gas, charcoal, and electric tandoors from India, but it does not establish a staffed service organization in all four target cities.

In Singapore, a local reseller lists commercial tandoors at approximately S$1,500–S$1,850 (https://www.buzzsgp.com/product/commercial-tandoor/). Export-oriented suppliers also advertise gas, electric, stainless-steel, coal, and clay tandoors, but their listed contacts are in India rather than the four target cities (for example, https://mohanlaltandoor.com/singapore/).

Recommended approach:

- Standardize the functional specification, footprint, connection, insulation, operating temperature, burner train, safety controls, outer stainless-steel casing, and hood duty—not necessarily the manufacturer.
- Prefer gas tandoors for authentic high-volume naan and kebab production where gas and exhaust are available.
- Consider electric tandoors where combustion restrictions, staff comfort, or ventilation capacity outweigh fuel cost.
- Avoid charcoal in enclosed mall or tower locations unless explicitly approved by the landlord, fire authority, environmental authority, and insurer.
- Hold spare clay pots/liners locally because the liner is a wear component that cannot normally wait for an international shipment.
- Require a documented liner-replacement method, burner/electrical component list, and training package.
- Treat the tandoor as a heavy thermal and grease/smoke load when sizing the hood; do not rely on general room ventilation.

2. Supplier comparison

2.1 Electrolux Professional

Best use:
- Premium modular range.
- Induction and lower-heat-load cooking.
- General cooking, refrigeration, dishwashing, laundry, and beverage categories under a broad corporate platform.
- Sites where a multinational customer-care framework is valuable.

Strengths:
- The therma line platform is explicitly designed for demanding, heavy-duty kitchens and offers modular 800/850/900 mm configurations (https://www.electroluxprofessional.com/commercial-kitchen-equipment/cooking-ranges/thermaline-modular-80-85-90/).
- Induction provides smooth surfaces, immediate response, low heat dissipation, and front service access (https://www.electroluxprofessional.com/gb/commercial-kitchen-equipment/cooking-ranges/thermaline-cooking-ranges/modular-cooking-range-line-thermaline-90-2-zone-induction-wok-and-plate-1-side-589038/).
- Electrolux reports 1,900 authorized service centers and worldwide spare-parts delivery in 24–48 hours, describing its network as its “most extensive” customer-care network. That is a corporate global claim and does not guarantee a 24–48-hour repair at each restaurant (https://www.electroluxprofessional.com/sg/customer-care/).
- A directly verified Singapore office is at 8 Commonwealth Lane, with a Singapore customer-care contact (https://www.electroluxprofessional.com/sg/contact-us/).

Limitations:
- City-specific staffed coverage in Bangkok, Manila, and Jakarta was not established by the collected evidence.
- The documented 5 kW induction wok may not meet all high-output Asian-menu requirements.
- Premium imported equipment may have higher capital and proprietary-parts costs.
- Contractual response times, technician locations, and country-level spare stocks must be verified before award.

Assessment:
- Preferred regional modular cookline candidate, subject to proof of service in all four cities.
- Pair with Nayati or another high-output wok supplier and a specialist tandoor.

2.2 RATIONAL

Best use:
- Programmable combi-steaming and production standardization.
- High-volume batch cooking, regeneration, steaming, roasting, baking, and menu flexibility.
- Reducing dependence on multiple conventional ovens, steamers, and some grills.

Strengths:
- Automatic cleaning and descaling with soil-based program recommendations (https://www.rational-online.com/media/downloads/anwendungshinweise/autodose/rational-anwendungshinweise-icombi-pro-wa62-en-gb.pdf).
- Manufacturer-claimed reduction from 5,000 to 1,500 kWh per month in its comparison example (https://www.rational-online.com/en_us/icombi-pro/cost-savings/index.php).
- RATIONAL reports more than 1,200 certified service partners worldwide and provides a Singapore contact number and service-partner database. The page labels this count “as at August 2026,” so the timing and current local list should be confirmed during procurement (https://www.rational-online.com/en_sg/customercare/rational-service-partner/).
- Indonesia has an identified distributor and service partner, Lotus Food Services, with locations in the Jakarta/Bekasi area, Surabaya, Bali, and Malang (https://lotusfoodservices.co.id/rational).

Limitations:
- It is not a replacement for a high-flame wok, clay tandoor, or open chargrill.
- Bangkok- and Manila-specific partner locations were not established in the gathered evidence.
- Savings are manufacturer claims and depend on replacing the correct baseline equipment, utilization, loading, menu, and staff behavior.
- Automatic cleaning depends on proprietary consumables, correct water treatment, and disciplined daily operation.

Assessment:
- Recommended as the common regional production platform.
- Purchase only with two-unit redundancy at critical kitchens and a country-specific preventive-maintenance/spares agreement.

2.3 Nayati

Best use:
- High-output Asian cooking.
- Gas and induction woks.
- Teppanyaki/griddle equipment.
- Value-oriented stainless-steel and general kitchen packages.
- Indonesia, where manufacturing and service proximity are strongest.

Strengths:
- More than 40 years of development and products spanning cooking, refrigeration, and dishwashing; equipment is designed and manufactured in Indonesia (https://www.nayati.com/).
- Broad wok selection, including high-output gas, turbo, induction, soup-warmer combinations, and ergonomic knee controls (https://www.nayati.com/product/asian-cooking/).
- The 28 kW documented gas wok is well aligned with high-intensity Asian production (https://www.nayati.com/product/ngtl-6-65-so/).
- Nayati lists its head office/manufacturing base in Semarang and dealer offices in Jakarta, Surabaya, Bandung, Denpasar, and Semarang (https://www.nayati.com/asking-for-information/sales-contact/).
- A Singapore corporate presence is reported, but the evidence for it is from business-directory and industry-directory listings rather than Nayati’s current official service locator.

Limitations:
- Equivalent verified service offices in Bangkok and Manila were not identified.
- Product-by-product efficiency certification and lifecycle cost need to be compared with premium imported brands.
- For multi-country standardization, parts interchangeability and software/controls may be less unified than a single premium global platform.

Assessment:
- Preferred wok and Indonesia package supplier.
- Strong candidate for regional stainless fabrication and selected value-engineered equipment.
- Before regional award, require named Bangkok and Manila technicians, parts inventories, and response-time commitments.

2.4 Halton

Best use:
- Engineered kitchen exhaust.
- Demand-controlled kitchen ventilation.
- Multi-hood zoning and tropical HVAC-load reduction.

Strengths:
- M.A.R.V.E.L. adjusts exhaust and supply air in response to real-time cooking activity and can control individual hoods or zones independently (https://www.halton.com/products/marvel-dckv-demand-controlled-ventilation-na-en/).
- Halton states typical ventilation-energy reductions of 30–50%, depending on application (same source).
- Another Halton description states that airflow reduction can reach 64% and highlights reductions in fan power and the energy used to condition replacement air (https://www.halton.com/technology/marvel-energy-saving-technology/).
- The controls can distinguish equipment states such as off, heating, and cooking, and can regulate both exhaust and replacement-air fans (https://www.halton.com/app/uploads/2020/08/Halton_M.A.R.V.E.L.Brochure_BR-002.pdf).

Limitations:
- Savings are application-dependent manufacturer figures, not guarantees.
- Hood capture and containment must never be sacrificed for savings.
- Sensor placement, commissioning, minimum airflow, fire interlocks, grease loading, and local code approval determine actual performance.
- The gathered evidence did not establish a staffed Halton office in every target city.

Assessment:
- Preferred basis of design for regional ventilation controls.
- Procure through a performance specification and local licensed installer, with witnessed smoke/capture testing and trend-log verification.

2.5 Hobart

Best use:
- Commercial dishwashing and warewashing.
- High-volume rack, hood-type, and automated wash systems.

Strengths:
- Hobart has a directly verified Singapore company and service operation at 158 Kallang Way (https://www.hobart.com.sg/technical-service/overview).
- It says service partners hold original spare parts and receive regular training.
- Hobart Thailand has an Indochina office and spare-parts center in Bangkok’s Thai CC Tower (https://www.hobartthailand.com/product/pro_cat.php).
- Hobart offers equipment ranging from small undercounter units to large semi- and fully automatic warewashing systems.

Limitations:
- Manila- and Jakarta-specific service operations were not established in the gathered evidence.
- Water treatment, local chemical support, rinse temperature, and rack-flow design still require local validation.

Assessment:
- Strong choice in Singapore and Bangkok.
- Conditional choice in Manila and Jakarta pending named service partners and local parts stock.

2.6 Specialist tandoor manufacturers

Best use:
- Dedicated Indian-menu production where clay-wall baking and radiant high heat are essential.

Strengths:
- Available in clay, stainless-steel, gas, electric, charcoal, and portable formats.
- Singapore has at least one local reseller listing commercial units at S$1,500–S$1,850 (https://www.buzzsgp.com/product/commercial-tandoor/).

Limitations:
- Evidence mainly points to Indian exporters, not a unified Southeast Asian service organization.
- Clay liners, burners, valves, insulation, and controls may not be standardized.
- Fire and ventilation acceptance can vary significantly by location.

Assessment:
- Do not award a four-country tandoor contract without pilot testing and local support proof.
- Standardize technical requirements and approve one or two models per country.

3. City-by-city solution

3.1 Singapore

Recommended configuration

- RATIONAL combi pair for the production backbone.
- Electrolux induction range and induction wok for lower- to medium-intensity production.
- One or more Nayati high-output gas wok stations only where the menu requires live-flame stir-fry.
- Gas or electric tandoor under dedicated heavy-duty exhaust.
- Halton-style demand-controlled exhaust with carefully conditioned make-up air.
- Hobart warewashing.
- Highest emphasis on energy monitoring, hood commissioning, accessible duct cleaning, and fire compliance.

Why

Singapore has the highest directional electricity cost among the four markets. EMA reports that regulated tariffs averaged S$0.281/kWh from July 2024 through June 2025, down from S$0.295/kWh, with energy cost accounting for S$0.215/kWh or 76.2% of the regulated tariff in the first half of 2025 (https://www.ema.gov.sg/resources/singapore-energy-statistics/chapter5). Commercial customers may procure electricity differently, so S$0.281/kWh is a planning benchmark rather than a restaurant quotation.

Ventilation and fire requirements are also the clearest and most prescriptive among the four reviewed cities:

- A restaurant or hotel kitchen’s cooking-area mechanical exhaust must be independent of systems serving other parts of the building.
- Hood and duct clearance from unprotected combustible material is 500 mm.
- Exhaust must discharge directly outdoors and at least 5 m from air-intake openings.
- No fire damper may be fitted in a kitchen exhaust duct.
- Ducts outside the kitchen require the prescribed fire-rated protection or enclosure (Singapore Civil Defence Force Fire Code: https://www.scdf.gov.sg/fire-safety-services-listing/fire-code-2023/table-of-content/chapter-7-mechanical-ventilation-smoke-control-systems/clause-7.1-air-conditioning-and-mechanical-ventilation-systems).

The National Environment Agency also requires kitchen exhaust fumes to discharge above the roof where practical and not face adjacent buildings; where roof discharge is impractical, an alternate outdoor discharge point must satisfy siting criteria (https://www.nea.gov.sg/docs/default-source/air-quality/clarifications-on-siting-of-kitchen-exhaust-outlets-cooling-towers.pdf).

Singapore’s SS 553 ventilation standard includes kitchen-exhaust air-cleaning guidance for medium and heavy cooking, including baffle/cyclone filters, ultraviolet treatment, electrostatic precipitation, multistage media filters, activated carbon, ozone, and minimum maintenance frequencies. The standard itself should be purchased and applied by the design engineer rather than inferred from its preview (https://www.singaporestandardseshop.sg/Product/GetPdf?fileName=260206091409SS+553-2026+Preview.pdf&pdtid=c417dc9a-0cca-4562-a19e-b076c9a4957e).

Operational priority

Because every cubic metre of exhausted conditioned air has to be replaced with warm, humid outside air, Singapore is the strongest case for zoned demand control. Induction should be used wherever culinary output permits, while gas should be reserved for cooking processes that demonstrably need flame or extreme recovery.

3.2 Bangkok

Recommended configuration

- RATIONAL combi backbone.
- Mixed Electrolux induction/general range and Nayati gas wok line.
- Gas tandoor where the Indian menu is material; electric where the site’s gas or flue restrictions dominate.
- Demand-controlled hood zones, with particular attention to peak-demand management.
- Hobart warewashing, supported by the verified Bangkok office and spare-parts center.
- Local mechanical engineer to reconcile Bangkok food-premises rules, building/fire requirements, EIT practice, and landlord criteria.

Why

Bangkok’s Metropolitan Electricity Authority tariff structure includes both energy and demand charges, making simultaneous electric cooking loads important.

For the published Type 5 “specific business” tariff applicable to hotels and other lodging businesses with demand of at least 30 kW, below-12-kV service is listed at:

- Normal tariff energy charge: THB3.1751/kWh.
- Demand charge: THB276.64/kW per month.
- Service charge: THB312.24 per month.
- VAT and the separate Ft fuel-adjustment charge are excluded (https://www.mea.or.th/en/our-services/service-rates/other/-xrkDjPOMaxJO).

The same page lists time-of-use energy charges below 12 kV of THB4.3297/kWh on-peak and THB2.6369/kWh off-peak, with an on-peak demand charge of THB210/kW per month. The 2025 Ft was THB0.3672/kWh from January–April, THB0.1972 from May–August, and THB0.1572 from September–December (https://www.mea.or.th/en/our-services/service-rates/ft/statistics).

Important limitation: Type 5 is a published hotel/lodging tariff and should not be assumed to apply to every stand-alone restaurant. A specific MEA tariff quotation is necessary.

Bangkok’s food-establishment regulation distinguishes premises over 200 m², which require a licence, from premises of no more than 200 m², which use a notification certificate. The cited regulation is in Thai and dates from 2003, so current district-level interpretation should be confirmed (https://foodsanitation.bangkok.go.th/assets/uploads/document/document/20210208_37913.pdf).

Operational priority

Bangkok should not become an all-electric kitchen without a load and demand-charge study. High-output gas woks may reduce electrical peak demand, while induction remains attractive for reduced room heat and cleaning. Sequence combi preheating, dishwashing booster operation, and electric tandoor start-up rather than allowing all major loads to peak together.

3.3 Manila

Recommended configuration

- RATIONAL combi backbone, with two-unit redundancy and local parts commitment.
- Electrolux induction where local service can be contracted.
- Nayati or locally supported gas woks for high-output Asian cooking.
- Gas tandoor or tested electric tandoor, depending site utilities.
- Type I grease hoods with at least the statutory room-air requirement and separate capture calculations for each appliance.
- Hobart only if a named Philippine service partner and spare inventory are contractually established.

Why

Meralco reported a 2024 average commercial retail electricity rate of PHP10.14/kWh, compared with PHP10.36 in 2023. Its overall average rate was PHP10.54/kWh in 2024 (https://www.meralco.com.ph/sites/default/files/inline-files/6b753bf10b504437321294f48fe6e789.pdf). The May 2025 residential rate was PHP12.2628/kWh, but that figure should not be used as a commercial-kitchen tariff (https://company.meralco.com.ph/news-and-advisories/lower-rates-may-2025).

The Philippine National Building Code requires artificial ventilation to prevent excessive accumulation of hot or polluted air. It specifies at least:

- Three air changes per hour for restaurants generally.
- Ten air changes per hour for hotel or restaurant kitchens above grade.

The kitchen requirement is therefore more than three times the general restaurant rate: 10 ÷ 3 = 3.33 (https://source.gosupra.com/widget/provision/71488).

This minimum whole-room air-change figure is not a substitute for an appliance-specific grease hood. Professional guidance summarizing commercial-cooking requirements states that equipment producing smoke or grease-laden vapour must have an exhaust system covering hoods, grease removal, ducts, fans, fire extinguishing, and associated components (https://psimph.org/ventilation-control-and-fire-protection-of-commercial-cooking-operations/). Fire-system design must be checked against the current Bureau of Fire Protection rules; the collected official source is the 2019 revised implementing rules for the Fire Code (https://bfp.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/RA9514-RIRR-rev-2019.pdf).

Operational priority

Given Manila’s relatively high electricity cost, combi utilization, induction efficiency, automatic shutdown, and demand-controlled ventilation have strong value. Nevertheless, gas may remain preferable for high-output woks and tandoors if the site’s fuel, fire, and exhaust arrangements support it. The chain should not accept “10 ACH” alone as proof that a wok, charbroiler, or tandoor hood will capture smoke and grease.

3.4 Jakarta

Recommended configuration

- Nayati-led Asian cookline and stainless-steel package.
- RATIONAL combi backbone supported by the identified Jakarta/Bekasi-area distributor.
- Electrolux induction only where lifecycle and support terms outperform the domestic alternative.
- Nayati gas or induction woks depending concept.
- Locally supportable gas/electric tandoor.
- Ventilation designed to the new SNI 6572-5:2025 commercial-kitchen standard.
- Warewashing award based on local service validation; do not assume Singapore or Bangkok Hobart coverage automatically extends to Jakarta.

Why

Jakarta has the strongest documented local Nayati support. Nayati manufactures in Semarang and lists a Jakarta dealer office as well as offices in Surabaya, Bandung, Denpasar, and Semarang (https://www.nayati.com/asking-for-information/sales-contact/). RATIONAL’s Indonesian distributor also lists an office in the Jakarta/Bekasi area, plus Surabaya, Bali, and Malang (https://lotusfoodservices.co.id/rational).

PLN’s published fourth-quarter 2025 business tariffs list:

- B-1 and B-2 business customers, 450–200,000 VA: IDR1,444.70/kWh.
- B-3 above 200 kVA: IDR1,035.78/kWh for the period described, with time-of-use metering applicable to large customers (https://web.pln.co.id/media/2025/12/tarif-listrik).

PLN states that tariffs are governed by the applicable Ministry of Energy regulation and adjusted according to macroeconomic inputs; the company also reported that third-quarter 2025 nonsubsidized tariffs were held unchanged (https://web.pln.co.id/cms/media/siaran-pers/2025/06/jaga-daya-beli-pemerintah-putuskan-tarif-listrik-triwulan-iii-tetap/).

Indonesia adopted SNI 6572-5:2025, “Design procedure for building ventilation system—Part 5: Commercial kitchen,” on 6 February 2025. It is a 59-page revision replacing the commercial-kitchen-relevant aspects of the older SNI 03-6572-2001 framework (https://pesta.bsn.go.id/produk/detail/657252025-sni6572-5:2025). The project mechanical engineer should purchase and apply the complete standard.

Indonesia’s catering hygiene regulation requires artificial ventilation when natural ventilation is insufficient and requires dirty-air or smoke discharge not to disturb the surroundings. It also calls for separate handwashing and equipment-washing facilities with smooth, easily cleaned surfaces (https://pelayanan.jakarta.go.id/download/regulasi/permen-kesehatan-nomor-1096-menkes-per-vi-2011-tentang-higiene-sanitasi-jasaboga.pdf). Restaurant-specific hygiene rules also require kitchen, dining, food-storage, sanitation, equipment, and processing controls; the precise currently applicable rule and local inspection practice should be confirmed because the collected sources include regulations from 1989, 2003, and 2011 with different scopes (for example, https://pdf2.sumselgo.id/ppiddinkes/unggah/71282883-KMK%20No.%201098%20ttg%20Persyaratan%20Hygiene%20Sanitasi%20Rumah%20Makan%20Dan%20Restoran.pdf).

Operational priority

Jakarta offers the clearest opportunity for a locally manufactured Nayati package, shorter domestic logistics, and lower energy cost. It should nevertheless retain the same corporate controls, hygiene geometry, cleaning schedules, hood-performance testing, and data monitoring used in the other cities.

4. Ventilation design for tropical high-volume kitchens

4.1 Required architecture

All four kitchens should use the same functional design:

- Heavy-duty grease hoods over gas woks, tandoors, charbroilers, fryers, and other smoke/grease sources.
- Separate hood zones for high-load and lower-load appliances.
- Listed baffle or cyclone grease filters that staff can remove without tools.
- Exhaust ducts with access panels at changes of direction and other cleaning points.
- Variable-speed exhaust and supply fans.
- Demand controls using temperature and, where suitable, optical or appliance-status sensing.
- Interlocked make-up air.
- Fire suppression and fuel/electric shutdown interlocks.
- Slight negative kitchen pressure relative to dining/public areas, without excessive door drafts.
- Conditioned or at least tempered/dehumidified make-up air, delivered so it does not disrupt hood capture.
- Monitoring of fan status, speed, faults, operating hours, and abnormal overnight operation.
- Commissioning by smoke visualization and capture/containment testing under worst-case appliance operation.

4.2 Why demand control matters

Commercial kitchens do not cook at full load all day. Halton’s M.A.R.V.E.L. platform adjusts airflow to actual equipment activity and can independently control multiple hoods or hood sections. Halton cites typical ventilation-related energy savings of 30–50%, with outcomes depending on the application (https://www.halton.com/products/marvel-dckv-demand-controlled-ventilation-na-en/).

The U.S. Department of Energy’s guidance similarly explains that demand-controlled kitchen ventilation saves fan and make-up-air conditioning energy by matching hood exhaust and incoming outside air to cooking activity; actual savings vary with location, operating hours, features, and system cost (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1755519).

A CaptiveAire case study illustrates the fan-law opportunity: an 18% average fan-speed reduction produced approximately 44% measured fan-energy savings over three months, with total reported savings of US$1,498 or 39% in that case. It is a single North American case and not a Southeast Asian forecast, but it demonstrates why modest speed reductions can materially reduce fan electricity (https://www.captiveaire.com/catalogcontent/electriccontrols/doc/CASLink_case-study_BFC.pdf).

4.3 Tropical-climate design implications

In Singapore, Bangkok, Manila, and Jakarta, exhaust replacement air is generally warm and humid. Excess exhaust therefore creates three simultaneous burdens:

- Fan electricity.
- Sensible cooling to reduce air temperature.
- Latent cooling/dehumidification to remove moisture.

The regional specification should consequently:

- Capture contaminants at the lowest airflow that passes witnessed testing.
- Prevent four-way ceiling diffusers or make-up jets from blowing across the hood face.
- Introduce replacement air at low velocity.
- Separate dining-room comfort air from dirty-kitchen exhaust.
- Use variable speed rather than constant full-speed exhaust.
- Insulate cold ducts and pipes sufficiently to prevent condensation.
- Trend kitchen temperature and humidity as well as fan speed.
- Keep minimum safe airflow when gas or solid-fuel appliances are operating.
- Lock out cooking fuel or appliances if exhaust fails, as required by the applicable design and authority.

5. Energy-cost comparison and explicit savings illustrations

5.1 Directional cross-market comparison

A 2025 regional comparison cited the following effective commercial/industrial rates:

- Singapore: US$0.238/kWh.
- Thailand: US$0.128/kWh.
- Philippines, Meralco standard case: US$0.1215/kWh.
- Indonesia: US$0.077/kWh.

Source: https://meralcomain.s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/2026-02/positioning_the_philippines_for_hyperscale_data_center_growth.pdf.

For a common 100,000 kWh annual load:

- Singapore: 100,000 × US$0.238 = US$23,800/year.
- Thailand: 100,000 × US$0.128 = US$12,800/year.
- Philippines: 100,000 × US$0.1215 = US$12,150/year.
- Indonesia: 100,000 × US$0.077 = US$7,700/year.

Singapore’s cost in this comparison is:

- 23,800 ÷ 7,700 = 3.09 times Indonesia’s.
- 23,800 ÷ 12,800 = 1.86 times Thailand’s.
- 23,800 ÷ 12,150 = 1.96 times the Philippines’.

Uncertainty: these are broad commercial/industrial comparisons rather than matched restaurant tariffs. Tax, contracted supply, service voltage, demand, power factor, time-of-use allocation, and subsidies can change the result. Capital decisions should use twelve months of actual or landlord-provided bills for each proposed premises.

5.2 Local-currency planning examples

Singapore

Using EMA’s July 2024–June 2025 regulated average of S$0.281/kWh:

100,000 kWh × S$0.281 = S$28,100/year.

Source: https://www.ema.gov.sg/resources/singapore-energy-statistics/chapter5.

Manila

Using Meralco’s 2024 average commercial rate of PHP10.14/kWh:

100,000 kWh × PHP10.14 = PHP1,014,000/year.

Source: https://www.meralco.com.ph/sites/default/files/inline-files/6b753bf10b504437321294f48fe6e789.pdf.

Jakarta

Using PLN B-2’s published IDR1,444.70/kWh:

100,000 kWh × IDR1,444.70 = IDR144,470,000/year.

Using the separately listed B-3 energy figure of IDR1,035.78/kWh:

100,000 kWh × IDR1,035.78 = IDR103,578,000/year.

Source: https://web.pln.co.id/media/2025/12/tarif-listrik.

This excludes any other applicable billing components and assumes the customer qualifies for the cited class.

Bangkok hotel example

Using the below-12-kV Type 5 normal tariff and September–December 2025 Ft:

- Base energy: THB3.1751/kWh.
- Ft: THB0.1572/kWh.
- Combined energy rate before VAT: 3.1751 + 0.1572 = THB3.3323/kWh.
- Annual energy cost for 100,000 kWh: 100,000 × 3.3323 = THB333,230.

If monthly billed demand is 100 kW:

- Annual demand cost: 100 kW × THB276.64/kW/month × 12 = THB331,968.
- Annual service charge: THB312.24 × 12 = THB3,746.88.
- Illustrative total before VAT: 333,230 + 331,968 + 3,746.88 = THB668,944.88.

Source: https://www.mea.or.th/en/our-services/service-rates/other/-xrkDjPOMaxJO and https://www.mea.or.th/en/our-services/service-rates/ft/statistics.

This example is material because demand cost is almost as large as energy cost. It applies to the cited hotel/lodging Type 5 category, not automatically to every restaurant.

5.3 Combi-oven savings illustration

RATIONAL’s example reduces monthly electricity consumption from 5,000 to 1,500 kWh:

- Monthly saving: 5,000 − 1,500 = 3,500 kWh.
- Annual saving: 3,500 × 12 = 42,000 kWh.

Applying the directional 2025 US-dollar rates:

- Singapore: 42,000 × US$0.238 = US$9,996/year.
- Thailand: 42,000 × US$0.128 = US$5,376/year.
- Philippines: 42,000 × US$0.1215 = US$5,103/year.
- Indonesia: 42,000 × US$0.077 = US$3,234/year.

RATIONAL claim: https://www.rational-online.com/en_us/icombi-pro/cost-savings/index.php. Rate comparison: https://meralcomain.s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/2026-02/positioning_the_philippines_for_hyperscale_data_center_growth.pdf.

These values are scenarios, not promised savings. A valid trial must compare identical menu output, batch size, food yield, production hours, ventilation interaction, and cleaning energy.

5.4 Demand-controlled ventilation illustration

If conventional kitchen ventilation consumes 100,000 kWh/year and a DCKV system achieves Halton’s cited 30–50% typical ventilation-energy reduction:

- Low saving: 100,000 × 30% = 30,000 kWh/year.
- High saving: 100,000 × 50% = 50,000 kWh/year.

At the same directional country rates:

Singapore:
- 30,000 × US$0.238 = US$7,140/year.
- 50,000 × US$0.238 = US$11,900/year.

Thailand:
- 30,000 × US$0.128 = US$3,840/year.
- 50,000 × US$0.128 = US$6,400/year.

Philippines:
- 30,000 × US$0.1215 = US$3,645/year.
- 50,000 × US$0.1215 = US$6,075/year.

Indonesia:
- 30,000 × US$0.077 = US$2,310/year.
- 50,000 × US$0.077 = US$3,850/year.

This calculation covers electricity only. In tropical kitchens, reduced outside-air cooling and dehumidification could add savings, but no reliable site-specific cooling-load data were gathered, so that additional benefit is not quantified.

6. Cleaning, sanitation, and inspection readiness

6.1 Common equipment specification

To make inspection readiness consistent across all four markets, require:

- AISI 304 stainless steel on exposed work and splash surfaces, as demonstrated in the documented Nayati wok construction (https://www.nayati.com/product/ngtl-6-65-so/).
- Fully welded, polished, coved, or smoothly sealed joints.
- No exposed hollow sections, inaccessible grease traps, unsealed bolt penetrations, or raw absorbent materials in food areas.
- Removable pot supports, drip trays, filters, grease cups, and splash guards without specialist tools.
- Front access to service components; Electrolux specifically documents front access on its induction wok/plate module (https://www.electroluxprofessional.com/gb/commercial-kitchen-equipment/cooking-ranges/thermaline-cooking-ranges/modular-cooking-range-line-thermaline-90-2-zone-induction-wok-and-plate-1-side-589038/).
- Raised equipment on sealed plinths or hygienic legs/castors with sufficient cleaning access.
- Smooth glass-ceramic induction surfaces where culinary needs allow.
- Automatic oven washing with chemical-use records.
- Clearly separated handwashing, food preparation, pot washing, and warewashing flows.
- Adequate floor drains for wet-cleaned appliances without creating standing water.
- Color-coded tools and documented clean-as-you-go procedures.
- Hood-filter washing capacity sized to the number of filters in service.
- Posted daily, weekly, monthly, and quarterly cleaning schedules.
- Duct-cleaning access and contractor certificates.

6.2 City-specific inspection emphasis

Singapore:
- Independent kitchen exhaust, fire-rated duct provisions, outdoor discharge, intake separation, and no duct fire dampers are explicit concerns (SCDF source above).
- Exhaust siting and nuisance control are important under NEA guidance.
- Specify records for hood, filter, duct, fire-suppression, and automatic-cleaning maintenance.

Bangkok:
- Licensing differs around the 200 m² threshold in the cited Bangkok rule.
- Because the gathered public evidence is not sufficient to state every technical inspection criterion, have a Bangkok food-sanitation consultant review layout, wash facilities, drainage, pest exclusion, LPG arrangements, and exhaust before construction.

Manila:
- Demonstrate at least 10 room air changes per hour for restaurant kitchens where the cited code applies.
- Separately prove smoke and grease capture at each hood.
- Coordinate hood, duct, grease removal, and extinguishing arrangements with the Bureau of Fire Protection and local building official.

Jakarta:
- Apply SNI 6572-5:2025 through a qualified designer.
- Provide artificial ventilation where natural ventilation is inadequate.
- Ensure dirty-air/smoke discharge does not disturb surroundings.
- Provide separate hand- and equipment-washing facilities with smooth, cleanable surfaces, consistent with the cited catering hygiene regulation.

7. Service-network evaluation and procurement safeguards

Verified coverage from the gathered evidence is uneven:

Singapore:
- Electrolux Professional: direct Singapore office and customer-care contact.
- RATIONAL: Singapore service contact and global certified-partner database.
- Hobart: direct Singapore company and service operation.
- Nayati: reported Singapore presence, but current official service details should be reconfirmed.

Bangkok:
- Hobart: direct Thailand/Indochina office and spare-parts center.
- Other reviewed brands: city-level support not sufficiently evidenced and must be documented in bids.

Manila:
- No city-specific office or spare-parts center was established in the gathered evidence for the reviewed suppliers.
- This does not prove that support is absent; it means procurement must require proof rather than relying on global network statements.

Jakarta:
- Nayati: Jakarta dealer plus wider Indonesian dealer network and domestic factory.
- RATIONAL: identified distributor/service partner in the Jakarta/Bekasi area.
- Other reviewed brands: current city-level support should be confirmed.

Every regional framework agreement should require:

- Named legal service entity in each country.
- Technician count and base location.
- Normal and emergency response times.
- 24/7 escalation for critical equipment.
- First-time-fix and uptime reporting.
- Country-level critical-parts inventory.
- Maximum parts lead times.
- Preventive-maintenance frequency and checklist.
- Remote diagnostic capability where available.
- Staff training at opening and refresher training.
- Loaner or contingency plan for critical combi, warewash, and refrigeration failures.
- Standard warranty terms across countries.
- Fixed labor rates and travel-zone charges.
- Consumable availability and price protection.
- End-of-life software and electronics support.
- References from high-volume restaurants or hotels in each city.

Recommended critical spares held at each site or metropolitan depot include door gaskets, probes, fan belts where applicable, contactors, fuses, ignition components, thermocouples, wok burner jets, faucet cartridges, hood-controller sensors, VFD cooling fans, dishwasher wash/rinse arms, chemical pumps, and tandoor liners.

8. Final supplier and city decision matrix

Regional production platform:
- Preferred: RATIONAL.
- Reason: strongest documented programmable cooking and automatic-cleaning case.
- Condition: named service partner and parts stock in every city.

Modular general cookline:
- Preferred: Electrolux Professional therma line.
- Reason: heavy-duty modular system, induction precision, lower kitchen heat, smooth cleanable surfaces.
- Condition: verify Bangkok, Manila, and Jakarta support and compare lifecycle price.

High-output wok:
- Preferred: Nayati.
- Reason: purpose-built Asian range and documented 28 kW gas unit; domestic Indonesian manufacturing.
- Condition: secure service commitments in Bangkok and Manila.

Tandoor:
- Preferred: locally supportable approved gas/electric specialist rather than a single unverified regional vendor.
- Reason: no four-city network was established.
- Condition: common technical specification, local spare liner, burner/electrical support, and authority approval.

Ventilation:
- Preferred controls/basis of design: Halton M.A.R.V.E.L. or equivalent DCKV.
- Reason: appliance/zone-level modulation and documented 30–50% typical ventilation-energy savings claim.

Warewashing:
- Preferred in Singapore and Bangkok: Hobart.
- Reason: direct service operation in Singapore and an office/spares center in Bangkok.
- Manila and Jakarta: conditional on verified local support.

Best package by city:

Singapore:
- RATIONAL + Electrolux + limited Nayati gas wok + approved tandoor + Halton-style DCKV + Hobart.
- Highest priority: energy efficiency, heat reduction, stringent exhaust/fire details, automated cleaning.

Bangkok:
- RATIONAL + mixed Electrolux/Nayati line + gas wok/tandoor + DCKV + Hobart.
- Highest priority: control electrical peak demand, verify district and landlord requirements, maintain strong gas safety.

Manila:
- RATIONAL + mixed induction/gas cookline + high-output wok + approved tandoor + robust grease exhaust + locally supported warewashing.
- Highest priority: 10-ACH minimum plus appliance capture, electricity efficiency, documented BFP acceptance, and enforceable service coverage.

Jakarta:
- Nayati-led package + RATIONAL combis + locally supported tandoor + SNI 6572-5:2025 ventilation.
- Highest priority: exploit domestic supply/service economics without relaxing corporate hygiene, controls, commissioning, or uptime standards.

9. Procurement decision

The recommended award strategy is a multi-vendor regional framework with no more than two approved models in each major category:

- One combi platform.
- One premium modular range.
- One primary Asian cookline.
- Two approved tandoors where necessary.
- One ventilation-control standard with licensed local installers.
- One primary warewash platform plus a fallback where service coverage is inadequate.

Before full rollout, conduct a measured pilot in one restaurant using the chain’s actual menu. Record:

- Portions per hour.
- Preheat and recovery time.
- Electricity and gas by appliance.
- Hood fan speed and airflow.
- Kitchen temperature and humidity.
- Water and chemical consumption.
- Cleaning labor.
- Food yield and oil use.
- Faults and technician response.
- Chef acceptance for wok hei, tandoor bread, kebab, and grill finish.

The final choice should be based on five-year total cost of ownership, not purchase price alone. Singapore will generally justify the largest efficiency premium; Bangkok requires the most attention to demand peaks; Manila needs strong ventilation/fire coordination and contractual service proof; Jakarta offers the strongest case for locally manufactured Nayati equipment supported by RATIONAL’s identified Indonesian network.
