NEW ZEALAND CONSTRUCTION METALWORKS / STRUCTURAL-STEEL FABRICATION MARKET

Market assessment as at 2024, with historical indicators for 2018–2024

1. Executive summary

New Zealand’s structural-steel fabrication market is a relatively small, fragmented manufacturing sector serving commercial and industrial buildings, bridges, transport infrastructure, stadiums and seismic-strengthening work. The appropriate official industry classification is ANZSIC 2006 class C2221, “Structural Steel Fabricating” (Stats NZ classification page: https://datainfoplus.stats.govt.nz/item/nz.govt.stats/ff97cfbd-5ede-42b5-af73-e6dc2ffb2125/1).

The strongest defensible 2024 market indicators are:

• Paid employee count: approximately 4,450 at February 2024 under ANZSIC C2221, compared with 4,250 in 2018 and a peak of 4,600 in 2023. This is Stats NZ Business Demography data, republished in downloadable form by Figure.NZ (Stats NZ release dated 31 October 2024: https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/new-zealand-business-demography-statistics-at-february-2024; detailed C2221 series: https://figure.nz/chart/tAQeOoJ0aDCZo3ER-k2pX8VwdLmexeE2c).

• Economically significant enterprises: 285 in February 2024, down from 294 in 2023 and the same number as in 2018. This is broader than Steel Construction New Zealand’s count of specialist structural-steel fabrication companies because Stats NZ classifies all economically significant enterprises whose predominant activity is C2221 (https://figure.nz/chart/IW0xisEu03j4YW09-nMdeErmezWdjoYQk).

• Fabricated output: approximately 100,000 tonnes a year. Steel Construction New Zealand, or SCNZ, reported about 100,000 tonnes of plate, hot-rolled sections and hollow sections fabricated into buildings and bridges in 2018 and again in 2022–23. This should be treated as an industry estimate rather than an official Stats NZ or MBIE tonnage series (SCNZ March 2018: https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/SCNZ_Industry-Update_March-2018.pdf; December 2022: https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/SCNZ-IU-DEC2022_WEB.pdf; September 2023: https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf).

• Installed annual fabrication capacity: SCNZ estimated 120,000 tonnes a year from at least 2018 through mid-2023, increasing to 150,000 tonnes by September 2023. At annual output of approximately 100,000 tonnes, the latter implies underlying utilisation of about 67%, although SCNZ’s forward-workload survey reported 41% spare forward capacity at September 2023. The two measures are not identical: one compares trailing output with nominal annual capacity, while the other measures committed forward workload (SCNZ September 2023: https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf).

• Revenue: Stats NZ’s public material located for this assessment does not publish a reliable annual C2221 revenue series for 2018–2024. The Annual Enterprise Survey is the correct official source, but the publicly surfaced AES tables are generally released at more aggregated industry levels. It would therefore be misleading to present an invented C2221 revenue series. The only directly surfaced 2024 market-size figure—NZ$1.5 billion—is for all “Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing,” not structural-steel fabrication, and is an IBISWorld estimate rather than Stats NZ or MBIE data (https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/market-size/fabricated-metal-product-manufacturing/247/). It is an upper-bound context figure, not the structural-fabrication market’s revenue.

• Tariffs: the raw and semi-finished iron and non-alloy steel headings most relevant to structural fabrication—HS 7207 through 7216—generally enter New Zealand at a “Free” normal customs-duty rate. The direct tariff burden on raw structural-steel inputs is consequently 0% of customs value before any goods and services tax, trade-remedy duty, freight, port, testing or compliance costs. The governing source is the New Zealand Customs Service Working Tariff Document; the 2024 tariff/concessions material is available at https://www.customs.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/tariff-documents/wtd-2024/concessions-1-jan-2024.pdf. Customs’ later extracted import data confirm that headings 7208, 7211 and 7216 are actively used for New Zealand steel imports (Customs OIA extract covering 2020–2024: https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/yyshc4tn/oia-25-677-iron-and-non-alloy-steel-imports-2020-to-2024.pdf).

• Major demand examples: City Rail Link used approximately 29,595 tonnes of steel in total, including about 25,000 tonnes of locally produced reinforcing steel; Christchurch’s Te Kaha/One New Zealand Stadium requires about 13,000 tonnes; and Hamilton’s Te Ara Pekapeka/Peacocke Bridge contains about 2,650 tonnes of structural steel. These three projects alone represent approximately 45,245 tonnes of steel, although the totals mix reinforcing and fabricated structural steel and span several construction years.

The central strategic conclusion is that New Zealand had sufficient installed fabrication capacity in 2024, but not necessarily enough secured forward orders to use it fully. The sector’s principal exposure is therefore less a formal import tariff than the combination of imported-material price and exchange-rate volatility, concentration among overseas mills and distributors, and an uneven domestic project pipeline. Conversely, certification, seismic capability, short lead times and a large infrastructure pipeline give local fabricators a defensible position against offshore fabricated imports.

2. Scope and definitions

This report covers steel prepared for construction and structural applications: building frames, beams, columns, trusses, plate girders, seismic systems, bridge steel, stadium structures and associated detailing, cutting, drilling, fitting, welding, coating and erection.

SCNZ describes a structural-steel fabricator’s work as material management, shop detailing, cutting, drilling, fitting by bolting or welding, painting or galvanising where required, and shipping for erection (SCNZ March 2023, published March 2023: https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/SCNZ-IU-Mar-23.pdf).

Excluded from the core market are:

• primary steelmaking except where it supplies structural fabricators;
• reinforcing-bar rolling as a manufacturing market in its own right;
• architectural aluminium;
• sheet-metal products not used structurally;
• machinery, pressure vessels and marine fabrication;
• steel distribution with no fabrication component; and
• non-construction fabricated-metal products.

There is an unavoidable boundary issue in the official data. ANZSIC C2221 includes businesses whose predominant activity is structural-steel fabricating, but some large contractors combine fabrication, erection, heavy engineering and other activities. Conversely, distributors and construction contractors may process structural steel while being classified outside C2221. SCNZ’s approximately 5,000-person sector estimate is consequently broader than Stats NZ’s 4,450 paid employees assigned to C2221 in February 2024.

3. Market size and growth, 2018–2024

3.1 Official employment and enterprise series

Stats NZ Business Demography is the most consistent official source for annual employment at the detailed C2221 level. It is an annual February snapshot of economically significant enterprises. “Employee count” is a headcount of salary-and-wage earners sourced from taxation data; it is not Stats NZ’s official labour-market employment measure and may count jobs rather than unique full-time-equivalent workers (Stats NZ methodology: https://datainfoplus.stats.govt.nz/item/nz.govt.stats/bdb02aa2-866e-418f-83e8-342234867a0f; employee-count definition: https://www.stats.govt.nz/services/customised-data-services/statistics-for-university-staff-and-students/business-demography-data-package/).

C2221 structural-steel fabrication indicators:

Year | Paid employee count | Annual change | Economically significant enterprises
2018 | 4,250 | — | 285
2019 | 4,200 | -1.2% | 288
2020 | 4,350 | +3.6% | 282
2021 | 4,250 | -2.3% | 273
2022 | 4,450 | +4.7% | 291
2023 | 4,600 | +3.4% | 294
2024 | 4,450 | -3.3% | 285

Sources: detailed Stats NZ Business Demography data republished by Figure.NZ, employee series https://figure.nz/chart/tAQeOoJ0aDCZo3ER-k2pX8VwdLmexeE2c and enterprise series https://figure.nz/chart/IW0xisEu03j4YW09-nMdeErmezWdjoYQk; Stats NZ’s 2024 release was published 31 October 2024 at https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/new-zealand-business-demography-statistics-at-february-2024.

Quantitative growth:

• Employment growth, 2018–2024:
  (4,450 / 4,250) − 1 = 4.71%.

• Compound annual employment growth:
  (4,450 / 4,250)^(1/6) − 1 = approximately 0.77% a year.

• Employment change from the 2023 peak to 2024:
  (4,450 / 4,600) − 1 = -3.26%.

• Enterprise growth, 2018–2024:
  (285 / 285) − 1 = 0%.

• Average paid employees per enterprise:
  2018: 4,250 / 285 = 14.9.
  2023: 4,600 / 294 = 15.6.
  2024: 4,450 / 285 = 15.6.

The employee series therefore shows modest net expansion since 2018 rather than rapid structural growth. Employment proved relatively resilient through 2020–21, rose strongly in 2022–23, and softened in 2024 as the construction cycle weakened.

Stats NZ cautions that fine-industry figures can be affected by classification changes and Business Register timing, particularly for smaller industries. Business Demography covers enterprises meeting an economic-significance test—such as more than NZ$30,000 in annual GST-subject sales or expenses, a rolling employee count above three, group membership, or certain tax-return thresholds—and is not a census of every informal or very small operator (Stats NZ/Figure.NZ metadata: https://figure.nz/chart/tAQeOoJ0aDCZo3ER-k2pX8VwdLmexeE2c).

3.2 Fabricated tonnage and capacity

Neither Stats NZ nor MBIE publishes a discovered annual physical-tonnage series for C2221. The best available construction-specific series comes from SCNZ’s fabricator surveys and industry updates.

Year | Estimated fabricated output | Estimated annual capacity | Evidential status
2018 | approximately 100,000 t | approximately 120,000 t | SCNZ directly reported
2019 | approximately 100,000 t indicative | approximately 120,000 t | recurring SCNZ run-rate; no separate annual total located
2020 | approximately 100,000 t indicative | approximately 120,000 t | no annual output total located; capacity directly reported in SCNZ updates
2021 | approximately 100,000 t indicative | approximately 120,000 t | no separate annual total located
2022 | approximately 100,000 t | approximately 120,000 t | SCNZ directly reported
2023 | approximately 100,000 t | 120,000 t through mid-year; 150,000 t by September | SCNZ directly reported
2024 | approximately 100,000 t run-rate, not an official outturn | approximately 150,000 t | carried forward from September 2023 capacity; 2024 outturn not independently located

Direct sources:

• March 2018: SCNZ said the sector had turned approximately 100,000 tonnes of plate, hot-rolled and hollow sections into buildings and bridges in the previous 12 months, with annual capacity of approximately 120,000 tonnes and 86 fabricators nationwide (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/SCNZ_Industry-Update_March-2018.pdf).

• September 2018: approximately 100,000 tonnes of annual output and 120,000 tonnes of capacity; 26% spare forward capacity for the year ending June 2019 (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/SCNZ_Industry-Update_September-2018.pdf).

• June 2020: SCNZ reported 47% spare capacity for the year ending June 2020 against 120,000 tonnes of annual capacity. The update index, published online from 9 September 2020, lists the historical reports at https://scnz.org/steel-construction/structural-steel-industry-updates/.

• December 2022: approximately 100,000 tonnes fabricated into buildings and bridges in the previous 12 months, 120,000 tonnes capacity, 153 fabrication companies and approximately 5,000 workers. SCNZ reported 26% spare capacity for the year ending December 2023 (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/SCNZ-IU-DEC2022_WEB.pdf).

• March 2023: approximately 100,000 tonnes of trailing annual output, 120,000 tonnes capacity, approximately 5,000 workers and 153 companies. Forward spare capacity for the year ending March 2024 was 28% (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/SCNZ-IU-Mar-23.pdf).

• September 2023: SCNZ increased its estimate of industry capacity from 120,000 to 150,000 tonnes a year, saying capacity had risen over the preceding five years through investment in workshops, machinery and technology and an increase in fabricators. It continued to report trailing output of about 100,000 tonnes, 153 companies, approximately 5,000 workers and 41% spare forward capacity (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf).

Output and capacity calculations:

• Implied trailing utilisation in 2018:
  100,000 / 120,000 = 83.3%.

• Implied trailing utilisation after the 2023 capacity revision:
  100,000 / 150,000 = 66.7%.

• Capacity growth, 2018 to September 2023:
  (150,000 / 120,000) − 1 = 25%.

• Approximate output per Stats NZ C2221 paid employee:
  2018: 100,000 / 4,250 = 23.5 tonnes per paid employee.
  2023: 100,000 / 4,600 = 21.7 tonnes per paid employee.
  2024 run-rate proxy: 100,000 / 4,450 = 22.5 tonnes per paid employee.

These calculations should not be interpreted as shop-floor labour productivity. The output denominator is SCNZ’s broader sector estimate, while the employee count is Stats NZ’s predominant-industry C2221 classification and includes office, detailing and management staff.

The 2019–21 and 2024 tonnage entries are not official observations. They are shown as an approximately flat indicative run-rate because the directly located SCNZ reports repeatedly used about 100,000 tonnes before and after that interval. A proper annual series would require SCNZ’s underlying quarterly survey records or a custom Stats NZ/MBIE production dataset.

3.3 Revenue and market value

A complete official annual revenue series for C2221 was not available in the public evidence reviewed. Stats NZ’s Annual Enterprise Survey is New Zealand’s most comprehensive source of business financial statistics and covers more than 500,000 businesses, but the surfaced public release does not give C2221 structural-steel revenue separately (Stats NZ AES 2023 provisional release, published 1 July 2024: https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/annual-enterprise-survey-2023-financial-year-provisional; survey metadata: https://datainfoplus.stats.govt.nz/item/nz.govt.stats/b3619438-0e76-43a0-a405-565c3ba5a117).

Accordingly:

Year | Structural-fabrication revenue, NZD
2018 | Not separately disclosed in the located Stats NZ/MBIE public tables
2019 | Not separately disclosed
2020 | Not separately disclosed
2021 | Not separately disclosed
2022 | Not separately disclosed
2023 | Not separately disclosed
2024 | Not separately disclosed

This is an evidence limitation, not a zero value.

The available NZ$1.5 billion figure for 2024 relates to the much broader “Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing” market and includes activities outside this report’s construction/structural scope. It cannot be presented as C2221 revenue (IBISWorld 2024 market-size page: https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/market-size/fabricated-metal-product-manufacturing/247/).

Likewise, Steel & Tube Holdings’ NZ$589.1 million FY2023 revenue and NZ$479.1 million FY2024 revenue cover a national steel distribution and processing group, including plate, purlins, ComFlor, fasteners, roofing, mesh, reinforcing bar, piping and other products. They are not structural-fabrication market revenue. Steel & Tube’s total volume fell from 146,400 tonnes in FY2023 to 115,500 tonnes in FY2024, while gross margin dollars per tonne rose from NZ$850 to NZ$901 (Steel & Tube FY2024 results presentation, published in 2024: https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20FY24%20Results%20Presentation.pdf).

The Steel & Tube figures are nevertheless useful as a cyclical indicator:

• Revenue decline:
  (479.1 − 589.1) / 589.1 = -18.7%.

• Volume decline:
  (115.5 − 146.4) / 146.4 = -21.1%.

• Gross-margin dollars per tonne:
  (901 − 850) / 850 = +6.0%.

The company attributed part of the weakness to a 15% decline in commercial sales and a 15% year-on-year reduction in non-residential consents to June 2024, affecting structural and reinforcing products. This supports the view that 2024 was a softer demand year, but it must not be used as a direct measure of structural-fabricator revenue.

4. Leading structural-steel fabricators

4.1 Ranking limitations

A definitive top-five ranking by 2023 revenue is not publicly supportable from the evidence reviewed. Most specialist fabricators are privately held New Zealand companies and do not publish segment revenue. Companies Office filings establish legal entities, directors and shareholders, but qualifying private companies are not necessarily required to file public, revenue-bearing financial statements. Even where group accounts exist, they may combine fabrication, erection, engineering and unrelated construction operations.

The most defensible comparison is therefore disclosed annual or weekly fabrication capacity. Only three businesses in the available primary/company material disclose sufficiently clear capacity figures. CH Steel discloses ownership and major-project scale but not a total annual tonnage capacity. Steel & Tube publishes group revenue and volume, but it is principally a distributor and processor rather than a directly comparable specialist structural fabricator.

The table below is consequently a “leading disclosed operators” ranking, not a claim that every private competitor has been exhaustively ranked.

4.2 Capacity-based ranking and company profiles

Rank | Company | Disclosed structural-fabrication capacity/output | Approximate annualised amount | Ownership/status | Source
1 | D&H Steel Construction | 250–400 tonnes per week, depending on complexity | approximately 13,000–20,800 t/year at 52 weeks | Privately held New Zealand structural-steel contractor; company website identifies Wayne Carson as managing director | D&H fabrication page: https://www.dhsteel.co.nz/how-we-do-it/fabrication/
2 | Grayson Engineering | More than 10,000 tonnes of finished product annually | >10,000 t/year | Privately held New Zealand engineering/fabrication company; also has subsidiary Cellbeam NZ Ltd | Easysteel case study: https://www.easysteel.co.nz/web/assets/Easysteel-Case-Study-Grayson-Engineering.pdf
3 | Calder Group steel fabrication | 100 tonnes per week | approximately 5,200 t/year | Part of privately held New Zealand Calder Group | Calder Group page dated 15 January 2024: https://caldergroup.nz/manufacturing/steel-fabrication/
4 | CH Steel | Annual capacity not disclosed; demonstrated an 8,500-tonne structural package | Not rankable on annual capacity | 50/50 joint venture between Culham Engineering of Whangārei and The Herrick Corporation of California, in place since 2015 | CH Steel company page: https://www.chsteel.co.nz/
5 | Steel & Tube Holdings / processed structural-steel operations | Group sold 146,400 tonnes across all products in FY2023; structural fabrication not separated | Not comparable with specialist-fabricator capacity | NZX-listed New Zealand company; ownership dispersed among shareholders | FY2024 results presentation: https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20FY24%20Results%20Presentation.pdf

D&H Steel Construction

D&H reports more than 4,000 in-house production labour-hours per week before outsourcing, converting to between 250 and 400 tonnes a week depending on project complexity. Annualising the stated rate:

• Low end: 250 × 52 = 13,000 tonnes.
• High end: 400 × 52 = 20,800 tonnes.

At the high end, D&H’s stated capacity would equal approximately 13.9% of SCNZ’s 150,000-tonne national capacity estimate; at the low end, approximately 8.7%. D&H says its production and quality-control systems enable it to undertake structural-steel projects of any size in New Zealand and the South Pacific (https://www.dhsteel.co.nz/how-we-do-it/fabrication/).

Grayson Engineering

Grayson produces more than 10,000 tonnes of finished product annually from a purpose-built 12,000-square-metre Manukau facility. The cited company case study identifies experience in commercial and industrial structures, stadiums, bridges, towers and other heavy structures, and projects including the Forsyth Barr Stadium, Eden Park upgrade, SkyCity Casino, the New Zealand International Convention Centre, the University of Auckland Business School and Princes Wharf. It also identifies Cellbeam NZ Ltd as a subsidiary fabricating cellular beams under licence (https://www.easysteel.co.nz/web/assets/Easysteel-Case-Study-Grayson-Engineering.pdf).

Using the minimum disclosed output, Grayson represents at least:

• 10,000 / 150,000 = 6.7% of estimated national installed capacity; or
• 10,000 / 100,000 = 10% of the approximately 100,000-tonne annual industry output.

Calder Group

Calder Group states that its fabrication plant can process 100 tonnes a week. Annualised without allowing for shutdowns:

100 × 52 = 5,200 tonnes a year.

That equals approximately 3.5% of SCNZ’s 150,000-tonne national capacity estimate. Calder markets an integrated detailing-through-installation service and describes its equipment as among New Zealand’s most advanced (company page dated 15 January 2024: https://caldergroup.nz/manufacturing/steel-fabrication/).

CH Steel, Culham Engineering and Herrick

CH Steel is owned equally by Culham Engineering and California-based Herrick. The company states that the joint arrangement has operated since 2015, combining Culham’s New Zealand heavy-engineering and site-delivery capability with Herrick’s high-volume fabrication capability. CH Steel cites eight on-site fabrication workshops in Whangārei and an 8,500-tonne structural-steel package, but does not disclose annual capacity (https://www.chsteel.co.nz/).

The 8,500-tonne package is evidence of project scale, not annual throughput. It is therefore inappropriate to place CH Steel numerically above or below Calder solely from that project amount. Culham should not be separately counted as another independent top-five company when the structural-steel delivery entity being compared is the 50/50 CH Steel joint venture.

Steel & Tube Holdings

Steel & Tube is included only to provide the requested public-company revenue comparator. It reported FY2023 group revenue of NZ$589.1 million and total volume of 146,400 tonnes, followed by FY2024 revenue of NZ$479.1 million and volume of 115,500 tonnes. Its range includes processed plate and structural products, but also roofing, reinforcing, mesh, piping, fasteners and other products. Its group revenue cannot be treated as specialist structural-fabrication revenue (https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20FY24%20Results%20Presentation.pdf).

Overall concentration cannot be calculated reliably because comparable capacities are not disclosed by every private firm. The disclosed minimum capacities of D&H, Grayson and Calder sum to:

13,000 + 10,000 + 5,200 = 28,200 tonnes a year at D&H’s low end,

or:

20,800 + 10,000 + 5,200 = 36,000 tonnes at D&H’s high end.

That corresponds to approximately 18.8%–24.0% of SCNZ’s 150,000-tonne national capacity estimate, before CH Steel and other large private operators are included.

5. Import tariffs on structural-steel inputs

5.1 Relevant HS headings

The principal Chapter 72 headings used by construction-focused structural fabricators are:

HS 7207 – Semi-finished products of iron or non-alloy steel.

HS 7208 – Flat-rolled products of iron or non-alloy steel, width 600 mm or more, hot-rolled, not clad, plated or coated. This includes structural plate and hot-rolled coil used for built-up members, base plates, stiffeners and connection plates.

HS 7209 – Flat-rolled products of iron or non-alloy steel, width 600 mm or more, cold-rolled, not clad, plated or coated.

HS 7210 – Flat-rolled products of iron or non-alloy steel, width 600 mm or more, clad, plated or coated.

HS 7211 – Flat-rolled products of iron or non-alloy steel, width under 600 mm, not clad, plated or coated.

HS 7212 – Flat-rolled products of iron or non-alloy steel, width under 600 mm, clad, plated or coated.

HS 7213 – Bars and rods, hot-rolled, in irregularly wound coils.

HS 7214 – Other bars and rods of iron or non-alloy steel, not further worked than forged, hot-rolled, hot-drawn or hot-extruded, including twisted bars.

HS 7215 – Other bars and rods of iron or non-alloy steel.

HS 7216 – Angles, shapes and sections of iron or non-alloy steel, including structural beams, columns, channels and angles.

The most directly relevant headings for conventional structural fabrication are 7208 for plate, 7211 for narrower strip/plate and 7216 for rolled structural sections. Customs’ import extract specifically covers 7208, 7211 and 7216 and reports quantities and NZ-dollar values by origin for 2020–2024 (New Zealand Customs response extracted 2 September 2025: https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/yyshc4tn/oia-25-677-iron-and-non-alloy-steel-imports-2020-to-2024.pdf).

5.2 Duty rates

The normal New Zealand customs-duty treatment for raw and semi-finished steel under HS 7207–7216 is Free, subject to checking the exact statistical key, origin, date of entry and any applicable trade remedy in the Working Tariff Document.

Summary:

Heading | Construction use | Normal tariff rate
7207 | Semi-finished steel feedstock | Free
7208 | Hot-rolled plate/coil ≥600 mm | Free
7209 | Cold-rolled flat steel ≥600 mm | Free
7210 | Coated flat steel ≥600 mm | Free
7211 | Uncoated flat steel <600 mm | Free
7212 | Coated flat steel <600 mm | Free
7213 | Hot-rolled rod in coils | Free
7214 | Structural/reinforcing bars | Free
7215 | Other bars and rods | Free
7216 | Beams, columns, channels, angles and other sections | Free

Primary tariff source: New Zealand Customs Service, Working Tariff Document and 2024 concessions material, effective 1 January 2024: https://www.customs.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/tariff-documents/wtd-2024/concessions-1-jan-2024.pdf. Customs also explains that its downloadable tariff data contain tariff-item details, normal and preferential rate groups, commencement/end dates and levy formulas: https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/y1dmuyec/tariff-and-concession-readme.pdf.

“Free” means zero customs duty; it does not mean zero landed-border cost. Imports can still incur:

• 15% goods and services tax, generally recoverable as input tax by a GST-registered fabricator;
• ocean freight, insurance and inland transport;
• port and customs-clearance charges;
• exchange-rate exposure;
• testing, traceability and certification expenses;
• inventory financing and storage;
• possible anti-dumping or countervailing duties on a specific product and country; and
• losses from non-compliant material, delay or rework.

5.3 Effective tariff impact on fabricator margins

For ordinary imports under the listed zero-duty headings:

Customs duty = customs value × 0% = NZ$0.

Illustrative calculation for NZ$10 million of qualifying raw structural-steel imports:

• Customs value: NZ$10,000,000.
• Normal customs-duty rate: 0%.
• Customs duty: NZ$10,000,000 × 0% = NZ$0.
• Direct tariff cost as a share of revenue or gross margin: 0%, before any trade remedy or non-tariff landed costs.

If steel represents 40% of a fabricated contract’s sales value, a hypothetical 5% tariff would reduce contract gross margin by approximately:

40% × 5% = 2.0 percentage points,

unless fully passed through to the customer.

Because the actual normal tariff is zero, that 2-point direct burden does not arise. The formal tariff therefore has a neutral direct effect on local fabricator margins.

The commercially important consequence is competitive rather than fiscal. Zero duty lowers input costs for New Zealand shops, but it can also allow imported finished or semi-finished structural steel to compete without a protective raw-material tariff wall. Margin exposure comes from the overseas mill price, NZ-dollar exchange rate, shipping, certification and project-price pass-through rather than the scheduled tariff itself.

Steel & Tube’s FY2024 results illustrate why non-tariff price management matters: despite a 21.1% volume reduction, gross-margin dollars per tonne rose 6% from NZ$850 to NZ$901. This reflects commercial pricing and product mix, not tariff protection (https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20FY24%20Results%20Presentation.pdf).

6. Major infrastructure and large public-project steel demand

6.1 City Rail Link, Auckland

Project: A 3.45-kilometre twin-tunnel underground railway linking Waitematā/Britomart with the western line at Maungawhau/Mount Eden, including new underground stations at Te Waihorotiu and Karanga-a-Hape and redevelopment of Maungawhau station.

Steel demand:

• Total steel across the City Rail Link structures: approximately 29,595 tonnes.
• Concrete: approximately 185,000 cubic metres.
• Locally produced reinforcing steel: approximately 25,000 tonnes over three to four years.
• The project’s sustainability/design work reported a reduction of 100,259 kg of structural steel from reducing plunge columns and a further approximately 823,158 kg from reduced temporary struts and walers. It also reused 85,000 kg of steel for temporary propping and returned nearly 70,000 kg of temporary struts for potential reuse.

Sources:

• The 29,595-tonne total is reported in a 2023 Structural Engineering Society New Zealand conference paper on CRL design and construction: https://www.sesoc.org.nz/static/Documents/Conference/2023/SESOC2023-0043-Page-43-98-Page-Ethan-43-98-Page-Ethan.pdf.

• New Zealand Steel’s project announcement states that approximately 25,000 tonnes of locally produced reinforcing steel would be used over three to four years: https://www.nzsteel.co.nz/news-and-media/local-steel-for-aucklands-city-rail-link/.

• Project description and status are given by WSP at https://www.wsp.com/en-za/projects/city-rail-link.

Timeline:

The New Zealand Steel announcement described the project as due for completion in 2024, but that date was superseded. WSP now describes the project as “in delivery” with 2026 status. For an as-of-2024 market assessment, the appropriate conclusion is that steel-intensive civil construction was substantially advanced, while railway testing, systems integration and opening extended toward 2026.

Structural-fabrication interpretation:

The 29,595 tonnes should not be treated as 29,595 tonnes of addressable workshop-fabricated beams and columns. It includes reinforcing and other steel embedded in concrete infrastructure. With approximately 25,000 tonnes explicitly identified as reinforcing steel, the difference is:

29,595 − 25,000 = approximately 4,595 tonnes.

Even that residual is not a clean fabricated-structural-steel total because the underlying boundaries and temporary works may differ. CRL was nevertheless a major source of demand for fabricated temporary works, station steelwork, supports and specialist heavy structural components.

6.2 Te Kaha / One New Zealand Stadium, Christchurch

Project: Christchurch’s new covered stadium and events venue.

Steel demand: approximately 13,000 tonnes in total across the stands and roof. By September 2024, more than 8,000 tonnes had been installed.

Completion: project reporting in September 2024 said the stadium remained on budget and on track for an April 2026 opening.

Source: The Press project update, published 19 September 2024, https://www.thepress.co.nz/nz-news/350423579/more-half-steel-te-kaha-installed.

Quantitative progress:

• Installed by September 2024: >8,000 tonnes.
• Total: approximately 13,000 tonnes.
• Minimum installed proportion: 8,000 / 13,000 = 61.5%.

This is a more directly addressable structural-fabrication package than CRL’s total-steel figure because it includes major stand and long-span roof structures. The project update described roof trusses spanning the field and being installed in three sections, with each truss taking approximately one month to install before the supporting hydraulic frames were moved.

6.3 Te Ara Pekapeka / Peacocke Bridge, Hamilton

Project: A four-lane bridge over the Waikato River, including bus lanes and paths, linking Hamilton East with the Peacocke growth area. The bridge uses weathering-steel structural members.

Steel demand: approximately 2,650 tonnes of structural steel.

Timeline: construction began in 2020 and the bridge opened to pedestrians and cyclists on 30 August 2024.

Source: Structurae project record, https://structurae.net/en/structures/te-ara-pekapeka-bridge.

This is the cleanest of the three project figures for workshop structural fabrication because the reported amount is specifically structural steel. The project includes large weathering-steel Y-shaped supports and steel girders.

6.4 Combined demand and timing

Reported steel in the three projects:

• City Rail Link: 29,595 tonnes total steel.
• Te Kaha: 13,000 tonnes.
• Te Ara Pekapeka: 2,650 tonnes.

Combined:

29,595 + 13,000 + 2,650 = 45,245 tonnes.

Relative to the industry’s approximate 100,000-tonne annual output:

45,245 / 100,000 = 45.2%.

However, these projects span multiple years and CRL’s amount is dominated by reinforcing steel. The combined figure must not be interpreted as a single-year, 45% order-book share for structural fabricators.

A narrower illustrative total excluding CRL’s stated 25,000 tonnes of reinforcing is:

(29,595 − 25,000) + 13,000 + 2,650
= 4,595 + 13,000 + 2,650
= 20,245 tonnes.

That is a more plausible upper-order estimate of non-rebar steel across the three projects, but it is still not a precise fabricated-tonnage measure.

7. Strategic risks

7.1 Risk 1: imported-input concentration and landed-cost volatility

Formal tariffs are zero, but New Zealand is geographically remote and reliant on imported plate, sections and specialty grades. Customs data for HS 7208 show supply from countries including Australia, China, Indonesia, Japan, Korea and Malaysia, among others, illustrating both diversification and dependence on overseas mills and shipping (Customs extract covering 2020–2024: https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/yyshc4tn/oia-25-677-iron-and-non-alloy-steel-imports-2020-to-2024.pdf).

Key exposures are:

• NZ-dollar depreciation;
• mill-price volatility;
• freight and port disruption;
• long replenishment lead times;
• concentration in a limited number of compliant mills and domestic distributors;
• project delay while material certificates or conformity are checked; and
• working-capital requirements for imported inventory.

A 10% rise in the landed cost of steel would be much more material than the 0% tariff. If raw steel is 40% of contract revenue and the increase cannot be passed through:

Margin impact = 40% × 10% = 4 percentage points.

Fixed-price contracts without steel escalation clauses are therefore a more significant margin threat than the normal customs schedule.

Mitigation includes dual sourcing, hedging foreign exchange, early material procurement, customer escalation clauses, approved-mill frameworks and retaining traceability documentation from mill to erected member.

7.2 Risk 2: excess capacity and an uneven project pipeline

SCNZ increased estimated installed capacity from 120,000 to 150,000 tonnes while reporting output of only about 100,000 tonnes. That implies around 50,000 tonnes of unused capacity on a simple trailing basis:

150,000 − 100,000 = 50,000 tonnes,

or:

50,000 / 150,000 = 33.3%.

SCNZ’s September 2023 forward survey was even softer, reporting 41% spare capacity, although forward committed workload is conceptually different from trailing utilisation (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf).

The demand slowdown became more visible in 2024. Steel & Tube reported commercial sales and non-residential consents down 15%, group volume down 21.1%, and revenue down 18.7% in FY2024 (https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20FY24%20Results%20Presentation.pdf).

Fabricators face:

• price competition to keep workshops loaded;
• under-recovery of fixed plant, certification and skilled-labour costs;
• gaps between completion of mega-project packages and mobilisation of replacements;
• dependence on a small number of stadium, hospital, rail, bridge and commercial projects; and
• cancellations or deferrals caused by public-budget or private-financing constraints.

The 2024 fall in C2221 employee count from 4,600 to 4,450 is consistent with, though does not by itself prove, the beginning of capacity adjustment.

7.3 Risk 3: offshore fabricated-steel competition and quality/compliance exposure

A zero-duty environment reduces input costs but does not create tariff protection against offshore supply. SCNZ’s 2018 update referred to project failures associated with poor procurement decisions and imported product and emphasised that AS/NZS 5131 had been cited in the Building Code as an approved fabrication and erection standard (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/SCNZ_Industry-Update_September-2018.pdf).

The risk has two dimensions:

• Commercial: offshore fabricators can quote large packages from lower-cost production bases.
• Technical/reputational: non-conforming steel, incomplete traceability, welding defects or dimensional errors can cause inspection, rework and programme costs that ultimately affect the whole steel category.

By September 2023, 65 fabrication companies representing 92.5% of annual output participated in the independent Steel Fabrication Certification scheme (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf). That high coverage raises the baseline for domestic quality but also imposes ongoing audit, training and documentation costs.

Mitigation includes specifying independently certified fabrication, whole-of-life procurement rather than lowest initial price, early contractor involvement, digital model coordination and clear allocation of responsibility for overseas inspection and non-conformance.

8. Strategic opportunities

8.1 Opportunity 1: convert the infrastructure pipeline into steady domestic workload

Large transport, stadium, bridge, water, health and education projects can absorb meaningful portions of the industry’s capacity. Te Kaha alone represents 13,000 tonnes, or approximately:

13,000 / 100,000 = 13%

of one year’s current national output, although delivered over several years. Te Ara Pekapeka represents another 2.65% of one year’s output.

Local fabricators can increase capture by:

• early contractor involvement during concept and detailed design;
• packaging projects to suit domestic workshop and transport constraints;
• standardising bridge girders and connection details;
• coordinating procurement calendars across public agencies;
• avoiding simultaneous peaks followed by workload cliffs; and
• demonstrating regional employment and schedule benefits.

SCNZ’s estimate of 150,000 tonnes of annual capacity indicates that the domestic industry has headroom for additional infrastructure work without automatically requiring offshore fabrication.

8.2 Opportunity 2: premium for seismic, certified and rapid-delivery capability

New Zealand fabricators possess specialised knowledge in seismic design, low-damage systems, buildability and erection in constrained urban sites. The domestic industry’s advantages include:

• rapid design clarification and rework;
• direct coordination among engineer, detailer, fabricator and erector;
• shorter transport and replacement lead times;
• independent certification;
• local accountability for welding, coatings and tolerances; and
• experience with New Zealand earthquake and Building Code requirements.

SCNZ reported more than 92% of output covered by Steel Fabrication Certification by September 2023. This creates a procurement differentiator if clients evaluate compliance risk and programme certainty rather than comparing only ex-works steel prices.

8.3 Opportunity 3: productivity, automation and low-carbon/reuse services

Capacity rose 25% from 120,000 to 150,000 tonnes over about five years, reflecting investment in workshops, machinery and technology (SCNZ September 2023: https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf). Individual disclosures support this trend:

• Grayson operates a 12,000-square-metre purpose-built CNC-equipped plant and produces more than 10,000 tonnes annually (https://www.easysteel.co.nz/web/assets/Easysteel-Case-Study-Grayson-Engineering.pdf).
• Calder can process 100 tonnes per week with advanced fabrication machinery (https://caldergroup.nz/manufacturing/steel-fabrication/).
• D&H has more than 4,000 in-house production hours per week and capacity of 250–400 tonnes per week (https://www.dhsteel.co.nz/how-we-do-it/fabrication/).

Further opportunity lies in robotic welding, automated beam lines, model-to-machine data, digital traceability, off-site assembly and design-for-manufacture.

CRL also demonstrates a circular-economy service opportunity. Its design reportedly avoided approximately:

100,259 kg + 823,158 kg = 923,417 kg,

or about 923 tonnes, of structural steel in selected temporary/permanent works changes, while reusing 85 tonnes and returning nearly 70 tonnes of temporary struts for potential reuse (https://www.sesoc.org.nz/static/Documents/Conference/2023/SESOC2023-0043-Page-43-98-Page-Ethan-43-98-Page-Ethan.pdf).

Fabricators can monetise this trend through:

• reusable temporary works;
• bolted rather than permanently welded modular assemblies where appropriate;
• member passports and digital material records;
• design optimisation;
• deconstruction and remanufacture services; and
• verified embodied-carbon reporting.

9. Overall outlook as at 2024

The market entered 2024 with substantially more physical capacity than in 2018 but only modestly more employment and no demonstrated increase in annual tonnage output.

Key changes from 2018 to 2024 were:

• paid employees: 4,250 to 4,450, up 4.7%;
• enterprises: 285 to 285, no net change;
• estimated annual capacity: 120,000 to about 150,000 tonnes, up 25%;
• estimated annual output: broadly around 100,000 tonnes at the directly observed endpoints;
• implied utilisation: from approximately 83% to approximately 67%;
• certification coverage: 65 companies representing 92.5% of output by September 2023; and
• near-term demand: weakening commercial activity but continuing large public and infrastructure packages.

The market is therefore best characterised as technologically capable and capacity-rich but cyclically underutilised. Its most important competitive issue is not the customs tariff on raw steel—the normal rate is zero—but whether local fabricators can secure a stable, well-sequenced project pipeline and pass through volatile imported-material costs while maintaining certified quality.

10. Data-quality qualifications

1. Revenue: No public Stats NZ or MBIE annual revenue series at the exact C2221 level was established from the available releases. The NZ$1.5 billion 2024 fabricated-metal figure is broader than this market and must not be substituted for structural-fabrication revenue.

2. Tonnage: SCNZ figures are industry-survey estimates, not Stats NZ or MBIE production statistics. Direct approximately 100,000-tonne observations were located for 2018, 2022 and 2023. Values for 2019–21 and 2024 are indicative run-rates rather than independently measured annual outturns.

3. Employment: Stats NZ Business Demography employee count is a February headcount of paid jobs in economically significant enterprises, not full-time equivalents or the official Household Labour Force Survey employment measure. SCNZ’s approximately 5,000-worker estimate uses a broader sector boundary.

4. Top five: Private-company revenue and annual-capacity disclosure is incomplete. D&H, Grayson and Calder can be ranked from disclosed rates; CH Steel’s 8,500 tonnes is a project package rather than annual capacity; Steel & Tube’s revenue and volume cover a much broader product portfolio. The list is therefore not an audited national league table.

5. Tariffs: The stated Free rate is the normal customs-duty treatment for the relevant raw/semi-finished Chapter 72 products. Every import should still be checked at the full tariff-item/statistical-key level for the entry date, origin, concession and any anti-dumping or countervailing measure.

6. Project steel: CRL’s 29,595 tonnes includes reinforcing and other steel and is not wholly addressable structural-fabrication demand. Te Kaha’s 13,000 tonnes and Te Ara Pekapeka’s 2,650 tonnes are more directly relevant structural quantities. Project totals span multiple years and should not be added as if they were one year’s market demand.

final.content:
# Suggestion Timing, Developer Flow, Code Quality, and Trust in AI Code-Completion Interfaces

## Executive summary

The available evidence supports a differentiated interface policy rather than a single universal timing rule:

- **Short, high-confidence inline completions can appear proactively when end-to-end latency is about 200 ms or less.** GitHub reports operating Copilot at a mean response time below 200 ms at production scale, while Meta’s industrial code-completion research shows that lower latency materially increases the number of suggestions developers actually see. This is the strongest evidence-backed target for “flow-preserving” automatic completion, although it is an operational target rather than a experimentally proven cognitive boundary.
- **Between roughly 200 and 750 ms, proactive presentation should be selective.** Suggestions should be triggered at syntactic or task boundaries, suppressed while the developer is continuously typing or debugging, and canceled when their originating code state becomes stale.
- **Above approximately 750 ms, longer or multi-line generation should normally become visibly pending or on-demand rather than silently appearing.** Meta only counted suggestions as meaningfully displayed for acceptance-rate purposes if they remained visible for more than 750 ms, and found that longer generations could take more than two seconds and often became obsolete before the developer saw them. The 750 ms figure is therefore an exposure and UI-policy threshold, not a demonstrated human-perception optimum.
- **Silent proactive completions taking more than two seconds are poorly matched to continuous coding.** If a block is valuable enough to justify that delay, the interface should show a non-disruptive progress indicator, allow cancellation, and preferably require an explicit invocation or a strong semantic boundary such as the end of a newly declared function.
- **Multi-line suggestions have high leverage but also higher interruption and verification costs.** In Meta’s deployment, multi-line completions were only 16% of displayed suggestions but supplied 42% of accepted characters, and increased keystrokes saved from 9% to 17%. Yet both Meta and JetBrains found that large gray blocks can be “jarring,” harder to review, and disruptive when they move existing code. Multi-line suggestions should therefore be proactively shown much less often than single-line suggestions.
- **For new-feature implementation, proactive assistance is most appropriate during predictable, implementation-oriented work:** boilerplate, tests, API use, repetitive transformations, and completion of a scope the developer has just opened. Comment-to-code generation should be initiated after a developer has stated an intent in a comment or docstring, not inferred while the developer is still deciding what to build.
- **For debugging, use negotiated or on-demand intervention.** Suggestions should appear after a test result, debugger stop, explicit request, completed edit, or other boundary—not during hypothesis formation, code reading, or stepping. Research on debugging found negotiated interruptions superior to immediate interruptions, and broader interruption studies show that programming context can take much longer to rebuild than the interruption itself.
- **Acceptance rate is useful but not a code-quality measure.** GitHub’s research found acceptance rate to be more predictive of perceived productivity than lines contributed or persistence, but Microsoft’s CUPS study found that developers sometimes accept code before fully evaluating it, then verify or edit it later. Enterprise systems should measure accepted-and-retained code, subsequent edits, test outcomes, reverts, defects, and security findings in addition to immediate acceptance.
- **Explanation support should be available progressively, not attached to every low-risk completion.** Developers’ trust is situational: comprehensibility, perceived correctness, task stakes, process integrity, and alignment with goals matter. Quality indicators, provenance, relevant tests, and user controls can improve trust calibration. But lengthy automatic explanations would themselves become interruptions. A layered design—concise suggestion first, explanation/rationale/tests on demand—is the best-supported approach.
- **The evidence does not support exact acceptance-rate or quality comparisons between GitHub Copilot, Tabnine, and Amazon CodeWhisperer for developers with 2–5 versus 10+ years of experience.** No retrieved independent study provides that complete cross-product × experience × task matrix. GitHub has much stronger public field and experimental evidence; Amazon publishes a productivity challenge but not a comparable acceptance-rate breakdown; and the retrieved Tabnine materials document architecture and speed claims but not controlled experience-stratified acceptance or quality metrics. Product-specific numerical comparisons should therefore be treated as unavailable rather than estimated.

The practical recommendation is a **two-lane interface**:

1. **Proactive lane:** sub-200 ms, short, high-confidence, syntactically stable, easily ignored, and immediately cancelable.
2. **Deliberate lane:** multi-line generation, comment-to-code, debugging help, explanations, security-sensitive code, or expected latency above 750 ms; invoked explicitly or offered only at clear workflow boundaries.

---

## 1. What the evidence can and cannot establish

There is considerably more public evidence for GitHub Copilot than for Tabnine or Amazon CodeWhisperer. Moreover, the studies use different tasks, populations, versions, interfaces, and outcome measures:

- GitHub/Microsoft research includes a randomized task-completion experiment, large-scale telemetry and surveys, and a detailed interaction study.
- Amazon’s public figure comes from a company-run “productivity challenge.”
- The retrieved Tabnine documentation describes local/cloud architecture and responsiveness, but provides no comparable controlled acceptance-rate or task-quality study.
- JetBrains provides production deployment metrics for its own completion systems, not for the three named products.
- Meta’s CodeCompose research is not a Tabnine study, but it is the strongest retrieved evidence about the interaction properties of the same relevant presentation pattern: automatic multi-line inline completion at enterprise scale.

Consequently, there is **no defensible direct ranking** such as “Tabnine is best for 10+ year developers during debugging” or “CodeWhisperer has a specific acceptance advantage among 2–5 year developers.” Any such statement would exceed the evidence.

There is also no research result in the gathered evidence establishing a universal latency optimum in the form “exactly X ms maximizes flow and code quality.” The thresholds in this report are operational design bands synthesized from:

- GitHub’s sub-200 ms production latency;
- Meta’s use of a 750 ms meaningful-display criterion;
- Meta’s evidence that multi-line generations exceeding two seconds are often invalidated by the developer’s next action;
- JetBrains’ finding that several-second completion is noticeably disruptive;
- interruption research showing that task boundaries and negotiated interruptions matter.

These are evidence-based design thresholds, but not psychophysical constants.

---

## 2. Comparison of the three presentation models

### 2.1 GitHub Copilot: automatic inline “ghost text”

Copilot’s core interaction pattern is an inline suggestion produced whenever the programmer pauses, with acceptance through a keyboard command such as Tab. The Microsoft Research CUPS study describes the 2022 version as using the code around the cursor as a prompt and allowing the programmer to accept, reject, or browse up to three alternatives. Natural-language comments can also be used to steer generation (https://arxiv.org/html/2210.14306).

This presentation has three major advantages:

1. **Low switching cost:** the suggestion remains inside the editor and at the insertion point.
2. **Immediate comparison with intent:** a developer who already knows the next line can recognize a correct completion quickly.
3. **Minimal invocation overhead:** the developer does not need to open chat or construct a full prompt.

Its main cost is that every shown suggestion creates a micro-decision: inspect, accept, ignore, reject, or wait. Microsoft’s CUPS work emphasizes that code-recommendation systems introduce previously absent activities—prompt crafting, waiting, verifying, editing generated code, and sometimes accepting first and evaluating later. The study analyzed 21 developers, 3,137 retrospectively labeled coding segments, and 1,096 Copilot suggestions. Its state-based accounting attributed nearly twice as much developer time to interaction with the recommendation system as simpler telemetry metrics did (https://arxiv.org/html/2210.14306).

That matters for “flow”: an unobtrusive visual treatment does not mean the suggestion has zero cognitive cost.

#### Copilot productivity and experience effects

In a controlled experiment, 95 professional developers were randomized to implement a JavaScript HTTP server with or without Copilot. Among those completing the task and survey, the mean completion time was:

- Copilot: **71.17 minutes**
- Control: **160.89 minutes**

The explicit calculation is:

\[
\frac{160.89-71.17}{160.89}
= \frac{89.72}{160.89}
= 0.5576
\approx 55.8\%
\]

Thus the Copilot group completed the task **55.8% faster**, with a reported 95% confidence interval of 21%–89% and a t-test p-value of 0.0017. Task success was seven percentage points higher, but that difference was not statistically significant. The study also found that less experienced developers benefited more, although its experience interaction was only marginal by conventional significance standards: p = 0.0629. The authors explicitly state that the study did not evaluate code quality and may not generalize to large proprietary projects, other tasks, or other languages (https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590).

A separate large GitHub analysis of 934,533 users reported that users accepted nearly **30%** of suggestions on average and that benefits were greatest for less experienced users (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.15033). Another enterprise deployment involving more than 400 developers at ZoomInfo reported:

- suggestion acceptance rate: **33%**
- line acceptance rate: **20%**
- satisfaction: **72%**
- perceived time savings: approximately **20%**

Developers also cited lack of domain-specific logic and inconsistent quality as reasons for additional scrutiny (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.13282).

These figures are broadly consistent with a practical Copilot acceptance baseline around 30%–33%, but they should not be interpreted as an expected rate for every language, task, or experience group.

#### Latency

GitHub’s production service reportedly handles hundreds of millions of completion requests daily, with a mean response time below **200 ms** and peaks around 8,000 requests per second. GitHub describes suggestions as taking over when a developer pauses typing (https://www.infoq.com/presentations/github-copilot/).

This makes sub-200 ms the strongest available production benchmark for proactive inline assistance. It is fast enough that the suggestion can arrive during a natural pause rather than creating a conspicuous wait. It is not proof that 201 ms harms flow, but it is a credible engineering target.

### 2.2 Tabnine: multi-line prediction with local/cloud deployment options

Tabnine’s relevant interaction style is predictive completion inside the IDE, including longer code continuations. Its architecture documentation says that the IDE plugin sends relevant context-window requests to a remote Tabnine cluster for inference, while other Tabnine materials describe local deployment options (https://docs.tabnine.com/main/welcome/readme/architecture).

An older Tabnine Xcode integration claimed that it produced a list of suggestions in less than **10 ms on average**, while also warning that local-model latency could vary by computer and that its cloud option used GPU-accelerated inference (https://github.com/tabnine/tabnine-xcode). That number should not be treated as a modern multi-line LLM latency benchmark: it refers to an older product/integration and a list of suggestions, not necessarily generation of a full multi-line block.

The gathered Tabnine evidence does **not** provide:

- a published multi-line acceptance rate;
- acceptance split between debugging and new-feature work;
- retention, defect, or security outcomes;
- results for developers with 2–5 versus 10+ years of experience;
- a controlled latency-versus-acceptance curve.

Accordingly, the appropriate comparison is architectural and interactional rather than numerical.

For understanding how Tabnine-style multi-line presentation is likely to affect flow, the strongest comparable evidence is Meta’s CodeCompose research and JetBrains’ deployment work.

#### Evidence from enterprise multi-line completion

Meta expanded CodeCompose from single-line to multi-line suggestions across tens of thousands of engineers. The system automatically generated inline suggestions as developers typed. The researchers found that multi-line blocks could be “jarring” because they moved existing code and mixed trusted human-written code with unverified generated code. They therefore limited multi-line display to semantically stable positions such as:

- the end of the innermost scope;
- the end of a line defining a new scope;
- the end of a notebook cell;
- explicit keyboard invocation.

They avoided automatic multi-line generation where characters followed the cursor or where the developer was not at the end of the relevant scope (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141).

The resulting value was substantial:

- Multi-line suggestions were **16% of displayed suggestions**.
- They supplied **42% of all accepted characters**.
- Keystrokes saved increased from **9% to 17%**.
- Less than **1%** of engineers opted out of multi-line suggestions.

Two calculations clarify the leverage:

1. Share-of-value enrichment:

\[
\frac{42\%}{16\%}=2.625
\]

Multi-line suggestions contributed accepted characters at **2.625 times their share of displays**.

2. Comparing accepted-character share per display share for multi-line versus all other suggestions:

\[
\text{Multi-line ratio} = \frac{0.42}{0.16}=2.625
\]

\[
\text{Other-suggestion ratio} = \frac{0.58}{0.84}=0.6905
\]

\[
\frac{2.625}{0.6905}\approx3.80
\]

On this normalized measure, a displayed multi-line suggestion contributed about **3.8 times as much accepted-character share** as a displayed non-multi-line suggestion.

This does **not** mean multi-line suggestions had a 42% acceptance rate. The published figure is accepted-character contribution, not the fraction of blocks accepted.

The increase in keystrokes saved was:

\[
17\%-9\%=8 \text{ percentage points}
\]

and relative improvement was:

\[
\frac{17-9}{9}=0.8889\approx88.9\%
\]

Thus multi-line assistance produced an approximately **89% relative increase** in keystrokes saved.

The design implication for Tabnine-style multi-line completion is clear: long suggestions are valuable enough to retain, but their automatic display should be sparse, semantically gated, and easy to accept partially.

### 2.3 Amazon CodeWhisperer: comment-to-code generation

CodeWhisperer’s interaction model combines normal code context with natural-language comments in the IDE. Amazon describes it as generating recommendations from comments and prior code, making the user’s comment an explicit statement of intent (https://pages.awscloud.com/rs/112-TZM-766/images/DEV201-Maximizing%20Developer%20Productivity%20with%20Amazon%20CodeWhisperer.pdf).

In Amazon’s preview productivity challenge, participants using CodeWhisperer were reported to be:

- **27% more likely to complete tasks successfully**
- **57% faster** than participants who did not use it

(https://pages.awscloud.com/rs/112-TZM-766/images/DEV201-Maximizing%20Developer%20Productivity%20with%20Amazon%20CodeWhisperer.pdf).

Those figures are not directly comparable to Copilot’s randomized HTTP-server experiment:

- Amazon’s exact sample, task distribution, experience strata, and acceptance denominator are not provided in the gathered source.
- “57% faster” may be computed differently from a 57% reduction in completion time.
- No acceptance rate or retained-code rate is supplied.
- No debugging-versus-feature split is supplied.

Comment-to-code has an important timing advantage: the comment itself supplies an intentional boundary. Once the developer finishes a comment such as “validate the request and return 400 for missing fields,” the interface has stronger evidence that the developer wants implementation help. This reduces the need to interrupt while intent is still forming.

It also carries a risk: generated code may look like a direct implementation of the comment while silently embedding an incorrect interpretation, omitted edge case, insecure API, or unsupported assumption. Therefore comment-to-code should pair generation with quick access to an explanation, inferred assumptions, tests, and security analysis—especially in enterprise and high-stakes code.

## 3. Recommended latency thresholds

### 3.1 There is no single experimentally proven optimal threshold

The research supports latency bands, not one exact universal optimum. Latency interacts with:

- suggestion length;
- whether the developer is typing or paused;
- task state;
- model confidence;
- location in the syntax tree;
- whether generation was explicitly requested;
- experience and familiarity with the codebase;
- network and local rendering delay.

End-to-end latency should be measured from the developer’s triggering action to the suggestion being visibly stable—not just server inference time.

### 3.2 Evidence-based operational bands

| End-to-end latency | Recommended policy | Evidence and interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **0–200 ms** | Proactive inline suggestions are appropriate if short and high-confidence. | GitHub reports mean production response below 200 ms. This is the best available real-world benchmark for continuous inline completion (https://www.infoq.com/presentations/github-copilot/). |
| **200–750 ms** | Proactive only at stable boundaries and only when predicted utility is high. Cancel immediately if the code state changes. | Meta shows latency governs whether a suggestion is displayed before the next keystroke; suggestions become stale as soon as the developer types or moves the cursor (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141). |
| **750–2,000 ms** | Prefer explicit invocation, visible pending state, or carefully gated multi-line generation. Do not make the developer wonder whether anything is coming. | Meta counted acceptance only for suggestions visible more than 750 ms and added an inline spinner because uncertainty about pending multi-line generation frustrated users (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141). |
| **Above 2,000 ms** | Avoid silent automatic inline generation. Use on-demand generation, streaming, a progress indicator, or a separate preview surface. | Meta reports long multi-line generation could take more than two seconds, during which another keystroke often invalidated the response. JetBrains similarly reports that extensive LLMs taking several seconds caused noticeable delays (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141; https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2024/10/complete-the-un-completable-the-state-of-ai-completion-in-jetbrains-ides/). |

The **750 ms boundary must not be misreported as a proven cognitive interruption threshold**. It was Meta’s criterion for a suggestion being visible long enough to count in its acceptance denominator. It is useful for UI design because it separates near-immediate completion from a delay that may need feedback, but it is not a universal human-factors constant.

### 3.3 Why latency changes acceptance

Meta’s production experiments show the mechanism directly:

- Multi-line suggestions are invalidated when the developer types another character or moves the cursor.
- Lower latency therefore raises the **display rate** before quality or user preference even enters the funnel.
- Flash Attention produced a median **2.53× reduction in first-token latency** and **1.15× reduction in final-token latency**. In the associated experiment, displayed suggestions increased **13%**, acceptance rate increased **8%**, and accepted suggestion length increased **3%**.
- CUDA graphs and fused kernels reduced median generation latency **29%** and 90th-percentile latency **40%**. Displayed suggestions rose **26%**, and the total number accepted rose **17%**, even though acceptance rate declined **1%**.

The latter result is especially important: reducing latency can expose suggestions in additional, lower-value contexts. Faster is beneficial, but not sufficient. Trigger quality and context filtering are also necessary (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141).

Meta’s overall model-hosting optimizations sped multi-line suggestion latency by approximately **2.5×**. The study treats latency as both a guardrail and a driver of display throughput rather than as an isolated performance statistic.

### 3.4 JetBrains deployment evidence

JetBrains reported millions of local full-line completions per day, an acceptance rate of **35% or more**, and an explicit cancel rate around **5%**. It described earlier cloud completion as too conservative because it triggered only after Enter; according to JetBrains, a developer presses Enter only around **70 times per day**, limiting opportunity. But making generation more frequent also required lower latency and more careful single-line/multi-line selection (https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2024/10/complete-the-un-completable-the-state-of-ai-completion-in-jetbrains-ides/).

JetBrains’ redesigned cloud completion:

- triggers while typing rather than only after Enter;
- limits the locations where multi-line suggestions appear;
- uses syntax-aware highlighting rather than undifferentiated gray text;
- supports word-by-word and line-by-line acceptance;
- deliberately reduced average completion length;
- uses project context while filtering undesirable output.

JetBrains later reported that its Mellum model reduced completion latency to **one-third** of its previous level, achieved about a **40% acceptance rate**, reduced cancel rate by **3–4×**, and more than doubled the number of completions shown (https://blog.jetbrains.com/blog/2024/10/22/introducing-mellum-jetbrains-new-llm-built-for-developers/).

These figures do not establish how much of the acceptance increase was caused by latency rather than model quality, filtering, or UX changes. They do reinforce that low latency, concise output, appropriate trigger locations, and readable presentation have to be optimized together.

## 4. Interruption timing: debugging versus new-feature development

### 4.1 New-feature development

New-feature implementation includes at least two distinct cognitive modes:

1. **Acceleration mode:** the developer knows what to build and is translating a clear plan into code.
2. **Exploration mode:** the developer is deciding on APIs, architecture, behavior, or implementation strategy.

Microsoft’s CUPS paper cites prior work distinguishing these modes and provides more detailed states such as thinking about new code, writing new code, prompt crafting, waiting for a suggestion, verifying, editing generated code, testing, and looking up documentation (https://arxiv.org/html/2210.14306).

#### Best timing during acceleration

Proactive suggestions are most likely to help when:

- the developer has started a predictable line;
- a naming or syntactic pattern is established;
- boilerplate is being repeated;
- a new function or scope has just been declared;
- a natural-language comment clearly specifies the next behavior;
- tests or surrounding code strongly constrain the expected completion.

This is where Copilot-style short inline suggestions and carefully triggered Tabnine-style multi-line blocks can save keystrokes without redirecting thought.

For a developer writing a new function, the recommended sequence is:

1. Let the developer state the function name, signature, docstring, or initial control structure.
2. Generate short inline completion within approximately 200 ms where possible.
3. Offer multi-line completion only at the end of the new scope declaration or after an explicit request.
4. Permit token-, word-, or line-level partial acceptance.
5. Avoid moving existing code or obscuring the next handwritten line.

Meta’s semantic trigger rules and JetBrains’ conservative multi-line strategy both support this approach (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141; https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2024/10/complete-the-un-completable-the-state-of-ai-completion-in-jetbrains-ides/).

#### Best timing during exploration

During exploration, a large automatic completion can prematurely anchor the developer on one implementation. The interface should instead:

- wait for an explicit comment or command;
- offer alternatives in a preview, not continuously moving ghost text;
- show relevant project APIs or examples;
- expose assumptions and uncertainties;
- make it easy to request explanation before insertion.

Comment-to-code is particularly appropriate here because the developer decides when their intent is sufficiently formed to write the comment. The completion is reactive to an explicit intent marker rather than a guess made during deliberation.

### 4.2 Debugging

Debugging is less compatible with unsolicited generation because the developer is often:

- reading rather than typing;
- maintaining a causal model of program state;
- comparing expected and actual behavior;
- stepping through execution;
- forming or eliminating hypotheses;
- making small diagnostic edits whose purpose is not the same as production code.

Research comparing interruption styles in end-user debugging found **negotiated-style interruptions superior to immediate-style interruptions** on several important measures and suggested that immediate interruption changed debugging strategies (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/985692.985729).

The broader programming-interruption literature reinforces the cost. An analysis involving 10,000 recorded sessions from 86 programmers, supplemented by a survey of 414 programmers, found:

- only **10%** of interrupted sessions resumed programming activity within one minute;
- only **7%** resumed editing without first navigating elsewhere.

This shows that recovery often requires reconstructing location and context, although these were larger task interruptions rather than inline code-completion microinterruptions (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11219-010-9104-9).

A controlled study of resumption cues found that developers using automated cues completed interrupted programming tasks at **twice the success rate** of developers relying on note-taking alone, and participants preferred chronological code-snippet cues (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1753326.1753342). The design lesson is not merely “avoid all interruption”; it is also to preserve and restore context when interruption occurs.

#### Recommended debugging timing

Proactive debugging suggestions should appear only at negotiated boundaries such as:

- after a test fails and output stabilizes;
- after the debugger pauses at a breakpoint;
- after an exception is surfaced;
- after the developer completes an edit and pauses;
- after an explicit “explain,” “diagnose,” or “suggest fix” action;
- after a build or static-analysis result;
- when the developer returns to the IDE after consulting documentation.

They should not appear:

- while the developer is stepping;
- while scrolling or reading code;
- in the middle of a rapid edit sequence;
- while hovering or inspecting state;
- immediately after every diagnostic character typed;
- when the current suggestion would move or obscure inspected code.

Debugging suggestions should default to **diagnosis and evidence before code replacement**:

1. summarize the likely failure;
2. identify the relevant state or trace;
3. state assumptions;
4. propose one or more candidate changes;
5. show or generate a validating test;
6. insert code only after confirmation.

This is more compatible with calibrated trust than immediately offering a large patch.

### 4.3 What is known about acceptance by task timing

The gathered evidence does not provide a reliable numeric table of acceptance rates for:

- debugging versus new-feature development;
- each of Copilot, Tabnine, and CodeWhisperer;
- each experience group.

The closest direct timing evidence comes from a two-month professional-developer deployment of an adaptive timing mechanism. It reported suggestion acceptance of:

- **4.9%** with no delay;
- **15.4%** with static delays;
- **18.6%** with adaptive timing;

and a reduction in “blind rejections” from **8.3% to 0.36%**, while reducing wasted inference calls by **75%**. The mechanism incorporated a high-level estimate of whether the developer was implementing or debugging (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1109/ASEW67777.2025.00049).

Quantitative work:

- Static delay versus no delay:

\[
15.4\%-4.9\%=10.5 \text{ percentage points}
\]

Relative increase:

\[
\frac{15.4}{4.9}=3.14
\]

- Adaptive timing versus no delay:

\[
18.6\%-4.9\%=13.7 \text{ percentage points}
\]

Relative increase:

\[
\frac{18.6}{4.9}=3.80
\]

- Adaptive versus static:

\[
18.6\%-15.4\%=3.2 \text{ percentage points}
\]

Relative increase:

\[
\frac{18.6-15.4}{15.4}=20.8\%
\]

- Blind-rejection reduction:

\[
8.3\%-0.36\%=7.94 \text{ percentage points}
\]

Relative reduction:

\[
\frac{8.3-0.36}{8.3}=95.7\%
\]

This is strong evidence that “immediately show everything” is inferior to timing adapted to the developer’s state. However, the gathered abstract does not disclose the exact millisecond delays or provide separate final acceptance rates for debugging and implementation, so those values cannot be reconstructed.
