## 5. Developers with 2–5 years versus 10+ years of experience

### 5.1 What the studies show

GitHub’s randomized study found that less experienced developers benefited more from Copilot on the HTTP-server task. The average participant had six years of coding experience, but the published results retrieved here do not provide separate outcomes for exactly 2–5 years and 10+ years (https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590).

The large GitHub user analysis similarly reports the greatest benefits for less experienced users, with average acceptance near 30%, but does not give the requested exact experience bands in the gathered material (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.15033).

JetBrains surveyed 640 early AI Assistant adopters; 91% reported saving time, 37% reported saving 1–3 hours per week, 22% reported saving 3–5 hours, and 4%—23 people—reported saving more than eight hours. JetBrains stated that developers with fewer than two years of experience appeared to benefit most, commonly reporting savings of 3–5 hours per week (https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2024/04/developers-save-up-to-8-hours-per-week-with-jetbrains-ai-assistant/). This is self-reported evidence and does not directly answer 2–5 versus 10+.

A comparative thesis summarized in the retrieved evidence reported that novices used Copilot primarily for debugging and learning, while experienced developers used it more broadly but were more critical of context awareness and security. Both groups used exploration mode, and experienced developers were more likely to enter acceleration mode (https://exa.ai/library/publication/18mg7lbkg31). Because this is a thesis summary rather than a large field deployment, it should be treated as suggestive.

### 5.2 Likely interaction differences, with uncertainty

#### Developers with 2–5 years

Evidence suggests this group is more likely to obtain visible task-completion gains, but may also face higher verification and calibration risk.

Appropriate defaults:

- Proactively show short, common-pattern inline suggestions at low latency.
- Allow comment-to-code for scaffolding and API discovery.
- Provide easy access to explanations, examples, tests, and project-specific conventions.
- Visibly identify generated code or preserve provenance.
- Use partial acceptance rather than encouraging wholesale insertion.
- Suppress long blocks when confidence, project relevance, or security posture is uncertain.
- Encourage validation before considering a suggestion complete.

Potential failure modes:

- accepting plausible code without understanding it;
- being anchored by the first suggestion;
- mistaking fluent explanations for evidence;
- missing security, performance, or concurrency issues;
- relying on generated code rather than learning the project’s abstractions.

A study of novice Copilot use found cognitive and metacognitive difficulties and argued for stronger scaffolding in the interface (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3617367).

#### Developers with 10+ years

Senior developers may benefit more from high-selectivity acceleration than from frequent exploratory suggestions. They generally have a stronger internal plan and a lower tolerance for irrelevant or context-insensitive output.

Appropriate defaults:

- Use a stricter proactive threshold.
- Prefer very fast single-line completion for repetitive implementation.
- Trigger multi-line generation at explicit semantic boundaries or on demand.
- Optimize for project-specific APIs, architecture, security, and consistency.
- Provide concise rationale, dependency provenance, and change-impact information rather than tutorial-style explanation.
- Let users suppress entire categories or tune suggestion frequency by task.
- Avoid interrupting code review, debugging, architectural reasoning, and unfamiliar high-risk areas.

Potential failure modes:

- productivity loss from reviewing low-value suggestions;
- overconfidence caused by a suggestion matching familiar surface patterns;
- rejecting useful assistance because initial context quality is poor;
- hidden architectural inconsistency despite locally correct code.

### 5.3 Recommended adaptive policy by experience

| Dimension | 2–5 years | 10+ years |
|---|---|---|
| Short inline completion | Proactive at high confidence and low latency | Proactive, but with stricter relevance filtering |
| Multi-line completion | Offer at scope boundaries with partial acceptance and validation cues | Prefer explicit invocation or very high-confidence scope completion |
| Comment-to-code | Useful for learning, scaffolding, and APIs; pair with explanation/tests | Useful for delegating well-specified boilerplate; keep explanations concise |
| Debugging | Negotiated assistance with causal explanation and test guidance | On-demand diagnosis; avoid unsolicited fixes during reasoning |
| Explanation | More accessible detail, examples, API references, and validation steps | Compact assumptions, risks, architecture impact, provenance, and evidence |
| Security-sensitive code | Require warning, tests/scans, and explicit confirmation | Same safeguards; experience should not bypass controls |
| Personalization | Learn accepted patterns but avoid reinforcing indiscriminate acceptance | Learn task-specific suppression and preferred invocation style |

These are design recommendations inferred from the direction of experience effects, not measured product-specific acceptance rates.

## 6. Acceptance rate, flow, and code quality

### 6.1 Acceptance rate predicts perceived usefulness

GitHub’s productivity research matched 2,631 user survey responses to IDE telemetry and found that acceptance rate—the fraction of shown suggestions subsequently accepted—was a better predictor of perceived productivity than more detailed contribution measures. Acceptance varied substantially across users and over time. Earlier IntelliCode Compose online trials had reported an acceptance/click-through rate around 10% (https://cacmb4.acm.org/magazines/2024/3/280076-measuring-github-copilots-impact-on-productivity/fulltext).

The approximate industry figures gathered are:

- GitHub Copilot large user analysis: nearly **30%**
- Copilot enterprise deployment at ZoomInfo: **33% of suggestions**, **20% of lines**
- JetBrains local/full-line: **35% or more**
- JetBrains Mellum: approximately **40%**
- Earlier IntelliCode Compose: about **10%**

These values should not be used as a leaderboard. Denominators, suggestion length, visibility rules, trigger frequency, language mix, and user populations differ.

### 6.2 Acceptance is not equivalent to quality

Microsoft’s CUPS research identifies several reasons immediate acceptance can mislead:

- Developers may accept monochrome text so they can inspect it with normal syntax highlighting.
- They may accept line-by-line suggestions before evaluating the combined block.
- They may defer thought, planning to verify the suggestion later.
- Verification and editing may happen after acceptance.
- Prompt construction costs are absent from the acceptance metric.

The CUPS study therefore found nearly twice as much interaction time as conventional telemetry would attribute (https://arxiv.org/html/2210.14306).

A later trust-dynamics study reported that developers often changed their decisions and retained only **52% of original suggestions**, with comprehensibility and perceived correctness being the most common trust factors (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/ICSE55347.2025.00199).

For enterprise evaluation, acceptance should be supplemented by:

- accepted-and-retained characters after a defined period;
- edit distance after acceptance;
- deletion or revert rate;
- tests passed and new tests created;
- static-analysis and security findings;
- review comments;
- defects linked to generated lines;
- build failures;
- production incidents;
- time spent verifying;
- interruption and waiting time;
- task completion time;
- developer satisfaction and perceived control.

GitHub itself has moved toward accepted-and-retained characters as a meaningful metric; a newer custom model was reported to improve accepted-and-retained characters by 20%, acceptance rate by 12%, throughput by 3×, and latency by 35% (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/the-road-to-better-completions-building-a-faster-smarter-github-copilot-with-a-new-custom-model/).

### 6.3 Quality evidence remains incomplete

The randomized Copilot productivity study explicitly states that it did not measure code quality. Faster completion could improve quality if the assistant contributes better implementation, or reduce quality if developers scrutinize code less (https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590).

Amazon’s result that CodeWhisperer users were 27% more likely to complete tasks successfully is evidence about task success, not long-term maintainability, security, or production defect rates (https://pages.awscloud.com/rs/112-TZM-766/images/DEV201-Maximizing%20Developer%20Productivity%20with%20Amazon%20CodeWhisperer.pdf).

A study in which 28 participants validated and repaired Copilot-generated code found that developers often failed to identify code as LLM-generated when provenance was not explicit. Informing them of provenance improved performance and increased search effort, but also increased cognitive workload (https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10576279). This supports keeping provenance available while minimizing unnecessary visual burden.

The quality implication is that timing and explanation design should not optimize solely for “more acceptances.” The objective should be **useful, retained, validated code with minimal disruption**.

## 7. Explanation availability and trust calibration

### 7.1 Trust is situational, not a fixed attitude toward the product

A two-stage qualitative study first interviewed 17 developers and then conducted design-probe sessions with 12 more. Developers judged AI code-generation tools using:

- perceived practical benefit;
- alignment with short- and long-term goals;
- integrity of the generation process;
- task stakes;
- task complexity.

They continuously reassessed trust in context. The researchers found that missing trust affordances could produce inefficient or biased evaluations. Proposed supports included quality indicators, usage-statistics dashboards, and controls for communicating user intent (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3630106.3658984).

Another mixed-method study found that comprehensibility and perceived correctness were the most frequently used criteria for judging a suggestion, while developers retained only 52% of original suggestions (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/ICSE55347.2025.00199).

The implication is that an explanation should help the developer decide **when not to rely** on a suggestion, not merely persuade them to accept it.

### 7.2 Explanations can both improve and distort trust

Explanation availability can improve calibration by exposing:

- what the generated code is intended to do;
- assumptions inferred from surrounding code or comments;
- relevant project files or APIs;
- likely edge cases;
- confidence or quality indicators;
- tests or evidence supporting correctness;
- security and licensing/provenance concerns.

But explanations can also create automation bias if they are fluent yet ungrounded. A developer may mistake a convincing rationale for proof. Detailed explanations also consume attention and can become a larger interruption than the code itself.

Therefore, explanations should be:

- **available, not mandatory**, for routine low-risk completion;
- **automatically surfaced** for high-risk or low-confidence cases;
- **grounded** in code, tests, static analysis, documentation, and project context;
- **separable** from the generated code so that accepting code does not imply accepting the explanation;
- **concise by default**, with progressive expansion.

### 7.3 Recommended explanation layers

**Layer 0: inline completion**

- Show only the code.
- Use syntax-aware rendering rather than undifferentiated gray blocks.
- Allow immediate dismissal and partial acceptance.

**Layer 1: compact rationale**

Available through hover or shortcut:

- one-sentence intent;
- key assumption;
- files/APIs used;
- warning if generated from incomplete context.

**Layer 2: validation**

- generated or relevant tests;
- expected inputs and outputs;
- static-analysis result;
- security warning;
- citations to internal documentation or definitions;
- provenance marker.

**Layer 3: detailed explanation**

On explicit demand:

- step-by-step behavior;
- alternatives considered;
- complexity and performance;
- error handling;
- architectural implications;
- known limitations.

For junior developers, Layer 1 or 2 can be easier to discover. For senior developers, the default should remain terse, while risk and architectural-impact information should be prominent.

### 7.4 Timing explanations without breaking flow

Do not append an explanation to every sub-200 ms inline completion. Instead:

- show explanation affordances after the suggestion stabilizes;
- surface them when the developer pauses over the suggestion;
- automatically expand risk information only for security-sensitive code, unfamiliar dependencies, broad multi-line edits, or low-confidence output;
- provide an explanation before applying a multi-file or behavior-changing patch;
- during debugging, show causal evidence before an automatic fix;
- after acceptance, retain a lightweight provenance marker that can be inspected during review.

This preserves the speed advantage of inline completion while still supporting calibrated reliance.

## 8. Proactive versus on-demand presentation policy

### 8.1 Show proactively when all or most of these conditions hold

- Expected end-to-end latency is **≤200 ms**.
- The completion is one line or otherwise visually compact.
- The cursor is at the end of a line or stable scope.
- There is no existing code that would be displaced.
- The developer is typing implementation code, not reading or stepping.
- Context strongly constrains the continuation.
- Historical acceptance for this developer, repository, language, and trigger type is high.
- The suggestion can be ignored without an explicit action.
- The code is low risk and easy to verify.
- The request will be canceled if another keystroke makes it stale.

Typical examples:

- variable names and call arguments;
- repetitive mappings or serializers;
- closing predictable control structures;
- common test assertions;
- implementation following a precise signature or comment;
- repetitive enterprise framework boilerplate.

### 8.2 Show proactively but only at a boundary when these conditions hold

- Expected latency is **200–750 ms**.
- The suggestion is multi-line but confined to the new innermost scope.
- The developer has just completed a signature, comment, docstring, or test name.
- A test/build/debugger event has completed.
- The developer is returning from an external context and a resumptive cue is useful.
- The output is a non-modal recommendation rather than an immediate patch.

Use semantic gating like Meta’s: only at the end of the owning scope, at a newly declared scope, at the end of a notebook cell, or through explicit invocation (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141).

### 8.3 Make generation visibly pending or on-demand when

- Expected latency is **750–2,000 ms**.
- The completion is a large block.
- The developer is exploring rather than executing a known plan.
- The request depends on project-wide retrieval.
- The operation may introduce a dependency.
- Multiple valid approaches exist.
- The suggestion needs an explanation or test plan.

Show a subtle spinner or pending marker so the developer knows whether waiting is rational. Meta’s inline indicator improved predictability and gave developers control over whether to pause or keep typing (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141).

### 8.4 Require explicit invocation when

- Expected latency is **>2,000 ms**.
- The task is debugging or root-cause analysis.
- The proposed change spans files or architectural boundaries.
- The code handles authentication, authorization, cryptography, money, privacy, data deletion, or concurrency.
- The model has weak project context.
- The developer is reading, navigating, stepping, or reviewing.
- The generated output could obscure or move trusted code.
- An explanation is essential for safe evaluation.
- The action would execute commands, alter infrastructure, or commit changes.

## 9. Enterprise measurement and experiment design

An enterprise rollout should instrument the complete suggestion funnel:

1. **Eligible trigger**
2. **Request issued**
3. **Canceled before completion**
4. **Suggestion rendered**
5. **Visible for at least 750 ms**
6. **Partially or fully accepted**
7. **Edited**
8. **Retained**
9. **Validated by tests/static analysis**
10. **Committed**
11. **Reviewed**
12. **Reverted or associated with a defect**

At minimum, segment results by:

- 2–5 versus 10+ years of professional experience;
- debugging, new-feature work, testing, documentation, and refactoring;
- single-line versus multi-line;
- proactive versus explicit invocation;
- latency bucket: ≤200, 201–750, 751–2,000, >2,000 ms;
- language and framework;
- repository familiarity;
- security sensitivity;
- suggestion confidence;
- explanation opened/not opened;
- remote versus local model;
- cold versus warm context.

### Recommended primary metrics

- accepted-and-retained characters;
- task completion time;
- validated task success;
- test and build pass rate;
- defect and revert rate;
- time spent waiting and verifying;
- uninterrupted coding intervals;
- developer-reported flow and control.

### Secondary metrics

- raw acceptance rate;
- partial acceptance rate;
- explicit rejection/cancel rate;
- suggestion display rate;
- percentage of keystrokes saved;
- explanation-open rate;
- time to accept;
- prompt/comment construction time;
- opt-out rate.

### Experiments to run

**Experiment A: latency bands**

Randomize otherwise identical suggestions among short delays within safe ranges. Test whether acceptance, retained code, and flow differ at ≤200, 201–500, and 501–750 ms. Do not intentionally delay high-stakes operations merely to raise acceptance.

**Experiment B: trigger policy**

Compare:

- every pause;
- syntactic boundaries only;
- adaptive prediction based on recent acceptance;
- explicit invocation.

**Experiment C: task state**

Detect or let users indicate:

- implementing;
- debugging;
- reading/reviewing;
- testing;
- refactoring.

Measure whether debugging benefits from negotiated timing and implementation from proactive timing.

**Experiment D: explanation availability**

Compare:

- no explanation affordance;
- explanation on demand;
- compact automatic risk/assumption indicator;
- full automatic explanation for high-risk blocks.

Measure correct acceptance and correct rejection, not just perceived trust.

**Experiment E: experience personalization**

Compare conservative versus frequent proactive policies separately for 2–5 and 10+ year developers. Examine whether junior developers gain speed at the cost of more post-acceptance correction, and whether senior developers benefit from lower frequency but higher project relevance.

---

## 10. Product-specific design recommendations

### GitHub Copilot-style inline interface

- Maintain sub-200 ms mean end-to-end response where possible.
- Keep default completions short during continuous typing.
- Predict when the developer is implementing versus debugging or reading.
- Suppress low-probability suggestions instead of maximizing display count.
- Preserve an explicit command for longer alternatives.
- Track accepted-and-retained code and verification time.
- Make provenance, rationale, and tests available without attaching them to every completion.
- For senior developers, allow stronger suppression and repository-specific tuning.
- For less experienced developers, make validation and explanation affordances easier to discover.

### Tabnine-style multi-line prediction

- Do not rely on the older “less than 10 ms” suggestion-list claim as a multi-line performance target; measure current end-to-end block generation separately (https://github.com/tabnine/tabnine-xcode).
- Treat multi-line generation as a distinct interaction class.
- Trigger automatically only at scope boundaries.
- Avoid shifting existing code.
- Stream or show a pending indicator if generation exceeds about 750 ms.
- Use partial acceptance by token or line.
- Default to explicit invocation if expected generation exceeds two seconds.
- Evaluate accepted-character leverage and retained-code value rather than only block acceptance.
- Offer local deployment for privacy where appropriate, but monitor hardware-dependent latency.

### Amazon CodeWhisperer-style comment-to-code

- Treat completion of a natural-language comment as an explicit intent boundary.
- Wait until the comment or docstring is complete rather than generating on every word.
- Generate proactively only when the comment is specific and the expected delay is low.
- For broad comments, offer an explicit “generate” action and preview.
- Pair the output with inferred assumptions, relevant APIs, tests, and security checks.
- During debugging, interpret comments such as “why does this fail?” as requests for diagnosis, not immediate code insertion.
- Do not infer acceptance or code quality from Amazon’s 57% speed and 27% success figures; collect enterprise-specific retained-code and defect outcomes.

---

## 11. Bottom-line decision framework

The research supports the following enterprise defaults:

### New-feature development

- **Short completion, ≤200 ms:** proactive.
- **Multi-line, 200–750 ms:** proactive only at a new scope or explicit intent boundary.
- **Multi-line, 750–2,000 ms:** visible pending state or on-demand.
- **Above 2,000 ms:** explicit generation with preview.
- **Explanation:** on demand, with automatic risk indicators for sensitive code.

### Debugging

- **While reading, stepping, or forming a hypothesis:** suppress proactive code.
- **After test failure, breakpoint, exception, or completed diagnostic edit:** offer a negotiated diagnostic action.
- **Fix generation:** on demand, with causal explanation and validation.
- **Large patch:** preview, tests, and explicit confirmation.
- **Latency:** less important than timing at a cognitive boundary; a fast interruption at the wrong moment is still an interruption.

### Developers with 2–5 years

- Permit somewhat more proactive low-risk assistance.
- Emphasize explanations, examples, tests, provenance, and partial acceptance.
- Monitor whether apparent speed gains are offset by correction or security costs.

### Developers with 10+ years

- Use stricter proactive filtering.
- Prioritize project context, architecture, and low-noise acceleration.
- Keep detailed explanations available but not automatically expanded.
- Use on-demand assistance for debugging, review, and high-impact changes.

## Conclusion

The central finding is that **timing quality matters as much as model quality**. Low latency raises the chance that a suggestion arrives before the developer moves on, but indiscriminate speed can merely expose more low-value suggestions. The best-performing systems combine low latency with semantic trigger rules, conservative multi-line presentation, partial acceptance, cancellation, and visible progress for longer work.

The defensible practical thresholds are:

- **≤200 ms:** suitable for proactive inline completion;
- **200–750 ms:** selective proactive presentation at stable boundaries;
- **750–2,000 ms:** pending indicator or on-demand generation;
- **>2,000 ms:** explicit invocation and preview.

These are operational synthesis thresholds, not universal cognitive constants.

For task timing, proactive suggestions fit predictable new-feature implementation; debugging should use negotiated or on-demand assistance. For experience, available evidence indicates larger productivity gains among less experienced developers, but does not provide exact product-by-task acceptance rates for 2–5 versus 10+ years. Senior developers should generally receive fewer, more contextually precise suggestions; less experienced developers need stronger explanation and validation scaffolding.

Finally, explanations improve trust calibration only when they provide grounded evidence and preserve user control. They should help developers recognize both when a suggestion is trustworthy and when it is not. The enterprise objective should therefore be neither maximum suggestion frequency nor maximum immediate acceptance, but **validated, retained code delivered at moments that preserve the developer’s cognitive flow**.

final.content:
COLLAR DELTA RANGES

Sold Call Delta: 0.20 to 0.30 (reason: this generally provides a useful compromise between premium income and retaining upside. Use approximately 0.20 when keeping the shares and preserving upside are priorities; use approximately 0.30 when financing the put is more important. The quoted call has positive delta, but because it is sold, its contribution to position delta is negative.)

Bought Put Delta: −0.20 to −0.30, or 0.20 to 0.30 in absolute terms (reason: this range usually provides meaningful protection without paying for near-the-money insurance. A −0.30 put establishes a higher, more expensive floor; a −0.20 put is cheaper but leaves a larger deductible before protection begins.)

Practical wider ranges:

- Sold call: approximately 0.15–0.35
- Bought put: approximately −0.15 to −0.35
- Conservative about surrendering stock: sell 0.15–0.20 delta
- Stronger downside protection: buy −0.25 to −0.35 delta
- Catastrophe-only protection: buy approximately −0.10 to −0.20 delta

Important clarification: a “30-delta put” does not mean protection begins 30% below the stock. Delta is an option-price sensitivity and, secondarily, an approximate model-based indication of finishing in the money. The percentage distance to the strike depends on volatility, expiration, interest rates, dividends and volatility skew. OIC defines delta principally as the estimated option-price change for a $1 underlying move; using it as an ITM probability is only an approximation (https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/delta; https://www.optionseducation.org/videolibrary/probability-i-delta-as-a-probability-metric).

Likewise, a 0.30-delta call does not literally guarantee a 30% assignment probability. Assignment can occur before expiration, particularly around ex-dividend dates, while delta is not the same mathematical quantity as terminal ITM probability.


SYMMETRIC VS. ASYMMETRIC

Recommendation: Start with the desired downside floor, and then choose the call that meets the acceptable cost and upside cap. Do not require equal deltas.

A symmetric collar—such as selling a 0.25-delta call and buying a −0.25-delta put—is a clean probability-based starting point, but it is not necessarily zero-cost. Equal absolute deltas mean roughly comparable modeled tail locations, not equal premiums.

In equity options, downside puts commonly have higher implied volatility than equidistant upside calls. Consequently:

- Equal-delta collars often require a net debit.
- A zero-premium collar may require selling a higher-delta/closer call, buying a lower-delta/farther put, or both.
- Alternatively, the investor can accept a debit or use a put-spread collar.

A useful decision hierarchy is:

1. Choose the maximum tolerable loss and therefore the put strike.
2. Choose expiration to cover the required risk period.
3. Decide how much upside can be surrendered.
4. Select the call producing the desired net debit, credit or approximately zero premium.
5. Check both deltas afterward to understand the resulting exposures.

Thus, an asymmetric structure such as selling a 0.25-delta call and buying a −0.20-delta put is entirely reasonable when preserving more upside while obtaining lower-cost, deeper downside protection. If tight protection is more important, the asymmetry may go the other way—for example, buying a −0.30 put and selling a 0.30–0.35 call or paying a net debit.

There is no credible market-wide census demonstrating that “most traders” use equal deltas. Published institutional methodologies more often specify a target loss floor, target upside cap, or premium budget rather than insisting on delta symmetry. OIC likewise describes strike selection in terms of the put floor, call ceiling, hedge cost and desired protection—not a mandatory equal-delta rule (https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/collar-protective-collar).


PERCENTAGE DISTANCE FROM CURRENT PRICE

“Sell the 10% OTM call and buy the 10% OTM put” is a valid simple rule, but it is not volatility-neutral.

For example, 10% OTM over one month could be extremely remote for a low-volatility utility but relatively close for a volatile technology or biotechnology stock. The corresponding deltas could differ substantially. The same strike percentage also produces very different deltas at 30 days versus one year.

Recommended approach:

- Use percentage distance when the investor’s economic limits are explicitly stated in return terms: “I can absorb a 10% loss and will surrender gains above 12%.”
- Use delta when seeking approximately consistent option exposure across stocks, volatility regimes or expiration periods.
- For a single concentrated holding, prioritize the dollar loss floor and tax/assignment consequences over an arbitrary delta.

Representative percentage ranges are:

- Put: commonly 5%–15% OTM
- Call: commonly 5%–15% OTM
- Shorter expirations generally require smaller percentage distances to reach 20–30 delta.
- Longer expirations or high-volatility stocks generally place the same delta farther from spot.

The Cboe S&P 500 95-110 Collar Index illustrates a fixed-percentage rather than equal-delta design: it buys a 5% OTM quarterly SPX put and sells a 10% OTM monthly SPX call. Cboe expressly notes that there is no unique “best” collar because investors have different risk/return preferences (https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/newcollardescriptionoct1909.pdf).


EXAMPLE COLLAR

Stock: $100

Illustrative assumptions:

- 90 days to expiration
- Interest rate: 4.5%
- Dividend yield: 1.5%
- Call implied volatility: 24%
- Put implied volatility: 28%, reflecting illustrative downside skew
- European-style Black-Scholes estimates; actual American equity-option prices, deltas and fills will differ

Sell call: $110 strike, Delta +0.248 for the option, or −0.248 position delta because it is sold  
Call premium received: approximately $1.66 per share, or $166 per contract

Buy put: $90 strike, Delta −0.189  
Put premium paid: approximately $1.54 per share, or $154 per contract

Net credit/debit: $1.66 − $1.54 = $0.12 credit per share, or approximately $12 credit for one 100-share collar, before commissions and bid/ask slippage

This is approximately:

- A 10% upside ceiling
- A 10% downside deductible
- An asymmetric delta collar: roughly 25-delta call versus 19-delta put
- A near-zero-cost structure, despite equal 10% strike distances

Expiration payoff calculations, including the $0.12 credit:

- Maximum expiration value above the call strike: $110.12 per share
- Maximum gain from a $100 starting stock price:  
  $110 − $100 + $0.12 = $10.12 per share, or $1,012
- Minimum effective expiration value below the put strike: $90.12 per share
- Maximum loss from a $100 starting stock price:  
  $100 − $90 − $0.12 = $9.88 per share, or $988

The quoted credit is illustrative, not a live market quote. Real net cost must use executable bid/ask prices, and single-stock volatility skew may be materially different.


INSTITUTIONAL COLLAR STRUCTURES

Institutional holders generally treat the collar as an outcome-design and risk-budgeting exercise rather than applying one universal retail delta rule.

Common institutional characteristics include:

1. Index overlays

Pension funds and diversified portfolios frequently use SPX or other index options over an equity portfolio rather than placing separate collars on every stock. This can reduce operational complexity, although basis risk remains if the portfolio differs from the index.

2. Longer-dated protection

Institutions may buy six- to twelve-month puts so that protection aligns with annual funding or risk-budget horizons. An April 2024 LGIM America pension example bought a one-year 90% put and sold a one-year 112% call, producing a zero-upfront-premium 90/112 collar under the market conditions then prevailing (https://am.landg.us.com/asset/4994de/globalassets/lgima/insights/whitepapers/tailor-your-risk-by-buttoning-up-with-an-equity-collar.pdf).

3. Zero-premium structures

Institutions often determine the desired put first and solve for the call strike that finances it. “Zero cost” is more accurately “zero initial premium”: the economic cost is the surrendered upside, plus transaction, implementation and possible tax costs.

4. Put-spread collars

A put-spread collar buys a protective put, sells a farther OTM put and sells a call. Selling the second put reduces hedge cost and can permit a higher call cap, but protection ends below the short-put strike. The Cboe CLLZ methodology, for example, buys a monthly 2.5% OTM put, sells a 5% OTM put and sells an OTM call chosen to fund the put spread (https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/governance/Cboe_Zero-Cost_Put_Spread_Collar_Indices_Methodology.pdf).

5. Staggered or overlapping maturities

Instead of rolling the entire hedge on one date, institutions may stagger positions to reduce timing and path-dependency risk. Allspring presents an institutional calendar put-spread-collar model using 12-month puts alongside repeated sales of four-week 15-delta calls and 5-delta puts. This demonstrates that institutional short-call deltas can be lower than the retail 20–30 range when upside retention and systematic repetition are priorities (https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/whitepapers/Allspring_options-based-downside-protection.pdf).

6. OTC customization and collateral management

Large pension plans may use OTC options or listed-lookalike OTC contracts to customize strikes, maturities and eligible collateral. Exchange-listed options provide standardized terms and clearing, while OTC contracts add customization but introduce counterparty, documentation and valuation considerations.

7. Partial portfolio coverage

Institutions do not necessarily collar 100% of the equity allocation. A SEC-filed pension disclosure from Kimberly-Clark reported zero-net-premium equity collars covering approximately 45% of its U.S. pension plan’s $1.3 billion equity allocation, explicitly to reduce potential losses and limit gains (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/55785/000005578511000045/R11.htm).


BOTTOM LINE

Sold Call Delta: 0.20 to 0.30 (reason: balanced premium versus upside retention; favor 0.20 when retaining shares matters and 0.30 when financing protection matters)

Bought Put Delta: −0.20 to −0.30, or 0.20 to 0.30 absolute delta (reason: meaningful protection at a moderate insurance cost; favor −0.20 for cheaper catastrophe protection and −0.30 for a tighter floor)

Symmetric vs Asymmetric: Use equal absolute deltas only as a neutral starting point. For an actual zero-premium collar, choose the put based on the required floor and then solve for the call strike. Asymmetric deltas are normal because downside skew, rates, dividends and investor objectives make equal-delta premiums unequal.

Example Collar:
Stock: $100  
Sell call: $110 strike, Delta 0.248  
Buy put: $90 strike, Delta −0.189  
Net credit/debit: approximately $0.12 credit per share, or $12 per collar, under the stated hypothetical assumptions

Sources:

1. Options Industry Council, “Collar (Protective Collar)” — https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/collar-protective-collar  
2. Options Industry Council, “Options Delta” — https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/delta  
3. Fidelity, “What Is a Collar Position?” — https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/investment-products/options/options-strategy-guide/collar  
4. Cboe, “S&P 500 95-110 Collar Index Methodology” — https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/newcollardescriptionoct1909.pdf  
5. Cboe, “Zero-Cost Put Spread Collar Indices Methodology” — https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/governance/Cboe_Zero-Cost_Put_Spread_Collar_Indices_Methodology.pdf  
6. Allspring, “Options-Based Downside Protection” — https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/whitepapers/Allspring_options-based-downside-protection.pdf  
7. LGIM America, “Tailor Your Risk by Buttoning-up with an Equity Collar” — https://am.landg.us.com/asset/4994de/globalassets/lgima/insights/whitepapers/tailor-your-risk-by-buttoning-up-with-an-equity-collar.pdf

Industrial IoT Predictive-Maintenance Platform Assessment  
Australian mining operation, extreme heat and dust, 50 km² site

Executive recommendation

For a geographically dispersed 50 km² Australian mine, the preferred architecture is a LoRaWAN-based sensor layer with local edge processing and MQTT/OPC-UA integration into the existing SCADA/historian environment. On the evidence available:

1. Best overall fit: local S5 System RotaMon, subject to validation of its operating-temperature specification, hazardous-area approvals, radio performance and firm fleet pricing. It offers IP68 sealing, LoRaWAN or NB-IoT, on-device failure prediction and machine learning, claimed five-year-plus battery life, and explicit integration with SCADA, PI historians and work-order systems. Its Perth-based engineering and mining focus reduce support and integration risk (https://s5system.com/rotamon/; https://s5system.com/faq/).

2. Lowest technical-risk multinational option for a dispersed site: Honeywell Versatilis with Experion EHM or an open LoRaWAN/MQTT integration. Versatilis is IP66/IP67, rated from -40°C to +80°C, uses LoRaWAN rather than short-range Bluetooth for site communications, performs FFT and event triggering at the transmitter, and offers three- to five-year indicative battery life. It is especially attractive if the mine already operates Honeywell Experion (https://process.honeywell.com/us/en/products/field-instruments/iot-sensor-solutions/equipment-health-monitoring-hvt/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter; https://process.honeywell.com/us/en/products/field-instruments/iot-sensor-solutions/equipment-health-monitoring-hvt/honeywell-versatilis-experion-ehm).

3. Best enclosure rating but weakest wide-area network topology: Siemens SITRANS MS200/CC220/SCM IQ. The MS200 has the strongest published ingress rating of the compared sensors—IP69 in the Siemens technical sheet—and operates from -30°C to +80°C. However, each sensor uses Bluetooth Low Energy to reach a nearby CC220 gateway, and each current CC220 supports only up to eight sensors. That makes the solution practical inside a compact processing plant but comparatively expensive and infrastructure-heavy for dispersed conveyors, pumps and remote assets over 50 km². Its machine-learning anomaly detection is primarily in the Siemens Insights Hub cloud rather than at the sensor (https://cache.industry.siemens.com/dl/files/158/109804158/att_1150464/v1/sitrans_ms200_cc220_scmiq_fi01_en.pdf?download=true).

4. Lowest-cost local-integrator route: an Australian controls integrator such as ElcoTech or Meshed, using AU915 LoRaWAN, industrial gateways and a selected sensor such as the Advantech WISE-2410 or an IP68 Dragino IVS-LN. This offers strong protocol openness and potentially much lower capital cost, but predictive-maintenance model quality, cybersecurity ownership, sensor calibration and long-term product support must be specified contractually. ElcoTech supports edge processing with Node-RED, Python and MQTT and integration through MQTT, OPC-UA, REST and SQL; Meshed advertises private industrial LoRaWAN, up to 20 km reach under suitable conditions, and integration with SCADA, SAP, Maximo, CMMS, GIS and BI platforms (https://www.elcotech.com.au/services/iiot-lorawan; https://www.meshed.network/industries/industrial-automation/smart-mining/).

A prudent procurement path is a competitive 90-day pilot involving S5 and Honeywell on the same 10–20 representative assets, with Siemens included only if those assets are concentrated in a processing plant or the mine already has a strong Siemens Insights Hub/automation footprint. S5 publishes a fixed A$4,900 pilot for one critical asset over 90 days, including installation and a written business case, providing a low-cost first qualification step (https://s5system.com/rotamon/).

Scope and cost-model basis

Because Siemens, Honeywell and S5 do not publish complete Australian fleet prices, the totals below are planning-level estimates rather than vendor quotations. They are intended for budget comparison and should be treated as approximately ±40–50% until an RF survey, asset list, sampling specification and commercial quotation are completed.

The base case assumes:

- Site area: 50 km².
- Approximate equivalent circular radius:

  r = √(area/π)  
  r = √(50/3.1416)  
  r ≈ 3.99 km.

- Equivalent square dimensions:

  side = √50 ≈ 7.07 km.

- 100 rotating or mechanically critical assets.
- Two monitoring positions per asset, for 200 sensor points. Two points could represent drive-end and non-drive-end bearings, or motor and gearbox positions.
- Four to six outdoor LoRaWAN gateways for practical coverage, overlap and resilience. Although a clear line-of-sight gateway can reach much farther, pits, crushers, stockpiles, steel structures and elevation changes make catalogue maximum range unsuitable as a design basis.
- Existing Ethernet, fibre, microwave or cellular backhaul is available at some site locations. New long-distance fibre installation is excluded.
- Costs are in Australian dollars, excluding GST.
- The model covers condition monitoring, dashboards, SCADA/historian integration, commissioning and an allowance for support. It does not include major SCADA replacement, private LTE/5G construction, explosion-proof cabling projects, production losses during installation, or extensive power/solar civil works.
- Sensor data are advisory condition-monitoring inputs, not safety instrumented functions or shutdown protection.

The 200-point assumption materially drives the result. For a different point count, sensor hardware and installation scale almost linearly, while network servers, integration and gateway costs are more fixed. A 400-point deployment would not necessarily double the total because the LoRaWAN gateways and SCADA interfaces could be reused; Siemens gateway requirements would rise more directly because each CC220 has a small fixed sensor capacity.

1. Siemens SITRANS MS200, CC220 and SCM IQ

Durability and environmental fit

The Siemens MS200 monitors triaxial vibration and temperature. Siemens specifies:

- IP69 enclosure in the current technical sheet.
- Operating ambient temperature: -30°C to +80°C.
- Storage temperature: -40°C to +85°C.
- Temperature measurement range: -30°C to +80°C.
- Vibration frequency range: 15 Hz to 3.3 kHz.
- Sampling rate: 6.6 kHz.
- Battery life: two to five years at 25°C.
- BLE 5.0 communication.
- A nominal polling/data cycle of one transmission per 100 seconds in the 2023 sheet.

These figures come from Siemens’ product technical documentation (https://cache.industry.siemens.com/dl/files/158/109804158/att_1131957/v1/sitrans_ms200_cc220_scmiq__fi01_en.pdf and updated material at https://cache.industry.siemens.com/dl/files/158/109804158/att_1150464/v1/sitrans_ms200_cc220_scmiq_fi01_en.pdf?download=true).

The sensor itself is therefore well sealed against dust and water. Ingress protection does not, however, guarantee survivability under direct Pilbara or outback solar loading. A black or metal-mounted enclosure in full sun can exceed ambient air temperature, so qualification should include solar-radiation exposure and the actual bearing-housing surface temperature.

The gateway is the environmental weak point. Siemens specifies the CC220 as IP20, with an operating range of 0°C to +50°C. Siemens states that it is normally installed inside a cabinet (same Siemens technical sources). Outdoor or crusher-area deployment would therefore require an IP66/IP67 cabinet, thermal design, surge protection, 24 VDC power and backhaul. In an exposed Australian mine, cabinet internal temperature is likely to be the limiting factor rather than the MS200 sensor rating.

Edge processing and analytics

The MS200 collects vibration and temperature, while the CC220 polls sensors and forwards data over MQTT to SITRANS SCM IQ. SCM IQ, running on Siemens Insights Hub, manages machine-learning models, detects anomalies, labels events and sends email or SMS notifications (https://cache.industry.siemens.com/dl/files/158/109804158/att_1131957/v1/sitrans_ms200_cc220_scmiq__fi01_en.pdf).

This is a cloud-oriented analytics model. It provides trained anomaly detection but offers less autonomous field intelligence than S5’s claimed on-device prediction or Honeywell’s onboard FFT/event triggers. A loss of upstream backhaul could therefore interrupt new cloud analysis, although sensor/gateway buffering behaviour should be confirmed during tendering.

Siemens also offers a newer Connection Module IoT with local KPI calculation, three-axis vibration, temperature, magnetic-field and acoustic sensing, MQTT to a local broker, dual-band Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 5.2. Siemens describes that module as IP66 and says an Ex-certified version is forthcoming, but this is a different architecture from the MS200/CC220 system assessed in the cost model (https://www.siemens.com/en-us/products/digital-drivetrain/connection-module-iot/).

Legacy SCADA integration

The CC220 sends data using MQTT, and Siemens describes its cloud ecosystem as open to integration with existing systems. MQTT is useful, but many legacy SCADA systems expect OPC DA, OPC-UA, Modbus TCP, DNP3 or native historian tags. Unless the site already uses Siemens Insights Hub or a compatible MQTT ingestion layer, an edge broker or protocol converter will be needed.

Expected integration chain:

MS200 → BLE → CC220 → MQTT over plant network → Siemens Insights Hub/SCM IQ → API or middleware → SCADA/historian/CMMS.

This is workable but adds a cloud-to-OT integration layer. The condition-monitoring system should remain read-only toward control and should not be placed in a safety shutdown path.

Wide-area network implications

Current Siemens documentation states that a CC220 can collect from up to eight MS200 sensors; older 2023 documentation stated five. Procurement should use eight only after confirming the exact current hardware and firmware supplied (https://cache.industry.siemens.com/dl/files/158/109804158/att_1150464/v1/sitrans_ms200_cc220_scmiq_fi01_en.pdf?download=true; https://cache.industry.siemens.com/dl/files/158/109804158/att_1131957/v1/sitrans_ms200_cc220_scmiq__fi01_en.pdf).

For 200 points:

- At eight sensors per gateway:

  200 ÷ 8 = 25 CC220 gateways minimum.

- At five sensors per gateway:

  200 ÷ 5 = 40 CC220 gateways.

That is a hard capacity calculation before allowing for BLE range, steel shielding, redundancy or assets distributed too far apart to share a gateway. Consequently, 25–40 protected, powered gateway locations are a realistic planning basis, versus approximately four to six LoRaWAN gateways for Honeywell or S5.

Siemens planning-level cost

Assumptions:

- 200 MS200 sensors at A$1,500–A$2,500 each as a procurement allowance, not a published Siemens price.
- 25–40 CC220 gateways at A$2,000–A$3,000 each, including allowance for Australian supply but excluding field cabinet.
- Protected powered cabinet/backhaul installation at A$4,000–A$7,000 per gateway location.
- Cloud onboarding, licensing, dashboards and SCADA integration: A$100,000–A$250,000.
- Engineering, asset hierarchy, installation, commissioning and training: A$160,000–A$300,000.

Calculation:

- Sensors: 200 × A$1,500–A$2,500 = A$300,000–A$500,000.
- Gateways:  
  Low: 25 × A$2,000 = A$50,000.  
  High: 40 × A$3,000 = A$120,000.
- Cabinets/power/backhaul:  
  Low: 25 × A$4,000 = A$100,000.  
  High: 40 × A$7,000 = A$280,000.
- Software/integration: A$100,000–A$250,000.
- Engineering/installation: A$160,000–A$300,000.

Estimated implementation total:

A$300,000–500,000  
+ A$50,000–120,000  
+ A$100,000–280,000  
+ A$100,000–250,000  
+ A$160,000–300,000  
= A$710,000–A$1,450,000.

Five-year cloud support, subscriptions, battery replacements and maintenance allowance: A$100,000–A$300,000.

Estimated five-year TCO: A$810,000–A$1,750,000.

These are budget allowances, not quoted Siemens prices. One third-party listing showed a new sealed older CC220 at US$379.90 excluding tax and shipping, while another UK supplier listed a current CC220 variant at £846. Those international listings differ substantially and are not reliable Australian project prices; they reinforce the need for a formal Siemens Australia quotation rather than a catalogue conversion (https://www.all4sps.com/SITRANS-CC220-MULTISENSOR-7MP2200-1CB05-2AA1_1; https://www.parmley-graham.co.uk/7mp2200-2cb05-2aa1).

Assessment

Siemens is technically credible and has the best sensor ingress rating, but the BLE architecture is not economical for a site-wide 50 km² rollout. It is best used for a concentrated process plant, workshop or mill area where several monitored assets sit near each cabinet and Siemens cloud services are already approved.

2. Honeywell Versatilis and Experion EHM

Durability and environmental fit

Honeywell specifies the Versatilis transmitter as:

- IP66/IP67.
- Ambient temperature range: -40°C to +80°C.
- Surface-temperature range: -40°C to +80°C.
- Triaxial vibration range: 5 Hz to 2,500 Hz, up to ±16 g.
- Acoustics, ambient pressure, ambient temperature, humidity, surface temperature and vibration sensing.
- LoRaWAN for long-range communications.
- BLE for configuration and troubleshooting.
- AES-256 encryption for LoRa and BLE.
- Battery life up to three years with a five-minute sensor interval and 30-minute LoRaWAN update, or up to five years with a 10-minute interval and 60-minute update.

Source: Honeywell product information and technical specifications (https://process.honeywell.com/us/en/products/field-instruments/iot-sensor-solutions/equipment-health-monitoring-hvt/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter; https://prod-edam.honeywell.com/content/dam/honeywell-edam/pmt/hps/products/pmc/field-instruments/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter/pmt-hps-hvt-technical-specification.pdf?download=false).

IP67 is slightly below Siemens’ IP69 rating but remains appropriate for dust and temporary immersion. Its -40°C lower limit is broader than Siemens’ -30°C operating limit. Both have a +80°C upper limit.

Honeywell promotional material also states that Versatilis has intrinsic-safety and marine certifications and a built-in FFT algorithm. Exact Australian IECEx certificate numbers, gas/dust groups, temperature class and approved battery configuration must be verified in the tender rather than inferred from a brochure (https://process.honeywell.com/content/dam/process/en/campaigns/pmc/versatilis-transmitter/hon-pmc-brochure-versatilis-transmitter-en.pdf).

Edge processing and analytics

Versatilis supports onboard FFT, event triggers and FFT triggers. Published output includes RMS values and statistical indicators such as kurtosis, crest factor and skewness, with FFT data available for analysis. This is an important advantage on LoRaWAN because continuously transmitting raw high-frequency waveforms is neither bandwidth-efficient nor operationally desirable.

The practical processing split is:

- At sensor: sampling, statistical features, FFT and exception/event triggering.
- At LoRaWAN infrastructure: packet forwarding and MQTT delivery.
- At Experion EHM or another application: asset hierarchy, trends, alarms, ISO-based health reports and advanced fault verification.

Honeywell’s Experion EHM is an on-premises solution. A commercial LoRaWAN gateway forwards data to a ChirpStack network/application server, which publishes decoded data via MQTT to the Experion EHM virtual machine. Honeywell states that EHM provides plant hierarchy, historization, alarms, dashboards, ISO-based asset health reports and optional advanced vibration analytics (https://process.honeywell.com/us/en/products/field-instruments/iot-sensor-solutions/equipment-health-monitoring-hvt/honeywell-versatilis-experion-ehm).

This architecture avoids mandatory public-cloud dependence and is therefore suitable for a mine that requires local operation during WAN outages.

Legacy SCADA integration

Honeywell is the strongest option if the mine already uses Experion because EHM is built on Experion HS SCADA functionality and uses secure MQTT from the LoRaWAN application server. Honeywell states that web clients allow existing enterprise or OEM nodes to view health data without separate client deployment (https://ess.honeywell.com/content/dam/pmt/en/documents/document-lists/events/gat-wat-2023/Versatilis-transmitter-Technical-Spec.pdf).

For non-Honeywell SCADA, the same MQTT architecture can feed an OPC-UA bridge, historian connector or edge platform. Honeywell also emphasizes compatibility with commercial off-the-shelf LoRa-to-MQTT gateways, reducing lock-in at the radio gateway layer (https://process.honeywell.com/content/dam/process/en/campaigns/pmc/versatilis-transmitter/hon-pmc-brochure-versatilis-transmitter-en.pdf).

Wide-area network implications

A four- to six-gateway design is a reasonable planning basis for the 7.07 km by 7.07 km equivalent site, but only an RF survey can establish the final number.

Australian outdoor gateway evidence includes:

- Milesight UG67: IP67, -40°C to +70°C, AU915 support, up to 15 km line-of-sight, more than 2,000 nodes claimed, approximately A$881 from one Australian source and A$880.99 from another (https://www.agtech.dpi.nsw.gov.au/products/milesight-outdoor-gateway-ug67-915m-lorawan; https://oceancontrols.com.au/ULC-023.html).
- RAK WisGate Edge Pro: IP67, eight-channel gateway, A$594.95 including GST or A$540.86 excluding GST (https://core-electronics.com.au/rakwireless-wisgate-pro.html).
- Meshed states that private LoRaWAN networks can reach up to 20 km in suitable mine-site conditions, but that is a provider claim and should not replace site modelling (https://www.meshed.network/industries/industrial-automation/smart-mining/).

The gateway hardware itself is inexpensive relative to installed cost. Pole or structure mounting, antennas, lightning protection, solar/DC power, network backhaul, safe access, configuration and commissioning are likely to lift each installed site to approximately A$10,000–A$25,000.

Honeywell planning-level cost

Assumptions:

- 200 Versatilis transmitters at A$1,200–A$2,200 each as a procurement allowance. Honeywell’s Australian distributor offers them by quotation rather than publishing a price (https://www.territoryinstruments.com/instrumentation/honeywell/honeywell-versatilis/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter).
- Four to six installed industrial LoRaWAN gateway sites at A$10,000–A$25,000 each.
- EHM/on-premises server, virtual machines, licensing and analytics: A$80,000–A$200,000.
- MQTT/SCADA/historian/CMMS integration: A$60,000–A$150,000.
- RF survey, engineering, mounting, commissioning and training: A$140,000–A$250,000.

Calculation:

- Sensors: 200 × A$1,200–A$2,200 = A$240,000–A$440,000.
- Gateway sites:  
  Low: 4 × A$10,000 = A$40,000.  
  High: 6 × A$25,000 = A$150,000.
- EHM/server/software: A$80,000–A$200,000.
- Integration: A$60,000–A$150,000.
- Engineering/installation: A$140,000–A$250,000.

Estimated implementation total:

A$240,000–440,000  
+ A$40,000–150,000  
+ A$80,000–200,000  
+ A$60,000–150,000  
+ A$140,000–250,000  
= A$560,000–A$1,190,000.

Five-year licensing, support, battery replacement and gateway maintenance allowance: A$100,000–A$300,000.

Estimated five-year TCO: A$660,000–A$1,490,000.

Assessment

Honeywell offers the most balanced multinational package for a dispersed mine: suitable temperature and ingress ratings, efficient long-range radio, meaningful sensor-level FFT processing, on-premises deployment and strong SCADA integration. Its main uncertainties are proprietary pricing, EHM licensing and whether high-resolution waveform requirements can be met within LoRaWAN airtime constraints.

3. S5 System RotaMon: Australian local provider

Durability and environmental fit

S5 System is a Perth-based Australian provider that designs and manufactures condition-monitoring sensors for mining, agriculture and infrastructure. It describes RotaMon as:

- Battery powered.
- IP68 and hermetically sealed against dust, water and vibration.
- Bolt- or stud-mounted directly to the asset.
- LoRaWAN or NB-IoT connected.
- Suitable for pumps, conveyors, screens, crushers, gearboxes and other remote or unpowered equipment.
- Five-year-plus battery life.
- Installable without cable trays, conduit, junction boxes or production shutdown for cabling.

Sources: https://s5system.com/rotamon/ and https://s5system.com/faq/.

The product’s published ingress protection is appropriate for dust, wash-down and immersion. However, the gathered evidence did not provide a numerical operating-temperature range, storage range, UV rating, vibration survivability limit, accelerometer bandwidth or IECEx certification. These omissions are material for an extreme-heat mine and must be resolved before award.

Required contractual acceptance criteria should include:

- Sensor operation from at least -20°C to +80°C ambient, preferably -40°C to +80°C.
- Demonstrated operation at the maximum expected equipment surface temperature.
- UV and solar-radiation resistance.
- Salt/corrosion resistance where relevant.
- IECEx equipment-protection level and dust/gas group for hazardous areas.
- Accelerometer frequency range, dynamic range, sample rate and noise floor.
- Radio certification for AU915.
- Battery derating curves at 50°C, 60°C and 70°C.
- Enclosure warranty after repeated thermal cycling.

Edge processing and analytics

S5 claims that RotaMon samples continuously, runs failure prediction on-device and reports a machine-health index and anomaly alerts. Measurements include:

- Triaxial vibration velocity and acceleration.
- Surface and bearing-housing temperature.
- Acoustic signature.
- On-device machine learning intended to detect changes in sound before a clear vibration signature.
- Continuous machine-health index.

Source: https://s5system.com/rotamon/.

This is the strongest stated edge-processing proposition in the comparison because failure prediction is performed at the sensor rather than only in a central platform. If independently demonstrated, it reduces radio traffic, cloud dependence and latency.

The tender should nevertheless require evidence showing:

- How the model is trained.
- Whether baseline learning occurs locally or in a server.
- False-positive and missed-alarm rates.
- Ability to export raw waveform and FFT data.
- Detection performance for imbalance, misalignment, looseness, bearing defects, gear mesh and cavitation.
- Model version control and rollback.
- Behaviour after sensor replacement.
- Whether proprietary health scores can be independently audited.

Legacy SCADA integration

S5 says sensor data can be delivered to SCADA, OSIsoft PI or similar historians, CMMS/work-order systems and customer applications through an API. It positions itself as both an OT/SCADA engineering firm and sensor manufacturer rather than a dashboard-only supplier (https://s5system.com/faq/).

That local systems-engineering capability is valuable for brownfield mining sites. The recommended interface remains:

RotaMon → private AU915 LoRaWAN or NB-IoT → local broker/network server → MQTT/OPC-UA → historian and SCADA → CMMS work-order logic.

No wireless condition sensor should write directly to PLC interlocks. Alarms should enter the existing SCADA and reliability workflow as advisory tags, with role-based acknowledgement and audit trails.

Wide-area network implications

S5 states that one LoRaWAN gateway can typically cover a mine process plant, while NB-IoT can communicate directly over a mobile network where coverage exists (https://s5system.com/faq/). For the complete 50 km² site, four to six LoRaWAN gateways remain a prudent planning basis.

NB-IoT could eliminate private gateway infrastructure for isolated assets, but only if carrier coverage, latency, roaming, data costs and long-term service availability are acceptable. A hybrid model is attractive:

- LoRaWAN for dense process-plant, conveyor and pit-edge clusters.
- NB-IoT for isolated bores, pumps or distant infrastructure.
- Local LoRaWAN gateway buffering during backhaul outages.

S5 planning-level cost

Published S5 fleet sensor pricing was not available. S5 states that pricing depends on quantity, LoRaWAN/NB-IoT configuration, gateway needs and integration scope. It publishes only the A$4,900 one-asset, 90-day instrumentation pilot (https://s5system.com/faq/).

Assumptions:

- 200 RotaMon sensors at A$900–A$1,800 each as a planning allowance.
- Four to six installed gateway sites at A$10,000–A$25,000 each.
- Local edge platform, dashboard and SCADA/historian/CMMS integration: A$80,000–A$180,000.
- RF survey, installation, model commissioning, asset hierarchy and training: A$100,000–A$200,000.
- The A$4,900 pilot is assumed to be either credited or absorbed in the engineering allowance; this must be negotiated.

Calculation:

- Sensors: 200 × A$900–A$1,800 = A$180,000–A$360,000.
- Gateway sites:  
  Low: 4 × A$10,000 = A$40,000.  
  High: 6 × A$25,000 = A$150,000.
- Edge platform/integration: A$80,000–A$180,000.
- Engineering/installation: A$100,000–A$200,000.

Estimated implementation total:

A$180,000–360,000  
+ A$40,000–150,000  
+ A$80,000–180,000  
+ A$100,000–200,000  
= A$400,000–A$890,000.

Five-year local support, battery service, gateway maintenance and software allowance: A$75,000–A$225,000.

Estimated five-year TCO: A$475,000–A$1,115,000.

Assessment

S5 is potentially the best technical and commercial fit, particularly because it combines local mining knowledge, IP68 construction, on-device analytics and SCADA engineering. It should not receive a full fleet award based solely on website claims, however. Temperature, hazardous-area certification, vibration metrology, fleet pricing, cybersecurity and detection accuracy require documentary and pilot validation.

4. Other Australian/local-provider architecture

Local providers can supply an open, multi-vendor LoRaWAN and edge platform rather than a single vertically integrated sensor product.

ElcoTech

ElcoTech is a Perth-based controls contractor offering:

- LoRaWAN network design and commissioning.
- RF surveys, coverage modelling and gateway siting.
- Edge devices using Node-RED, Python and MQTT.
- Cellular, NB-IoT and LTE-M backhaul.
- Grafana, Node-RED and Ignition Perspective dashboards.
- MQTT, OPC-UA, REST and SQL interfaces.
- Integration to SCADA, historians, ERP and BI.
- Condition monitoring for vibration, temperature, current and flow.
- Ongoing battery, firmware, sensor replacement and dashboard support.

Source: https://www.elcotech.com.au/services/iiot-lorawan.

This is an attractive integration model where the mine wishes to retain control of data and avoid a proprietary cloud.

Meshed

Meshed describes itself as Australian-owned and offers:

- Private industrial LoRaWAN.
- IP67 industrial-grade infrastructure.
- 99.9%+ network uptime SLA on its MeshedX network.
- Up to 20 km private LoRaWAN reach in suitable environments.
- Predictive maintenance and asset intelligence.
- Integration with SCADA, SAP, Maximo, CMMS, GIS, BI and digital-twin platforms.

Source: https://www.meshed.network/industries/industrial-automation/smart-mining/ and https://www.meshed.network/lorawan-iot-smart-industries/iot-in-mining-automation-and-asset-management/.

The 20 km figure is a best-case provider claim, not a guaranteed mine-site radius. Open pits, highwalls, stockpiles, conveyors and plant steelwork require measured coverage.

Sentient Computing

Sentient Computing reports a Western Australian mining deployment using AU915 LoRaWAN vibration sensors across motors, conveyors, pulleys, pumps and other rotating equipment. It used a local gateway and in-house data processing/storage rather than depending on a third-party cloud, and integrated processed information into the client’s data centre or historian (https://sencom.com.au/case-studies/condition-vibration-monitoring-iiot/).

This supports the feasibility of a private LoRaWAN architecture in an Australian mining setting, although the case study does not publish enough performance or cost data for direct procurement comparison.

Commodity and industrial sensor options

- A$596 excluding GST from an Australian supplier.
- IP66.
- Battery powered.
- Operating temperature -20°C to +80°C.
- Three-axis accelerometer.

- ±16 g range.

Source: https://pacificautomation.com.au/advantech-wise-2410-lorawan-vibration-temperature-sensor-battery-powered/.

Dragino IVS-LN:

- A$279 excluding GST from an Australian seller.
- IP68 probe.
- Probe operating range -40°C to +80°C.
- AU915/AS923 LoRaWAN.
- RMS acceleration, RMS velocity, vibration frequency, displacement and temperature.
- ISO 20816-1-oriented evaluation.

Source: https://iot-store.com.au/products/dragino-ivs-ln-lorawan-vibration-detector.

Lower-cost event sensor:

- A locally stocked LoRaWAN three-axis vibration/shock sensor was advertised at A$127, with temperature/humidity, runtime counting and AU915 support, but its feature set is more suited to vibration presence, shock and operating-state detection than high-quality bearing diagnostics (https://www.prosense.com.au/product-page/lorawan-vibration-sensor-industrial-3-axis-shock-movement-detector).

These price points show that sensor hardware can be much cheaper than the planning allowances for Siemens, Honeywell or S5. They are not necessarily equivalent. Predictive maintenance depends on mounting repeatability, bandwidth, signal-to-noise ratio, waveform access, FFT quality, timestamp accuracy, calibration and diagnostic software—not merely the presence of a three-axis accelerometer.

- Integration: A$50,000–A$120,000.
- Engineering/installation: A$65,000–A$160,000.

A$119,200
