3. Solution-by-solution findings

3.1 Olam/ofi AtSource and OFIS

What it is

AtSource is primarily a sustainable-sourcing, sustainability-performance, assurance, and customer-transparency system. It was created by Olam in 2018. Its customer dashboard presents social and environmental data and offers more than 350 metrics across ten topics. AtSourceV offers traceability to farmer-group level or estates, while AtSource+ adds more granular metrics, environmental footprints, annual third-party verification, and deforestation due diligence (https://www.atsource.io/atsource.html).

Critically, AtSource’s methodology says the system is “open to ofi and Olam Group product supply chains.” Those supply chains include the entities handling products from farms to the final processing site, including farmer groups, suppliers, facilities, and ofi/Olam processing facilities (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html). This is not the same as an independent SaaS platform that a cooperative can buy while remaining buyer-neutral.

Usability and basic phones

The underlying Olam Farmer Information System, OFIS, was designed for field staff working with remote smallholders. Its multilingual Android application collects farm surveys, GPS points, photos, training records, input distribution, financing, crop purchases, and other first-mile transactions. It can communicate to field staff through app notifications and to farmers through SMS. A 2017 Olam publication reported implementation across 21 countries, eight products, and nine languages, with more than 100,000 farmers registered at that time (https://www.olamgroup.com/content/dam/olamgroup/files/uploads/2017/07/New-OFIS-Brochure-1.pdf and https://www.olamgroup.com/content/dam/olamgroup/files/uploads/2017/06/OFIS-Press-Release-05.06.2017.pdf).

This is suitable for an enumerator-mediated model, but the reviewed evidence does not show that farmers can independently use AtSource through feature phones for farm records or transaction verification. SMS advice is not equivalent to a feature-phone farm-management application.

GPS and mountain mapping

OFIS records GPS points on the ground, and more recent ofi material refers to polygon mapping linked to weekly satellite monitoring and Global Forest Watch alerts. The same material says ofi had mapped close to one million individual smallholder farms using its digital solutions (https://frucom.eu/component/attachments/attachments.html?id=2409&task=download).

AtSource’s public methodology, however, treats some GPS mapping metrics as optional and reports some data at farmer-group level. The cooperative should therefore not infer that every AtSource tier automatically supplies buyer-ready plot polygons for every member. It would need a written commitment covering:

- 100% plot-level mapping;
- farmer-to-plot-to-delivery linkage;
- polygon exports;
- accuracy and remapping rules;
- cooperative access to raw geodata;
- continued data access if the ofi buying relationship ends.

Certification integration

AtSource provides sustainability requirements, risk and performance assessments, third-party verification, and deforestation due diligence. Its AtSourceV and AtSource+ tiers were recognized as Silver and Gold equivalent, respectively, against the Sustainable Agriculture Initiative Platform’s Farm Sustainability Assessment 3.0 for spices, cocoa, coffee, and nuts (https://www.ofi.com/en-us/news-and-events/press-release/atsource-receives-equivalence-under-the-sai-platforms-farm-sustainability-assessment-fsa-3).

That recognition is valuable but is not Rainforest Alliance or Fairtrade certification. AtSource has projects and programs involving Rainforest Alliance, but the reviewed sources do not establish direct export into the Rainforest Alliance Certification Platform or a Fairtrade internal-control and transaction-reporting workflow. AtSource should therefore be treated as complementary sustainability assurance, not as proof of integration with both requested certification schemes.

Languages and offline use

Historical OFIS material says the Android application was multilingual and was deployed in nine languages, but it does not identify those languages. Spanish, Bahasa Indonesia, and Amharic must therefore be verified individually. The reviewed evidence describes use in isolated regions, but does not provide sufficiently explicit current documentation of complete offline workflows and synchronization behavior.

Cost

No public per-farmer or cooperative subscription price was found. More importantly, the platform is bound to Olam/ofi supply chains. The economic offer may be embedded in a sourcing contract, product tier, sustainability program, or buyer-funded intervention rather than a standalone software subscription.

Verdict

AtSource is appropriate only if ofi is a strategic buyer willing to fund deployment and give the cooperative contractually protected access and portability. It is not the best choice for the cooperative’s independent master database.

3.2 Fairtrade Fairtrace and Plot Insights

What they are

Fairtrace is FLOCERT’s online collaboration and assurance platform for Fairtrade-certified organizations. Supply-chain partners report and verify transactions through “virtual handshakes.” Traders report Fairtrade sales and direct purchases from producers; producers generally verify transactions reported by customers. Reporting includes volumes and, where applicable, price and premium information (https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf).

Only FLOCERT-certified customers receive access to Fairtrace (https://fairtrace-account.flocert.net/assets/SAM_FairtraceLoginManual_TR_18_en.pdf). It is therefore a certification transaction-reporting layer, not a general-purpose farm-management product.

Plot Insights is Fairtrade’s separate system for geolocation management. It lets certified coffee and cocoa producer organizations upload plot data, validate common errors, visualize plots, receive Satelligence deforestation-risk analysis, convert data to EUDR-compatible GeoJSON, and control which data are shared with buyers. Fairtrade states that it is free for all certified coffee and cocoa small-producer organizations (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf).

Usability and basic phones

Fairtrace is an online organizational reporting system, and the reviewed evidence does not establish an offline basic-phone farmer workflow. Farmers ordinarily do not record each farm activity or delivery directly in Fairtrace.

Plot Insights is likewise a cooperative data-management and sharing tool, not a boundary-walking application for farmers. It accepts geodata collected elsewhere. As a result, Fairtrade’s systems must sit above a mobile field-collection platform.

GPS and mountain mapping

Plot Insights is strong at validating, visualizing, managing, analyzing, and sharing geodata. It does not eliminate the need to collect accurate field coordinates. For the cooperative, this means using Farmforce, SourceTrace, Koltiva, INATrace, TerraTrac, or another mapping application and then uploading or synchronizing the results.

Fairtrade’s own rules make this relationship explicit:

- All certified members’ coffee plots require geolocation.
- A plot of exactly four hectares or larger should be a polygon.
- Smaller plots may use points where allowed.
- KML, GeoJSON, and Shapefile are accepted polygon formats.
- Fairtrade recommends field collection and particularly recommends polygons in larger or high-risk plots.
- Farmer and farm-unit IDs should be unique and stable.

Sources:  
https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf  
https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/2025-EN_Fairtrade-Best-practices-geolocation-data-collection-preparation_colour.pdf

Certification integration

For Fairtrade, this is the strongest option because it is the scheme owner’s own reporting and geodata environment. It handles Fairtrade transactions, prices, premiums, geodata, risk analysis, and controlled sharing with Fairtrade buyers.

It is not a Rainforest Alliance internal-control or certification platform. A dual-certified cooperative would still need to export data to Rainforest Alliance’s RACP and maintain the relevant Rainforest Alliance audit and corrective-action records.

Languages

Plot Insights is available in English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, and Vietnamese; Amharic is not listed (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf). This gives good coverage for Colombia and Indonesia but leaves an Ethiopian localization gap.

Offline functionality

No evidence reviewed establishes full offline field use. This is not necessarily a defect because Plot Insights is not intended to be the principal field application. The cooperative should collect offline, quality-check internally, and upload when connected.

Cost

Plot Insights is free for certified coffee and cocoa producer organizations. That is a software-access price of:

$0 ÷ 5,000 farmers = $0 per farmer per year

This excludes Fairtrade certification fees, staff time, Android devices, mapping labor, mobile data, remediation, and any separate farm-management system. Fairtrace access is tied to being a FLOCERT-certified customer and should not be treated as universally free outside that relationship.

Verdict

Use Fairtrace and Plot Insights for Fairtrade-certified production, but not as the cooperative’s only farm-management platform.

3.3 Fairfood Trace/Connect

This is a different system from Fairtrade/FLOCERT Fairtrace and should not be confused with it.

Basic-phone inclusion

Fairfood Trace Connect is the strongest model reviewed for farmers who have no smartphone. Collectors use the mobile application to enroll farmers and record transactions. Each farmer can receive an NFC/QR card and tap or scan it to confirm deliveries or payments. The farmer needs neither a phone nor an email account. Photos of signed receipts can be used if a card is unavailable (https://github.com/Fairfood/trace-app and https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect).

The application minimizes entry because collection is not the user’s primary task. It can work offline and synchronize later. It was tested for more than two years with two cooperatives in Indonesia and had digitized close to 15,000 nutmeg transactions from rural Indonesian islands, according to Fairfood’s documentation (https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect).

GPS plot mapping

The public evidence centers on farmer enrollment, deliveries, payments, receipts, NFC cards, and supply-chain transparency. It does not establish a mature workflow for walking and validating coffee plot polygons. The cooperative should therefore treat mapping as a gap unless Fairfood demonstrates it in a pilot or integrates an external mapping system.

Certification integration

The platform can collect evidence for sustainability or payment claims and integrate with external cooperative or ERP systems. The reviewed evidence does not show ready-to-use current Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade internal-control templates, nonconformity management, audit workflows, or direct certification-platform exports.

Languages

The open-source application supports localization and translations, but the exact available production languages were not enumerated in the evidence. Spanish, Amharic, and Indonesian should be demonstrated, not merely promised.

Offline

Strong. The application was explicitly designed for limited, slow, or infrequent internet and can synchronize after offline collection.

Cost

The mobile application is open source, which makes the software-license cost potentially $0. Fairfood warns, however, that an open-source app without the backend is not the complete platform. Deployment still requires a backend, hosting, security, support, integration, cards, Android devices for collectors, and operations.

If the cooperative self-hosted the mobile code, the license-only calculation would be:

$0 software license ÷ 5,000 farmers = $0 per farmer

That is not a credible total-cost figure. The actual per-farmer cost must include the implementation and operating components discussed in Section 5.

Verdict

A strong complementary transaction and farmer-inclusion tool, but not the leading all-in-one choice without proven polygon mapping and certification modules.

3.4 Farmforce

Functional fit

Farmforce maintains a digital farmer database, assigns unique farmer and field IDs, maps individual fields as GPS polygons, records farm activities and chemical use, and provides bag-level traceability from a field through aggregation into lots and containers. Its certification-related records support compliance with Rainforest Alliance and other programs (https://farmforce.com/products/information-management-system-ims/).

Usability and basic phones

Farmforce’s operational model is primarily field-staff mediated. The mobile system is designed for staff who register and visit farmers. Its dedicated farmer-facing Farmforce Connect product was described as being piloted, not as a universally mature production offering (https://farmforce.com/products/farmer-app/).

This means farmers with basic phones can still be included in the cooperative database, but the main app would be on cooperative-owned Android devices. A basic-phone SMS or NFC-card channel may require another tool or custom integration.

Farmforce states that its design principles include low literacy, gamification, offline operation, farmer identity, education, weather, coaching, and buying offers. These goals are positive, but the procurement decision should be based on demonstrated current modules rather than roadmap language.

GPS and mountainous terrain

Farmforce offers:

- GPS-mapped field polygons;
- one or multiple fields per farmer;
- mobile boundary mapping;
- shapefile import;
- Google Maps visualization;
- Global Forest Watch integration;
- remapping workflows when errors are detected.

Source: https://farmforce.com/solutions/farmers-database-gps-mapping/

Most importantly for this cooperative, Farmforce has a directly relevant Ethiopia example. In a Farm Africa/ECOM forest-coffee pilot, more than 4,500 smallholder producers and approximately 4,550 hectares were mapped over eight months, with more than 3,500 signed EUDR consent surveys. More than 80 field collectors used offline-first Android GPS workflows in the forested highlands of Bale and Illubabor, synchronizing when they returned to connectivity (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/).

That example closely matches the cooperative’s Ethiopian conditions, although it is a vendor case study rather than an independent accuracy audit. The cooperative should request actual data-quality statistics: rejected polygons, remapping rate, median Android accuracy, duplicate plots, and average time per plot.

Certification integration

Farmforce says its records are used for Rainforest Alliance and other certification programs and that its workflows support organic, fair-trade, and other compliance schemes. It can store certification IDs, surveys, field activity, chemical application, household data, child-labor information, procurement, and traceability (https://farmforce.com/products/information-management-system-ims/ and https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/).

This is a strong functional fit, but “supports fair-trade” does not necessarily mean a live API to FLOCERT Fairtrace or Fairtrade Plot Insights. The RFP should demand a demonstration of:

- Fairtrade member and plot export;
- price and premium records;
- lot-to-plot linkage;
- Fairtrace transaction workflow or export;
- Plot Insights-compatible GeoJSON;
- Rainforest Alliance farm-unit templates;
- KML/JSON export for RACP;
- nonconformity and corrective-action management.

Languages

A third-party software listing identifies Chinese, English, French, Hindi, Indonesian, Portuguese, Serbian, Spanish, Thai, Turkish, and Vietnamese (https://www.getapp.com.au/software/2071368/farmforce). Spanish and Indonesian are therefore covered; Amharic was not verified. Farmforce also supports configurable multilingual surveys, which could mitigate but not fully solve an untranslated application interface (https://farmforce.com/articles/sustainability-starts-with-data-empowering-farmer-engagement-through-digital-traceability/).

Offline

Strong. Farmforce states that field staff can collect farmer, household, training, plot, and observation data offline. Case studies describe offline synchronization in low-connectivity settings, including the Ethiopian forest-coffee pilot and a Ghana deployment involving more than 6,000 digitized farmers (https://farmforce.com/articles/sustainability-starts-with-data-empowering-farmer-engagement-through-digital-traceability/ and https://farmforce.com/case-studies/red-river-foods/).

Cost

Farmforce does not provide a dependable public enterprise rate card. A third-party Capterra listing is internally difficult to interpret: it displays NOK 330 “flat rate, per year” and also US$1,950 per user per year (https://www.capterra.com/p/189458/Farmforce/). These figures should not be treated as a vendor quote.

An illustrative calculation using only the more clearly labeled user figure is:

- Assumed mobile/web users: 50 cooperative field and management staff.
- Listed third-party annual user price: $1,950.
- Indicative annual subscription: 50 × $1,950 = $97,500.
- Cost across 5,000 farmers: $97,500 ÷ 5,000 = $19.50 per farmer per year.

This is not a forecast. It excludes setup, devices, support, integrations, SMS, mapping labor, and taxes, and Farmforce may license by module, tenant, mobile user, or negotiated enterprise volume. Conversely, the cooperative may need substantially fewer than 50 paid users, and a negotiated price may be lower.

Verdict

Best evidenced all-round commercial option, provided it passes the pricing threshold and adds Amharic.

3.5 SourceTrace DATAGREEN

Functional fit

SourceTrace is designed for agricultural supply chains and smallholder organizations in developing economies. DATAGREEN covers farmer registration, farm data, agronomic monitoring, GPS mapping, input distribution, procurement, payments, certification, traceability, analytics, and integrations. It links farmer IDs and certification/practice data to product records and supports barcodes and QR codes (https://sourcetrace.com/agriculture-solutions/).

Basic-phone usability

SourceTrace has the broadest documented device compatibility:

- Java-enabled regular phones;
- smartphones;
- tablets;
- POS-like devices;
- laptops and desktop computers.

Its remote application is intended for low bandwidth or no permanent connection and uses small data packets to reduce transmission cost (https://sourcetrace.com/the-platform/).

This makes it particularly attractive where cooperative agents already use simple devices or where procurement stations need rugged POS workflows. Nevertheless, GPS polygon collection should still use Android or appropriate GNSS hardware; a simple Java phone should not be assumed to provide sufficient mapping capability.

GPS and mountainous terrain

SourceTrace records farm GPS coordinates, computes farm area, georeferences farms, captures photos, and supports digital mapping. A Cargill case study says GPS-enabled mobile applications were used to calculate the area of certified productive farms for 240,000 cocoa farmers across Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, and Ghana (https://sourcetrace.com/case-studies/cargill-cocoa-and-chocolate-cote-divoire-cameroon-ghana/).

The evidence is strong on general GPS capability but less specific than Farmforce or Koltiva on polygon-quality validation and mountainous coffee. The field pilot should therefore test:

- boundary walking rather than only point capture;
- GeoJSON/KML/Shapefile output;
- accuracy metadata;
- overlap and self-intersection rules;
- use with external Bluetooth GNSS;
- remapping queues;
- performance under shade canopy.

Certification integration

SourceTrace is especially strong here. It provides a digital internal-control system, keeps nonconformities and corrective-action plans, and advertises ready-to-use certification templates for Organic, UTZ/Rainforest, Fairtrade, GlobalG.A.P., and other schemes (https://sourcetrace.com/solutions/).

Its Cargill deployment digitized 240,000 farmers producing under UTZ, Rainforest Alliance, and Fair Trade requirements, using English and French data collection (https://sourcetrace.com/case-studies/cargill-cocoa-and-chocolate-cote-divoire-cameroon-ghana/). This is more direct evidence of multi-certification support than was found for AtSource or Fairfood Trace.

Because standards change, the cooperative should verify template version dates and exact interoperability with current RACP, Fairtrace, and Plot Insights workflows.

Languages

SourceTrace has been described as deployed in 15 languages (https://solve.mit.edu/solutions/38651). A third-party review lists 22 interfaces, including Spanish and Bahasa, but not Amharic (https://solevant.com/software/sourcetrace). The cooperative should require Amharic localization and verify that local language extends to forms, validation messages, training material, and support—not just custom question labels.

Offline

Strong. SourceTrace explicitly targets remote and low-bandwidth environments and supports offline operation (https://sourcetrace.com/farm-management/ and https://sourcetrace.com/the-platform/).

Cost

A GSMA digital-agriculture profile reports that SourceTrace pricing includes a one-time onboarding fee followed by a monthly subscription. The subscription may depend on the number of registered farmers; some cases use acreage, while traceability pricing may depend on the number of commodity ecosystems (https://www.sourcetrace.com/wp-content/themes/sts-v3/img/media/GSMA-Agritech-Digital-Agriculture-Maps-2020.pdf).

No reliable amount was published. The cooperative should request all three possible pricing bases and normalize them to annual cost per active farmer.

Verdict

Potentially the best budget-sensitive choice, especially if feature-phone/POS compatibility and ready-made certification controls outweigh the need for a modern farmer-facing interface.

3.6 Koltiva KoltiTrace

Functional fit

KoltiTrace combines farm and supplier mapping, product traceability, sustainability management, risk assessment, certification management, and EUDR due diligence. Koltiva supports mobile and web deployment, API-first ERP integration, supplier and shipment screening, and GPS points or polygons (https://www.koltiva.com/eudrcompliance).

Basic-phone usability

The principal field workflow uses FarmXtension on mobile devices operated by field agents. Koltiva describes the rural problem accurately—many farmers have unstable internet, low English ability, and limited smartphone or laptop access—but the reviewed evidence does not establish a farmer-facing feature-phone application (https://www.koltiva.com/post/koltiva-joins-cool-farm-alliance-to-boost-regenerative-and-climate-smart-farm-practices).

It should therefore be evaluated as an offline field-agent solution, not as a platform farmers will necessarily operate themselves.

GPS and mountainous terrain

Koltiva explicitly supports offline plot mapping. Field agents walk plot boundaries and collect polygon, GPS, area, land-legality, and assessment data through FarmXtension. Koltiva recommends polygon mapping for better deforestation-risk accuracy and future compliance (https://www.koltiva.com/eudrcompliance and https://www.koltiva.com/post/unleashing-the-power-of-deforestation-monitoring-tools-for-eudr-compliance).

This is a strong stated capability, but no mountain-accuracy case study comparable to Farmforce’s Ethiopia deployment was found. Pilot testing remains necessary.

Certification integration

Koltiva says field teams support suppliers in certification under Rainforest Alliance, Fairtrade, FSC, and other voluntary standards. Its application description says it can integrate supply-chain certification standards and provide internal-management-system dashboards for certificate holders, auditors, and standards organizations (https://www.koltiva.com/global-eudr-compliance-tools-for-upstream-and-downstream-businesses and https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.koltiva.datacollection.neo&hl=en_US).

As with the other commercial systems, the cooperative should demand a live demonstration using its specific Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade data, not rely on the generic phrase “any certification standard.”

Languages

The FarmXtension listing includes English, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Japanese, Chinese, and Korean (https://chrome-stats.com/d/com.koltiva.datacollection.neo). The evidence reviewed did not explicitly confirm Amharic or Indonesian interface localization. Koltiva is headquartered in Indonesia and operates there, but corporate origin is not proof that all required screens and support are available in Bahasa Indonesia. Both Bahasa and Amharic should therefore be contractual requirements.

Offline

Strong. Koltiva explicitly advertises offline plot mapping and uses field-agent applications to overcome plantation network limitations (https://www.koltiva.com/eudrcompliance).

Cost

No published rate card was found. Pricing likely combines software, configuration, integrations, and optional “boots on the ground” services. These service options may lower the cooperative’s internal staffing burden but could increase per-farmer cost.

Verdict

A strong contender, particularly in Indonesia and where outsourced mapping or verification is desired. Require transparent separation of software, implementation, and field-service charges.

3.7 INATrace

Functional fit

INATrace is an open-source traceability and cooperative-management system funded by Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development and implemented by GIZ. It supports full supply-chain transparency, multiple organizations and value chains, farmer registration, GPS polygon mapping, offline mobile data, quality and compliance, pricing and payment tracking, and EUDR-related traceability (https://docs.agstack.org/inatrace/ and https://github.com/INATrace/mobile).

It is particularly relevant to coffee: the public codebase includes a coffee network and separate frontend, mobile, and backend components.

Basic-phone usability

The field application is mobile-first and designed for field officers. No evidence establishes a Java-feature-phone app, SMS farmer interface, or NFC-card workflow comparable to SourceTrace or Fairfood. Farmers can still be registered without owning smartphones, but staff would need Android devices.

GPS and mountainous terrain

The mobile app supports offline GPS polygon mapping and later synchronization. Because the software is open source, the cooperative could modify accuracy thresholds and quality rules, but that work would require technical expertise.

Certification integration

User guides allow organizations to upload Organic, Fairtrade, and other certificates, and the platform is designed to support regulatory compliance. Evidence of ready-to-use, current Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade inspection templates or direct APIs was not found. These would likely require configuration or development.

Languages

The documented languages are English, Kinyarwanda, Spanish, and German (https://www.sustainable-supply-chains.org/fileadmin/INA/Wissen_Werkzeuge/INATrace/SASI_INATrace_2.0_User_guide_2025_Producers.pdf). Spanish is covered; Indonesian and Amharic would need translation and testing.

Offline

Strong for farmer registration and GPS polygon collection.

Cost

The software is open source, so license fees can be zero:

$0 license ÷ 5,000 farmers = $0 per farmer

Total cost is not zero. The cooperative would need hosting, database administration, backups, cybersecurity, implementation, training, translations, maintenance, bug fixing, Android devices, and help-desk support. An open-source solution can be cheaper over several years if the cooperative shares these costs with buyers, donors, or other cooperatives; it can also be more expensive than SaaS if custom development is poorly controlled.

Verdict

The leading data-sovereignty and low-license-cost option, but only with a credible implementation and support partner.

3.8 TerraTrac

TerraTrac is a free Android application developed by TechnoServe Labs for coffee and cocoa geolocation and EUDR readiness. It:

- captures points for plots smaller than four hectares;
- captures boundary polygons for larger plots;
- operates offline;
- stores data locally;
- exports CSV and GeoJSON;
- allows data sharing with buyers;
- supports synchronization and server restore in its open-source implementation.

Sources:  
https://www.technoserve.org/tns-labs/terratrac-eudr-compliance/  
https://github.com/TechnoServe/EGNSS4COFFEE

This makes it a useful low-cost mapping tool or pilot benchmark. It is not, by itself, a complete solution for farmer management, agronomy, Rainforest Alliance inspections, Fairtrade prices and premiums, inventory, lots, warehouse movement, and buyer traceability.

The license-only cost is:

$0 ÷ 5,000 farmers = $0 per farmer

Again, mapping labor, devices, support, data cleaning, and integration remain material.

4. Language assessment for the three countries

4.1 Colombia

Spanish is well supported by Farmforce, SourceTrace, Koltiva, Fairtrade Plot Insights, and INATrace. Spanish support for current AtSource/OFIS deployments and Fairfood Trace should be demonstrated.

4.2 Indonesia

Indonesian is explicitly listed for Farmforce and Fairtrade Plot Insights. SourceTrace lists Bahasa in third-party interface documentation. Fairfood’s Connect has direct evidence of field testing with two Indonesian cooperatives and nearly 15,000 nutmeg transactions, although this does not itself prove that every management screen is localized.

Koltiva operates from Indonesia, but the reviewed interface listing did not explicitly name Indonesian. The cooperative should require a Bahasa Indonesia demonstration across the mobile app, web interface, help material, and support.

4.3 Ethiopia

Amharic is the largest common localization gap. It was not verified for Farmforce, SourceTrace, Koltiva, Fairtrade Plot Insights, or INATrace. Farmforce nevertheless has strong operational evidence from Ethiopian forest coffee using more than 80 field collectors, suggesting that a deployment can work with English or configured surveys, but a national rollout should not rely on that assumption.

The contract should require:

- Amharic interface and forms;
- Unicode rendering and search;
- translated validation errors and help text;
- support for Ethiopian names and identifiers;
- offline language packs;
- training content in the relevant local languages;
- the ability to add other Ethiopian languages where needed.

A platform’s claim to be “multilingual” should not receive full credit unless the cooperative sees all three required languages in a working demonstration.

5. Cost-per-farmer framework

5.1 Why public prices are insufficient

With the exception of free/open-source tools and Fairtrade Plot Insights, dependable vendor prices were not public. AtSource is linked to Olam/ofi sourcing; SourceTrace uses variable subscription metrics; Farmforce’s third-party price listings are inconsistent; and Koltiva uses tailored commercial proposals.

The cooperative should compare five-year total cost of ownership, not only annual software fees.

Define:

C₅ = S + 5(A + H + D + T + I + M)

where:

- S = one-time setup, configuration, migration, and integration;
- A = annual software subscription and support;
- H = annualized hardware replacement and device management;
- D = annual data/SMS/cloud cost;
- T = annual training and refresher training;
- I = annual internal staff and field-enumeration cost;
- M = annual maintenance, localization, and change requests.

Five-year cost per farmer per year is:

C₅ ÷ (5 years × 5,000 farmers)

Every bidder should populate the same template.

5.2 License-cost findings

AtSource:
- Published price: none found.
- Denominator may be volume, sourcing program, or customer tier rather than farmer.
- Require a separate software/service value even if bundled into coffee purchasing.

Fairtrade Plot Insights:
- Eligible software-access cost: $0.
- Per farmer: $0 ÷ 5,000 = $0.
- Excludes certification, mapping, hardware, and field labor.

Fairfood Trace mobile:
- Open-source mobile license: potentially $0.
- Per farmer license: $0.
- Complete backend, cards, hosting, integration, and support are not demonstrated as free.

Farmforce:
- No reliable vendor quote.
- Third-party illustrative figure: $1,950 per user per year.
- At 50 users: 50 × $1,950 = $97,500 annually.
- Per farmer: $97,500 ÷ 5,000 = $19.50 annually.
- Treat solely as a budget stress test, not a forecast (https://www.capterra.com/p/189458/Farmforce/).

SourceTrace:
- One-time onboarding plus monthly subscription.
- Pricing may depend on farmer count, acreage, or commodity ecosystems.
- No reliable dollar rate found (https://www.sourcetrace.com/wp-content/themes/sts-v3/img/media/GSMA-Agritech-Digital-Agriculture-Maps-2020.pdf).

Koltiva:
- Quote required.
- Separate optional field-agent services from software because combining them obscures software cost per farmer.

INATrace:
- Open-source license: $0.
- License cost per farmer: $0.
- Hosting, implementation, development, translation, and support remain.

TerraTrac:
- Free/open source.
- License cost per farmer: $0.
- It covers geolocation rather than the full platform requirement.

5.3 Required commercial quote structure

Ask each vendor to quote:

1. One-time configuration for three countries.
2. Migration of all 5,000 farmers and existing certification records.
3. Number and cost of web users.
4. Number and cost of mobile/offline users.
5. Cost for inactive or seasonal farmers.
6. Cost per additional farmer.
7. Spanish, Bahasa Indonesia, and Amharic localization.
8. API access and data exports.
9. Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade configuration.
10. Buyer portals and number of buyer accounts.
11. Cloud hosting and storage.
12. SMS, NFC cards, QR labels, barcode labels, and printers.
13. Training and field support.
14. Polygon mapping or remapping services.
15. External GNSS integration.
16. Five-year price escalation.
17. Exit export and termination support.
18. Data ownership and deletion.
19. Disaster recovery and service levels.
20. Taxes and travel.

The cooperative should insist on reporting both:

- Annual recurring software cost per registered farmer.
- Five-year total cost per active farmer, including implementation.

6. Recommended target operating model

For 5,000 farmers across three countries, the most inclusive and technically sound model is a shared-service architecture:

Farmer layer
- Every farmer receives a permanent cooperative ID and preferably a durable QR/NFC card.
- Farmers do not need smartphones.
- Delivery receipts, price, weight, quality, and premium information are printed or available by SMS where feasible.
- Farmers have a process to dispute transactions and correct personal or plot data.

Field layer
- Cooperative enumerators use offline Android devices.
- Each device supports farmer registration, consent, photos, internal inspections, training, deliveries, and GPS points/polygons.
- Higher-risk or ambiguous plots are remapped with a dual-frequency phone or external GNSS receiver.

Cooperative layer
- One master farmer and plot database.
- Country-specific roles and data access.
- Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade internal-control workflows.
- Lot, warehouse, and export traceability.
- Corrective-action and document management.
- Dashboards showing synchronization, mapping quality, missing inspections, expiring certificates, and traceability breaks.

Certification/buyer layer
- Rainforest Alliance-compatible KML/JSON exports.
- Fairtrade Plot Insights-compatible files and Fairtrace transaction records.
- Controlled buyer access by contract or lot.
- Complete audit logs and data-sharing consent.
- GeoJSON exports for due-diligence use.

7. Pilot and acceptance plan

Do not make the final award from demonstrations alone. Run a paid, competitive pilot with the top two or three platforms.

7.1 Pilot scope

A practical pilot would include representative farmers from:

- Colombia: steep Andean plots with Spanish-speaking staff.
- Ethiopia: shaded or forest coffee in mountainous terrain, using Amharic forms.
- Indonesia: remote plots with Bahasa Indonesia and intermittent connectivity.

Include:

- small plots under four hectares;
- plots at or above four hectares;
- multiple plots per farmer;
- irregular boundaries;
- dense shade canopy;
- overlapping or disputed boundaries;
- dual-certified farmers;
- farmers with no smartphone;
- delivery and premium transactions;
- offline use lasting several days.

7.2 Measurable acceptance criteria

Farmer usability
- Farmer need not own a smartphone or email account.
- A delivery can be recorded and acknowledged offline.
- Receipt, NFC/QR confirmation, or SMS provides an understandable transaction record.
- Consent and correction workflows are documented.

Mapping
- 100% of pilot farmers have stable IDs.
- 100% of plots have stable plot IDs.
- Required points or polygons export in accepted formats.
- No unresolved self-intersecting polygons.
- Duplicates and major overlaps are automatically flagged.
- Supervisors can identify and reassign remapping tasks.
- A sample is checked against a higher-accuracy receiver or trusted imagery.
- The vendor reports mapping accuracy and does not merely claim that “GPS is accurate.”

Certification
- Produce a valid Rainforest Alliance farm-unit upload file.
- Produce a Fairtrade-compatible farmer/plot file and GeoJSON.
- Demonstrate internal inspections, nonconformities, corrective actions, and evidence.
- Link farmer and plot records to deliveries, lots, warehouse movements, and an export sale.
- Record Fairtrade price and premium fields where relevant.

Languages
- Complete representative workflows in Spanish, Amharic, and Bahasa Indonesia.
- Include validation errors, help text, exports, and training—not only survey labels.

Offline
- Register farmers, map plots, record inspections, and record purchases with no connection.
- Synchronize later without duplicates or data loss.
- Resolve two users editing the same farmer.
- Restore a lost or damaged device.

Data portability
- Export all farmer, farm, polygon, inspection, transaction, and audit data in non-proprietary formats.
- Verify that farmer-to-plot-to-lot relationships survive the export.
- Demonstrate deletion and revocation of user access.

8. Final ranking by criterion

Best for farmers with basic phones

1. SourceTrace — documented support for Java-enabled regular phones, POS-like devices, smartphones, tablets, and low-bandwidth operation.
2. Fairfood Trace/Connect — strongest no-phone-required model using collector Android devices plus farmer NFC/QR cards.
3. Farmforce/Koltiva/INATrace — farmers can be included without owning smartphones, but field staff perform most digital interaction.
4. AtSource/OFIS — staff-mediated Android and SMS, but tied to ofi/Olam.
5. Fairtrade Fairtrace/Plot Insights — organizational online systems rather than farmer tools.

Best for GPS mapping in mountainous terrain

1. Farmforce — strongest directly relevant Ethiopian forest/highland coffee evidence and mature polygon/remapping workflow.
2. Koltiva — strong offline polygon-boundary walking and geospatial risk workflow.
3. SourceTrace — substantial GPS and area-mapping experience, but mountain-specific quality controls need demonstration.
4. INATrace — capable and modifiable, but quality assurance depends heavily on implementation.
5. TerraTrac — strong free mapping utility but narrower overall scope.
6. AtSource/OFIS — capable within the Olam ecosystem, but tier, export, and cooperative-access questions remain.
7. Fairtrade Plot Insights — excellent validation and management after field collection, not the main field collector.
8. Fairfood Trace — polygon capability not established.

Best for Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade requirements

1. SourceTrace — clearest evidence of ready certification templates and large-scale multi-certification use.
2. Farmforce — strong farm, activity, certification, traceability, and compliance workflows.
3. Koltiva — strong stated certification internal-management and field-service capabilities.
4. Fairtrade Fairtrace/Plot Insights — strongest Fairtrade-specific layer but not Rainforest Alliance or complete farm management.
5. INATrace — flexible compliance base but likely requires configuration.
6. AtSource — strong sustainability assurance but not proven as direct integration with both certification systems.
7. Fairfood Trace — evidence and transparency strengths, but certification ICS templates not established.
8. TerraTrac — geolocation/EUDR only.

Best language coverage

- Colombia: Farmforce, SourceTrace, Koltiva, Fairtrade Plot Insights, and INATrace cover Spanish.
- Indonesia: Farmforce and Plot Insights explicitly cover Indonesian; SourceTrace lists Bahasa; Fairfood has Indonesian field experience.
- Ethiopia: no candidate reviewed had verified Amharic. Localization is a mandatory procurement item.

Best offline capability

Farmforce, SourceTrace, Koltiva, Fairfood Trace, INATrace, and TerraTrac all have strong explicit offline evidence. AtSource/OFIS appears designed for remote collection but current complete offline behavior should be verified. Fairtrade Fairtrace/Plot Insights should be treated as online synchronization and reporting layers.

Best cost position

- Lowest software-license cost: INATrace or TerraTrac, but neither is a cost-free complete deployment.
- Lowest certification-specific cost: Fairtrade Plot Insights, free to eligible certified producer organizations.
- Most promising commercial value: SourceTrace, because its device flexibility and certification templates may reduce integration and hardware costs, but this remains contingent on its quote.
- Most complete commercial fit with price risk: Farmforce.
- Potentially service-intensive and therefore higher-cost: Koltiva, depending on use of field agents.
- Least transparent/selectable: AtSource, because access and economics are tied to Olam/ofi sourcing.

Final recommendation

Select a neutral platform owned or contractually controlled by the cooperative, rather than making the master farmer database dependent on one buyer.

Invite Farmforce, SourceTrace, and Koltiva to a common RFP and pilot. Farmforce should be the provisional technical leader because of its offline polygon, traceability, certification, multilingual, and Ethiopian coffee evidence. SourceTrace should receive equal commercial attention because it may be more inclusive of basic devices and has the clearest Rainforest Alliance/Fairtrade internal-control evidence. Koltiva should remain on the shortlist because of its strong offline mapping, traceability, certification, and Indonesian service capacity.

Use Fairtrade Plot Insights and Fairtrace alongside the selected system for Fairtrade-certified supply; their free or certification-linked functions can lower the incremental cost of Fairtrade geodata validation and buyer sharing. Do not mistake them for a complete farm-management platform.

Retain INATrace plus TerraTrac as the negotiating benchmark and fallback. Their zero license cost demonstrates that commercial bids must justify their recurring charges through support, certification automation, reliability, integrations, and lower operating burden.

AtSource should be considered only as an ofi-funded buyer channel layered onto the cooperative’s neutral database. It should not become the sole system of record unless ofi provides farmer-level data portability, full cooperative access, all required language and offline functions, direct certification exports, and a transparent five-year cost.

The final award should go to the platform that passes all three country pilots and offers the lowest five-year total cost per active farmer—not the platform with the lowest headline license fee.

final.content:
# 9-Day Thailand Itinerary for 7 Travellers from Hyderabad

## Executive summary

This itinerary uses Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Doi Inthanon and Chiang Dao in a continuous northbound-and-return route:

- **Days 1–3:** Bangkok, including an Ayutthaya day trip
- **Night 3:** Overnight sleeper train to Chiang Mai
- **Days 4–5:** Chiang Mai and Doi Inthanon
- **Days 6–7:** **Chiang Dao countryside — two full rural days**
- **Night 8:** Overnight sleeper train back to Bangkok
- **Day 9:** Bangkok and flight home

The two overnight trains replace two hotel nights, while Chiang Dao provides the required rural component without an expensive domestic flight or major detour.

### Budget result

A conservative planning exchange rate of **₹2.90 per THB** is used. The observed March 2026 average was approximately **₹2.882 per THB**, with a range of roughly ₹2.839–₹2.921, so ₹2.90 is a reasonable planning rate, though travellers should check the live rate before departure (https://www.exchangerates.org.uk/THB-INR-spot-exchange-rates-history-2026.html).

- **International-flight allocation:** ₹18,000 per person
- **Ground-budget ceiling:** ₹52,000 per person
- **Planned ground spending:** **THB 16,206 = approximately ₹46,997 per person**
- **Ground-budget contingency:** **approximately ₹5,003 per person**
- **Planned all-in total:** **approximately ₹64,997 per person**
- **Total group cost for seven:** approximately **₹454,982**
- **Total group ceiling:** ₹490,000
- **Group contingency:** approximately **₹35,018**

Thus, the itinerary fits within the requested ₹70,000 ceiling, provided the Hyderabad–Bangkok return ticket is actually secured for no more than ₹18,000.

## Important airfare qualification

The ₹18,000 international-flight assumption is the least certain part of the budget. Evidence gathered for 2026 shows:

- Air India Express advertised Hyderabad–Bangkok **one-way** fares from approximately ₹16,664–₹16,711 on selected dates (https://www.airindiaexpress.com/en-in/book-flights/hyderabad-to-bangkok-flights and https://flights.airindiaexpress.com/en-in/hyderabad-to-bangkok-flights).
- A recent fare comparison cited a lowest found Hyderabad–Bangkok return price of approximately **₹28,840**, with typical return pricing around ₹24,388–₹32,711 (https://www.momondo.in/flights/hyderabad/suvarnabhumi-bkk).

Therefore, ₹18,000 return is an aggressive promotional-fare target rather than a dependable year-round price. The ground itinerary itself remains below ₹52,000, but travellers should:

1. Search flexible midweek dates.
2. Avoid Thai and Indian festival weekends.
3. Compare HYD–BKK and HYD–DMK combinations.
4. Book the airfare before committing to non-refundable Thai accommodation.
5. Treat checked baggage, seat selection and airline meals as part of the ₹18,000 cap.

If the actual return airfare is ₹28,000 rather than ₹18,000, the same ground itinerary would produce an all-in cost of roughly ₹74,997 per person. In that case, either the overall ceiling must rise or approximately ₹5,000–₹10,000 must be removed through cheaper flights, fewer paid attractions and lower food/nightlife spending.

---

# Recommended route and overnight plan

| Night | Location | Suggested accommodation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bangkok | Station8 Hostel, 8-person mixed dorm |
| 2 | Bangkok | Station8 Hostel, same dorm |
| 3 | Bangkok–Chiang Mai train | Second-class air-conditioned sleeper |
| 4 | Chiang Mai | i-Smile & U2 Hostel, private 9-person room |
| 5 | Chiang Mai | i-Smile & U2 Hostel, same room |
| 6 | Chiang Dao | Chiang Dao Hostel, 6-bed dorm plus twin/private room |
| 7 | Chiang Dao | Chiang Dao Hostel, same arrangement |
| 8 | Chiang Mai–Bangkok train | Second-class air-conditioned sleeper |

This gives the group:

- Two Bangkok hostel nights
- Two Chiang Mai hostel nights
- Two rural Chiang Dao nights
- Two sleeper-train nights
- No accommodation expense after arriving in Bangkok on Day 9

---

# Accommodation recommendations

## Bangkok: Station8 Hostel

**Suggested room:** Reserve all seven beds in its eight-person male/female dorm, ideally reserving the eighth bed as well if the hostel offers a whole-dorm arrangement.

The property’s published information describes:

- An eight-person mixed dorm
- THB 350 per bed per night
- Proximity to Wongwian Yai BTS, within approximately 50 metres
- No breakfast included
- Twenty beds across three rooms (https://s8hostel.com/th/products/713368-male%26female-dormitory)

### Planned cost

- THB 350 per person per night
- Two nights: **THB 700 per person**
- Seven travellers: **THB 4,900 total for two nights**

Because there are eight beds, ask whether the group can pay for seven occupied beds while keeping the room private. If privacy requires buying the eighth bed, the additional group cost would be THB 350 per night, or only THB 100 per traveller over two nights.

### Alternative Bangkok options

- **Marni BKK Hostel:** An eight-bed mixed dorm listed for eight adults, with air-conditioning, privacy curtains, shared bathroom and a location about 500 metres from Khao San Road. Prices are live rather than fixed on its page (https://marnibkkhostel.com/rooms/8-bed-mixed-dorm).
- **Airbnb-style hostel room in Bangkok Old Town:** An Airbnb listing offers an eight-bed hostel room for up to eight guests, within walking distance of the Grand Palace, Wat Pho, Khao San Road and the Flower Market, but the gathered listing did not expose a reliable fixed price (https://www.airbnb.com/rooms/37765246).
- **Lub d Bangkok Chinatown:** Eight-bed dorm beds were shown from THB 324 per person, subject to date and membership pricing (https://lubd.com/rooms/bangkok-chinatown/1-bed-in-our-tribe-hideout-8-shared-beds/).

Use Station8 as the budget baseline; switch only if an Old Town hostel matches the THB 350-per-person ceiling after taxes.

## Chiang Mai: i-Smile & U2 Hostel

This is particularly suitable for seven because it publishes private group-room prices:

- Air-conditioned dorm bed: THB 180
- Private room for six: THB 1,200
- Private room for nine: THB 1,600
- En-suite bathroom
- Free water, tea, coffee, fruit and biscuits
- Shared refrigerator, microwave and toaster
- Located by Chang Phueak Gate on the edge of the Old City (https://u2chiangmai.com/)

### Recommended booking

Reserve the **nine-person private room for the seven travellers**.

Calculation:

- THB 1,600 ÷ 7 = **THB 229 per person per night**
- Two nights = **THB 458 per person**
- Group total for two nights = **THB 3,200**

This is cheaper and more cohesive than seven unrelated dorm beds.

## Chiang Dao: Chiang Dao Hostel

Published accommodation information indicates:

- A six-bed mixed dorm
- Twin rooms and double rooms
- Shared kitchen, garden, terrace and free parking
- Rates shown from approximately THB 250 per night on one booking source (https://www.roomsaint.com/hotels/th/chiang-dao/chiang-dao-hostel/1782763)
- Another listing shows the six-bed dorm, twin rooms and double rooms, though exact live rates vary by date (https://www.trip.com/hotels/chiang-dao-hotel-detail-7694323/chiang-dao-hostel/)

### Recommended configuration

Book:

- The complete six-bed dorm for six travellers
- One bed in a twin room or one private room for the seventh traveller

Use a hard booking ceiling of:

- **THB 350 per person per night**
- THB 2,450 maximum for the entire group per night
- Two nights: **THB 4,900 maximum for the group**

If Chiang Dao Hostel cannot meet that ceiling, ask it or another countryside guesthouse for a seven-person group quote. Do not reserve a property that pushes the per-person cost over THB 350 unless savings are made elsewhere.

---

# Day-by-day itinerary and costs

All costs below are **per person**. Group expenses are divided by seven. Minor local fares and meals are deliberately rounded upward.

## Day 1 — Arrive in Bangkok: royal and riverside Bangkok, then Khao San nightlife

### Morning

Arrive at Bangkok Suvarnabhumi Airport, complete immigration and travel to the hostel.

For Suvarnabhumi arrivals, the Airport Rail Link operates from approximately 05:30 to midnight, with fares between THB 15 and THB 45. The full airport-to-Phaya Thai trip is THB 45 (https://thailand.go.th/issue-focus-detail/001_01_107-2).

Continue by BTS, MRT, bus or a metered/Grab taxi shared by the group to Station8 Hostel near Wongwian Yai BTS.

If the flight lands at Don Mueang rather than Suvarnabhumi, use the airport bus, SRT train or a divided seven-person van/taxi fare, keeping within the Day 1 local-transport allowance.

### Afternoon: cultural core

Visit:

1. **Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew**  
   Foreign-adult admission is THB 500 and includes Wat Phra Kaew and the Queen Sirikit Museum of Textiles (https://www.royalgrandpalace.th/en/visit/practical-information).

2. **Wat Pho and the Reclining Buddha**  
   Budget THB 300. Recent visitor information lists a THB 300 foreigner price and daily hours around 08:00–18:30 (https://traveltriangle.com/thailand-tourism/bangkok/places-to-visit/wat-pho).

Wear clothing that covers shoulders and knees.

### Evening: nightlife

Have an inexpensive street-food dinner, then visit Khao San Road or Rambuttri. The THB 350 nightlife allocation is enough for modest drinks or music, but not a bottle-service club.

### Day 1 budget

| Item | THB |
|---|---:|
| Station8 dorm | 350 |
| Food and water | 600 |
| Airport and city transport | 250 |
| Grand Palace | 500 |
| Wat Pho | 300 |
| Khao San/Rambuttri nightlife | 350 |
| **Day 1 total** | **2,350** |
| **Approximate INR** | **₹6,815** |

---

## Day 2 — Ayutthaya day trip: ruins, cycling and Bangkok nightlife

This is a cultural and light-adventure day trip without changing hotels.

### Early morning: Bangkok to Ayutthaya

Take an ordinary third-class train from Hua Lamphong. Ordinary services have been reported at approximately THB 15–20 each way and take around 1.5–2 hours; tickets are generally purchased at the station on the day (https://www.thaiholidayguide.com/services/bangkok-to-ayutthaya-train-tickets/).

The budget allows:

- THB 30 for the round-trip train
- THB 16 for two short local ferry crossings
- THB 100 for other local transport

If the group uses a faster express from Krung Thep Aphiwat instead, it must absorb the higher fare from the contingency.

### Ayutthaya historical circuit

Hire bicycles near the station or historical park and visit a manageable selection such as:

- Wat Mahathat
- Wat Ratchaburana
- Wat Phra Si Sanphet
- Wat Chaiwatthanaram if time permits

The historical-park fee source lists a combined foreigner price of THB 300 for seven major sites, while individual temple pricing varies (https://ayutthaya-history.com/ce_admissionfee.html). Use the combined-ticket budget only if visiting enough paid monuments to justify it.

The cycling portion adds an adventure element, but avoid the hottest hours and use tuk-tuks instead if traffic or heat makes cycling unsafe.

### Evening

Return to Bangkok. Choose either:

- Chinatown/Yaowarat for food and bars, or
- A second Khao San evening

Keep nightlife modest because Day 3 ends with an overnight train.

### Day 2 budget

| Item | THB |
|---|---:|
| Station8 dorm | 350 |
| Food and water | 600 |
| Return train, ferry and local Bangkok/Ayutthaya transport | 146 |
| Bicycle and historical sites | 400 |
| Nightlife | 300 |
| **Day 2 total** | **1,796** |
| **Approximate INR** | **₹5,208** |

The THB 400 activity allocation consists of approximately THB 300 for monuments and THB 100 as the bicycle-rental ceiling.

---

## Day 3 — Bangkok neighbourhoods and overnight sleeper to Chiang Mai

### Morning and afternoon

Check out but leave luggage at the hostel if permitted.

Choose low-cost or free neighbourhood exploration:

- Pak Khlong Talat flower market
- Chinatown lanes
- Talat Noi street art
- Chao Phraya riverside
- Bangkok’s local markets

The THB 100 activity allowance can cover a short ferry ride, donation or incidental entrance.

### Late afternoon: transfer to Krung Thep Aphiwat

Collect luggage and reach Krung Thep Aphiwat station early.

### Overnight train

Book **Special Express No. 9**, second-class air-conditioned sleeper.

Published schedule and fares:

- Departure from Krung Thep Aphiwat: approximately 18:40
- Arrival Chiang Mai: approximately 07:15 next morning
- Upper berth: THB 941
- Lower berth: THB 1,041
- Tickets can be purchased through the official SRT D-Ticket system, and advance booking is strongly recommended (https://www.thaitrainguide.com/timetables/no-9/)

The budget uses **THB 1,041 for everyone**, allowing the group to choose lower berths or cover a mixture of upper and lower beds. Seven adjacent berths are not guaranteed, so reserve as soon as the travel date opens.

Eat dinner before boarding or buy simple train food. The sleeper cost serves as both transport and the night’s accommodation.

### Day 3 budget

| Item | THB |
|---|---:|
| Second-class sleeper | 1,041 |
| Food and water | 600 |
| Bangkok local transport and station transfer | 250 |
| Ferries/donations/incidental sightseeing | 100 |
| Light Chinatown or pre-train nightlife | 300 |
| **Day 3 total** | **2,291** |
| **Approximate INR** | **₹6,644** |

---

## Day 4 — Chiang Mai Old City, Thai cooking and Night Bazaar

### Morning

Arrive around 07:15, then take a red songthaew or divided Grab fare to i-Smile & U2 Hostel near Chang Phueak Gate.

Leave bags if the private room is not ready.

Walk through Chiang Mai Old City, visiting free or donation-based temples such as:

- Wat Chedi Luang
- Wat Phan Tao
- Wat Chiang Man
- Tha Phae Gate

### Afternoon and evening: Thai cooking class

Book a half-day or evening course at **Siam Garden Cooking School**.

Its published programme includes:

- THB 800 per person
- Morning course approximately 09:30–14:00, or evening approximately 14:30–19:30
- Six dishes
- Curry paste, curry, stir-fry, soup, appetiser and dessert categories
- Pickup window listed for the group course (https://www.siamgardencookingschool.com/en/courses)

The dishes function as a substantial meal, so Day 4’s separate food allowance is reduced to THB 450.

### Nightlife

After the course, visit:

- Chiang Mai Night Bazaar
- Zoe in Yellow/Old City bar area, if the group wants a livelier evening
- A quieter jazz or live-music venue

### Day 4 budget

| Item | THB |
|---|---:|
| Share of private nine-person hostel room | 229 |
| Food outside cooking class | 450 |
| Local songthaews/Grab | 150 |
| Cooking class | 800 |
| Night Bazaar or bar allowance | 350 |
| **Day 4 total** | **1,979** |
| **Approximate INR** | **₹5,739** |

---

## Day 5 — Doi Inthanon countryside: summit, waterfalls and Karen village

Although Chiang Dao supplies the formal two rural days, Day 5 adds another full countryside excursion.

### Transport

Hire a private air-conditioned van for all seven from Chiang Mai.

A published Doi Inthanon private-van offer is:

- THB 3,500 per van
- Nine to twelve seats
- Driver, water and hotel/guesthouse transfers
- Approximately eight to nine hours
- Guide available separately, but not required for the basic transport itinerary (https://chiangmaiguideline.com/private-tour-doi-inthanon/)

Calculation:

- THB 3,500 ÷ 7 = **THB 500 per person**

Confirm in writing that fuel, driver and Chiang Mai pickup/drop-off are included. Entrance fees and meals should be assumed excluded.

### Suggested sequence

1. Depart Chiang Mai around 07:30–08:00.
2. Visit Wachirathan Waterfall.
3. Continue to the summit area and Ang Ka nature trail.
4. Visit the twin royal pagodas.
5. Stop at a Karen or Hmong village/market and purchase coffee or crafts directly from local vendors.
6. Return to Chiang Mai before evening.

### Fees

Doi Inthanon is in the national-park category charging foreign adults **THB 300** (Thailand’s Department of National Parks announcement: http://news.dnp.go.th/news/17112).

Allow:

- THB 300 park admission
- THB 100 for the twin-pagoda area, consistent with published Doi Inthanon tour exclusions (https://happytovisit.com/chiang-mai-to-doi-inthanon-full-day-shared-tour/)
- THB 100 contingency for a local trail guide, parking or village contribution

### Day 5 budget

| Item | THB |
|---|---:|
| Share of Chiang Mai private room | 229 |
| Food and water | 600 |
| Share of private van | 500 |
| Park, pagoda and local-guide contingency | 500 |
| **Day 5 total** | **1,829** |
| **Approximate INR** | **₹5,304** |

The day is logistically easier with the private van than with seven individual tour tickets. A private van also lets the group control stops and avoid paying seven separate shared-tour markups.

---

## Day 6 — Chiang Mai to rural Chiang Dao: cave exploration and village surroundings

**This is rural/countryside day 1.**

### Morning transport

Check out and travel to Chang Phueak Bus Station.

An air-conditioned bus/minivan listing for Chiang Mai–Chiang Dao shows:

- Approximately THB 170 per person
- Ten departures daily
- Departures between approximately 08:00 and 17:00 (https://www.busonlineticket.co.th/bus-from-chiang-mai-to-chiang-dao/)

Choose an 08:00–09:00 service. The journey is roughly a few hours including station access and waiting, leaving the afternoon for the cave.

### Check-in

Check into Chiang Dao Hostel: six-bed dorm plus one twin/private-room space. Leave luggage and arrange a local songthaew through the property.

### Chiang Dao Cave

The cave is about 7 km from town and is known for limestone chambers, stalactites, shrines and Buddha images.

Published charges include:

- Foreign admission: THB 40 per person
- Dark inner cave: approximately THB 200 per guide-and-lantern group
- A guide is required for the unlit chambers
- Community members or students may provide local guiding (Chiang Dao local-government information: https://www.chiangdaosao.go.th/v/catalog/151 and visitor details at https://www.sayhithailand.com/view-attractions/?pro_id=1692)

Because some sources describe a guide-and-lantern group as suitable for up to five, seven travellers should budget for **two lantern groups**:

- Admission: 7 × THB 40 = THB 280
- Two guide/lantern groups: 2 × THB 200 = THB 400
- Total for seven: THB 680
- Per traveller: approximately THB 97, rounded to **THB 100**

Wear closed shoes and clothing appropriate for a religious cave. Anyone uncomfortable with narrow, dark or slippery spaces can remain in the illuminated chambers.

### Evening

Walk or cycle through town, eat at a local market or family-run restaurant, and enjoy a quiet hostel evening. This is intentionally not a nightlife day.

### Day 6 budget

| Item | THB |
|---|---:|
| Chiang Dao accommodation | 350 |
| Food and water | 600 |
| Chiang Mai–Chiang Dao bus plus local songthaew | 370 |
| Cave admission and guide/lantern share | 100 |
| **Day 6 total** | **1,420** |
| **Approximate INR** | **₹4,118** |

---

## Day 7 — Chiang Dao countryside cycling, rice fields, temples and hot springs

**This is rural/countryside day 2.**

This day deliberately avoids changing hotels or making a long intercity transfer.

### Recommended cycling route

Rent bicycles and explore at an easy pace:

1. Chiang Dao town and morning market
2. Rural lanes and rice-field views
3. Wat Tham Pha Plong or another countryside temple
4. Coffee shops or farms near the mountain
5. Chiang Dao hot springs
6. Return before dark

Chiang Dao Nest publishes mountain-bike rental at **THB 200 per day** and describes a local cycling route linking hot springs and waterfalls (https://www.chiangdao.com/nest/fulldaytours.htm).

The local hot spring has been described as free, with optional paid private or improved bathing areas around THB 50 (https://nashaplaneta.net/asia/thai/chiangmai-province-chiang-dao-hot-springs_en).

### Safer non-cycling option

Travellers who do not want to cycle should hire a local songthaew with driver. One traveller report describes a local full-day songthaew arrangement at approximately THB 1,000 for the vehicle (https://aboringtravelblog.com/guide-to-chiang-dao-from-wat-tham-pha-plong-to-hot-springs).

For seven:

- THB 1,000 ÷ 7 = approximately THB 143 per person

This is lower than the THB 200 bicycle allowance and is a sensible choice in rain, intense heat or for anyone uncomfortable riding on rural roads.

### Evening

Have a relaxed local dinner. A THB 200 social allowance is included for drinks at the hostel, a café or a quiet local venue rather than an urban nightclub.

### Day 7 budget

| Item | THB |
|---|---:|
| Chiang Dao accommodation | 350 |
| Food and water | 600 |
| Bicycle or share of local songthaew | 200 |
| Hot-spring/private-bath allowance | 50 |
| Quiet evening drinks/social allowance | 200 |
| **Day 7 total** | **1,400** |
| **Approximate INR** | **₹4,060** |

---

## Day 8 — Return to Chiang Mai, Doi Suthep and sleeper to Bangkok

This is the most schedule-sensitive day, but it is feasible if the group leaves Chiang Dao early.

### Early morning

Check out and take the earliest practical bus or minivan to Chiang Mai. Ask the hostel to verify the current return departure the day before.

Budget:

- THB 170 for Chiang Dao–Chiang Mai
- THB 200 for Chiang Mai songthaews and station transfers

Aim to be back in Chiang Mai by late morning.

### Midday: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep

Leave luggage at i-Smile/U2 if permitted, at Chiang Mai station, or with a paid luggage facility.

Take a shared red songthaew to Doi Suthep. Shared songthaews are commonly quoted around THB 40–50 per person each way, and the temple foreigner fee is approximately THB 30 (https://www.thaiholidayguide.com/attraction/wat-phra-that-doi-suthep/).

Budget:

- THB 100 return songthaew
- THB 30 temple entrance
- Remaining transport allocation for Chiang Mai station transfers

The main-road temple visit does not incur the newer national-park trail fee. The THB 100 foreigner national-park charge applies to specified trail and waterfall areas, while visits to Wat Doi Suthep by the main road are exempt from that additional charge (https://www.chiangmaicitylife.com/citynews/general/entrance-fees-required-at-doi-suthep-pui-starting-october-2025/).

Return to the city by approximately 15:00, eat an early dinner, collect bags and reach Chiang Mai railway station at least one hour before departure.

### Overnight train to Bangkok

Book **Special Express No. 10**, second-class air-conditioned sleeper.

Published information lists:

- Chiang Mai departure: approximately 18:20
- Bangkok arrival: approximately 06:30 next morning
- Upper berth: THB 941
- Lower berth: THB 1,041
- Advance reservations available for long-distance trains (https://www.thaitrainguide.com/timetables/no-10/)

As on Night 3, budget THB 1,041 per person.

### Day 8 budget

| Item | THB |
|---|---:|
| Second-class sleeper | 1,041 |
| Food and water | 600 |
| Chiang Dao bus, Doi Suthep songthaew and station transfers | 370 |
| Doi Suthep temple admission | 30 |
| **Day 8 total** | **2,041** |
| **Approximate INR** | **₹5,919** |

If the Chiang Dao return bus is delayed, skip Doi Suthep rather than risking the overnight train. Doi Suthep is optional; the sleeper is not.

---

## Day 9 — Arrive Bangkok, final meal and fly to Hyderabad

### Morning

The sleeper is scheduled to reach Bangkok around 06:30.

Book the Hyderabad flight no earlier than:

- **14:00 from Suvarnabhumi**, or
- A similarly conservative afternoon departure from Don Mueang

This allows for train delays, breakfast, airport transfer, airline check-in and immigration.

If departing Suvarnabhumi:

- Use MRT/BTS plus Airport Rail Link.
- Airport Rail Link to Suvarnabhumi costs no more than THB 45 from Phaya Thai (https://thailand.go.th/issue-focus-detail/001_01_107-2).

If the flight is later in the evening, leave luggage at the station and choose a short final activity. The THB 500 Day 9 activity allowance may cover:

- A budget massage
- Souvenirs
- A museum or another paid sight
- Additional airport food
- Unexpected baggage-storage expense

### Day 9 budget

| Item | THB |
|---|---:|
| Food and water | 400 |
| Bangkok and airport transport | 200 |
| Massage, souvenir or final-activity allowance | 500 |
| **Day 9 total** | **1,100** |
| **Approximate INR** | **₹3,190** |

---

# Complete daily budget

| Day | Destination | THB per person | INR at ₹2.90/THB |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | Bangkok: Grand Palace, Wat Pho, Khao San | 2,350 | ₹6,815 |
| 2 | Ayutthaya day trip | 1,796 | ₹5,208 |
| 3 | Bangkok and sleeper to Chiang Mai | 2,291 | ₹6,644 |
| 4 | Chiang Mai and cooking class | 1,979 | ₹5,739 |
| 5 | Doi Inthanon countryside | 1,829 | ₹5,304 |
| 6 | Chiang Dao cave — rural day 1 | 1,420 | ₹4,118 |
| 7 | Chiang Dao cycling/hot springs — rural day 2 | 1,400 | ₹4,060 |
| 8 | Doi Suthep and sleeper to Bangkok | 2,041 | ₹5,919 |
| 9 | Bangkok and flight home | 1,100 | ₹3,190 |
| **Total** |  | **16,206** | **₹46,997** |

Rounding explains any ₹1 discrepancy when individual converted days are added.

---

# Budget by category

| Category | THB per person | INR per person |
|---|---:|---:|
| Hostels and sleeper berths | 3,940 | ₹11,426 |
| Food and drinking water | 5,050 | ₹14,645 |
| Local and intercity transport, excluding sleeper portion above | 2,436 | ₹7,064 |
| Cultural/adventure activities | 3,280 | ₹9,512 |
| Nightlife and social spending | 1,500 | ₹4,350 |
| **Ground total** | **16,206** | **₹46,997** |
| **Available ground budget** | **17,931 THB equivalent** | **₹52,000** |
| **Unallocated contingency** | **approximately 1,725 THB** | **approximately ₹5,003** |

The equivalent THB ceiling is:

- ₹52,000 ÷ ₹2.90 = **THB 17,931**

Margin:

- THB 17,931 − THB 16,206 = **THB 1,725**
- THB 1,725 × ₹2.90 = **₹5,003**

## Seven-person group calculation

- Planned ground spending: THB 16,206 × 7 = **THB 113,442**
- In rupees: ₹46,997.4 × 7 = **₹328,982**
- Ground ceiling: ₹52,000 × 7 = **₹364,000**
- Group ground contingency: approximately **₹35,018**
- Flight allocation: ₹18,000 × 7 = **₹126,000**
- Planned all-in group total: approximately **₹454,982**
- Overall group ceiling: ₹70,000 × 7 = **₹490,000**

---

# Food plan within THB 5,050 per person

The itinerary allows an average of approximately THB 560 per person per day, with Day 4 lower because the cooking class supplies a substantial meal.

A workable daily approach is:

- Breakfast: THB 60–100
- Lunch: THB 100–180
- Dinner: THB 150–250
- Fruit, snacks and water: THB 50–100

To stay within budget:

- Use street-food stalls, markets and food courts.
- Share dishes at family-run restaurants.
- Refill water where the hostel provides it.
- Avoid hotel breakfasts and international chains.
- Confirm dietary requirements in Thai before ordering.
- Vegetarian travellers should clarify that fish sauce, oyster sauce and shrimp paste must also be excluded.
- Muslim travellers can ask the Doi Inthanon van operator to stop at halal restaurants; one private-tour provider specifically notes that halal arrangements are possible (https://mychiangmaitour.com/tour14/).

Alcohol is not included in the food line; it is confined to the separate nightlife allowance.

---

# Local transport strategy

## Bangkok

Use a combination of:

- Airport Rail Link from Suvarnabhumi
- BTS and MRT
- Chao Phraya ferries
- Ordinary SRT train for Ayutthaya
- Metered taxi or Grab divided among seven when rail is inconvenient

For a group of seven, compare two Grab cars against one larger van before booking. Always confirm whether tolls are included.

## Bangkok–Chiang Mai–Bangkok

Use SRT overnight trains instead of domestic flights.

Advantages:

- Saves two hostel nights
- Delivers the group directly between city centres
- Avoids airport-transfer and baggage costs
- Adds a distinctive Thai rail experience

Use SRT’s official D-Ticket platform where possible. Train No. 9 and No. 10 sleeper fares and schedules are documented at https://www.thaitrainguide.com/timetables/no-9/ and https://www.thaitrainguide.com/timetables/no-10/.

## Chiang Mai

Use:

- Red songthaews for short urban trips and Doi Suthep
- Walking within Old City
- A private 9–12-seat van for Doi Inthanon

The Doi Inthanon private van is more economical for seven than paying seven individual tour rates.

## Chiang Mai–Chiang Dao

Use the shared bus/minivan rather than a private transfer. The published air-conditioned price is approximately THB 170 each way (https://www.busonlineticket.co.th/bus-from-chiang-mai-to-chiang-dao/).

## Chiang Dao

Local public transport is limited. Use:

- Bicycles where road and weather conditions are suitable
- Hostel-arranged songthaew for the cave
- A full-day local songthaew for Day 7 if cycling is unsuitable

Do not rely on ride-hailing availability in the countryside.

---

# Activity balance

The itinerary includes all three requested activity types.

## Cultural

- Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew
- Wat Pho
- Ayutthaya historical temples
- Chiang Mai Old City temples
- Thai cooking class
- Doi Suthep
- Chiang Dao Cave’s shrines and Buddha images

## Adventure and nature

- Ayutthaya cycling
- Overnight sleeper trains
- Doi Inthanon waterfalls and nature trails
- Guided dark-cave exploration
- Chiang Dao countryside cycling
- Hot springs

## Nightlife and social experiences

- Khao San Road/Rambuttri
- Chinatown evening
- Chiang Mai Night Bazaar and Old City bars
- A quieter Chiang Dao hostel/café evening

The nightlife allowances are deliberately moderate. Anyone planning clubs, cocktails or heavy drinking should increase that category using personal funds rather than the shared trip budget.

---

# Booking sequence

1. **Secure Hyderabad–Bangkok return flights first**, because the ₹18,000 airfare ceiling is uncertain.
2. Ensure the inbound flight reaches Bangkok early enough for Day 1 and the outbound flight leaves after 14:00 on Day 9.
3. Book SRT sleeper trains No. 9 and No. 10 as soon as reservations open.
4. Reserve the Bangkok eight-bed dorm.
5. Reserve the Chiang Mai private nine-person room.
6. Obtain a written Chiang Dao Hostel quote for the six-bed dorm plus one additional bed/room.
7. Reserve the THB 3,500 Doi Inthanon van and confirm inclusions.
8. Book the THB 800 Chiang Mai cooking class.
9. Confirm Chiang Mai–Chiang Dao bus times shortly before travel.
10. Ask Chiang Dao accommodation to arrange the cave songthaew and, if needed, a Day 7 songthaew.

---

# Entry formalities and practical cautions

All non-Thai nationals must complete the **Thailand Digital Arrival Card**, which replaced the paper arrival card. The official guidance says it should be submitted online within three days before arrival, and a group submission can include up to ten travellers—enough for all seven in one submission (https://tdac.immigration.go.th/manual/en/).

Use only the official portal:

https://tdac.immigration.go.th

The TDAC is not a visa. Visa rules can change, so Indian passport holders should verify their exact entry status with Thailand’s official immigration or Ministry of Foreign Affairs sources immediately before travel.

Other practical points:

- Carry passports or secure copies for railway and accommodation check-in.
- Keep shoulders and knees covered at major temples.
- Carry cash in small denominations for caves, songthaews, buses and rural vendors.
- Use closed shoes for Chiang Dao Cave and Doi Inthanon trails.
- Avoid cycling after dark or during heavy rain.
- Do not schedule a morning international flight on Day 9.
- Keep at least THB 1,000 of the contingency untouched until the last day.
- Verify whether online accommodation prices include tax and service charges.
- Travel insurance is advisable and is not included in the ₹52,000 ground calculation.

---

# Final assessment

The route is logistically coherent:

**Bangkok → Ayutthaya day trip → overnight train → Chiang Mai → Doi Inthanon → Chiang Dao for two rural nights → Chiang Mai → overnight train → Bangkok**

It avoids backtracking other than the necessary return to Bangkok for the international flight, uses sleeper trains efficiently, gives the group two full countryside days in Chiang Dao, and provides a balanced mix of cultural sights, outdoor activity and nightlife.

The planned ground expenditure is **approximately ₹46,997 per person**, leaving approximately **₹5,003 under the ₹52,000 ground ceiling**. The complete trip is approximately **₹64,997 per person only if the return flight is secured for ₹18,000**. The itinerary itself fits the requested budget; the principal uncertainty is the international airfare, which should be confirmed before any non-refundable bookings are made.
