final.content:
Anthropology of Gift Economies: From Kula Exchange to Digital Platforms and Cryptocurrency Governance

Executive summary

The classical anthropology of the gift did not identify a pristine realm of altruism opposed to commerce. Rather, Bronisław Malinowski, Marcel Mauss, and Marshall Sahlins showed that apparently voluntary transfers can organize obligation, prestige, political authority, and enduring social relations.

Malinowski’s 1922 account of the Trobriand kula established the ethnographic foundation. Shell valuables circulated through durable partnerships and ceremonial voyages, alongside—but analytically distinguished from—utilitarian barter. Kula objects were valued less for consumption than for their histories, renown, and capacity to constitute relationships. Mauss generalized from the kula, the Northwest Coast potlatch, Polynesian materials, and ancient law. Gifts, he argued, create three interlocking obligations: to give, to receive, and to make a return. Gift exchange is therefore a “total social phenomenon,” simultaneously legal, moral, economic, religious, political, and aesthetic. Sahlins subsequently classified reciprocity as generalized, balanced, or negative, relating the form of exchange to social distance.

Feminist anthropologists exposed the gendered selectivity of this canon. Annette Weiner’s Trobriand restudy documented women’s production and ceremonial distribution of banana-leaf bundles and skirts, especially in mortuary exchange—activities marginalized in Malinowski’s male-centered account. Her theory of “keeping-while-giving” further showed that power may lie not only in circulating wealth but in controlling inalienable possessions and the authority they authenticate. Gayle Rubin demonstrated how theories that describe women themselves as gifts can reveal, but also risk naturalizing, male alliance and women’s subordination. Marilyn Strathern went further by questioning whether Western oppositions—individual/society, subject/object, production/exchange, male/female, gift/commodity—can adequately represent Melanesian persons and relations. Feminist work thus shifts attention from the visible transaction to the often-hidden labor of producing people, valuables, hospitality, care, and social continuity.

Contemporary digital practices confirm the continuing importance of gifts but undermine any strict gift-versus-commodity dichotomy:

• Free and open-source software resembles generalized reciprocity and commons-based production: contributors make code available without requiring a direct equivalent return. Yet reputational rewards, licenses, employment, corporate appropriation, and unequal control over project governance make it a hybrid of gift, commons, and commodity relations.

• Social-media platforms turn attention, content, friendship, and personal data into “pseudo-gifts.” Likes and shares create Maussian obligations and measurable prestige, but platforms appropriate the resulting interaction data and sell advertisers the capacity to influence users. Gift relations are therefore not outside capitalism; they can be infrastructure for commodity production and private accumulation.

• Cryptocurrency communities combine voluntary technical labor and common-good aspirations with explicitly priced tokens. Governance rights can be bought, sold, delegated, and accumulated. This makes political voice an alienable commodity even when discourse emphasizes community and decentralization. Empirical research finds substantial concentration of voting power and low participation in many decentralized autonomous organizations, reproducing hierarchy in a formally open system.

The strongest conclusion is that gift and commodity should be treated as relational tendencies or transaction forms, not mutually exclusive kinds of society or object. A piece of code, social-media post, token, or shell valuable can move between regimes, or participate in several simultaneously. Contemporary systems reinforce the classical claim that exchange constitutes social relations, while feminist and digital scholarship show that any adequate model must also ask who performs the underlying labor, who controls the infrastructure, what remains inalienable, and who converts collective gifts into privately controlled value.

1. Conceptual problem: what is a gift economy?

In ordinary usage, a gift is often imagined as a unilateral, voluntary, and altruistic transfer. The anthropological tradition destabilizes that image. A gift may be formally free yet socially obligatory; materially uncompensated yet rewarded through prestige or political allegiance; or transferred to another person while remaining connected to its giver.

The central contrast is therefore not simply:

gift = free, altruistic, non-economic  
commodity = priced, interested, economic

A more useful ideal-typical contrast, developed in political-economic anthropology, concerns the relationship among objects and transactors. Chris Gregory defines commodity exchange as involving alienable things exchanged among reciprocally independent actors, while gift exchange involves inalienable things among reciprocally dependent actors (https://haubooks.org/viewbook/gifts-and-commodities/08_ch01). “Inalienable” does not necessarily mean physically impossible to transfer. It means that an object may retain the identity, history, rights, or social force of its source after transfer.

This distinction is analytically powerful but should not be converted into a division between entire “gift societies” and “market societies.” Gregory’s analysis of colonial Papua New Guinea found that indigenous gift exchange and commodity production expanded together rather than the former being displaced by the latter. Commodities could become gifts and gift economies intensified in response to modern colonial conditions (https://doi.org/10.30676/jfas.v44i3-4.91424). The relevant questions are consequently:

1. What is transferred?
2. What relationship does the transfer create or express?
3. Is a return required, and on what timetable?
4. How is value measured—or deliberately left unmeasured?
5. Who produced the transferable object or service?
6. Who has authority to give it?
7. What remains attached to the giver or group?
8. Who controls the infrastructure through which exchange occurs?
9. Can social recognition, personal data, or political authority be converted into money?

These questions connect the classical literature to open-source software, attention economies, and cryptocurrency governance.

2. Malinowski and the Trobriand kula

2.1 Ethnographic and methodological contribution

Bronisław Malinowski’s Argonauts of the Western Pacific, published in 1922, is the canonical ethnography of the kula. Malinowski lived in the Trobriand Islands, learned local languages, and observed everyday and ceremonial activity directly. The book helped establish extended participant observation as a defining anthropological method (full text: https://gutenberg.org/files/55822/55822-h/55822-h.htm).

The methodological point matters theoretically. Kula exchange could appear irrational if isolated from its social setting: people undertook difficult sea voyages to exchange apparently impractical shell valuables. Malinowski instead embedded the transactions in kinship, magic, mythology, politics, canoe construction, garden production, rank, and long-term inter-island partnerships. The institution could not be understood by assigning market utility to the valuables alone.

2.2 Organization of the kula

The kula is an inter-island circuit in the Massim region of what is now Papua New Guinea. Its most famous valuables are:

• soulava: shell necklaces circulating in one direction around the circuit;
• mwali: shell armbands circulating in the opposite direction.

Participants acquire a valuable and later pass it onward. The point is not permanent accumulation or practical consumption. Temporarily holding a famous valuable brings prestige because the object carries a history of previous possessors and transactions. Kula partnerships can last for years and connect communities across considerable geographical distance.

The system therefore links persons through objects while linking objects to named histories. A valuable does not become socially anonymous when transferred. This is a foundational example of what later anthropology would call the partial inalienability of gifts.

Kula valuables also move according to conventions different from ordinary barter or gimwali. Malinowski did not claim that Trobrianders lacked trade, bargaining, or material self-interest. Kula expeditions were accompanied by trade in useful goods. His argument was that ceremonial exchange was not reducible to a calculation of utility, profit, and loss. The book’s preface emphasizes that ordinary trade accompanied kula but that the ceremonial valuables served emotional, aesthetic, political, and social purposes rather than straightforward utility (https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55822/pg55822-images.html).

This juxtaposition is critical: gift and commodity-like transactions coexisted in the same voyages, among the same people, and sometimes around the same events. Malinowski’s ethnography therefore does not support a simple historical succession from “primitive gift economy” to “modern commerce.”

2.3 Reciprocity, delay, and prestige

Kula exchange is reciprocal, but the return is neither an immediate purchase nor necessarily a numerically equivalent counter-transfer. Delay is socially productive. It keeps a relationship open, creates expectations, permits strategic action, and allows reputations for generosity or meanness to develop.

Its political economy has several features:

• Valuable objects circulate rather than being consumed.
• Returns occur through established social relations, not an anonymous spot market.
• The identity and reputation of giver and recipient matter.
• Status depends on the capacity to attract, hold, and pass on renowned valuables.
• Exchange is inseparable from hospitality, magic, ceremonial display, alliance, and dangerous travel.
• Formal generosity does not exclude rivalry or political calculation.

Kula thus challenges the figure of an isolated “economic man.” But it does not describe disinterested altruism. It describes strategic action embedded in social obligation and cultural definitions of value.

2.4 Limits of Malinowski’s account

Malinowski’s work was transformative but selective. His ethnography foregrounded male voyagers, leaders, partnerships, and circulating shell valuables. It consequently helped establish “exchange” as a public, male-centered domain while leaving much of the female labor that reproduced Trobriand persons and social relations analytically peripheral.

Annette Weiner’s later restudy demonstrated that this was not a minor omission. Trobriand women conducted large ceremonial exchanges of banana-leaf wealth, especially in mortuary contexts. The male-centered framing therefore shaped what later theorists, including Mauss, treated as the paradigmatic gift.

3. Mauss: the gift as obligation and “total social phenomenon”

3.1 Scope and argument

Marcel Mauss’s Essai sur le don was first published in the 1923–24 issue of L’Année Sociologique and is conventionally dated 1925. Unlike Malinowski’s single-site ethnography, it was a comparative theoretical essay drawing on Polynesia, Melanesia, the Northwest Coast of North America, the Andaman Islands, and ancient legal systems. A recent expanded edition restores the essay to its original intellectual context (https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/distributed/G/bo22485556.html; full English edition: https://haubooks.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Marcel-Mauss-The-Gift-Expanded-Edition-Selected-Annotated-and-Translated-by-Jane-Guyer.pdf).

Mauss begins from a paradox: transfers appear voluntary and generous, yet are in practice obligatory. In the original French text, he emphasizes that gifts and counter-gifts are offered in a formally voluntary manner but can be “rigorously obligatory,” with refusal potentially leading to conflict (https://classiques.uqam.ca/classiques/mauss_marcel/socio_et_anthropo/2_essai_sur_le_don/essai_sur_le_don.pdf).

His famous formulation distinguishes three obligations:

1. The obligation to give: giving initiates or affirms social standing and relationship.
2. The obligation to receive: refusing a gift rejects the giver, alliance, or shared social world.
3. The obligation to return: accepting creates a debt that must eventually be answered.

These obligations make the gift a mechanism of solidarity and rivalry simultaneously. Generosity can establish peace, but it can also rank giver and receiver, create dependency, or humiliate an actor unable to respond.

3.2 Total prestation and total social facts

Mauss argued that archaic exchange was commonly conducted not by autonomous individuals but by collectivities—families, clans, tribes, or groups represented by leaders. What circulated was not merely useful property. Exchanges included hospitality, feasts, rituals, military services, women, children, dances, festivals, offices, and rights. Market exchange was only one moment within a larger and more durable contract (French primary text: https://classiques.uqam.ca/classiques/mauss_marcel/socio_et_anthropo/2_essai_sur_le_don/essai_sur_le_don.pdf).

Gift exchange is therefore a “total social phenomenon.” It simultaneously expresses:

• economic production and distribution;
• legal rights and duties;
• moral expectations;
• kinship and family relations;
• religious or cosmological commitments;
• political hierarchy and alliance;
• aesthetics, performance, and honor.

This remains Mauss’s most durable contribution. Transactions cannot be understood by price or material movement alone because exchange may reproduce the institutional order as a whole.

3.3 The “spirit” of the gift

In discussing Māori materials, Mauss used the concept of hau, often rendered as the spirit of the thing given, to explain why a gift presses toward return. A transferred object remains connected to its source; retaining it without reciprocating is socially or spiritually dangerous.

The strongest interpretation is not that every gift literally contains a supernatural entity. Rather, gifts carry persons, histories, and claims. The giver is present in the thing, and the thing therefore cannot be treated as wholly detached property. This insight connects the kula valuable, the family heirloom, attribution attached to software, and even the social meaning of a visible “like.”

Sahlins later criticized the ethnographic and textual basis of Mauss’s hau interpretation. He noted, among other things, that hau at most explains why gifts are repaid, not why actors are obligated to give or receive in the first place. He also cautioned that the relevant Māori text is disputed (Stone Age Economics: https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf). Mauss’s wider theory does not, however, depend entirely on a literalized hau. Its broader claim is that exchange transmits social identity and obligation as well as objects.

3.4 Gift, hierarchy, and power

Mauss is sometimes read as a theorist of communal solidarity, but the essay gives equal attention to rivalry, honor, credit, debt, and agonistic display. In a potlatch, a leader may assert superiority by giving or destroying more wealth than rivals can match. A recipient is not simply enriched; the recipient may be subordinated by an unanswerable gift.

The gift thus has an ambivalent politics:

• It incorporates outsiders but also binds them.
• It distributes wealth but may concentrate prestige.
• It creates mutuality but can generate debt.
• It appears voluntary while enforcing collective norms.
• It can make peace, yet refusal or failed reciprocation can provoke conflict.

Digital “free” services and token distributions reproduce this ambiguity: a transfer can be simultaneously useful to the recipient and constitutive of the giver’s power.

3.5 Limits and feminist problem

Mauss’s formulation included women, children, labor, and services among things exchanged. That breadth exposed how kinship and political orders are produced through circulation, but it could also reproduce the viewpoint of male transactors who treat women as objects of alliance.

A feminist critique notes that describing women as gifts can erase them as producers, political actors, and interpreters of exchange. One review of women-and-gift theory observes that Mauss repeated materials in which “food, women, children, possessions, charms, land, labour, services, religious offices, [and] rank” all appear as things to be given and repaid, a formulation later amplified by Lévi-Strauss’s theory of marriage alliance (https://doi.org/10.30674/scripta.67247). The analytical task is not to deny that patriarchal systems may exchange rights over women, but to distinguish an account of that process from its naturalization.

4. Sahlins: reciprocity as a continuum of social distance

4.1 Substantivist orientation

Marshall Sahlins’s Stone Age Economics, published in 1972, developed an “anthropological economics” opposed to reducing all societies to universal business calculation. The book explicitly situated itself on the substantivist side of the formalist–substantivist debate: economic conduct must be understood within historically specific social and cultural institutions rather than assumed to instantiate a universal microeconomic model (https://files.libcom.org/files/Sahlins%20-%20Stone%20Age%20Economics.pdf).

His essay “On the Sociology of Primitive Exchange” systematized reciprocity into three forms:

• generalized reciprocity;
• balanced reciprocity;
• negative reciprocity.

These are not rigidly separate boxes. They form a spectrum related to social distance, moral community, and the expected timing and equivalence of return.

4.2 Generalized reciprocity

Generalized reciprocity involves assistance or giving without calculation of an immediate or precisely equivalent return. It is common among close kin or others treated as kin. Examples include feeding children, caring for elderly relatives, or sharing resources within a household.

The relation is reciprocal in a broad and temporally open sense, not necessarily transaction by transaction. The giver may expect that support will circulate within the relationship or group, but demanding prompt equivalence would itself signal excessive distance.

Characteristics include:

• indefinite return time;
• weak or absent calculation of equivalence;
• strong interpersonal identification;
• emphasis on need and capacity;
• durable social interdependence.

Open-source contributions to a shared repository can approximate this form when programmers contribute without identifying a particular recipient or demanding direct repayment.

4.3 Balanced reciprocity

Balanced reciprocity is a direct exchange in which actors expect a return of reasonably equivalent value within a socially appropriate period. The exact measure may remain culturally defined rather than monetized, but symmetry and timeliness matter.

Ceremonial gift partnerships often fall in this middle range. Giving sustains a relationship, yet failure to return can end it or damage reputation. Many exchanges of birthday gifts, favors, endorsements, reciprocal social-media engagement, and professional assistance likewise take this form.

Characteristics include:

• identifiable counterpart;
• expectation of an equivalent or fitting return;
• bounded return period;
• greater calculation than in generalized reciprocity;
• maintenance of a relationship through repeated equivalence.

Digital metrics can intensify this logic. When users can count likes, shares, follows, and response times, formerly ambiguous recognition becomes easier to audit.

4.4 Negative reciprocity

Negative reciprocity describes attempts to obtain something for as little as possible. It includes hard bargaining, opportunism, appropriation, theft, and other transactions in which actors pursue opposed interests.

It is most likely at the greatest social distance: dealings with outsiders, enemies, or people outside the operative moral community. Market bargaining may approach this pole, although Sahlins did not imply that every market transaction is theft or that negative reciprocity is absent among kin.

Characteristics include:

• maximization of unilateral advantage;
• weak mutual identification;
• adversarial bargaining or appropriation;
• readiness to exploit informational or power asymmetry.

A platform that encourages users to exchange content and attention as gifts while privately appropriating their data may be interpreted as combining peer-level generalized or balanced reciprocity with structurally negative reciprocity between platform and user.

4.5 Social distance rather than evolutionary stages

Sahlins’s central explanatory variable is not technological “advancement” but the social relation between transactors. Generalized reciprocity predominates near the center of the moral community; balanced reciprocity appears at an intermediate distance; negative reciprocity becomes more likely toward the periphery. A later edition’s discussion summarizes this as three circles: generalized reciprocity among close kin, balanced reciprocity in a middle zone governed by fairness, and negative reciprocity beyond that social boundary (https://archive.org/stream/StoneAgeEconomics_201611/StoneAgeEconomics-MarshallSahlins_djvu.txt).

The same society—and the same person—can therefore engage in all three. This improves on an absolute gift/market opposition. It also helps analyze online environments, where strangers may collaborate as if they were kin in one setting and compete anonymously in another.

4.6 Comparison with Malinowski and Mauss

Malinowski asks ethnographically how a particular exchange system works. Mauss asks comparatively why gifts obligate and how exchange constitutes society. Sahlins asks how different kinds of reciprocity vary with social relations.

Their complementary emphases can be summarized as follows:

Malinowski:
• Object: kula as a concrete regional institution.
• Method: participant observation and contextual ethnography.
• Key mechanism: ceremonial circulation through partnerships.
• Contribution: separation without isolation of ceremonial exchange and barter.
• Limitation: male-centered representation of exchange.

Mauss:
• Object: gifts across several societies and legal traditions.
• Method: comparative synthesis.
• Key mechanism: obligations to give, receive, and return.
• Contribution: gift as a total social phenomenon.
• Limitation: dependence on secondhand ethnography and insufficient attention to women as producers and subjects.

Sahlins:
• Object: reciprocity as a range of transactional forms.
• Method: comparative typology informed by substantivist economics.
• Key mechanism: social distance and expectations of return.
• Contribution: generalized, balanced, and negative reciprocity.
• Limitation: a tidy continuum may understate institutions, gender, colonial history, and the coexistence of multiple relations within a single transaction.

5. Feminist anthropology: gendered labor, objects, and authority

5.1 From transaction to social reproduction

The classical accounts tended to privilege visible transfers: voyages, speeches, valuables, political representatives, and named partnerships. Feminist anthropology asks what makes those public performances possible.

Relevant forms of often-obscured labor include:

• growing and preparing food for feasts;
• making textiles, leaf bundles, clothing, decorations, and ritual valuables;
• bearing and raising children through whom groups continue;
• maintaining households and hospitality;
• mourning, burial, and mortuary commemoration;
• emotional mediation and care;
• preserving genealogies and group identity;
• organizing the everyday relationships later activated in ceremonial exchange.

If analysis begins only when a recognized man publicly hands over a valuable, much of the economic and political process has already disappeared from view.

5.2 Annette Weiner and Trobriand women’s wealth

Annette Weiner’s Women of Value, Men of Renown directly restudied the society made canonical by Malinowski. Whereas Malinowski and many successors focused on male exchange, Weiner showed that women play central roles in Trobriand social reproduction and wealth circulation (https://doi.org/10.2307/2801107).

Her research examined:

• internal exchanges of male and female wealth;
• women’s banana-leaf bundles and skirts;
• annual yam distributions;
• land and matrilineal continuity;
• life-cycle events;
• father–son and affine relations;
• women’s mortuary distributions;
• differentiated male and female domains of authority.

The eHRAF synopsis emphasizes that Weiner analyzed women’s wealth in mortuary ceremonies and the differential roles of women and men throughout the life cycle (https://ehrafworldcultures.yale.edu/cultures/ol06/documents/025).

The empirical force of her critique is illustrated by a ceremony she encountered shortly after arriving in Kiriwina: hundreds of people watched an exchange conducted by and for women, involving decorated leaf-fiber skirts and bundles of dried banana leaves. Hundreds of wealth items could change hands in one transaction. Such mortuary distributions recognized work associated with death and mourning, reciprocated debts to the deceased’s father’s people and affines, and reclaimed the deceased’s identity and substance for the matrilineal group (https://repository.upenn.edu/han/vol38/iss2/4).

This was not merely the addition of “women’s activities” to an intact male model. It changed the theory of exchange. Men’s renown in prominent exchange systems rested partly on female production and on matrilineal identities reproduced through women’s work. Public male circulation and less-visible female work were mutually constitutive.

5.3 Inalienable possessions and “keeping-while-giving”

In Inalienable Possessions, Weiner argued that exchange is always accompanied by efforts to retain certain things, identities, or rights. The paradox is “keeping-while-giving”: groups transfer valuables while preserving their connection to ancestral authority, rank, sacred identity, or reproductive power.

The motive force of exchange is therefore not only a desire to restore equivalence. Actors may circulate wealth in order to preserve what should not be fully alienated. Control over inalienable possessions authenticates hierarchy and difference. A review summarizes Weiner’s argument that reciprocity is centered not simply in the gift but in the authority vested in keeping inalienable possessions, and that the authentication of difference may be more fundamental than balance (https://digitalcollections.byuh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2248&context=pacific-studies-journal).

This revises Mauss in two ways:

1. The gift’s continuing attachment to the giver is not merely a spiritual force compelling return; it can be a deliberately managed political resource.
2. Circulation cannot be understood without retention. Power may lie in deciding what can be given, what must be withheld, and whose identity survives transfer.

The framework also applies to intellectual property and digital systems. Open-source code circulates, but authorship, project authority, trademark control, or commit privileges may be retained. Cryptocurrency tokens circulate, while protocol founders, large delegates, or core developers may retain disproportionate governance power.

There is an important caveat. Producing wealth does not automatically entail controlling it. One critical review of Weiner argues that women’s production of valued cloth does not by itself prove political authority; production must be distinguished from control over distribution and accumulation (https://digitalcollections.byuh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2256&context=pacific-studies-journal). This is a useful feminist methodological rule: document labor, but also trace ownership, authority, appropriation, and decision-making.

5.4 Gayle Rubin and the “traffic in women”

Gayle Rubin’s 1975 “The Traffic in Women” drew critically on Lévi-Strauss’s kinship theory and the anthropological gift tradition. If marriage alliance is produced by men exchanging women, then women occupy the position of gifts while men are positioned as transactors. Rubin used this insight to analyze the “sex/gender system”—the social arrangements through which biological females are made into subordinated social categories such as wives (primary text: https://glc.yale.edu/sites/default/files/pdf/rubin_the_traffic_in_women.pdf).

The intervention exposes a central ambiguity. Saying that “women are exchanged” may accurately describe the allocation of marital and reproductive rights, but the grammar also risks denying women agency. Feminist analysis must ask:

• Who is entitled to give?
• Who is entitled to receive?
• Whose consent counts?
• Is a person exchanged, or are rights over sexuality, labor, fertility, and descendants transferred?
• Can women act as exchange partners, not merely objects?
• What violence or dependency underwrites apparently reciprocal alliances?

Rubin’s critique also complicates Mauss’s claim that gifts create solidarity. Solidarity among male-controlled groups may be purchased through women’s loss of autonomy. Reciprocity for some can therefore rest on dispossession for others.

5.5 Marilyn Strathern: gender, gifts, and the problem of Western categories

Marilyn Strathern’s The Gender of the Gift, published in 1988, is both a major work on Melanesia and a critique of anthropological comparison. It argues that gender relations became a casualty of unexamined assumptions shared, in different ways, by Western social science and some feminist analysis (https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.1525/j.ctt1ppj9n).

Strathern does not simply add women to an existing map of “society.” She questions the map’s categories. Western analysis often assumes:

• individuals exist prior to relationships;
• persons own their labor and objects;
• society constrains autonomous individuals;
• production precedes exchange;
• objects are distinct from persons;
• gender is a fixed attribute possessed by individuals;
• domination must take a familiar public-versus-domestic form.

Her Melanesian analysis instead treats persons as constituted through relations. A person can be understood as divisible or “partible,” containing contributions and relations from multiple others. Gifts do not merely travel between already formed individuals; they make visible the relations of which persons are composed.

Gender, accordingly, is not only a permanent male/female property. It can be activated as a relational capacity or mode of action. A modern commentary summarizes Strathern’s intervention as transforming gender from a property of people into a capacity for action and relation. It notes that in her account, women were associated with producing exchange goods and men with public transaction, but that these roles cannot be read straightforwardly through Western assumptions about fixed identity or power (https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/14647.003.0071).

Strathern’s relation to feminism is deliberately “awkward.” Feminist critique reveals male bias, but feminist categories formed in Euro-American political struggles can themselves distort Melanesian sociality if treated as universal. Her chapter “A Place in the Feminist Debate” emphasizes that feminism is not simply another incomplete social-scientific perspective; it challenges how knowledge is organized (https://academic.oup.com/california-scholarship-online/book/21765/chapter/181727625).

The value of Strathern’s approach for contemporary digital economies is substantial. Users, code, profiles, data, and tokens are not necessarily independent entities brought together by exchange. They are produced through networks of relations. A software contribution contains prior code, standards, maintainers’ decisions, and collective labor. A social-media profile is assembled from other people’s attention and platform classifications. A cryptocurrency token embodies software rules, investor expectations, exchange infrastructure, and community belief.

5.6 The cumulative feminist revision

Feminist anthropology changes gift theory along four dimensions.

First, visibility: what classical ethnographers called “the exchange system” often reflected publicly visible male activity.

Second, production: gifts require labor. The capacity to give depends on growers, makers, caregivers, organizers, and maintainers whose work may not be recognized in the prestige economy.

Third, subject/object position: women and subordinated people may be treated as transferable objects or sources of labor while dominant actors appear as reciprocal partners.

Fourth, control: producing a gift is not the same as controlling its circulation, retaining its symbolic force, or receiving the prestige it generates.

These insights are indispensable for analyzing digital economies, where community management, moderation, documentation, emotional support, data generation, and maintenance can be less visible than code, financial investment, or public leadership.

6. Open-source software: gift, commons, or subsidized commodity?

6.1 Why it resembles a gift economy

Free and open-source software is produced through voluntary or mixed voluntary/paid collaboration, with source code made available under licenses that permit use, study, modification, and redistribution. Because digital information is non-rival—one person’s possession of a copy does not deprive another—the giver can retain the code while others receive it. This differs fundamentally from transferring land, food, or a shell valuable.

An anthropological study of open-source development suggests that some software groups resemble kinship subgroups: direct economic calculation is inappropriate internally, contributions need not be directly reciprocated, and symbolic capital or reputation rewards contributors and their groups (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0048733303000532).

The Maussian parallels are clear:

• To give: contributors release code, fixes, documentation, or support.
• To receive: users download, inspect, adapt, and incorporate contributions.
• To return: recipients may report bugs, submit patches, answer questions, improve documentation, acknowledge authorship, or contribute to another project.

The return is often delayed and indirect. Developer A may help an unknown user who never assists A personally; A nevertheless benefits from a much larger pool produced by thousands of others. This approximates Sahlins’s generalized reciprocity.

Open-source participation can also yield renown. Visible contributions, maintainership, and authorship establish reputations that may lead to influence, employment, consulting, or invitations. Like kula valuables, code circulates while carrying histories of authorship and project association. The object is reproducible, but attribution and reputation can remain attached to it.

6.2 Commons-based peer production as a third mode

Yochai Benkler describes open-source software and related projects as commons-based peer production: large groups coordinate the production of information goods without relying primarily on either market prices or managerial hierarchy. Its sustained success challenges assumptions that material incentives, exclusive property, and firms are always central to innovation (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1476127016652606).

The argument is not that incentives disappear. Intrinsic interest, learning, enjoyment, ethical commitment, social recognition, reputation, and career benefit coexist. What changes is the coordination mechanism.

This suggests at least four analytically different modes:

1. Commodity production coordinated by price and contract.
2. Hierarchical production coordinated by managerial authority.
3. State or public production coordinated politically and administratively.
4. Commons-based peer production coordinated through open resources, licenses, technical architectures, community norms, and modular contribution.

Open source is therefore not adequately described merely as a gift economy. “Commons” draws attention to shared resources and governance rules, while “gift” highlights interpersonal obligation, reputation, and circulation.

6.3 Licenses as institutionalized reciprocity

Open-source licenses formalize the conditions under which code circulates. Some are permissive, allowing extensive proprietary reuse; copyleft licenses require derivative distributions to preserve specified freedoms. This resembles an institutionalized obligation to return—not necessarily by paying the original contributor, but by keeping modified code available under reciprocal terms.

Gabriella Coleman’s ethnography of free-software communities emphasizes that practitioners treat software as an ethical and political project involving free speech, transparency, access, and opposition to restrictive intellectual property. Her work examines hacker ethics, licenses, governance, conferences, humor, and technical collaboration rather than reducing participation to economic motivation (https://press.princeton.edu/books/ebook/9781400845293/coding-freedom).

Research on Debian describes “ethical volunteerism” based on institutional independence, volunteer labor, and networks of trust. Ethical commitments are reinforced through sustained work on code, licenses, and project policy (https://mako.cc/academic/coleman_hill-social_production.pdf). Here the gift is simultaneously technical, legal, and moral—a Maussian total social phenomenon in digital form.

6.4 Why open source is not a pure gift economy

Open-source software is intertwined with commodity relations:

• Contributors may be salaried by corporations.
• Firms may sell hosting, support, hardware, integration, or complementary services.
• Employers use public contribution histories as labor-market signals.
• Platforms hosting repositories may commercialize attention, data, or infrastructure.
• A project’s freely available code can become an input into proprietary products.
• Maintainers may provide unpaid labor for infrastructures on which profitable companies depend.

The “high-tech gift economy” is therefore hybrid. One study summarizes the relationship as a symbiosis in which money, commodities, and gift relations coexist (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2053951719897092). This reinforces Gregory’s finding that gift and commodity economies can expand together.

Open source also complicates inalienability. Code is highly alienable in the sense that it can be copied and transferred, but authorship, reputation, license obligations, project identity, and authority over the canonical repository can remain attached. It is possible to give the software while retaining status or governance power: a digital version of “keeping-while-giving.”

6.5 Gendered and invisible labor in open source

Feminist analysis reveals that the prestigious gift is often “code,” while essential work such as documentation, mentoring, moderation, issue triage, community care, accessibility, release coordination, and conflict management can receive less recognition. Research defines invisible open-source labor as work that is inadequately documented, attributed, or compensated and argues that shifting analysis from isolated repositories to ecosystems makes these interdependencies visible (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3757417).

Quantitative evidence demonstrates substantial gender inequality, although results vary by dataset and definition:

• A study of 711 projects found that only 2.3% of core developers were women (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3382494.3410682).
• Expressed as a rate, 2.3% = 2.3 ÷ 100 = 0.023, or approximately 23 women per 1,000 core developers if the study’s proportion is applied to a hypothetical group of 1,000.
• A systematic review synthesized 51 studies published from 2000 through 2021. It reported that about 5% of projects had women as core developers and that women authored under 5% of pull requests, while their pull-request acceptance rates were similar to or higher than men’s (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3510460).
• Five percent is 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05, equivalent to one in twenty. Because one figure concerns the gender composition of core developers and another concerns the proportion of projects with women core developers, they are not directly comparable and should not be averaged.

The systematic review identified social barriers such as low peer parity, non-inclusive communication, and toxic culture. These findings qualify claims that open access to code automatically creates equality. Formally universal participation can coexist with unequal leisure time, prior training, financial security, exposure to hostility, and recognition.

The feminist lesson from Weiner applies closely: the production of collective wealth may be misdescribed if analysts count only the most prestigious, publicly visible transfer. The Strathernian lesson is that contributors are made through relations—mentorship, review, community acceptance, and infrastructure—not simply autonomous individuals donating pre-existing talent.

7. Social-media attention economies

7.1 Likes, shares, and follows as digital gifts

On social media, users routinely provide content, acknowledgment, recommendations, comments, follows, and likes without direct monetary payment. A netnographic study of Facebook characterizes likes as “cyber-gifts” that form alliances and increase users’ digital social capital (https://mimesisjournals.com/ojs/index.php/antropologia-pubblica/article/view/3755).

This resembles Maussian exchange:

• Posting offers content and an opportunity for recognition.
• Liking or commenting recognizes both content and poster.
• Receiving attention may create pressure to respond, follow back, or reciprocate later.
• Refusal or silence can communicate distance.
• Public metrics turn recognition into prestige.

Attention can exhibit all three Sahlinsian modes.

Generalized reciprocity:
Friends or community members support one another without exact accounting, and creators distribute material to broad audiences without knowing who will return value.

Balanced reciprocity:
Users exchange likes, comments, follows, tags, or reposts with identifiable partners and may notice imbalances. Metrics make equivalence and delay unusually visible.

Negative reciprocity:
Spam, engagement manipulation, clickbait, harassment, data appropriation, and opportunistic influence seek unilateral advantage.

Sahlins’s correlation between reciprocity and social distance remains useful, but platforms complicate it. A stranger may give attention to a creator with whom they feel an intimate parasocial connection, while a platform operator occupies every transaction despite appearing socially distant.

7.2 From attention gift to commodity

Social-media exchange is triangular rather than simply dyadic:

1. Users give content, attention, interaction, and data.
2. Other users return attention and interaction.
3. The platform records, organizes, predicts, and monetizes the resulting activity.

Fourcade and Kluttz call this “accumulation by gift.” Enrollment is framed through benign invitations to join, share, connect, or use a “free” service. Gift-like participation obscures asymmetric appropriation and permits personal data to become a privately controlled commodity (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2053951719897092).

A related relational analysis describes platform interactions as asymmetrical gift exchange that supports a three-stage process:

• platforms appropriate user data as use values to optimize services;
• data undergo secondary commodification;
• platforms sell third parties the capacity to influence users.

This account stresses that the community’s interaction field, rather than only isolated individuals, is the source of value (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/20539517241259639).

The platform thus gives a service, but the “free” service generates obligations and valuable information. The asymmetry lies in commensuration and control: users often cannot know the full value of their data, while the platform can aggregate and monetize information at scale.

7.3 Reinforcing Mauss

Social media strongly reinforces several Maussian propositions.

First, apparently free transfers are obligatory. Social norms govern response, visibility, and acknowledgment.

Second, gifts carry persons. A like from a close friend, celebrity, employer, or stranger has a different meaning even when the interface renders each as one unit.

Third, giving produces hierarchy. Accounts that attract more attention gain prestige and may convert it into revenue or influence.

Fourth, exchange is total. Social-media activity mixes friendship, self-presentation, politics, commerce, leisure, sexuality, and work.

Fifth, the gift can dominate. A flood of attention may create demands, harassment, or dependence rather than uncomplicated benefit.

Research on internet fame finds that platforms strategically deliver visibility metrics that creators learn to experience as pleasurable, even as virality exposes them to hypervisibility, context collapse, and hateful commentary. The pursuit of metrics can therefore function as a mode of labor control (https://academic.oup.com/socpro/article-pdf/doi/10.1093/socpro/spaf028/63510641/spaf028.pdf).

7.4 Challenging Mauss and Sahlins

Digital attention also challenges the classical framework.

Scale:
A person can give one post to millions of unknown recipients. Classical gift theory often assumes identifiable partners or bounded groups.

Automation:
Algorithms determine who sees a gift and how much visibility it receives. The mediator is neither a neutral channel nor a traditional exchange partner.

Commensuration:
Likes and follower counts make attention numerical. Prestige, once qualitatively interpreted, becomes continuously ranked.

Near-zero reproduction cost:
A digital post can be copied without depriving its source, although human attention remains scarce.

Platform ownership:
The community produces interaction, but a corporation owns or governs much of the infrastructure and data.

Compressed temporality:
Notifications and visible response times accelerate expectations of return, moving some relations from generalized toward balanced reciprocity.

The classical concepts remain useful only if expanded from person-to-person exchange to infrastructures that classify, measure, and appropriate relations.

7.5 Gendered attention labor

A feminist analysis asks who performs the work of continual visibility, responsiveness, self-presentation, audience care, and moderation. Like women’s ceremonial and domestic production, this work can be treated as natural sociability rather than labor.

It also asks who receives prestige and who bears the costs of exposure. Numerical visibility is not equivalent to authority or income. A creator may produce highly valuable engagement while the platform controls data, advertising access, recommendation systems, and monetization rules. As in the critique of Weiner, producing value does not necessarily mean controlling it.

8. Cryptocurrency and decentralized governance

8.1 Cryptocurrency as an attempted alternative to institutional trust

Bitcoin and related systems promise peer-to-peer transfer through cryptographic protocols rather than conventional banks or state-managed payment systems. Bill Maurer, Taylor Nelms, and Lana Swartz characterize Bitcoin’s discourse as a “practical materialism”: advocates foreground code, mining, and protocol rules while backgrounding the credit relations and infrastructures that make money possible (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/7w616491; full paper: https://llaannaa.com/papers/maurer_nelms_swartz_bitcoin.pdf).

The ideal appears to challenge Mauss. Instead of trust emerging through long-term gift relationships, protocol rules make transactions irreversible without personal familiarity. Money is imagined as detached from institutions and interpersonal obligation.

Yet anthropological analysis reveals continuing dependence on:

• developers and maintainers;
• miners or validators;
• exchanges and wallet providers;
• online communities;
• shared narratives of value;
• legal and energy infrastructures;
• governance procedures;
• reputations and trust in code.

Protocol does not abolish social relations; it reorganizes and sometimes obscures them.

8.2 DAOs as hybrid organizations

Decentralized autonomous organizations use blockchains and smart contracts to coordinate resources and decisions. Members commonly vote with governance tokens, while transactions and proposals are recorded on public ledgers.

An organizational account defines DAOs as non-hierarchical organizations that perform and record routine tasks on peer-to-peer, cryptographically secured public networks and rely on stakeholders’ voluntary contributions to operate and evolve. Bitcoin itself has been described as an early real-world DAO, with protocol changes requiring agreement among relevant stakeholders such as miners and developers (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s41469-018-0038-1).

DAOs contain elements of all three classical models:

Malinowskian:
Named tokens, founding events, and prestigious governance positions circulate within communities, while technical and financial transactions coexist.

Maussian:
Airdrops, contributor grants, protocol rewards, and voluntary labor can create membership, obligation, and prestige. Governance is a total social process involving law, code, finance, politics, and moral claims about decentralization.

Sahlinsian:
Communities combine generalized contribution to common infrastructure, balanced exchange of work for tokens, and negative reciprocity through speculation, governance capture, or exploitative extraction.

8.3 Contribution systems and attempts to value gifts

Some Web3 communities try to compensate contributors for dispersed and otherwise invisible work. The SourceCred “CredSperiment,” for example, used community-developed software to calculate “Cred scores” and allocate payment according to recognized contributions. Its ethnography describes this as an attempt to let a community define what it values through everyday activity, while also reporting concerns about extractive behavior in a permissionless system (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4570035).

This is significant because it tries to convert gift labor into explicit, machine-assisted compensation. It challenges the classical assumption that gift value should remain unquantified, but it also creates new questions:

• Which activities can an algorithm see?
• Who defines the weighting system?
• Does numerical recognition crowd out care and intrinsic motivation?
• Can contributors game the metric?
• Does compensation make a contribution a commodity, or can it remain part of a reciprocal community?
• Who performs work that the contribution system cannot measure?

The feminist history of invisible labor suggests caution. Measurement may correct some exclusions while producing others.

8.4 Token voting and commodified political voice

Governance tokens make participation alienable and accumulable. If one token equals one vote, those able to buy or retain more tokens exercise more authority. Political membership and property ownership converge.

This challenges a classical distinction:

• A gift establishes reciprocal dependence through an object that remains socially attached.
• A commodity establishes exchange among independent owners of alienable property.
• A governance token can be both: it marks community membership and shared history, yet can be sold anonymously and accumulated for voting power.

Cryptoeconomics explicitly uses economic incentives and engineering to design decentralized coordination systems. Its intellectual history connects it to crypto-anarchist efforts to achieve autonomy and self-organization through technical means, though later cryptoeconomics did not preserve the same commitment to anonymity (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/24701475.2023.2183643).

8.5 Empirical concentration of governance power

Evidence indicates that formal decentralization does not guarantee evenly distributed authority.

A 2024 census-like analysis examined approximately 30,000 DAO communities across major platforms. It found that most had short lifespans and low participation, and that larger communities tended to have greater voting-power concentration. The authors describe this as an online version of an “iron law” of oligarchy, while noting that some DAOs were comparatively egalitarian by design (https://doi.org/10.1145/3589335.3651481).

A study of Compound, Uniswap, and Ethereum Name Service likewise found that most voting power was held by a small number of addresses. It also found that these powerful entities rarely overturned the outcome preferred by the broader set of participating voters, showing that concentrated capacity does not necessarily mean constant overt domination (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2096720924000216).

Research on 21 on-chain DAOs reported:

• high concentration of voting rights;
• hidden monetary costs of on-chain governance;
• substantial governance activity with little practical effect;
• questions about whether some DAO structures operate partly as marketing claims rather than meaningfully decentralized governance.

The associated dataset and analysis are described at https://arxiv.org/html/2302.12125v2.

A study of Aave, Compound, Lido, and Uniswap found that the “minimal quorum”—the smallest number of active voters capable of deciding a result—was often around three addresses, although acquiring enough tokens externally to attack the systems could be extremely expensive (https://arxiv.org/html/2407.10945v1).

A separate analysis of more than 370 Compound and Uniswap proposals through August 2024 found:

• ten voters controlled 50.53% of Compound voting power;
• ten voters controlled 35.73% of Uniswap voting power;
• an average of 3.18 Compound voters and 4.7 Uniswap voters was sufficient to account for at least half of votes on proposals (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17655v4).

Explicit comparison:

• Concentration gap between Compound and Uniswap among the top ten voters:
  50.53% − 35.73% = 14.80 percentage points.

• Compound’s average majority-forming voter count relative to Uniswap:
  3.18 ÷ 4.7 ≈ 0.677.
  Thus, Compound required on average about 67.7% as many voters as Uniswap to reach half the votes, or approximately 32.3% fewer.

• These numbers describe participating voting power, not necessarily ten verified human beings. One entity can control multiple blockchain addresses, while a delegate may aggregate tokens from many holders. Address-level concentration can therefore either understate or overstate person-level concentration.

The results reinforce Mauss’s insight that exchange produces rank and dependency, but they challenge narratives in which transparent protocols automatically eliminate hierarchy. Token voting often converts wealth into authority more directly than conventional one-person, one-vote systems.

8.6 Gender and care in crypto governance

The gathered empirical governance studies concentrate primarily on token distribution, voting, and participation rather than gender, so strong quantitative claims about gender composition would require additional evidence. Nevertheless, feminist gift theory identifies questions that token metrics alone cannot answer:

• Who writes documentation and explains proposals?
• Who moderates forums and resolves conflict?
• Who maintains community continuity between votes?
• Which contributors possess sufficient uncompensated time to participate?
• Who receives tokens for early technical or financial contributions?
• Are relational, care, and communication activities counted as governance?
• Does ownership of tokens confer control over value produced by non-token-holding users?

The Weinerian issue is control: contributing to a protocol does not ensure authority over it. The Strathernian issue is relational personhood: a “token holder” is not an isolated individual but a position assembled through delegation, capital, code, community recognition, and platform infrastructure. The Rubin-inspired issue is subject versus object: participants may understand themselves as members while governance systems treat their activity and liquidity as resources to be mobilized by larger holders.

9. Cross-case comparison

9.1 What contemporary cases reinforce

Contemporary digital economies reinforce five classical propositions.

First, gifts are rarely free of obligation.

Open-source contributors expect acknowledgment, responsible reuse, bug reports, or broader participation. Social-media users expect recognition and response. Crypto communities expect token holders or beneficiaries to contribute to governance or protocol growth.

Second, gifts make persons and groups.

Programmers become recognized maintainers through contributions. Influencers become social identities through accumulated attention. DAO members become stakeholders through tokens, participation, and shared narratives.

Third, circulation produces prestige.

Kula valuables generate renown; open-source commits generate reputation; social-media metrics generate visibility; governance participation can generate influence.

Fourth, exchange mixes solidarity and competition.

Open-source collaborators compete for authority or employment. Social-media users support one another while competing for scarce attention. DAO participants cooperate on infrastructure while pursuing token appreciation.

Fifth, gifts and commodities coexist.

Kula accompanied ordinary trade. Open-source code supports commercial firms. Social interaction produces advertising commodities. Cryptocurrency communities depend on volunteer effort while making governance rights tradable.

9.2 What contemporary cases challenge

Digital systems also challenge classical models in at least six ways.

Non-rivalry:
Digital code and content can be copied without physically leaving the giver’s possession. “Keeping-while-giving” is technically routine, although attention, labor, and authority remain scarce.

Algorithmic mediation:
Exchange is shaped by recommendation engines, repository permissions, smart contracts, and interfaces. These are active institutional actors, not neutral channels.

Mass anonymity:
Generalized reciprocity can occur among millions of strangers, weakening the assumption that it depends on kinship or face-to-face familiarity.

Radical commensuration:
Likes, commits, reputation scores, token balances, and votes quantify social contribution and prestige.

Triangular appropriation:
A third party may own the infrastructure and convert peer gifts into commodities. The primary commodity may be produced from the exchange rather than transferred between the visible participants.

Programmable obligation:
Software licenses and smart contracts can encode some duties automatically. Yet interpretation, maintenance, conflict resolution, and legitimacy remain social.

9.3 Comparative matrix

Kula:
• Primary gift: shell valuables.
• Return: delayed counter-gift through partners.
• Value: history, prestige, alliance.
• Retained element: name, provenance, relationship.
• Commodity interface: accompanying barter.
• Main hidden labor issue: women’s production and mortuary exchange marginalized by male-centered ethnography.

Open source:
• Primary gift: code, fixes, documentation, support.
• Return: indirect code improvements, recognition, learning, employment, or community standing.
• Value: functionality, freedom, reputation, collective capacity.
• Retained element: attribution, authorship, license, repository authority.
• Commodity interface: paid employment, corporate services, proprietary reuse.
• Hidden labor issue: maintenance, moderation, documentation, mentoring, and gendered exclusion.

Social media:
• Primary gift: content, attention, interaction, and personal data.
• Return: likes, visibility, belonging, entertainment.
• Value: recognition and predictive/advertising data.
• Retained element: personal identity and social connection, though platforms retain extensive records.
• Commodity interface: advertising and influence markets.
• Hidden labor issue: continual self-presentation, audience care, moderation, and exposure costs.

Cryptocurrency governance:
• Primary gift: code, community labor, liquidity, grants, airdrops, and participation.
• Return: tokens, protocol access, reputation, appreciation, or voting rights.
• Value: financial price, community membership, coordination capacity.
• Retained element: founder status, delegated authority, core-development influence, concentrated token holdings.
• Commodity interface: tokens and governance rights are traded.
• Hidden labor issue: maintenance, education, deliberation, moderation, and other contributions poorly captured by token ownership.

10. Toward a revised model of gift and commodity exchange

A comprehensive model should distinguish at least four dimensions instead of labeling an entire economy either “gift” or “commodity.”

10.1 Alienability

Can the object be detached from its producer or previous holder?

Kula valuables retain histories; open-source code retains attribution and license conditions; social-media data remain linked to identities; governance tokens are highly transferable but can retain symbolic connections to founding communities.

10.2 Reciprocity

What return is expected, from whom, and when?

Returns range from open-ended generalized reciprocity to precisely quantified token rewards. Lack of an explicit price does not mean lack of obligation.

10.3 Commensuration

Is value measured numerically?

Kula value is ranked but not reducible to a universal price. Social platforms and blockchains intensify commensuration through metrics and token prices. Quantification can make exchange more transparent while narrowing what counts.

10.4 Control over conversion

Who can convert one form of value into another?

This is the decisive political question. A contributor may generate social value, but a firm converts it into profit. A user may generate attention, but a platform sells influence. A community may create a protocol, but large token holders convert financial ownership into governance power.

To these four dimensions, feminist anthropology adds a fifth: social reproduction.

10.5 Reproductive and maintenance labor

Who produces the persons, relationships, objects, and infrastructures that make exchange possible? Who feeds, teaches, documents, moderates, cares, repairs, and remembers?

This labor cannot be treated as an external background. It is constitutive of the exchange system.

11. Conclusions

Malinowski’s kula ethnography demonstrated that economically significant conduct is embedded in ritual, prestige, partnership, and political order, and that ceremonial gifts can coexist with utilitarian trade. Mauss transformed that ethnographic lesson into a general theory: gifts create obligations to give, receive, and return and therefore operate as total social phenomena. Sahlins differentiated reciprocity according to the timing and equivalence of return and the social distance between actors.

Feminist anthropologists showed what these models had obscured. Weiner documented women’s wealth and mortuary distributions in the very society made canonical by Malinowski and recast exchange around the paradox of keeping-while-giving. Rubin exposed the unequal politics concealed when women appear as gifts through which men establish alliances. Strathern questioned the Western categories of individual, property, production, and fixed gender that underwrite much comparative theory. Together, these interventions show that exchange cannot be understood without production, reproduction, retention, and authority.

Open-source software validates the possibility of large-scale generalized reciprocity among strangers, but it is better understood as a hybrid gift-commons-commodity system than as a pure gift economy. Licenses, reputations, employment, and corporate use link generosity to institutionalized reciprocity and markets. Gender data—2.3% women among core developers in one 711-project study, and fewer than 5% of pull requests authored by women in the literature synthesized by a 51-study review—show that formal openness does not eliminate unequal participation or recognition.

Social-media platforms demonstrate that gifts can be engines of capitalist accumulation. Users exchange recognition and content, while platforms convert collective interaction into proprietary data and sell the ability to influence audiences. The gift does not stand outside commodification; it can conceal and facilitate it.

Cryptocurrency governance goes further by making the border between gift, money, and political authority programmable. Voluntary code and community labor support systems in which tokens are simultaneously property, reward, membership sign, and vote. Empirical evidence from thousands of DAOs and hundreds of proposals indicates that voting power is frequently concentrated: in one study, ten voters controlled 50.53% of Compound power and 35.73% of Uniswap power, while only 3.18 and 4.7 voters respectively were needed on average to constitute half of proposal votes. Decentralized architecture therefore does not by itself yield decentralized social power.

The contemporary evidence ultimately reinforces the deepest classical insight while rejecting a classical binary. Gift and commodity exchange are not mutually exclusive spheres, nor are they successive stages of social evolution. They are relational logics that can coexist within one object, transaction, platform, or institution. Gifts create solidarity, but also debt and rank. Commodities promise alienability, but remain embedded in histories and infrastructures. Digital systems make this interpenetration unusually visible: free contributions generate commodities, metrics turn recognition into calculable capital, and tradable property becomes governance.

The central anthropological questions are consequently not whether a transfer is “really” a gift or “really” a commodity. They are: What relationships does it make? What obligations does it impose? Whose labor does it conceal? What cannot be fully alienated? Who controls circulation? And who has the power to convert collective social value into prestige, money, or political authority?
