final.content:
Adaptive Input UX for Musicians with Hand Tremor in Digital Audio Workstations

Executive summary

The evidence does not support the premise that Ableton Live, Logic Pro, and SteadyMouse offer three comparable, music-aware tremor-compensation systems:

• Ableton Live’s built-in Velocity device remaps, clips, gates, fixes, compresses, or expands MIDI note velocities. It is not documented as a temporal “velocity smoothing” algorithm, does not estimate tremor frequency, and cannot distinguish pathological tremor from intentional expression. Some Max for Live modulation and MPE devices do offer rise/fall smoothing, but that is generic low-pass-like signal conditioning, not tremor-aware classification (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/live-midi-effect-reference/; https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/max-for-live-devices/).

• Logic Pro Smart Controls are documented as parameter-mapping and control-consolidation facilities. Apple’s documentation covers mapping screen controls, automatic controller assignment, parameter mapping graphs, hardware assignments, and automation, but no dedicated “tremor compensation” mode is documented (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/smart-controls-overview-lgcp7e59f24b/mac; https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/edit-mapping-parameters-lgcpc1eebede/mac). Smart Controls can reduce the amount and precision of movement required by exposing a small set of useful parameters, but that is indirect accommodation, not pathological-tremor detection.

• SteadyMouse is a Windows-wide pointing aid for essential tremor, Parkinson’s disease, and related conditions. It smooths mouse trajectories, blocks accidental clicks, offers target snapping, and provides several strength/filter presets. It does not process MIDI note, velocity, pitch-bend, aftertouch, MPE, or audio data. Its central UX tradeoff is stronger tremor removal versus increasing cursor lag, with a global toggle as an escape hatch for tasks where unfiltered motion is wanted (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/; https://www.steadymouse.com/).

The core scientific difficulty is that frequency alone cannot separate disease from musicianship. Essential tremor is commonly a 4–12 Hz action tremor, and classic Parkinsonian rest tremor is usually 4–7 Hz (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8350038/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6530552/). Professional violin and vocal vibrato commonly occupies approximately 5–8 Hz: one artist-level violin case measured 5.7 Hz in first position and 6.3 Hz in fifth position, a professional-violin study reported a mean of 6.63 Hz, and ten singers averaged 6.0 Hz (https://doi.org/10.1177/1948499209os-400103; https://doi.org/10.1177/194849921000100105; https://doi.org/10.1121/1.410141). A simple 4–12 Hz rejection band would therefore suppress much intentional vibrato.

No located controlled study reports composition-completion times, flow-state scores, or satisfaction scores across sensitivity thresholds among professional musicians with essential tremor or Parkinson’s disease. Likewise, no direct study was found on motor-skill retention when musicians alternate between tremor-adaptive and standard DAW interfaces. Existing quantitative evidence comes mainly from clinical tapping, mouse pointing, touchscreen interaction, rehabilitation, and accessible digital-musical-instrument prototypes. These adjacent results support personalization and cautious filtering, but they cannot be converted into claims about professional composition productivity.

1. Clinical and interaction context

1.1 Tremor frequencies and why the nominal “4–12 Hz” range is insufficient

An updated clinical review identifies the usual upper-extremity action-tremor frequency in essential tremor as 4–12 Hz (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8350038/). The International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society consensus states that classic Parkinsonian rest tremor is characteristically 4–7 Hz, although higher frequencies occur; it also cautions that most pathological tremors lie around 4–8 Hz and that frequency is usually not very diagnostic by itself (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6530552/).

The corresponding oscillation periods are:

• 4 Hz: 1 / 4 second = 250 ms per cycle  
• 7 Hz: 1 / 7 second ≈ 143 ms per cycle  
• 8 Hz: 1 / 8 second = 125 ms per cycle  
• 12 Hz: 1 / 12 second ≈ 83 ms per cycle

Thus a pathological oscillation may reverse direction every roughly 42–125 ms, depending on whether one considers a half-cycle.

Clinical phenomenology also matters:

• Essential tremor is principally an action or postural tremor.
• Parkinsonian tremor is characteristically a rest tremor, but postural and kinetic tremors may coexist.
• A diagnostic EMG study found PD tremor around 4–6 Hz, ET around 5–8 Hz, and enhanced physiological tremor around 6–12 Hz, with substantial overlap. Muscle-contraction pattern, latency, concentration effects, and response to loading provided additional discriminatory information beyond frequency (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5573102/).

This makes a fixed DAW-wide frequency cutoff especially risky. The same measured rate could represent ET, PD, enhanced physiological tremor, a deliberately oscillated controller, or a normal expressive musical gesture.

1.2 Intentional musical vibrato occupies the same band

Musical vibrato is not outside the pathological-tremor band:

• Historical singing measurements cited rates of 5.9–7.8 pulses per second, while more recent singers were reported around 4.9–6 pulses per second. Historical violin measurements were around 5.5–7 pulses per second (https://pubs.aip.org/asa/jasa/article/80/S1/S87/731036/Acoustic-parameters-of-violin-vibrato).

• An artist-level violin case study measured mean rates of approximately 5.7 Hz in first position and 6.3 Hz in fifth position. Mean widths were about 40 cents and 108 cents respectively (https://doi.org/10.1177/1948499209os-400103).

• A study of recorded violin soloists reported a mean vibrato rate of 6.63 Hz and mean width of 63 cents (https://doi.org/10.1177/194849921000100105).

• Ten singers performing Schubert’s “Ave Maria” averaged 6.0 Hz; rate tended to increase by 15% at tone endings, and within-performer rate variation was about ±8% around each artist’s average (https://doi.org/10.1121/1.410141).

• A review of vibrato and vocal tremor notes that Western lyric vibrato is typically 5–8 Hz, under approximately ±1 semitone, and nearly sinusoidal. Vocal tremor can have similar mean rate and extent, although its variability is greater (https://pubs.aip.org/asa/jasa/article/130/1/EL1/907816/Vibrato-and-tremor-extent-spectrum-Algorithm-and).

The overlap is nearly complete. Taking the common musical-vibrato range as 5–8 Hz and the requested pathological band as 4–12 Hz:

Overlap width = min(8,12) − max(5,4) = 8 − 5 = 3 Hz.

Because the musical range itself is 3 Hz wide, 100% of the nominal 5–8 Hz musical-vibrato band lies inside the 4–12 Hz pathological band. Frequency-only rejection cannot preserve vibrato reliably.

2. Comparison of the three systems

2.1 Ableton Live: velocity shaping rather than tremor-aware smoothing

Ableton’s official Live 12 documentation describes the Velocity MIDI effect as a mapper for MIDI Note On and/or Note Off velocity values from 1 to 127. It provides:

• Input and output ranges
• A velocity transfer curve
• Clip, Gate, and Fixed modes
• Random modulation
• Drive
• Compand, which expands or compresses output velocities toward extremes or the middle of the range

In Gate mode, velocities outside a configured range are removed. In Fixed mode, every passing note receives the same configured velocity. Negative Compand compresses output values toward the middle of the range (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/live-midi-effect-reference/).

This is not temporal smoothing in the signal-processing sense. A velocity value normally exists once at Note On—and sometimes once again as release velocity at Note Off. It is not a continuous time series like pitch bend or MIDI CC. Consequently:

• Velocity compression can reduce unwanted dynamic variance caused by inconsistent key strikes.
• An output floor can prevent weak accidental strikes from becoming inaudible.
• An input gate can reject very weak or very strong strikes.
• Fixed velocity can eliminate dynamic variation entirely.
• None of these operations determines whether a particular strike was intentional.
• Gate mode creates the clearest false-rejection risk because an intentional pianissimo note below the threshold is discarded.
• Fixed or strongly compressed velocity preserves note timing and pitch but erases intended accents and dynamic phrasing.

The user’s phrase “Ableton Live’s MIDI velocity smoothing” is therefore best interpreted as velocity range compression/remapping, not a documented accessibility feature. Ableton also offers a Velocity Shaper MIDI transformation for selected notes, but that is an editing operation applying an envelope to note velocities, not a real-time tremor classifier (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/midi-tools/).

Live’s Max for Live devices do provide actual smoothing for continuous modulation. The Max for Live documentation describes linear or logarithmic smoothing and separate rise/fall times from 0 to 1000 ms; MPE Control can smooth Press, Slide, and per-note pitch bend with independent rise/fall settings (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/max-for-live-devices/). Such smoothing could attenuate tremor transmitted through a continuous controller, but it remains generic. It does not infer pathology, musical context, note boundaries, gesture intent, or vibrato.

Implications for intentional vibrato:

• If vibrato is represented by pitch bend, MPE per-note pitch bend, aftertouch, or CC modulation, a long smoothing time will reduce its width and add lag.
• If vibrato is encoded in audio from a microphone or acoustic/electric instrument, MIDI Velocity does not affect it.
• If a keyboard patch generates vibrato internally from a sustained key or mod-wheel setting, velocity remapping may change initial timbre or loudness but does not directly remove the oscillation.
• If unintended tremor causes extra Note On events, velocity compression alone cannot reliably distinguish them from deliberate trills, tremolos, repeated notes, or grace notes.

A useful quantitative illustration follows from a first-order low-pass model, although Ableton does not document its smoother as this exact filter. The amplitude ratio for a first-order low-pass filter is:

Aout/Ain = 1 / √(1 + (2πfτ)²)

At a representative vibrato/tremor frequency of 6 Hz:

• τ = 20 ms: ratio ≈ 1 / √(1 + 0.754²) ≈ 0.80
• τ = 50 ms: ratio ≈ 1 / √(1 + 1.885²) ≈ 0.47
• τ = 100 ms: ratio ≈ 1 / √(1 + 3.770²) ≈ 0.26
• τ = 200 ms: ratio ≈ 1 / √(1 + 7.540²) ≈ 0.13

This illustrates the generic UX problem: settings strong enough to remove a 6 Hz tremor can also remove most 6 Hz intentional vibrato. These are model-derived examples, not measured Ableton performance figures.

2.2 Logic Pro Smart Controls: simplified mapping, not documented tremor compensation

Apple describes Smart Controls as screen controls for adjusting relevant parameters of the selected track, patch, plug-ins, EQ, and master effects. The documented facilities include:

• Choosing Smart Control layouts
• Automatic MIDI-controller assignment
• Mapping screen controls
• Editing mapping parameters
• Parameter-mapping graphs
• Assigning hardware controls
• Automating screen-control movements
• Comparing edited settings with saved settings

See Apple’s Smart Controls overview and mapping documentation: https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/smart-controls-overview-lgcp7e59f24b/mac and https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/edit-mapping-parameters-lgcpc1eebede/mac.

No Apple documentation located in this research describes “tremor compensation,” pathological-tremor estimation, adaptive notch filtering, accidental-gesture rejection, or preservation of intentional vibrato. It would therefore be inaccurate to treat Logic Smart Controls as having a built-in clinical tremor compensator.

Smart Controls can nevertheless improve accessibility indirectly:

• A producer can expose only a few high-value parameters rather than navigating dense plug-in windows.
• A large knob can be mapped over a deliberately restricted parameter range, reducing both travel and error consequence.
• Several underlying parameters can be made accessible through a consistent control layer.
• Hardware controls can be assigned to avoid precise mouse manipulation.
• Mapping curves can reduce sensitivity in the most frequently used region.

These are examples of reducing control difficulty and error cost, not automatically classifying unintended input.

Implications for vibrato are mapping-dependent:

• A flattened or restricted mapping can reduce accidental modulation but also reduce intended vibrato depth.
• A dead zone around the controller’s rest position can prevent small tremor-driven changes, but makes light expressive onset harder.
• A narrow output range protects against large parameter excursions, but limits expressive range.
• Automation captured from a trembling knob is not documented as being automatically cleaned by Smart Controls.
• Intent preservation must therefore come from deliberate mapping, editing, use of a different control modality, or an external filter.

There is also an important platform distinction. Logic Pro is a macOS application, whereas the current SteadyMouse 2 manual lists Windows XP through Windows 11 and Windows Server versions as supported and says macOS support is not yet available, with no known completion date (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/). SteadyMouse therefore cannot presently be assumed to assist the mouse pointer inside a standard Logic Pro/macOS setup.

2.3 SteadyMouse: cursor stabilization, click rejection, and explicit mode switching

SteadyMouse is designed for essential tremor and variants associated with Parkinson’s disease and multiple sclerosis. Its functions include:

• Anti-tremor cursor filtering
• Automatic blocking of unintentional clicks
• Icon targeting to select a nearby clickable item
• A system-wide on/off toggle
• Support for ordinary mice, trackpads, pointing sticks, RollerMouse devices, and other pointing hardware

The product description is at https://www.steadymouse.com/ and the detailed controls are in https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/.

The manual makes its latency tradeoff explicit: moving the strength control toward weaker filtering makes the pointer “snappier” but allows tremor to pass; moving toward stronger filtering improves tremor removal but increases lag. It advises users to choose the weakest setting that still removes the shake.

SteadyMouse also offers filter sets with different responsiveness:

• Feather: especially responsive but possibly insufficient for stronger tremor
• Allegro: a medium balance and default
• Adagio: stronger and smoother but more laggy
• Classic: broad range between responsive and heavy
• Artistry: oriented toward drawing lines and curves
• Laggy: exceptionally heavy filtering
• Experimental
• Steadicam: intended primarily for camera stabilization

The recommended calibration begins with very low pointer speed and an approximately 95% filter strength, then tests filter sets and gradually reduces strength to regain responsiveness while retaining control (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/).

For DAW work, SteadyMouse can help with:

• Selecting clips, menus, transport buttons, and small plug-in controls
• Dragging automation points
• Reducing accidental clicks that delete, move, or activate objects
• Reaching nearby controls through target assistance

It cannot directly clean:

• MIDI notes
• MIDI velocity
• Pitch bend
• MPE expression
• Modulation-wheel data
• Audio vibrato
• Performance gestures from a keyboard, pad controller, violin sensor, breath controller, or camera

Its treatment of intentional vibrato therefore depends on where that vibrato enters the system. Keyboard/MPE performance data bypasses SteadyMouse. But if a musician intentionally draws rapid oscillatory automation with the mouse, the cursor filter may smooth that motion away. The global toggle is the principal documented mechanism for preserving such intentional motion: filtering can be disabled for an expressive drawing task and restored for ordinary navigation. Unlike a classifier, this places intent specification in the user’s hands.

2.4 Comparative summary

Ableton Velocity:

• Input domain: discrete MIDI note velocity
• Main operation: range mapping, compression/expansion, clipping, gating, or fixed output
• Adaptive to tremor frequency: no documented support
• Risk to expression: loss of pianissimo, accents, and dynamic variation
• Vibrato handling: generally irrelevant unless vibrato is indirectly triggered by velocity
• User override: bypass device or change rack/mapping

Ableton Max for Live smoothing:

• Input domain: continuous modulation, MPE pressure/slide/pitch bend
• Main operation: configurable rise/fall smoothing
• Adaptive to tremor frequency: no documented pathology model
• Risk to expression: attenuated vibrato depth and delayed transitions
• User override: device bypass, shorter smoothing time, separate mappings

Logic Smart Controls:

• Input domain: mapped screen and hardware controls
• Main operation: parameter consolidation and mapping
• Adaptive to tremor frequency: no documented support
• Risk to expression: dead zones or restricted curves can suppress subtle intended gestures
• Vibrato handling: entirely dependent on mapping and any external processing
• User override: edit mappings, use another controller, or bypass the mapped layer

SteadyMouse:

• Input domain: Windows pointer motion and clicks
• Main operation: motion smoothing, accidental-click blocking, target assistance
• Adaptive to user: strength and filter-set selection, but no published music-intent classifier
• Risk to expression: cursor lag and attenuation of intentionally drawn oscillations
• Vibrato handling: does not affect MIDI/audio vibrato unless expressed through mouse movement
• User override: global toggle and choice of responsive versus heavy filter sets

3. HCI and signal-processing research on separating tremor from intended action

3.1 Established approaches

The tremor-suppression literature generally treats observed motion as:

measured motion = voluntary motion + tremor + sensor noise.

Common separation methods include:

1. Low-pass smoothing

Because voluntary motion is often slower than tremor, a low-pass filter removes high-frequency oscillation. Its disadvantages are lag and attenuation of fast voluntary movement. A computer-interface paper notes that pathological tremor is commonly 3–12 Hz and that low-pass filtering can lag faster intentional movements (https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pub_files/pub3/hsu_d_s_1996_1/hsu_d_s_1996_1.pdf).

2. Adaptive notch or sinusoidal cancellation

The Weighted-Frequency Fourier Linear Combiner estimates tremor frequency and amplitude, then subtracts the modeled oscillation rather than broadly low-pass filtering motion. It was developed because tremor amplitude and frequency vary over time and because preserving the phase of voluntary movement is important (https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pub_files/pub3/riviere_cameron_1995_2/riviere_cameron_1995_2.pdf; https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pub_files/pub3/hsu_d_s_1996_1/hsu_d_s_1996_1.pdf).

3. Adaptive LMS and Kalman estimation

A real-time gyroscope system separates voluntary and tremulous motion using their different frequency content, then estimates instantaneous amplitude and frequency with an adaptive least-mean-squares algorithm and Kalman filter (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3264472/).

4. Mean filtering plus path reconstruction

Adaptive Path Smoothing via B-splines uses mean filtering and B-spline trajectory reconstruction, adjusting treatment to the user’s tremor level and type. Seven participants with unwanted tremor evaluated the method and perceived it as easy and useful, although the available summary does not supply per-threshold task-time or false-positive data (https://doi.org/10.1080/10400435.2013.845271).

5. Context or state gating

A tremor-frequency filter for essential-tremor EMG observed that filtering also attenuated signals produced during voluntary movement. It therefore used tremor frequency as a switch to activate filtering selectively during posture maintenance. Recognition partly improved because less voluntary signal was attenuated, but the result was not complete separation (https://doi.org/10.1109/biorob.2012.6290905).

6. Learned or multimodal classifiers

Touchscreen research has combined phone motion sensors with a small wearable sensor on the tapping finger, reducing missed selections by up to 40% without changing the displayed interface (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3161169). A 102-person study using touch-path, timing, pressure, and inertial features distinguished early PD from controls with AUC 0.95, sensitivity 0.89, and specificity 0.88; it was a diagnostic classification study rather than an online rejection system for musicians (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3290605.3300313).

3.2 Why music needs more than generic tremor cancellation

A music-aware classifier must distinguish gestures that can be kinematically similar but semantically opposite:

• Unwanted periodic pitch modulation versus deliberate vibrato
• Accidental repeated notes versus a trill or tremolo
• Tremor-driven pressure variation versus expressive aftertouch
• Cursor shake versus intentional freehand automation
• A brief accidental click versus rhythmic triggering
• Bradykinetic pauses versus deliberate rests
• Small-amplitude tremor versus intentionally delicate control

Frequency alone fails because musical and pathological oscillations overlap. More useful features would include:

• Note-state context: intentional vibrato generally occurs while a note is sounding.
• Parameter identity: oscillation in pitch bend or MPE pitch is more plausibly expressive than oscillation in a file-menu pointer.
• Musical synchronization: intentional tremolo may align with tempo subdivisions.
• Onset and offset shape: artistic vibrato can develop after note onset and change near tone endings.
• Amplitude envelope: vibrato width may vary with dynamics or phrase position.
• Cross-modal correlation: intended vibrato may correlate with finger pressure, bowing, breath, audio fundamental-frequency modulation, or note sustain.
• Spatial dimensionality: tremor may occur across multiple axes, while a mapped musical gesture may use a constrained axis.
• Personal templates: a musician’s intended vibrato rate, width, and phase behavior can be learned separately from tremor measured at rest and during posture.
• Explicit mode or clutch input: a pedal, switch, dwell, or note-state condition can tell the system when oscillation is expressive.
• Reversibility: raw data should be retained so that rejected gestures can be restored.

A movement-to-MIDI experiment illustrates one feasible intentional-gesture detector. “Pidato” used accelerometer data, the YIN periodicity/frequency algorithm, and a periodicity probability threshold above 0.91 to trigger MIDI pitch bend. It updated the modeled frequency when pitch changed by more than 0.25 Hz and decayed the generated bend after detection (https://0110.be/posts/The_Pidato_Experiment%3A_Vibrato_on_a_Digital_Piano_Using_an_Arduino; https://github.com/JorenSix/Pidato/blob/master/pidato/pidato.pde). It demonstrates that periodic motion can intentionally generate vibrato, but it was not evaluated as a pathological-tremor discriminator. Indeed, a tremor can also be highly periodic and might satisfy the same detector.

3.3 Detection delay versus creative responsiveness

A frequency estimator needs enough temporal evidence to establish periodicity. As a simple lower-bound illustration:

At 4 Hz:

• Two cycles require 2 / 4 = 0.50 s
• Three cycles require 3 / 4 = 0.75 s

At 6 Hz:

• Two cycles require 0.333 s
• Three cycles require 0.50 s

At 12 Hz:

• Two cycles require 0.167 s
• Three cycles require 0.25 s

These calculations do not describe any particular product, but they expose a real-time UX tension. Waiting for several cycles reduces false classification of one-off movement but can add 167–750 ms of evidence-gathering time across the 4–12 Hz band. Predictive or adaptive filters can react faster, but then risk learning an intentional vibrato as “noise.” A practical music system may therefore need immediate weak assistance followed by stronger suppression only after confidence rises, rather than a binary reject/accept decision.

4. Documented false positives and false rejection

4.1 A directly quantified threshold tradeoff

The most relevant located quantitative false-positive evidence comes from a 2024 study detecting emergent Parkinsonian rest tremor from repetitive alternating finger tapping, not musical MIDI performance. It classified strikes with inter-strike-interval and dwell-time thresholds (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-024-00754-7).

Reported calibration points included:

• ISI threshold 216 ms and dwell threshold 70 ms:
  – Sensitivity: 50.00%
  – False-positive rate: 4.30%

• ISI threshold 225 ms and dwell threshold 85 ms:
  – Sensitivity: 73.45%
  – False-positive rate: 7.49%

The threshold change therefore produced:

• Sensitivity increase = 73.45 − 50.00 = 23.45 percentage points
• False-positive increase = 7.49 − 4.30 = 3.19 percentage points
• Relative sensitivity increase = 23.45 / 50.00 = 46.9%
• Relative false-positive increase = 3.19 / 4.30 ≈ 74.2%

The study further reported:

• Increasing ISI from 225 to 230 ms, with dwell held at 85 ms:
  – Sensitivity increased 2.26 percentage points
  – False positives increased 1.23 percentage points

• Increasing dwell from 80 to 85 ms, with ISI held at 225 ms:
  – Sensitivity increased 5.26 percentage points
  – False positives increased 0.67 percentage points

A simple marginal comparison is:

• ISI increase: 2.26 / 1.23 ≈ 1.84 sensitivity points gained per false-positive point.
• Dwell increase: 5.26 / 0.67 ≈ 7.85 sensitivity points gained per false-positive point.

Within that dataset, changing dwell time was therefore about 7.85 / 1.84 ≈ 4.3 times more favorable by this crude ratio than increasing the ISI threshold. This is an illustrative calculation, not a general optimality result.

The chosen 225 ms/85 ms thresholds, when applied to a held-out test set, achieved:

• Sensitivity: 79%
• Precision: 63%
• False-positive rate: 6.7%

The paper attributes many false positives to healthy controls who could voluntarily perform rapid alternating finger tapping with short dwell times. That is highly relevant to music: trained performers deliberately produce fast, regular gestures that resemble a pathological pattern under simple timing rules. A classifier calibrated on non-musicians or ordinary computer use could reject precisely the high-speed control that expertise enables.

4.2 Why these figures cannot be treated as MIDI gesture-rejection rates

The tapping study detected a Parkinsonian digital signature; it did not reject MIDI notes during composition. Its “false positive” means that healthy voluntary tapping was classified as tremor-like. In a musical system, possible error categories would instead include:

• False rejection: an intended note, trill, vibrato cycle, automation move, or controller modulation is suppressed.
• False acceptance: a tremor-induced event passes into the MIDI recording.
• Distortion without rejection: the gesture remains but its timing, amplitude, or expressive contour is altered.
• Delayed acceptance: the event is captured only after a confidence window, changing timing.
• Mode error: filtering remains enabled when expressive movement is intended, or disabled when stabilization is needed.

Published mouse and touchscreen studies often report misses, completion time, or trajectory accuracy rather than semantic false-rejection rates. These measures are valuable but not interchangeable with the musical question “Did the system delete something the performer intended?”

4.3 Adjacent pointing evidence

A multicenter evaluation of a Tremor Control System included 36 people with multiple sclerosis and intention tremor. An optimal alternative interface significantly improved Point & Click time at p<0.01 and Drag & Drop at p<0.05; Double Click improved at p<0.1. Adding motion-filtering software significantly improved Double Click time at p<0.05. More patients could complete the tests, and users—especially those with marked intention tremor—reported less fatigue and greater comfort than with a standard mouse (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11392656).

A pilot study of hardware and software Tremor Control Mouse variants for essential tremor found significant paired differences, p<0.05, in ease-of-use responses compared with a traditional mouse; subjective reactions were positive overall (https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.5555/1766311.1766384). The accessible summary does not give the sample size, threshold settings, absolute completion times, or false-positive rates.

A mouse adapter offering digital smoothing, inadvertent-click rejection, and enhanced double-clicking produced self-reported improvements ranging from moderate to considerable for most participants in a preliminary essential-tremor test, but the available abstract does not provide false-rejection figures (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5386687).

These studies support stabilization for general DAW pointing. They do not show whether filtering preserves freehand automation, musical timing, or intentional oscillatory controller gestures.

5. Sensitivity thresholds, completion time, satisfaction, and creative flow

5.1 What can be concluded about threshold direction

Across the available systems and studies, stronger sensitivity generally has predictable effects:

Low or weak filtering:

• Lower latency and more immediate control
• Better preservation of fast intentional movement
• More tremor leakage
• More accidental pointer movement, clicks, or controller fluctuation
• More post-recording cleanup

High or strong filtering:

• Less tremor and steadier targeting
• More lag
• More amplitude attenuation
• Higher risk of rejecting or flattening subtle expression
• Greater risk of suppressing vibrato, trills, or rapid automation
• Potentially less fatigue if stabilization outweighs the lag

SteadyMouse explicitly recommends the weakest strength that still removes tremor because stronger settings increase lag (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/). The Parkinson tapping study shows a related classifier tradeoff: expanding acceptance of tremor-like cases raised sensitivity but also increased false positives (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-024-00754-7).

For a DAW, the optimum is likely task-specific:

• Editing clips and menus can tolerate more smoothing than live performance.
• Drawing slow fades can tolerate more lag than freehand rhythmic automation.
• Drum triggering needs very low latency and must preserve rapid repeated notes.
• Pitch-bend vibrato needs preservation in the 5–8 Hz region.
• Mixing may benefit from restricted parameter ranges and coarse/fine modes rather than broad temporal smoothing.
• Accidental-click suppression may be valuable during destructive editing but intrusive during rapid rhythmic triggering with a pointing device.

5.2 No evidence for the requested professional-musician completion-time comparison

No located study reports composition completion time as a function of sensitivity threshold among professional musicians with Parkinson’s disease or essential tremor. In particular, the evidence does not support statements such as “a medium threshold reduced composition time by X%” or “professional satisfaction increased by Y points.”

The closest quantitative findings concern:

• Pointing, dragging, double-clicking, and touchscreen selection
• Clinical finger tapping
• Motion tracking and tremor suppression
• Prototype accessible instruments
• Usability or ease-of-use judgments

Those endpoints cannot be translated directly into time to compose, arrange, mix, or complete a piece. Composition time is additionally affected by musical complexity, medication state, fatigue, disease severity, DAW expertise, preferred workflow, hardware, genre, and the amount of editing required after performance.

5.3 No validated flow-state results

No located case study measured flow with a validated flow-state instrument while systematically varying tremor-filter sensitivity in a DAW. Claims about “creative flow” should therefore remain qualitative.

The likely pathways are plausible but unquantified:

Potential flow benefits:

• Fewer accidental edits and clicks
• Less visual attention devoted to keeping the pointer steady
• Less fatigue and frustration
• More successful completion of operations
• Lower fear of destructive errors

Potential flow costs:

• Perceptible lag
• Unpredictable or opaque gesture rejection
• Flattened dynamics
• Loss of vibrato or other stylistic signatures
• Repeated toggling and recalibration
• The need to inspect every take for silently deleted events

The multicenter Tremor Control System study’s reports of lower fatigue and greater comfort support the first group of mechanisms (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11392656), but fatigue and comfort are not validated flow scores. For music, false rejection may be more disruptive than visible tremor leakage because it breaks trust: the performer cannot know whether the captured take reflects the intended gesture.

5.4 Existing accessible-music studies are small and not tremor-threshold trials

A 2013 study of accessible technology for composers and producers involved three musicians with motor impairments: a composer with degenerative motor-neuron disease, a guitarist who had experienced a stroke, and a college student with impaired finger movement. Participants identified limitations in adapting conventional software and suggested more intuitive interfaces, optimized control-surface layouts, and repurposed text-input techniques (https://doi.org/10.1145/2513383.2513412). It did not report tremor-classifier thresholds, false positives, completion times, or standardized satisfaction scores for professional musicians with ET or PD.

A browser-based accessible-music project tested three participants with conditions affecting fine motor ability and three with typical motor ability. Contrary to the designers’ expectation, avoiding buttons and mice did not automatically make the tools more accessible; motion speed mattered more than the size of the control action (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3561212.3561231). This is important for design because replacing a mouse with camera or sensor input does not by itself solve tremor. It also does not provide the requested composition metrics.

An accessible MIDI-controller prototype supports joysticks, game controllers, keyboards, eye tracking, and other inputs, and was tested in an Ableton Live setup. The reported study was an observational usability exercise intended to generate development feedback, not a trial of ET/PD filtering thresholds or professional completion time (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14337032).

A separate inclusive-controller project describes a Logic Pro and Max setup tailored to a musician with highly limited mobility, using eye tracking to choose colored on-screen buttons and micromuscular sensors to trigger MIDI notes, chords, sequences, and other events. This demonstrates the value of individualized mappings and alternative channels, but supplies no tremor false-positive or composition-time data.

6. MIDI capture specifically: what should and should not be filtered

6.1 MIDI velocity is not vibrato

MIDI velocity is a discrete attribute attached to note events, typically 1–127. Musical vibrato, by contrast, is a continuous or repeatedly sampled pitch/amplitude modulation and is usually represented through:

• Pitch-bend messages
• MPE per-note pitch bend
• Polyphonic or channel pressure
• Modulation-wheel or other CC messages
• Audio itself
• An instrument’s internal modulation engine

Therefore, velocity smoothing cannot directly distinguish tremor from vibrato. It can only reduce dynamic inconsistency in the onset or release of notes. A robust DAW accessibility design should separately process:

• Note creation/deletion
• Note timing
• Velocity
• Continuous pitch
• Pressure
• Timbre/slide
• Pointer motion
• Click events

Applying one sensitivity threshold to all channels would erase their different musical semantics.

6.2 Accidental-note filtering versus musical repetition

A short inter-onset interval is not sufficient evidence of an accidental note. Musicians intentionally use:

• Trills
• Tremolos
• Drum rolls
• Repeated-note ostinati
• Grace notes
• Flams
• Ornamentation
• Arpeggios
• Rapid finger substitutions

Parkinsonian tremor at 4–7 Hz corresponds to 143–250 ms between cycles, while a sixteenth-note stream at common tempi can fall in the same timing region:

• At 60 BPM, one quarter note is 1000 ms and a sixteenth note is 250 ms = 4 Hz.
• At 90 BPM, a sixteenth is 1000 × 60 / 90 / 4 ≈ 166.7 ms = 6 Hz.
• At 120 BPM, a sixteenth is 125 ms = 8 Hz.
• At 180 BPM, a sixteenth is approximately 83.3 ms = 12 Hz.

Thus the entire 4–12 Hz tremor band corresponds exactly to common tempo-synchronized sixteenth-note rates from roughly 60 to 180 BPM. A frequency gate would reject musically ordinary passages.

6.3 Better real-time decision architecture

A safer architecture would classify in layers:

Layer 1: channel semantics

Do not use the same model for pointer motion, Note On events, velocity, and pitch bend.

Layer 2: personal tremor model

Measure baseline motion at rest, while holding posture, and during slow voluntary movement. Track dominant frequency, amplitude, dimensional direction, and variability.

Layer 3: musical context

Use note state, tempo, score/grid position, active instrument, articulation, phrase position, and whether the current mapping is designated expressive.

Layer 4: confidence-weighted attenuation

Rather than deleting a suspected event, reduce its influence proportionally to confidence. For example, compress velocity outliers before gating them, or attenuate only the estimated narrowband tremor component of pitch motion.

Layer 5: explicit intent controls

A pedal or switch can temporarily enable vibrato capture, bypass filtering, or change sensitivity. SteadyMouse’s global toggle embodies this principle at pointer level.

Layer 6: non-destructive recording

Record raw and filtered MIDI streams together. The visible take can use the filtered version while allowing restoration of rejected events.

Layer 7: immediate explanation and undo

Flag filtered events in the piano roll or automation lane rather than silently deleting them. One-command restoration lowers the creative cost of false positives.

7. Motor learning and retention when moving between adaptive and standard interfaces

7.1 Direct evidence is absent

No located study directly examines professional musicians with movement disorders learning on a tremor-adaptive DAW interface and then returning to an unfiltered Ableton, Logic, or standard MIDI interface. There are no sourced retention percentages, transfer scores, washout times, or longitudinal practice results for this population.

7.2 Relevant but indirect motor-learning evidence

A robotic-training study in able-bodied participants compared fixed-gain and variable-gain controllers and assessed short-term retention after controller removal. Fixed-gain assistance stabilized motor adaptation better than either no controller or variable-gain control in the studied conditions. The authors concluded that effective assistance should be challenging but consistent; effects also depended on task difficulty (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6732847/).

This is not evidence about musicians or tremor, but it suggests two hypotheses:

• Stable and predictable assistance may be easier to incorporate into a motor model than assistance whose gain changes unpredictably.
• Excessive or inconsistent adaptation could create aftereffects or reduce transfer to a standard interface.

The extrapolation must remain tentative because the study used able-bodied participants, robotic control, and visuomotor adaptation rather than DAW performance.

7.3 Expected transfer issues

Several retention and transfer risks follow from the system designs:

• A musician who learns to overshoot against heavy smoothing may overshoot when returning to an unfiltered interface.
• Strong velocity compression can weaken the learned relationship between finger force and audible dynamics.
• Dead zones can encourage larger gestures; those gestures may become excessive on a standard controller.
• Automatic rejection of repeated notes may reduce practice in controlling note release and separation.
• Variable adaptive gains can make the same physical gesture produce different outputs from day to day.
• Conversely, a stable interface that merely removes a narrow tremor component while preserving overall gain may permit more normal practice and maintain skill.

The safest design principle is not maximal assistance but minimal sufficient assistance, matching SteadyMouse’s recommendation to use the weakest filter that still controls tremor (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/).

7.4 Retention-oriented design recommendations

To preserve transfer to standard interfaces:

• Keep control-display gain consistent across adaptive and standard modes where possible.
• Avoid silently changing sensitivity based on short-term fluctuations.
• Expose the current assistance level clearly.
• Permit graded practice: for example, 100%, 75%, 50%, and 0% suppression.
• Include brief unassisted calibration blocks.
• Save user-specific profiles rather than forcing relearning after each session.
• Preserve raw MIDI so the musician can compare physical intent with filtered output.
• Use fixed, predictable assistance during performance and adapt only between takes unless the adaptive behavior has been validated.
• Evaluate retention after minutes, days, and weeks—not only immediate task success.

8. Implications for professional DAW practice

8.1 Best use of Ableton Live

For inconsistent key velocity:

• Use moderate negative Compand or a constrained output range rather than Gate or Fixed mode.
• Retain enough range for accents and pianissimo.
• Avoid interpreting low velocity as accidental by default.
• Use separate settings by instrument: percussion may tolerate more compression than expressive piano.

For pitch bend, MPE, or pressure:

• Use the shortest rise/fall smoothing that makes the controller manageable.
• Bypass or reduce smoothing on instruments where vibrato is intentional.
• Consider separate mappings for “navigation/editing” and “performance.”
• Record raw expression on a parallel path if possible.

For unintended extra notes:

• Prefer post-capture flagging over real-time deletion.
• Combine timing, velocity, note duration, neighboring-note context, and tempo alignment rather than a single threshold.
• Treat rapid repeated notes as ambiguous, not automatically pathological.

8.2 Best use of Logic Pro

Smart Controls should be treated as a reduced-complexity control surface:

• Map only the most important parameters.
• Restrict ranges to musically useful values.
• Provide coarse and fine controls separately.
• Use larger hardware encoders, pedals, switches, or alternative devices where precise mouse motion is difficult.
• Do not assume Smart Controls remove tremor.
• Preserve expressive mappings such as pitch or vibrato separately from editing mappings.

Because SteadyMouse is currently Windows-only, Logic users need a different macOS-compatible pointing accommodation or alternative hardware; SteadyMouse cannot presently be assumed to stabilize Logic’s pointer (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/).

8.3 Best use of SteadyMouse in a DAW

SteadyMouse is most appropriate for:

• Arrangement and editing
• Menu navigation
• Plug-in parameter selection
• Clip manipulation
• Transport controls
• Reducing destructive accidental clicks

Use weaker/snappier presets for:

• Freehand automation
• Rapid editing
• Controller-like mouse gestures
• Drawing curves

Use stronger presets for:

• Small targets
• Fine static positioning
• Operations where stability is more important than speed

Use the global toggle when deliberately drawing oscillatory automation or making rapid gestures. The system’s own guidance—to choose the weakest effective filter—appropriately minimizes latency and transfer cost (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/).

9. Research gaps and a suitable future evaluation

The requested evidence—professional-musician composition completion time, satisfaction, flow, false rejection, and motor retention across threshold levels—remains a clear research gap.

A defensible study would recruit separate groups of:

• Professional musicians with essential tremor
• Professional musicians with Parkinson’s disease
• Age- and instrument-matched professional controls

Medication state and symptom severity should be recorded, because Parkinsonian performance can vary substantially with medication timing.

Conditions should include:

1. Standard interface
2. Weak filtering
3. Medium filtering
4. Strong filtering
5. Personalized adaptive filtering
6. Personalized filtering with explicit bypass/clutch

Tasks should cover:

• Recording a melody with planned dynamics
• Recording deliberate vibrato via pitch bend or MPE
• Trills and repeated-note passages
• Drum programming
• Drawing automation
• Clip arrangement
• Plug-in adjustment
• Completing a short composition or production brief

Ground truth should come from a combination of:

• Score or stated musical plan
• Raw unfiltered MIDI
• Audio
• Motion sensors
• Participant annotation immediately after each take
• Expert adjudication where intent remains ambiguous

Key metrics should include:

• False-rejection rate = intended gestures rejected / all intended gestures
• False-acceptance rate = unintended gestures retained / all unintended gestures
• Expression distortion in cents, velocity units, and timing milliseconds
• Task and composition-completion time
• Number and duration of corrective edits
• Undo operations
• NASA-TLX or equivalent workload
• System Usability Scale
• A validated flow-state scale
• Trust and perceived authorship
• Fatigue and discomfort
• Satisfaction by task, not just overall
• Retention on an unassisted interface immediately, after 24 hours, and after one week

Threshold order should be counterbalanced to separate genuine threshold effects from learning and fatigue. Raw and filtered data should both be retained. Because an adaptive system may improve within a session, analysis should separate early from late trials.

10. Conclusions

The main finding is not that one of the three named products has solved tremor-versus-expression classification. None has:

• Ableton’s Velocity device is a velocity transfer function, not a tremor detector.
• Ableton’s continuous-control smoothing can attenuate tremor but can equally attenuate 5–8 Hz vibrato.
• Logic Smart Controls simplify and remap control but have no documented tremor-compensation classifier.
• SteadyMouse effectively addresses pointer shake and accidental clicks, but does not process MIDI or audio and trades smoothing strength against lag.

The hardest case—distinguishing pathological tremor from intentional musical expression—is intrinsically ambiguous in the frequency domain. Essential tremor at 4–12 Hz and Parkinsonian tremor at approximately 4–7 Hz overlap directly with professional vibrato around 5–8 Hz. Common tempo-synchronized sixteenth-note rates also span 4–12 Hz from 60 to 180 BPM. Frequency-only gesture rejection is therefore unsuitable for music.

The strongest directly relevant false-positive lesson comes from Parkinsonian tapping detection: increasing sensitivity from 50.00% to 73.45% raised false positives from 4.30% to 7.49%, and healthy participants’ rapid voluntary tapping caused many false classifications (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-024-00754-7). This is exactly the kind of behavior trained musicians perform intentionally.

General tremor-interface studies show improved pointing, task completion, comfort, and fatigue, including significant benefits in a 36-person intention-tremor trial (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11392656). However, there are no credible quantitative data answering how threshold settings change full composition time, validated creative flow, or user-satisfaction scores among professional musicians with ET or PD. There is also no direct evidence on their retention when alternating between adaptive and standard DAW interfaces.

The most defensible UX strategy is consequently:

• Personalize by user, task, parameter, and musical context.
• Use the weakest effective intervention.
• Prefer narrowband attenuation or compression over binary rejection.
• Preserve note-state and tempo context.
• Offer an immediate clutch or bypass.
• Record raw and filtered streams non-destructively.
• Make rejected gestures visible and reversible.
• Keep assistance stable enough to support motor learning.
• Evaluate artistic intent, not merely pointer accuracy.

Until these principles are tested with professional musicians who have movement disorders, claims about faster composition, higher satisfaction, improved flow, or preserved motor skill should be presented as hypotheses rather than established findings.
