THE ILIAD AND THE EPIC CYCLE: NEOANALYSIS, ORALISM, AND THE EMERGING SYNTHESIS

Executive summary

The older opposition between neoanalysis and oralism can be stated sharply:

• Neoanalysis asks which pre-Iliadic narrative complexes have been transferred, reshaped, or suppressed in the Iliad. It treats the fragments and summaries of the Epic Cycle—especially the Cypria and Aethiopis—as imperfect but usable witnesses to traditions older than the surviving cyclic poems themselves. Apparent redundancies, narrative discontinuities, compressed references, and anticipations of events beyond the Iliad’s limits can therefore be evidence of deliberate allusion or “motif transference.”

• Oralism asks how flexible stories, formulas, themes, and performance conventions circulate within a multiform oral tradition. It resists treating the lost Cypria as a recoverable source-text or assuming that resemblance entails one poem’s borrowing from another. John Miles Foley and Justin Arft replace a linear sequence of interacting texts with a “constellation” of flexible narratives whose individual performances owe primary allegiance to the tradition as a whole (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/greek-epic-cycle-and-its-ancient-reception/epic-cycle-and-oral-tradition/14397ED473238E742B12447115062E67).

That contrast remains useful, but it no longer maps cleanly onto the named scholars. Jonathan Burgess and Christos Tsagalis are neoanalytic interpreters who have explicitly incorporated oral poetics; Gregory Nagy reads the Cypria as a distinct traditional plot while insisting on performance, multiformity, and evolutionary stabilization; Bruno Currie combines neoanalysis with comparative epic; and Foley’s “traditional referentiality” can explain many of the same effects that neoanalysts call allusion. Egbert Bakker’s performance-oriented account of epic reference similarly shifts attention from a fixed object in the past to the performer’s present act of “pointing” at that past (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/preface-36/).

The result is not a consensus on direct dependence. It is a partial methodological synthesis usually called “oral intertextuality,” “intertextuality without texts,” or “oral, intertextual neoanalysis.” The strongest current formulation is that the Iliad evokes identifiable story-traditions associated in later evidence with the Epic Cycle, but in most cases the evidence does not establish dependence on the fixed texts summarized by Proclus. The key unresolved question is therefore no longer whether the Iliad has a traditional background—it plainly does—but how specifically an audience could identify a particular allusion and how securely modern scholars can reconstruct the relevant pre-Iliadic song.

I. What each methodology is trying to recover

1. Classical and revised neoanalysis

Neoanalysis began as a genetic but generally unitarian method: instead of dissecting the Iliad into incompatible compositional layers, it explains peculiarities in the received poem through the reshaping of earlier material. Wolfgang Kullmann’s classic formulation distinguishes ordinary oral “themes,” such as arming, arrival, feasting, or lament, from more particular configurations of plot, character, and motif. For neoanalysis, an element insufficiently assimilated to its Iliadic setting may retain signs of its earlier narrative function (https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/download/5411/5311/15193).

The method is especially important for Achilles. Patroclus’ death, Thetis’ lament, the making of new armor, Achilles’ return to combat, and the hero’s foreknowledge of death can be read as Iliadic transformations of traditions concerning Achilles’ own death and funeral. The Cycle is valuable not because its extant or summarized poems must be earlier in written form than the Iliad, but because their subject matter may preserve pre-Iliadic myth and song.

Burgess’s formulation makes three analytically distinct levels:

A. cyclic myth: the broader traditional story-world;
B. cyclic epic: particular epic realizations of that story-world;
C. Homeric epic: the relatively monumental Iliadic realization.

That distinction allows a neoanalyst to use cyclic evidence without claiming that “Homer” read a fixed copy of the Cypria. Burgess expressly argues that a textualized model of early epics borrowing from one another is anachronistic and that one should instead study interactions among oral narrative traditions. His work nevertheless retains the neoanalytic claim that transferred motifs can evoke a relatively determinate story outside the Iliad (https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf; review of The Death and Afterlife of Achilles at https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2009/2009.07.67/).

Tsagalis pushes this position further under the label “oral, intertextual neoanalysis.” His method distinguishes:

• broad mythological reference from allusion to an identifiable epic tradition;
• textualization from “entextualization,” the repeated shaping of traditional material into a recognizable performance unit;
• generic formulas or type-scenes from clusters of diction, motif, character, and narrative placement that make a more specific allusion plausible.

His recent theoretical account explicitly addresses criteria for identifying another epic tradition, the transference of motifs and phraseology, and the difficulty of deciding whether a Homeric echo signals general mythic knowledge or a particular oral epic (https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780192870988.003.0002).

Currie belongs to the same broad revisionist tendency but casts a wider comparative net. He treats the Cycle, archaic hymns, Gilgamesh, and other epic materials as controls for recognizing inherited narrative patterns. Comparative evidence makes it less necessary to imagine line-by-line literary borrowing, but Currie is generally more willing than strict oralists to posit meaningful, directed allusion to a specific narrative configuration.

2. Oralist objections

Nagy, Foley, and Bakker share no single doctrine, but their work converges on three objections to older neoanalysis.

First, surviving texts are performances or memorialized realizations of traditions, not transparent windows onto fixed pre-Homeric poems. Foley and Arft therefore describe the Cycle as a “constellation” rather than an anthology: a consortium of flexible stories that can overlap or contradict one another without one necessarily responding to another. Iliad, Odyssey, fragments, and summaries are stabilized instances of narratives that had previously existed as malleable story-patterns (https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511998409.005).

Second, oral poetry communicates through “traditional referentiality.” A formula, scene, or name can activate a much larger field of audience knowledge without citing a source. Similarity may consequently reveal the immanent tradition rather than the migration of a motif from poem X into poem Y.

Third, performance and reception matter as much as origin. Bakker argues that epic reference is an event in the present of performance: the performer “points at” and thereby realizes the heroic past. Treating the Iliad solely as a written artifact turns this dynamic activity into a static relation between texts (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/preface-36/).

Nagy’s evolutionary model adds that Homeric poetry became progressively stabilized through repeated Panhellenic performance. “Our” Iliad may be less multiform than the Cypria without having begun as an absolutely uniform authored text. Nagy calls the opposition between unique literary artistry and oral multiformity a false dichotomy (https://www-current.chs.harvard.edu/curated-article/gregory-nagy-homer-and-greek-myth/).

These objections do not deny that Iliad 1 and 24 activate stories found in the Cypria. They deny that the safest explanation is necessarily source-and-recipient borrowing.

II. The evidentiary problem: what “the Cypria” means

The Cypria covered the causes and early course of the Trojan War and, in Proclus’ account, had eleven books. The major evidence consists of:

• Proclus’ prose summary, transmitted with Homeric manuscripts;
• ancient quotations or testimonia collected in modern fragment editions, notably Alberto Bernabé’s Poetae Epici Graeci;
• Homeric scholia, including those in Venetus A;
• mythographical accounts such as pseudo-Apollodorus;
• later literature and art;
• papyrus hypotheses and educational summaries.

These are not equivalent kinds of evidence. A verbatim hexameter quotation is different from a prose synopsis, and both are different from a mythographer’s retelling. Even a genuine quotation from the Cypria proves the content of some textual form of that poem, not automatically the form of an eighth- or seventh-century precursor known to the Iliad.

Bruno Currie emphasizes how difficult it is to identify influence by the particular Cypria rather than by “the epic tradition quite generally.” A depiction of the Judgment of Paris on the Chigi Olpe around 630 BCE, for example, shows knowledge of the story but does not prove direct illustration of the Cypria. Currie accordingly allows that “the Cypria or a poem like it” may have been known to early poets while reserving confidence for unusual cases of verbal correspondence (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/greek-epic-cycle-and-its-ancient-reception/cypria/4208173BFCF2F8E91945C7D87482AFE8).

Burgess is even more explicit about reconstruction: all attempts to reconstruct the lost poems ultimately involve guesswork conditioned by assumptions about what an Epic Cycle is and how it was formed (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/greek-epic-cycle-and-its-ancient-reception/coming-adrift-the-limits-of-reconstruction-of-the-cyclic-poems/24FB12CB47FEA2ECD7B20A22EE3F7703). This caution is central to revised neoanalysis, not an oralist objection imposed from outside.

III. “Cypria motifs” in Iliad 1

1. The Will or plan of Zeus

The Iliad’s proem declares that through Achilles’ wrath many heroic souls were sent to Hades and “the plan/will of Zeus was being fulfilled” (Dios d’ eteleieto boulē, Iliad 1.5). The phrase poses an immediate interpretive question: does “Zeus’ plan” mean only the action Zeus undertakes after Thetis’ supplication—to honor Achilles by granting Trojan success—or does it also invoke the larger plan to cause the Trojan War and reduce the heroic population?

The Cypria tradition makes the larger plan explicit. Proclus begins: “Zeus, together with Themis, plans the Trojan War,” followed by the strife at Peleus and Thetis’ wedding and the Judgment of Paris (https://chs.harvard.edu/primary-source/epic-cycle-sb/). A verse fragment transmitted in the Homeric scholia and conventionally printed as Cypria fragment 1 in collections such as Bernabé describes Earth burdened by excessive human numbers and Zeus planning destructive warfare to relieve her. The Theban and Trojan wars become stages of a demographic or cosmic design.

Neoanalytic reading:

The matching Zeus-plan language, the proem’s emphasis on the deaths of “heroes,” and the scale implied by the phrase can make the Iliad’s wrath plot a concentrated realization of the larger depopulation plan. Achilles’ quarrel does not merely produce a local reversal; it advances a trans-epic divine program of heroic destruction. On this account, the Iliad deliberately narrows a comprehensive cyclic theology into one psychologically and ethically intense episode while allowing the proem to disclose the larger horizon.

This does not require the surviving Cypria to predate the Iliad. It requires the depopulation story to have existed in earlier poetry or myth. Its analogues in Hesiod and comparative Indo-European traditions support its antiquity. Philippe Rousseau notes that Hesiod’s Works and Days likewise links the disappearance of the heroic race with the Theban and Trojan wars, and that comparison with Indo-European traditions suggests an old theme of eschatological warfare (https://www-current.chs.harvard.edu/curated-article/philippe-rousseau-the-plot-of-zeus/).

Oralist reading:

The phrase is traditional and potentially multivalent. It can mean the plot being generated in the performance—the consequences of Achilles’ wrath and Zeus’ promise to Thetis—while resonating with a wider divine design known from other songs. An oral audience need not choose one exclusive referent. Traditional language can activate both local and panoramic frames.

Nagy makes the distinction by speaking of different epic plots as different “Plans of Zeus.” In the Iliad the plan organizes Achilles’ anger and honor; in the Cypria it organizes the war’s origin. The plots can be distinct without being mutually exclusive because each performance realizes Zeus’ will on its own narrative scale (https://classical-inquiries.chs.harvard.edu/trying-to-read-the-will-of-zeus/).

A performance-oriented intermediary position appears in work on the “junction” between Cypria and Iliad. The Cypria’s plan assimilates the whole Trojan story under an overarching divine design, whereas the Iliad’s more restricted plan could work before audiences attached to divergent local traditions; in this sense the Iliad is more Panhellenic (https://www.jstor.org/stable/1192467).

Best current conclusion:

Iliad 1.5 almost certainly invites a larger traditional resonance, but it cannot prove that the Iliad borrowed Cypria fragment 1 from a fixed poem. The phrase’s effectiveness arguably depends on controlled ambiguity: the immediate plot fulfills Zeus’ promise to Thetis, while the slaughter also belongs to the broader destruction of the heroic generation.

2. Eris, quarrel, and the compression of beginnings

The Cypria begins its causal chain with eris or neikos among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite at Peleus and Thetis’ wedding. The Iliad begins with another eris: Achilles and Agamemnon “stood apart in strife,” and the narrator asks which god brought them together to fight. Apollo supplies the immediate answer, but the verbal and thematic movement from divine causation to quarrel resembles the Cycle’s war-origin pattern.

A strong neoanalytic account treats this as meaningful relocation. The broad quarrel that generates the Trojan War is miniaturized into the quarrel that generates the Iliad. The wrath of Achilles becomes both a new beginning and a recapitulation of the war’s old beginning.

A strict oralist does not need “transference” from the Cypria to explain this. Quarrels generated by divine anger are fundamental epic story-patterns, and eris is both a narrative engine and a traditional category. Specificity must come from a cluster of correspondences, not the motif alone.

Here POxy 3829 matters, though with important limitations. Its antehomeric narrative apparently gives Zeus an unusually direct role: the version reported from P.Oxy. 3829 ii.12, paralleled by Hyginus, has Zeus exclude Eris from the wedding and instruct her to cause the goddesses’ quarrel. This makes the quarrel itself an instrument of Zeus’ design and has encouraged comparison with Iliad 1.3–5 and Zeus’ relation to battle-strife (evidence summarized in the Scripta Classica Israel search result at https://scriptaclassica.org/index.php/sci/article/download/15365/11361). But the papyrus is a later hypothesis or educational narrative, not an archaic manuscript of the Cypria. It demonstrates the ancient availability of a more integrated Zeus–Eris version; it does not establish that this was the exact version presupposed by the Iliad.

3. Achilles’ withdrawal at the Cypria–Iliad boundary

Proclus’ summary eventually reaches an arrangement by which Zeus relieves the Trojans by withdrawing Achilles from the Achaean side, after which the Iliad follows the Cypria (https://chs.harvard.edu/primary-source/epic-cycle-sb/). This creates an apparently seamless junction between epics.

Neoanalysts regard the conjunction as evidence that Achilles’ withdrawal was traditional outside the Iliad and perhaps existed in variant forms. Burgess stresses “competing versions”: even the Cypria’s endpoint may have involved a withdrawal or quarrel not identical to the Iliad’s Chryseis–Briseis narrative. The Iliad may have monumentalized one realization of a mobile story-pattern rather than invented withdrawal ex nihilo.

Oralists reply that Proclus or the organization of the later Cycle may have engineered continuity around a canonical Iliad. A summary designed to make poems form a chronological sequence is not neutral evidence of their original relationship. The safest inference is that withdrawal belonged to the tradition; the strongest claim—that a pre-Iliadic Cypria supplied the Iliad’s opening plot—remains unprovable.

IV. The Zeus–Thetis scene

1. Iliadic function

At Iliad 1.493–516, Thetis supplicates Zeus to honor her short-lived son by allowing the Trojans temporary success. Zeus silently deliberates, acknowledges conflict with Hera, and seals his promise with the irrevocable nod. The scene performs several functions simultaneously:

• it converts Achilles’ private grievance into Zeus’ plot;
• it links honor with mortality;
• it establishes Thetis as mediator between mortal suffering and divine decision;
• it opens a divine conflict that structures much of the battle narrative;
• it anticipates the movement from Thetis’ successful supplication of Zeus in Book 1 to Priam’s successful supplication of Achilles in Book 24.

Tsagalis describes the scene as a miniature or nucleus containing themes that expand through the poem: Achilles’ short lifespan, heroic liminality, the opposition between honor and life, and fulfillment of the Dios boulē (https://muse.jhu.edu/article/2653/summary).

2. Neoanalytic reconstruction

Thetis’ power over Zeus is not fully explained by her status as Achilles’ mother. Achilles reminds her that she once rescued Zeus from a conspiracy of Hera, Poseidon, and Athena by summoning the hundred-handed Briareus. The allusion is compressed, and the underlying story is otherwise marginal in surviving epic. Laura Slatkin’s influential line of interpretation, adopted and developed in later neoanalytic work, treats this as evidence of a larger suppressed mythology of Thetis.

The Cypria supplies another indispensable background: Thetis’ wedding to Peleus is the occasion at which the causal chain leading to the Trojan War begins. Iliad 24 later returns explicitly to that wedding. On a neoanalytic reading, the Book 1 Zeus–Thetis scene reverses and reactivates the war’s origin:

• At her wedding, divine action condemns Thetis to a mortal marriage and produces the conflict in which her son will die.
• In Iliad 1, Thetis approaches Zeus to secure honor for that son.
• Zeus can grant honor only through the violent plot that brings Achilles closer to death.
• The goddess who helped preserve Zeus’ sovereignty becomes the suppliant whose request advances the destruction of her own child.

The scene thus gains tragic force from knowledge outside the immediate Iliadic narrative.

3. Oralist and Tsagalean alternatives

A type-scene analysis emphasizes that the meeting is an elaborately constructed supplication: approach, physical contact, claim of prior benefit, request, hesitation, assent. Its meaning arises through performance conventions and its relation to other Iliadic supplications, especially Priam’s in Book 24. The scene does not require a reconstructed lost Thetis epic.

Tsagalis’ oral-palimpest model offers a middle position. Intertextual references that do not originate in one specific epic can be arranged into an Iliadic chain. Thetis’ aid to Zeus, her marriage, Achilles’ short life, the plan of Zeus, and supplication traditions may derive from different versions or narrative environments. The Iliad places them in close sequence, “rewoving” dispersed traditional material into a dramatically intensified structure (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/part-iv-intertextuality-and-intratextual-sequences-10-the-rhetorics-of-supplication-and-the-epic-intertext-iliad-i-493-516/).

That model preserves the neoanalytic insight that the scene is thick with external tradition while accepting the oralist objection that the tradition need not have existed as a single recoverable source-poem.

V. “Cypria motifs” in Iliad 24

Book 24 contains the Iliad’s most explicit compressed references to stories summarized in the Cypria.

1. The Judgment of Paris, Iliad 24.25–30

When the gods debate Hector’s corpse, Hera and Athena continue to oppose Troy because Paris once insulted them and favored Aphrodite. This is the Iliad’s only direct reference to the Judgment of Paris. Proclus gives the familiar Cypria sequence: at Peleus and Thetis’ wedding Eris causes a beauty contest; Zeus orders Hermes to lead the three goddesses to Paris; Paris chooses Aphrodite because she promises Helen (https://chs.harvard.edu/primary-source/epic-cycle-sb/).

Ancient critical controversy is itself part of the modern debate. Aristarchus objected to Iliad 24.25–30 on the ground that Homer did not otherwise know the Judgment and treated the passage as suspect or interpolated from the supposedly later Cycle. That judgment depended partly on a Homer-centric chronology in which “Homer” was earlier and aesthetically superior to cyclic epic. The ancient objection and its assumptions are summarized at https://classicalstudies.org/annual-meeting/583mazurek.

Neoanalytic interpretation:

The passage is a paradigmatic allusion. Its extreme compression assumes audience familiarity; it does not pause to narrate the apple, wedding, beauty contest, or promise of Helen. The reference therefore testifies to the pre-Iliadic availability of the story, whether or not the surviving Cypria was the direct source. Placed near the Iliad’s end, the allusion brings the war’s first cause into the final settlement over Hector and frames the whole poem between cyclic beginnings and Iliadic closure.

Oralist interpretation:

Compression is precisely how traditional referentiality works. The names, praise-and-blame vocabulary, and divine antagonism activate a known story-pattern without citing the Cypria. Nagy reads the verbs for Paris’ blaming Hera and Athena and praising Aphrodite as carrying both social and poetic meanings: the Judgment itself becomes an act of praise and blame (https://classical-inquiries.chs.harvard.edu/a-sampling-of-comments-on-iliad-rhapsody-24/). That interpretation locates the passage in a performance poetics rather than a source-critical relation.

Synthesis:

The passage refutes a crude claim that the Judgment must have been invented by a post-Iliadic Cypria. It does not prove that Iliad 24 depends on the text summarized by Proclus. The strongest secure statement is that the Iliad expects familiarity with a Judgment tradition substantially like the one later attached to the Cypria.

2. The wedding of Peleus and Thetis, Iliad 24.55–63

Hera defends Achilles’ superior status by recalling that the gods attended Thetis’ marriage to Peleus and that Apollo sang at the feast. Proclus places divine strife at this same wedding. The Iliad suppresses Eris in Hera’s speech but recalls the gathering itself.

The omission is interpreted differently:

• A neoanalyst may see “thematic silence”: the Iliad selects the element needed to distinguish Achilles’ divine parentage while allowing an informed audience to remember that the feast also generated the chain ending in Troy’s destruction and Achilles’ death.

• An oralist may say that the wedding is a multivalent traditional node. Hera’s rhetorical purpose determines which aspect she activates; there is no need to imagine deliberate suppression of a fixed Cypria scene.

Nagy connects Hera’s reference directly to the primal story of the wedding and Judgment. In Proclus, Eris produces neikos at the feast; in Iliad 24, that old divine quarrel continues to shape Hera and Athena’s hostility (https://classical-inquiries.chs.harvard.edu/a-sampling-of-comments-on-iliad-rhapsody-24/).

3. Structural return to Book 1

Thetis again ascends to Zeus in Book 24, now to transmit his order that Achilles return Hector’s body. This reverses the direction of Book 1:

• Book 1: Thetis asks Zeus to intensify the war so that Achilles will receive honor.
• Book 24: Zeus sends Thetis to bring Achilles back within human exchange and mourning.
• Book 1 moves from supplication to mass death.
• Book 24 moves from divine decision to ransom, shared grief, and burial.

Tsagalis and other synthetic interpreters see the two scenes as intratextual anchors. The Cypria’s wedding and Judgment enlarge their significance, but the Iliad has reorganized that inherited material around its own architecture of supplication, honor, mortality, and reconciliation.

VI. Achilles’ awareness of his death

1. What Achilles knows in the Iliad

Achilles’ knowledge is distributed across several stages:

• In Book 1, Thetis calls him short-lived and doomed to an especially brief life.
• In Iliad 9.410–416, Achilles reports Thetis’ prophecy of two fates: if he remains at Troy, he will lose his homecoming but win imperishable fame; if he returns home, he will lose that fame but live a long life.
• In Book 18, after Patroclus’ death, Achilles accepts that his own death will follow Hector’s.
• Hector’s dying prophecy identifies Paris and Apollo at the Scaean Gates as Achilles’ killers.
• The divine horse Xanthus also predicts death through a god and a man.
• In Book 24, Achilles’ encounter with Priam makes his own father’s future bereavement emotionally present.

The two-fates passage is especially important because it turns traditional plot into apparent character choice. Its logic is explicit:

Remain at Troy → nostos lost, kleos aphthiton gained.
Return home → kleos lost, long life gained.

The text and translation are quoted at https://chs.harvard.edu/giuseppe-lentini-refusing-an-odyssean-destiny-the-end-of-the-iliad-and-the-%CE%BA%CE%BB%CE%AD%CE%BF%CF%82-of-achilles/.

2. Neoanalytic interpretation

For neoanalysis, the audience knows more than the poem narrates: Achilles will be killed by Paris and Apollo near the Scaean Gates, and the Aethiopis tradition continues through his death, funeral, and posthumous destiny. The Iliad incorporates this future symbolically.

The death of Patroclus is the central case of motif transference. Patroclus functions as Achilles’ double:

• he enters battle in Achilles’ armor;
• he drives the Trojans back;
• Apollo intervenes;
• a mortal opponent completes the killing;
• his corpse and armor become objects of conflict;
• Thetis and the Nereids lament in anticipation of Achilles’ own death;
• Achilles receives new divine armor;
• the funeral of Patroclus anticipates Achilles’ funeral.

On this account, Achilles’ knowledge is not just psychological information. It activates a traditional narrative known to the audience and converts the remainder of the Iliad into a proleptic enactment of a death the poem will not narrate. Burgess’s The Death and Afterlife of Achilles explicitly reconstructs the Achilles tradition and argues that the Iliad alludes to the hero’s traditional death through motif transference, while rejecting the need for direct textual borrowing (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2009/2009.07.67/).

A later synthetic study similarly argues that structural and thematic correspondences incorporate Achilles’ death symbolically. Achilles earns the fame associated with a heroic battlefield death without dying inside the Iliad: his victory over Hector prefigures Troy’s fall, while repeated foreshadowing gives his triumph the aura of his own death (https://doi.org/10.1163/1568525x-12342767).

The Cypria also contains or is associated with anticipations of Achilles’ death. In pseudo-Apollodorus’ account attributed by Martin West to Cypria material, Thetis warns Achilles not to kill Tennes because Apollo will eventually kill him. A D-scholion to Iliad 19.326 reports a tradition in which Peleus, foreseeing Achilles’ death at Troy, hides him among Lycomedes’ daughters. But there is no comparably early external source explicitly attesting the Iliad’s precise choice between two fates. Martina Hirschberger therefore distinguishes the firmly established tradition of death by Paris and Apollo from the more specifically Iliadic formulation of the alternative destinies (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110272017.185/html).

3. Oralist interpretation

Oralists agree that performers and audiences knew Achilles was destined to die at Troy. They differ over what follows from that knowledge.

For Nagy, Achilles’ death is inseparable from kleos. The formula kleos aphthiton, “imperishable fame,” belongs to inherited Indo-European praise poetics. Achilles’ decision dramatizes the hero’s exchange of biological life for perpetual existence in song. His “awareness” can therefore be metapoetic: by choosing death at Troy he chooses the Iliadic tradition that continually performs his fame.

From this perspective, differences among prophecies do not necessarily expose transferred source-material. They may reflect multiform traditions activated at different moments. Book 9 temporarily presents a meaningful choice; after Patroclus’ death, that choice closes. Performance produces the experience of movement from possibility to necessity even though the audience knows the traditional outcome.

Foley’s model likewise interprets references to Achilles’ death as signals to the whole tradition. No unique Aethiopis or Achilleis need stand behind each one. The audience supplies the traditional implication from a stable narrative skeleton whose details can vary.

Some oralist critics consequently question the strongest neoanalytic doublet arguments. A scene such as Thetis’ lament can be well motivated by Patroclus’ death, consistent with lament conventions, and powerful within the Iliad without having been transferred from a poem about Achilles’ death. A critique of the consensus argues that Thetis’ mourning in Book 18 is neither as anomalous nor as uniquely indicative of an Achilleis, Aethiopis, or Memnonis as neoanalysis has maintained (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:f6f16918-26f2-4035-be4e-675b40c0bf7d/files/m873fb86eabff593b51421a245495e580).

4. Best synthesis

The Iliad’s audience almost certainly knew a story in which Achilles died before Troy through Apollo and Paris. The poem repeatedly exploits that knowledge. What cannot ordinarily be demonstrated is that each proleptic scene derives from a particular lost poem rather than from the shared Achilles tradition.

The most defensible synthesis therefore has two levels:

• Traditional outcome: Achilles’ death was part of the stable story-world and conditioned audience response.
• Iliadic design: the poem organized that knowledge into an evolving subjective awareness—short life, alternative fates, acceptance after Patroclus, exact prophecy, and anticipatory mourning.

Neoanalysis explains the precision and cumulative architecture of the foreshadowing; oralism explains how that architecture could be generated and recognized without fixed textual source-and-recipient relations.

VII. Bernabé’s fragments and the limits of fragmentary evidence

“Bernabé fragments” should not be treated as a manuscript called the Cypria. Bernabé’s Poetae Epici Graeci assembles quotations and testimonia from heterogeneous transmitting sources. Numbering also differs among Bernabé, Davies, and West, so fragment numbers are less secure identifiers than the transmitting source itself.

Three evidentiary levels must be kept separate:

1. Verbatim fragments

A quoted hexameter can support arguments about diction, meter, and thematic formulation. Cypria fragment 1, transmitted through scholia on Iliad 1.5, is especially important because its Zeus-plan vocabulary can be compared with the Iliadic proem.

Even here, attribution and transmission matter. A scholion may preserve an ancient quotation accurately, but that does not date the quoted formulation or prove that it was the only Cypria version.

2. Proclus’ summary

Proclus supplies sequence and broad content: Zeus and Themis’ plan, the wedding, Eris, Judgment, Helen’s departure, the expeditions, and the transition to the Iliad. It is indispensable for reconstruction but offers little exact wording and may reflect later cyclic organization.

Foley and Arft therefore warn against imposing anthology-like sequence and textual interaction on what may have developed as a constellation of narratives (https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511998409.005).

3. Testimonia, scholia, and mythographers

The Achilles-at-Scyros tradition illustrates the difficulty. Proclus’ Cypria apparently placed Achilles on Scyros after the Mysian expedition, where he married Deidameia; Pausanias preserves the names Pyrrhus and Neoptolemus in material identified as Cypria fragment 21 in Bernabé. Other sources instead tell the better-known story in which Achilles is hidden on Scyros because of a prophecy and exposed by Odysseus. These may be different realizations rather than corrupt reports of one fixed plot (https://classics-at.chs.harvard.edu/achilles-at-scyros-and-the-cypria-tradition-and-myth-in-the-epic-cycle/).

Neoanalysis uses such materials comparatively to reconstruct the probable stable core. Oralism stresses the variation itself as evidence that “the Cypria” was multiform or drew upon multiform traditions. Revised neoanalysis accepts both points but demands multiple independent indicators before positing specific Iliadic allusion.

VIII. The Venetus A scholia and digital Homer

Venetus A is a tenth-century Iliad manuscript containing extensive scholia derived from diverse ancient scholarship. It is exceptionally important but is not a neutral archive of archaic epic. Its notes preserve Alexandrian criticism, mythography, variant readings, quotations, and later accretions through complicated transmission.

The Homer Multitext project provides a complete digital text of the Venetus A Iliad and scholia (https://www.homermultitext.org/texts.html), including a line-oriented edition (https://www.homermultitext.org/texts/venetus-a-by-line.txt) and manuscript-linked reading environment (https://beyond-translation.perseus.org/reader/urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0012.tlg001.msA:1.1-1.25).

This matters methodologically in several ways:

• Scholars can distinguish scholia attached to particular Iliadic lines and compare marginal zones.
• Searchable data make it easier to trace repeated terms such as boulē, eris, and references to cyclic poets.
• Images allow verification of editorial supplements and marginal placement.
• Different scholia can be separated by hand, location, and likely source instead of being cited as an undifferentiated “ancient scholion.”

But digitization has also strengthened caution. The Homer Multitext project emphasizes that Venetus A creatively combines material from multiple sources and that the exact transmission routes remain incompletely understood. By 2018 the project had a complete first text of its Iliad and scholia and was beginning to compare additional manuscripts systematically (http://homermultitext.github.io/chsseminar/scholia-2018/).

For the present debate, the scholia have two opposed uses:

• Neoanalytic use: ancient scholars preserve genuine cyclic verses and traditions, giving external controls for interpreting compressed Iliadic references.

• Oralist use: the scholia document ancient reception, editorial ideology, and later harmonization as much as archaic sources. Aristarchus’ rejection of the Judgment passage, for instance, reveals his Homer-centric assumptions; it cannot settle the passage’s archaic status.

The digital turn has not made the scholia automatically more authoritative. It has made their heterogeneity more visible and their use more reproducible.

IX. Comparative Indo-European poetics

Comparative evidence enters the dispute at two distinct levels.

1. Reconstruction of old narrative complexes

Neoanalytically inclined scholars use cross-cultural parallels to argue that a motif is older than the surviving Greek poems. The Earth burdened by excessive heroes, a supreme god’s plan of destructive war, and an eschatological reduction of a heroic generation have parallels beyond the Cypria. Such comparison makes it less plausible that a late cyclic poet simply invented the plan after reading Iliad 1.5.

The argument is probabilistic, not textual. An Indo-European analogue can support the antiquity of a narrative pattern; it cannot prove the wording or plot of a Greek source-poem.

Currie’s comparison of the Iliad with Gilgamesh extends the method beyond Indo-European evidence. Gilgamesh is Near Eastern rather than Indo-European, so it cannot by itself establish Proto-Indo-European inheritance. It can, however, reveal recurrent epic structures concerning mortality, heroic friendship, grief, and wisdom. Currie’s broader comparative procedure weakens simplistic source hunting while strengthening the case that the Iliad’s treatment of Achilles belongs to a deep epic discourse on mortality.

2. Formula, fame, and performance

Nagy’s use of comparative poetics centers on kleos aphthiton, “imperishable fame.” Its inherited character shows that Achilles’ choice is not merely a unique literary idea; it realizes an old ideology in which the hero accepts death in exchange for undying praise. The Iliad is the medium in which the bargain is fulfilled.

This is an important difference in interpretive emphasis:

• Neoanalysis asks which Achilles-death narrative the passage evokes.
• Nagy asks how inherited praise language defines Achilles as the exemplary hero and how performance continually renews his kleos.

Bakker similarly treats traditional language as action. An inherited expression does not merely preserve a fossil from an older text; in performance it actively brings the heroic past and its values into the present.

Foley’s principal comparative evidence comes not from reconstructed Indo-European language but from living oral epic traditions. Such traditions generate multiple bounded realizations of the same narrative field, with variation in names, sequence, and detail. That comparative record supports a model in which overlap among Iliad and Cypria need not be direct borrowing.

3. Evidentiary discipline

Comparative poetics is strongest when it establishes:

• the antiquity of a formula or broad narrative pattern;
• the range of variation normal in oral traditions;
• the ideological force of fame, death, divine design, or heroic succession.

It is weakest when used to reconstruct the exact contents of a lost Greek poem. Neither a Vedic verbal parallel nor a South Slavic narrative analogue can identify the specific Cypria known to an Iliadic performer.

X. POxy 3829: what changed, and what did not

1. Correcting the chronological premise

POxy 3829 should not be described straightforwardly as a papyrus “discovered since 2000.” It is catalogued as P.Oxy. LVI 3829. What has expanded markedly since 2000 is digital availability, imaging, indexing, and the integration of papyri with searchable Homeric and scholastic corpora. Oxford’s digital item was posted in 2022 (https://doi.org/10.25446/oxford.21175024). The relevant post-2000 development is therefore chiefly digital access and renewed analysis, not necessarily archaeological discovery.

2. Contents

Oxford identifies the papyrus as “Homer, Iliad: Catechism, and Hypotheses to Book I” and divides it into three sections:

• lines 1–7a: end of a catechism listing Iliadic characters;
• lines 7b–38: an antehomeric narrative from Zeus’ plan to destroy the heroic generation through the Judgment of Paris;
• lines 39–44: Iliad 1.1 and a summary of Book 1.

The official description is at http://archive.csad.ox.ac.uk/POxy/papyri/vol56/pages/3829.htm.

A rough quantitative description clarifies the papyrus’ emphasis. Treating lines 7b–38 as approximately 31.5 lines out of 44 gives:

31.5 ÷ 44 × 100 ≈ 71.6%.

Thus roughly 72% of the preserved line-space, by this crude line count, belongs to antehomeric narrative. The figure is only approximate because line 7 is divided between sections and written lines are not equal semantic units. It nevertheless shows that the document embeds the opening of the Iliad in a substantial account of pre-Iliadic causation rather than treating Book 1 in isolation.

3. Significance for the Zeus-plan question

The papyrus directly juxtaposes:

• Zeus’ intention to destroy the heroic generation;
• the wedding/Judgment complex;
• the first line and summary of the Iliad.

That juxtaposition confirms that at least one ancient pedagogical or exegetical tradition read Iliad 1 against the Cypria-like prehistory of the war. Its version apparently gives Zeus a more direct role in arranging Eris’ intervention than Proclus does.

This supports three conclusions:

• The broad Zeus-plan interpretation of Iliad 1 was not solely a modern neoanalytic construction.
• Ancient readers possessed multiple versions of the causal chain.
• The boundary between “background myth” and interpretation of the Iliad was permeable.

4. Why it does not decide the debate

POxy 3829 is not a manuscript of the Cypria. It is a later catechism/hypothesis whose purpose is explanatory. Its narrative may harmonize different materials precisely because students required a coherent prehistory.

Accordingly:

• Neoanalysts can cite it as evidence that the Iliad’s opening was intelligible against an old cyclic complex.
• Oralists can cite its divergence from Proclus as evidence of multiformity and later recombination.
• Textualists cannot safely infer that its wording reproduces a pre-Iliadic Cypria.

Its most important contribution is therefore not proof of dependence but evidence for reception and variant mythographic organization.

5. Broader digital effects

Digital analysis since 2000 has improved the debate more than it has transformed its answer. It has enabled:

• direct inspection of papyrus images and transcriptions;
• comparison of papyrus hypotheses with Venetus A and other scholia;
• searches across line-indexed scholia;
• identification of recurrent diction and narrative clusters;
• clearer separation of manuscript evidence from modern reconstructed editions.

These advances favor synthesis because they reveal both patterned correspondence and textual variation. They make a rigid “Homer copied the Cypria” model less plausible, while also making it difficult to dismiss cyclic correspondences as accidental.

XI. The current state of synthesis in recent books

1. Burgess

Burgess’s work is foundational for synthesis. His 2006 article explicitly states that neoanalysis, oral theory, and intertextuality are compatible once motif transference is detached from simplistic written borrowing (https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf). His Achilles monograph reconstructs the traditional fabula while treating Iliadic relations as interactions among oral narratives rather than texts (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2009/2009.07.67/).

The gain is explanatory precision without a historical “master text.” The residual problem is criteria: when does a motif cluster point to a specific external fabula rather than the general tradition?

2. Tsagalis

Tsagalis’ The Oral Palimpsest and Early Greek Epic: Language, Interpretation, Performance offer the most explicit theoretical merger. His 2023 volume’s opening chapter, “Towards an Oral, Intertextual Neoanalysis,” reviews the limits of both theories and advocates a flexible philological method combining meter, formula, allusive motifs, narrative structure, and performance (review at https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2024/2024.03.17/; publisher description at https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110981384/html).

The book also places this synthesis alongside narratology, cognitive approaches, Indo-European comparison, Near Eastern relations, and performance. It therefore treats the divide not as a binary choice but as one issue within a larger ecology of early epic.

3. The 2015 Cambridge Companion

The Greek Epic Cycle and its Ancient Reception deliberately stages the disagreement. Its contents place Burgess on the limits of reconstruction, Foley and Arft on oral tradition, Kullmann on motif and source research, and Currie on the Cypria within one volume (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/greek-epic-cycle-and-its-ancient-reception/21C01778DFE41E056583F8845E3012C9).

The juxtaposition reveals substantial common ground:

• cyclic material often preserves very old stories;
• surviving summaries are late and selective;
• direct textual dependence is difficult to demonstrate;
• performance and multiformity must be considered;
• the Iliad nevertheless differentiates itself from broader Trojan-war traditions through radical selection and concentration.

But the volume does not erase the central dispute. Foley and Arft’s constellation model undercuts “transference” from one poem to another, whereas Kullmann’s model still seeks identifiable source traditions and regards incomplete assimilation as evidence.

4. Andrew Porter, Homer and the Epic Cycle

Andrew Porter’s 2022 monograph, Homer and the Epic Cycle: Recovering the Oral Traditional Relationship, represents the strongest recent oral-traditional synthesis. It challenges the Homer-centric framework inherited from Aristotle, Proclus, and later criticism; distinguishes performers, patrons or collectors, and scribes or poets in the formation of memorialized songs; and emphasizes shared traditional devices rather than linear textual influence (https://brill.com/display/title/59806).

Porter’s synthesis is asymmetrical: it incorporates neoanalytic observations about meaningful correspondence but explains them primarily through oral-traditional relations. It is therefore more skeptical than Burgess or Tsagalis about reconstructing a specific source-tradition from an Iliadic anomaly.

5. Current balance of opinion

No recent monograph has produced a universally accepted test for distinguishing:

A. common inheritance,
B. generic traditional resonance,
C. allusion to an identifiable song-tradition,
D. dependence on a fixed text.

The field’s center has nevertheless moved decisively away from both extremes:

• Few scholars now treat the Cycle simply as a late, inferior compilation assembled from Homer.
• Few accept a naïve model in which a single literate Iliad-poet mechanically borrowed episodes from fixed pre-Homeric cyclic texts.
• Many accept that stories later attested in the Cycle were pre-Iliadic and available in oral traditions.
• Many also accept that the Iliad’s arrangement of these materials is selective and often self-conscious.
• The point of contention is the recoverable specificity of the antecedent tradition.

XII. Final assessment

The “Cypria motifs” in Iliad 1 and 24 are real in the minimal sense that the Iliad invokes the same story-complexes later attributed to the Cypria:

• Zeus’ destructive plan;
• divinely generated eris;
• Peleus and Thetis’ wedding;
• the Judgment of Paris;
• Achilles’ withdrawal;
• Thetis’ mediation between Zeus and Achilles;
• the chain connecting Achilles’ honor with his death.

Neoanalysis best explains why these motifs occur at structurally privileged positions. Iliad 1 converts the cosmic or trans-epic plan into the wrath plot; Iliad 24 recalls the wedding and Judgment as the poem resolves Hector’s death; Patroclus and Hector foreshadow Achilles’ fate; and the two Zeus–Thetis scenes frame the movement from injured honor to mortal reconciliation.

Oralism best explains how those effects can exist without written source dependence. Formulaic language, type-scenes, traditional story-skeletons, and audience competence allow a performance to evoke a large narrative field in a few words. Contradictory Cypria variants are expected rather than embarrassing under this model.

The Zeus–Thetis scene is therefore not adequately described either as a self-contained supplication or as a passage lifted from one lost epic. It is an Iliadic construction made from a dense traditional complex: Thetis’ power, her forced mortal marriage, the divine wedding, Achilles’ brief life, Zeus’ sovereignty, and the exchange of death for honor.

Achilles’ awareness similarly combines stable tradition and Iliadic development. The audience knows his death; Achilles is made to progress toward that knowledge and acceptance. Neoanalytic prolepsis and oral-traditional resonance are complementary descriptions of that effect, provided “allusion” is not made to imply a fixed written source.

POxy 3829 has reinforced this synthesis rather than settled the dispute. Its extensive antehomeric hypothesis—roughly 72% of its preserved 44-line layout by a simple line count—shows an ancient interpretive tradition joining Zeus’ destruction plan, the Judgment, and Iliad 1. But its status as a later catechism/hypothesis and its divergence from Proclus also demonstrate multiformity. The post-2000 digital transformation of this papyrus and the Venetus A scholia has made correspondences easier to verify while making the layered, unstable character of the evidence harder to ignore.

The current best model is consequently “oral intertextual neoanalysis”: the Iliad is a highly organized, relatively stabilized performance-tradition that meaningfully reworks and signals other Trojan-war traditions, some recoverable through cyclic fragments and scholia, but usually not reducible to direct borrowing from the poems known to later antiquity as the Epic Cycle. This synthesis narrows the divide but does not abolish it. Burgess, Currie, and Tsagalis retain greater confidence that motif clusters identify particular external narratives; Nagy, Foley, and Bakker place greater weight on multiform tradition, performance, and the audience’s activation of inherited meaning. The surviving evidence supports both the specificity of some allusions—above all the Judgment of Paris—and persistent agnosticism about the exact texts or performances that carried them before the Iliad.

3-MONTH INSTAGRAM LEAD-GENERATION ROADMAP  
Digital marketing service provider targeting Indian SMBs and emerging brands  
Monthly budget: ₹40,000

## 1. Executive summary

The strategy combines authority-building organic content with Instagram Lead Ads, click-to-Instagram Direct ads, and retargeting. The primary offer should be a free “15-minute Instagram Growth Audit” or “90-Day Lead-Generation Plan,” rather than a generic request for a sales call.

India is strongly mobile-first: mobile accounted for 78% of digital-media spending in FY24, while social media represented 30% of digital ad spending. Short-form video, automation and data-driven marketing are among the leading trends identified by Indian marketers ([Ipsos, State of Digital Marketing in India 2024–25](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/publication/documents/2024-12/The%20State%20of%20Digital%20Marketing%20in%20India%202024-25.pdf)). This supports a Reels-led, mobile-native strategy.

### Three-month outcome target

| Month | Total budget | Paid media | Organic/tools/support | Target valid leads | Target blended CPL* | Target qualified calls |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Month 1 | ₹40,000 | ₹30,000 | ₹10,000 | 55–60 | ₹667–₹727 | 14–18 |
| Month 2 | ₹40,000 | ₹32,000 | ₹8,000 | 70–80 | ₹500–₹571 | 21–28 |
| Month 3 | ₹40,000 | ₹34,000 | ₹6,000 | 85–100 | ₹400–₹471 | 30–40 |
| **Total** | **₹120,000** | **₹96,000** | **₹24,000** | **210–240** | **₹500–₹571** | **65–86** |

\*Blended CPL = total monthly marketing expenditure ÷ valid leads. Paid-media CPL should be reported separately.

A “valid lead” means a unique decision-maker who supplies usable contact information and represents an operating business. A “qualified call” means the business has a relevant service need, reasonable budget or commercial potential, and agrees to a discovery call.

These are planning targets, not guaranteed results. Indian Instagram CPL estimates vary enormously by niche, competition and lead definition; one published range spans ₹3.50–₹1,500 per lead ([Shiprocket](https://www.shiprocket.in/blog/instagram-advertising-cost/)). Since this offer targets business owners rather than mass-market consumers, the roadmap uses the more conservative ₹425–₹600 paid CPL range.

---

# 2. Positioning, audience and offer

## Core positioning

“Practical growth marketing for Indian SMBs and emerging brands that need measurable leads—not vanity metrics.”

Avoid positioning as a full-service agency for every industry. For the first 90 days, prioritize two or three segments in which the provider can create credible examples:

1. D2C and emerging consumer brands.
2. Education, coaching or professional services.
3. Local multi-location businesses such as clinics, fitness, interiors or hospitality.
4. B2B services with a clear minimum contract value.

Create separate messaging for each chosen segment, even if delivery is similar.

## Primary lead magnet

**Free 15-minute Instagram Lead-Generation Audit**

Deliverables:

- Profile and offer diagnosis.
- Three missed lead opportunities.
- One sample campaign concept.
- Indicative 90-day action plan.
- Optional proposal after the audit.

The audit creates more immediate value than “book a sales call.” It can be delivered using a reusable one-page template, keeping fulfillment time below 20 minutes per qualified lead.

## Secondary lead magnets

- “Instagram Content Calendar for Indian SMBs.”
- “₹50K Meta Ads Planning Calculator.”
- “25 Reels Hooks for Founders.”
- “Instagram Profile Conversion Checklist.”
- “D2C/Service Business Ad Creative Scorecard.”

Each lead magnet should have one keyword, such as **AUDIT**, **CALENDAR** or **LEADS**, to make attribution and DM automation easier.

---

# 3. Measurable goals

## Month 1: Build and validate

- Generate 55–60 valid leads.
- Keep paid CPL at or below ₹600 by the end of the month.
- Generate at least 14 qualified calls.
- Achieve at least 25% valid-lead-to-booked-call conversion.
- Respond manually or automatically to 90% of inquiries within five minutes.
- Identify two winning audience/creative combinations.
- Build retargeting pools from video viewers, profile visitors and engagers.

## Month 2: Optimize and establish proof

- Generate 70–80 valid leads.
- Reduce paid CPL to ₹475–₹525.
- Generate 21–28 qualified calls.
- Reach a 30% lead-to-booked-call rate.
- Publish at least one documented case study or campaign teardown.
- Shift at least 60% of prospecting spend to proven creative angles.
- Keep invalid/duplicate leads below 20%.

## Month 3: Scale qualified demand

- Generate 85–100 valid leads.
- Reduce paid CPL to ₹400–₹450.
- Generate 30–40 qualified calls.
- Reach a 35% lead-to-booked-call rate.
- Generate at least 6–10 proposals, depending on service price and qualification criteria.
- Attribute every proposal and closed client to campaign, ad, content post or DM keyword.

## Funnel assumptions

A Month 3 base case could be:

- 90 valid leads.
- 35% book a call: `90 × 35% = 31.5`, or approximately 32 calls.
- 70% attend: `32 × 70% = 22` attended calls.
- 35% receive proposals: `22 × 35% = 7.7`, or approximately 8 proposals.
- 25% of proposals close: `8 × 25% = 2 clients`.

Closing rates will depend more on offer strength, case studies, pricing and sales skill than Instagram reach.

---

# 4. Organic content system

## Four content pillars

### Pillar 1: Education and actionable strategy — 35%

Purpose: Establish expertise and create saves/shares.

Topics:

- How Indian SMBs should divide a ₹50K marketing budget.
- Why boosting posts is not a complete lead strategy.
- Three reasons Instagram leads fail to convert.
- Reels hooks for local businesses or D2C brands.
- Lead-form questions that filter poor prospects.
- How to calculate CPL, CAC and break-even ROAS.

CTA: “Save this,” “DM CALENDAR,” or “Comment CHECKLIST.”

### Pillar 2: Proof and campaign analysis — 25%

Purpose: Reduce perceived risk.

Topics:

- Before/after profile audits.
- Anonymized campaign results.
- “What I would change in this brand’s Instagram funnel.”
- Breakdown of a public brand campaign.
- Lead quality or CPL optimization experiments.
- Testimonials and client screenshots with permission.

CTA: “DM AUDIT for the same analysis.”

If there are no client case studies, clearly label examples as simulations or public teardowns. Do not imply fictional results are client outcomes.

### Pillar 3: Founder pain points and opinion — 20%

Purpose: Make content relatable and demonstrate commercial understanding.

Topics:

- “More followers will not fix a weak offer.”
- “Your agency report should answer these five questions.”
- “Why cheap leads can be expensive.”
- Founder reactions to common marketing advice.
- Agency red flags.
- What businesses should prepare before hiring a marketer.

CTA: Ask a diagnostic question, such as “Which problem is costing you more: reach, leads or follow-up?”

### Pillar 4: Offers, process and behind the scenes — 20%

Purpose: Convert attention into inquiries.

Topics:

- What happens during a free audit.
- How campaigns are researched and launched.
- Weekly optimization checklist.
- Screen recording of a dashboard or content workflow.
- Service packages and client-fit criteria.
- Limited monthly audit or onboarding slots.

CTA: “DM AUDIT” or “Apply through the link in bio.”

## Weekly posting cadence

| Day | Format | Pillar | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monday | 30–45 second Reel | Education | “Three reasons your Instagram ads produce poor leads” |
| Tuesday | 7–9 slide carousel | Education | “₹50K SMB marketing budget breakdown” |
| Wednesday | 30–60 second Reel | Pain point/opinion | “Stop measuring your agency by followers” |
| Thursday | Case-study carousel or static proof post | Proof | “How this landing page could cut CPL” |
| Friday | 20–40 second Reel | Offer/process | “What you receive in a free audit” |
| Saturday | Stories and optional live/Q&A | Mixed | Poll, FAQ, audit clip |
| Sunday | Stories only or no post | Community | Weekly recap and next-week teaser |

Minimum cadence:

- 3 Reels per week.
- 2 carousels/static posts per week.
- 3–7 Story frames per day, five days per week.
- One Live, collaboration or Q&A every two weeks.
- 15 minutes of purposeful engagement before and after posting.

This produces approximately 20 feed posts and 60–100 Story frames per month without requiring advanced production.

## Six reusable post templates

### Template 1: “Three mistakes” Reel

Structure:

1. Hook: “If your Instagram leads disappear after submitting the form, check these three things.”
2. Mistake one.
3. Mistake two.
4. Mistake three.
5. CTA: “DM AUDIT and I’ll identify the biggest leak in your funnel.”

Reuse for content, ads, landing pages, follow-up and reporting.

### Template 2: Problem–diagnosis–fix carousel

Slides:

1. Painful headline.
2. Symptom.
3. Likely cause.
4–6. Corrective steps.
7. Example.
8. CTA.

Example: “Getting leads but no sales? Your form may be attracting the wrong buyer.”

### Template 3: Campaign teardown

Structure:

- Show a public ad, profile or landing page.
- Identify what works.
- Identify one conversion obstacle.
- Present a revised hook or CTA.
- Invite the audience to request an audit.

Add a clear note that the analysis is independent unless the business is a client.

### Template 4: Mini case study

Structure:

- Client/industry context.
- Initial problem.
- Action taken.
- Measured result.
- Lesson for similar businesses.
- CTA.

If confidentiality applies, anonymize the client but retain the dates, metric definitions and scope.

### Template 5: Myth-versus-reality founder Reel

Examples:

- Myth: “More followers automatically mean more leads.”
- Reality: “A smaller, relevant audience with a clear offer often converts better.”
- Action: Explain one change the founder can make today.
- CTA: Ask viewers to comment with their current challenge.

### Template 6: Checklist/lead-magnet post

Structure:

- Strong headline: “The seven-point Instagram lead funnel checklist.”
- Show three points in the post.
- Gate the complete checklist behind a keyword.
- CTA: “Comment CHECKLIST or DM CHECKLIST.”

One template can be reskinned for multiple segments and repurposed into a Reel, carousel, Story sequence and ad.

---

# 5. Paid-ad strategy

## Campaign architecture

Use Meta Ads Manager rather than relying primarily on boosted posts.

### Campaign A: Cold-audience Lead Ads

Objective: Leads  
Conversion location: Instagram Instant Form  
Offer: Free audit or industry-specific marketing plan

Form fields:

- Name.
- Business email.
- Phone/WhatsApp number.
- Business name.
- Website or Instagram handle.
- Industry.
- Approximate monthly marketing/ad budget.
- Main marketing challenge.
- Preferred call time.
- Consent checkbox and privacy-policy link.

Use a higher-intent form or an additional review step if invalid leads become excessive. Meta’s lead-generation guidance notes that instant forms are mobile-first, fast-loading and can autofill information, while CRM integration can support direct lead retrieval and later optimization ([Meta lead-generation guide](https://www.psmbrokerage.com/hubfs/LeadGenerationGuide.pdf)).

### Campaign B: Click-to-Instagram Direct

Objective: Leads or messaging, depending on current account options  
CTA: “Send message”  
Opening prompt: “Tell me your industry and monthly marketing budget, and I’ll recommend the first three actions.”

This captures prospects who are not ready to complete a formal application. Count a DM as a lead only after obtaining business/contact details and establishing a relevant need.

### Campaign C: Retargeting

Audiences:

- 50% or 75% Reel/video viewers.
- Instagram profile engagers.
- Lead-form openers who did not submit, where available.
- Website visitors.
- People who saved or interacted with posts.
- Existing lead list, excluding converted clients.

Creative:

- Case studies.
- Testimonials.
- “What you get in the audit.”
- Objection-handling videos.
- Deadline or limited-slot messages.

### Campaign D: Creative/video-view testing

Use a small budget to test hooks and build low-cost video-viewing audiences. Do not optimize the majority of spend for engagement; the primary business objective remains qualified leads.

## Audience strategy

Test three prospecting groups:

1. **Broad entrepreneur audience:** India, age approximately 24–45, suitable geographies, with minimal interest restrictions.
2. **Interest/behavior audience:** entrepreneurship, small business, D2C, Shopify, business software, digital advertising and related interests.
3. **Segment-specific audience:** one ad set each for the selected priority verticals.

Location options:

- Tier 1: Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune, Kolkata and Ahmedabad.
- Tier 2 tests: Jaipur, Chandigarh, Indore, Surat, Lucknow, Kochi, Coimbatore and similar commercially relevant cities.

Do not over-constrain the audience with many stacked interests. Once there is enough high-quality first-party data, test lookalikes of qualified leads or clients—not merely all form submissions.

## Monthly campaign allocation

### Month 1: Testing

| Use | % of paid budget | Amount |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cold Lead Ads | 60% | ₹18,000 |
| Click-to-DM ads | 20% | ₹6,000 |
| Retargeting | 15% | ₹4,500 |
| Video/creative testing | 5% | ₹1,500 |
| **Total** | **100%** | **₹30,000** |

Test:

- Three audience groups.
- Two offers.
- Three hooks.
- At least two formats: vertical video and carousel/static.

Avoid creating too many low-budget ad sets. Start with approximately 3–4 active prospecting ad sets and consolidate as evidence emerges.

### Month 2: Optimization

| Use | % of paid budget | Amount |
|---|---:|---:|
| Winning Lead Ads | 60% | ₹19,200 |
| Click-to-DM | 15% | ₹4,800 |
| Retargeting | 20% | ₹6,400 |
| New creative tests | 5% | ₹1,600 |
| **Total** | **100%** | **₹32,000** |

Actions:

- Pause high-spend ads with weak lead quality.
- Move spend toward the best offer/audience pair.
- Launch case-study retargeting.
- Separate reporting for raw, valid and qualified leads.
- Test a segment-specific audit page or form.

### Month 3: Controlled scaling

| Use | % of paid budget | Amount |
|---|---:|---:|
| Scaled winning Lead Ads | 55% | ₹18,700 |
| Click-to-DM | 15% | ₹5,100 |
| Retargeting | 25% | ₹8,500 |
| New creative tests | 5% | ₹1,700 |
| **Total** | **100%** | **₹34,000** |

Increase winning budgets gradually rather than making abrupt daily changes. Retain at least 5% for fresh creative because ad fatigue and auction conditions can change quickly.

## Reach and lead projections

“Reach” below means estimated unique paid reach, not followers gained. Calculation:

`Paid impressions = spend ÷ CPM × 1,000`  
`Estimated reach = impressions ÷ average frequency`  
`Paid leads = spend ÷ paid CPL`

| Month | Paid spend | Planning CPM | Estimated impressions | Assumed frequency | Estimated paid reach | Paid CPL | Paid leads | Organic/DM leads | Total leads |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | ₹30,000 | ₹120 | 250,000 | 1.7 | 147,000 | ₹600 | 50 | 5–10 | 55–60 |
| 2 | ₹32,000 | ₹115 | 278,000 | 1.8 | 154,000 | ₹500 | 64 | 6–16 | 70–80 |
| 3 | ₹34,000 | ₹110 | 309,000 | 1.9 | 163,000 | ₹425 | 80 | 5–20 | 85–100 |

Example Month 1 calculations:

- Impressions: `₹30,000 ÷ ₹120 × 1,000 = 250,000`.
- Reach: `250,000 ÷ 1.7 = approximately 147,000`.
- Paid leads: `₹30,000 ÷ ₹600 = 50`.
- Total leads: `50 paid + 5–10 organic/DM = 55–60`.

The declining CPM and CPL assume improving creative, retargeting data and qualification—not automatic platform improvement. Published India cost figures vary materially by source, and even the same campaign can change with geography, seasonality, audience competition and ad relevance. Shiprocket specifically identifies objective, targeting, competition, seasonality, estimated action rate and ad relevance as cost drivers ([source](https://www.shiprocket.in/blog/instagram-advertising-cost/)).

## Ad creative concepts

1. **Founder-to-camera:** “If your business spends ₹50K a month on marketing but cannot explain where the leads came from, this audit is for you.”
2. **Checklist carousel:** “Seven leaks raising your Instagram CPL.”
3. **Screen-record audit:** Show how an Instagram profile or landing page is evaluated.
4. **Case-study creative:** Problem → intervention → result.
5. **Industry-specific video:** “Three Instagram lead mistakes D2C founders make.”
6. **Objection video:** “Do Instagram ads work for B2B services in India?”

Every ad should have one audience, one problem, one offer and one CTA.

---

# 6. Lead capture and nurturing workflow

## Funnel

Instagram content/ad  
→ Keyword DM or higher-intent lead form  
→ Automated acknowledgement  
→ CRM contact creation  
→ Qualification and scoring  
→ Calendar booking  
→ Human follow-up  
→ Audit/discovery call  
→ Proposal  
→ Won/lost/nurture

## DM automation

Connect the professional Instagram account to Meta Business Suite.

Set up:

- Instant reply.
- Away message.
- FAQs.
- Saved replies.
- Keyword-triggered flows where available.
- Comment-to-DM automation through an approved platform if required.

Recommended keywords:

- AUDIT.
- CALENDAR.
- LEADS.
- PRICING.
- CASE STUDY.

Example first response:

“Thanks, {{first_name}}. I can prepare a quick Instagram lead audit. Please send:  
1. Your business/Instagram handle  
2. Your industry  
3. Your main marketing challenge  
4. Approximate monthly marketing budget  
5. Best email or WhatsApp number  
By sharing these details, you agree that I may contact you about the audit. You can opt out at any time.”

After qualification:

“Based on what you shared, an audit looks relevant. Choose a 15-minute slot here: [calendar link]. I’ll review your profile before the call.”

Automation should acknowledge and collect data, not pretend to be a human consultant. Move high-value or complex inquiries to manual conversation quickly.

## CRM integration

Recommended lean stack:

- **CRM:** HubSpot Free, Zoho CRM, or a structured Airtable/Google Sheet during initial validation.
- **Automation:** Native Meta integration, Make, Zapier or Pabbly Connect.
- **Scheduling:** Calendly, Zoho Bookings or Google Calendar appointment scheduling.
- **Communication:** Email plus WhatsApp Business, with explicit consent.
- **Reporting:** Meta Ads Manager, Instagram Insights and Looker Studio/Google Sheets.

Required CRM fields:

- Lead ID.
- Date/time.
- Name and business.
- Email and phone.
- Instagram handle/website.
- Source: ad, Reel, Story, bio or referral.
- Campaign, ad set and ad name.
- DM keyword.
- Industry.
- Monthly marketing budget.
- Main challenge.
- Lead status.
- Qualification score.
- First-response time.
- Call booked/attended.
- Proposal value.
- Won/lost reason.
- Revenue.

HubSpot can sync connected lead-ad submissions and log them as CRM form submissions; its documentation also describes custom field mapping and lead-sync error monitoring ([HubSpot lead-sync documentation](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/ads/sync-leads-from-your-facebook-page-or-linkedin-ads-account-to-hubspot)). Test the integration with dummy leads before launch and maintain a daily backup export.

## Lead scoring

Example 10-point score:

- Decision-maker: +2.
- Clear marketing problem: +2.
- Active website/Instagram/business: +1.
- Marketing budget ₹30,000–₹50,000 or more: +2.
- Wants to start within 30 days: +2.
- Valid phone/email: +1.

Classification:

- 8–10: Hot; personal contact within 15 minutes during business hours.
- 5–7: Warm; send audit resource and booking invitation.
- 0–4: Nurture; send educational content and requalify later.

## Follow-up sequence

### Immediately

- DM or email confirms receipt.
- Show expected response time.
- Provide calendar link.
- Add source and consent status to CRM.

### Within 10–15 minutes during working hours

Personal WhatsApp, DM or call:

“Hi {{name}}, I saw your request for an Instagram audit for {{business}}. Your point about {{challenge}} stood out. I can show you three improvements on a short call. Would {{time option 1}} or {{time option 2}} work?”

### Day 1

Send one useful observation:

“I reviewed your profile. The main issue appears to be {{specific issue}}. Here is a 60-second explanation. If useful, book your audit here.”

### Day 3

Send proof:

“Here is an example of how I diagnose the path from Reel/ad to lead and follow-up. Your setup has a similar opportunity around {{issue}}.”

### Day 5

Handle the main objection:

“You do not need a huge content team to test this. A basic system can start with three Reels and two carousels weekly, provided the offer and follow-up are clear.”

### Day 7

Direct close:

“Would you like me to reserve an audit slot, or should I close the request for now?”

### Day 14

Move non-responsive leads to nurture and send a relevant checklist or case study.

### Days 21–30

Send one monthly insight and ask whether timing or budget has changed. Stop promotional follow-up when the person opts out.

---

# 7. Three-month execution schedule

## Month 1: Foundation and testing

### Week 1

- Choose two priority verticals.
- Finalize offer, qualification rules and privacy policy.
- Optimize Instagram bio and Highlights.
- Build lead form and booking page.
- Configure CRM pipeline and tracking.
- Produce the first two weeks of content.
- Install/test Meta Pixel and Conversions API if using a website.
- Submit test leads through every path.

Bio structure:

“Instagram & performance marketing for Indian SMBs  
Lead funnels, content and Meta Ads  
Get a free 15-minute audit ↓”

Highlights:

- Start Here.
- Services.
- Results.
- Audits.
- FAQs.
- About.

### Week 2

- Begin organic cadence.
- Launch Lead Ads and click-to-DM campaigns.
- Test three hooks and two offers.
- Check comments and DMs at least three times daily.
- Record response time and lead quality manually.

### Week 3

- Pause obvious low performers only after meaningful spend.
- Publish a teardown and FAQ Reel based on incoming objections.
- Launch retargeting to video viewers and profile engagers.
- Review invalid-lead reasons.

### Week 4

- Rank creatives by valid CPL and qualified-call CPL.
- Retain the top two creative angles.
- Rewrite the weakest form question or landing-page section.
- Prepare a short Month 1 proof post.

## Month 2: Optimization and authority

- Allocate most prospecting spend to winners.
- Create one vertical-specific ad/form.
- Publish at least two proof-based posts.
- Introduce fortnightly Live/Q&A.
- Improve qualification and calendar-show reminders.
- Build a 30-day nurture list.
- Compare Instant Form versus DM lead quality.
- Refresh at least one winning creative rather than waiting for fatigue.

## Month 3: Scaling and sales efficiency

- Raise paid spend to ₹34,000.
- Expand the strongest audience to additional Indian cities.
- Increase retargeting to 25%.
- Use testimonial, case-study and objection creatives.
- Build a qualified-lead or client lookalike if enough data exists.
- Feed CRM outcomes back into campaign decisions.
- Document the winning content/ad/follow-up system for the next quarter.
- Decide whether to scale, specialize further or change the lead offer based on qualified-call and revenue data.

---

# 8. KPIs

## Awareness and creative

- Paid reach.
- Impressions.
- Frequency.
- CPM.
- Three-second video views.
- Hook/hold rate.
- 25%, 50% and 75% video completion.
- Saves and shares.
- Profile visits.
- Follower growth, reported only as a secondary indicator.

## Traffic and engagement

- Link clicks.
- CTR.
- CPC.
- Landing-page views.
- DM conversations started.
- Cost per DM conversation.
- Form opens.
- Form completion rate.

## Lead generation

- Raw leads.
- Unique valid leads.
- Invalid/duplicate leads.
- Paid CPL.
- Blended CPL.
- Organic leads.
- Lead source by campaign/post/keyword.
- Qualified-lead rate.
- Cost per qualified lead.

## Sales pipeline

- Median first-response time.
- Calls booked.
- Booking rate.
- Show rate.
- Qualified calls.
- Proposals sent.
- Proposal value.
- Clients won.
- Customer acquisition cost.
- Revenue and expected recurring revenue.
- Return on ad spend or marketing investment where revenue is attributable.

## Diagnostic thresholds

Use these as operating alerts, not universal truths:

- CTR below 0.8% after adequate delivery: review hook, audience and offer.
- Strong CTR but weak form completion: simplify or improve form relevance.
- Low CPL but poor qualification: tighten copy and form questions.
- Many valid leads but few bookings: improve speed-to-lead and CTA.
- High bookings but low attendance: add reminders and pre-call value.
- High attendance but few proposals: revisit positioning, qualification or discovery process.
- Frequency rising while CTR declines: refresh creative or broaden the audience.

# 10. Resource and contractor plan

The creator can handle routine scripting, filming, basic editing, carousels, Stories, publishing and community replies. Contractor support should be concentrated on technical setup and occasional production bottlenecks.

## Monthly budget split

| Category | Month 1 | Month 2 | Month 3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Paid advertising | ₹30,000 | ₹32,000 | ₹34,000 |
| CRM/automation/scheduling/tools | ₹3,000 | ₹3,000 | ₹3,000 |
| Contractor support | ₹7,000 | ₹5,000 | ₹3,000 |
| **Total** | **₹40,000** | **₹40,000** | **₹40,000** |

“Organic budget” means cash spent supporting organic production and operations. Organic distribution itself does not require media spend. The creator’s own time is not included as a cash cost.

## Creator-owned tasks

- Content research and idea selection.
- Script writing.
- On-camera recording.
- Basic Reel editing and captions.
- Carousel creation from templates.
- Posting and scheduling.
- Daily Stories.
- Community management.
- Initial DM qualification.
- Sales calls and proposals.
- Weekly reporting and learning log.

Expected workload: approximately 12–16 hours per week, including lead follow-up.

## Tasks that should receive contractor support

### Month 1: Technical setup

Hire an automation/ads specialist for a fixed setup project covering:

- Business Manager and permissions audit.
- Pixel/Conversions API setup if a website is used.
- CRM field mapping.
- Lead-ad webhook or automation connection.
- DM flow configuration.
- Calendar and notification workflow.
- Test submissions and attribution checks.
- Reporting dashboard structure.

Do not outsource the full strategy at this budget. Purchase a narrowly defined setup and quality-assurance deliverable.

### Months 1–2: Editing overflow

Use a freelance editor when:

- The creator cannot maintain three Reels weekly.
- Talking-head footage needs stronger pacing, B-roll or subtitles.
- Winning ads need rapid variants.
- The creator is spending more than three hours editing each week.

Assign the contractor 4–6 short videos per month while keeping simpler videos in-house.

### Month 2: Design system

A designer can create:

- Six reusable carousel templates.
- Case-study layouts.
- Story highlight covers.
- Proposal/audit report template.
- Static ad variants.

This should be a one-time template system, not ongoing per-post design.

### Month 3: Optional appointment-setting assistance

Only consider a part-time assistant if:

- Valid leads exceed 80 per month.
- Median response time exceeds 15 minutes.
- Follow-ups are being missed.
- Sales calls consume time needed for content and fulfillment.

The assistant should update CRM records, send reminders and schedule calls—not conduct strategic sales conversations without training.

## Tasks that should not be outsourced initially

- Founder voice and opinions.
- On-camera presence.
- Client discovery.
- Final offer design.
- Case-study claims and approval.
- Sales calls.
- Weekly strategic decisions.

These are the trust-building elements that differentiate a small specialist provider from a generic agency.

---

# 11. Governance and risk controls

- Publish a clear privacy policy before running lead forms.
- Ask only for information needed to qualify and contact the lead.
- Record consent source and date.
- Provide a simple opt-out mechanism.
- Restrict CRM and ad-account access.
- Use two-factor authentication.
- Review contractor access monthly.
- Never fabricate testimonials or case-study results.
- Separate raw lead count from valid and qualified leads.
- Cap initial client onboarding so delivery quality does not collapse if ads outperform projections.
- Review projections after the first ₹7,500–₹10,000 of paid spend; replace assumptions with actual CPM, valid CPL and qualified-call CPL.

## Final decision rule

At the end of 90 days, scale only if:

1. Paid CPL is at or below approximately ₹450–₹500.
2. At least 30% of valid leads book calls.
3. At least 65% of booked calls attend.
4. Cost per qualified call is commercially viable.
5. Attributed client gross profit exceeds total marketing and fulfillment-acquisition cost.

If CPL is acceptable but sales are weak, fix qualification, response speed, offer and sales execution before increasing ad spend. If qualified-call economics are strong, move the next incremental budget into the winning Lead Ads and retargeting campaigns while preserving the organic content engine that supplies proof
