LEGAL STATUS, PROPERTY CLASSIFICATION, AND SLAVE CONTROL IN THE 1730s BRITISH EMPIRE

Executive findings

1. The Molasses Act 1733 did not classify enslaved people as property or regulate their conduct or punishment. Its operative language taxed foreign rum, molasses, syrup, sugar, and paneles imported into British colonies and imposed customs controls. Its declared object was “the better securing and encouraging the trade of his Majesty’s sugar colonies in America.” It protected an economy based on enslaved plantation labor, but it was not itself a slave code. Full text: https://statutes.org.uk/site/the-statutes/eighteenth-century/1733-6-george-2-c-13-the-molasses-act/

2. The statutes enacted in Jamaica and Barbados during 1730–1739 generally presupposed that enslaved people were owned rather than re-enacting a comprehensive definition of them as chattels. The explicit foundational property classifications came from older statutes that remained part of the islands’ operative legal order:
   - Jamaica’s 1683 law said enslaved people were, for payment of debts, to be “deemed & taken as all other goods and chattels,” while being treated as freehold for other inheritance purposes.
   - Barbados’s 1668 statute declared enslaved people “Estate real, and not Chattels,” although the law continued to permit commercial dealings in them. Thus “property” is accurate for Barbados, but “chattels personal” is not always the technically correct local classification.
   - South Carolina’s famous express declaration that enslaved people were “chattels personal” belongs to the Negro Act of 1740, immediately outside the requested date range. A South Carolina slave act was enacted in 1735, but the surviving evidence gathered here does not justify attributing the 1740 chattel clause to the 1735 act.

3. The 1730s laws nevertheless make ownership unmistakable through repeated references to “owners,” “possessors,” compensation for executed enslaved people, recovery of runaways, restrictions on movement and trading, and summary corporal or capital punishment. The legal structure combined personhood for purposes of criminal liability with property status for purposes of sale, inheritance, debt, compensation, and owners’ economic interests.

4. Parliament’s Molasses Act operated principally through imperial trade and customs law. Jamaica’s and Barbados’s plantation codes operated directly on people: movement passes, weapons, markets, runaways, assemblies, summary trial, whipping, branding, transportation, execution, and compensation to owners. This was not, however, a completely clean division between a metropolitan “law of commerce” and autonomous colonial “slave law.” Recent legal history emphasizes that English common-law courts, Crown policy, imperial review, property doctrine, and colonial statutes together created and sustained an imperial law of slavery.

5. Recent scholarship overwhelmingly treats the Molasses Act as protectionist imperial trade regulation obtained for British West Indian sugar interests—not as a slave-control or police measure in the same sense as a plantation code. The stronger modern argument is that trade regulation and slavery were structurally connected: the Act defended the market position and political vision of British slave-based sugar colonies. Calling it “slave control” without qualification, however, confuses regulation of the plantation economy with legal control and punishment of enslaved persons.

I. THE MOLASSES ACT 1733: ACTUAL LANGUAGE AND LEGAL EFFECT

Citation and title

The Act is 6 Geo. II, c. 13, commonly called the Molasses Act 1733 and historically titled:

“An act for the better securing and encouraging the trade of his Majesty’s sugar colonies in America.”

A transcribed full text is available through the Statutes Project: https://statutes.org.uk/site/the-statutes/eighteenth-century/1733-6-george-2-c-13-the-molasses-act/

A contemporary statutes-at-large volume for 1733–1747 is digitized by HathiTrust: https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nyp.33433035265135

An additional transcription identifies Pickering’s Statutes at Large, vol. XVI, pp. 374–379, as its source: https://www.originalsources.com/Document.aspx?DocID=IAFKKB9RUXAN3CV

Preamble

The Act’s preamble states:

“Whereas the Welfare and Prosperity of Your Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in America are of the greatest Consequence and Importance to the Trade, Navigation, and Strength of this Kingdom: And whereas the Planters of the said Sugar Colonies have of late Years fallen under such great Discouragements, that they are unable to improve or carry on the Sugar Trade upon an equal Footing with the Foreign Sugar Colonies, without some Advantage and Relief be given to them from Great-Britain…”

The preamble is important for interpretation. Parliament expressly described the beneficiaries as “Your Majesty’s Sugar Colonies” and their “Planters,” and the purpose as giving them an “Advantage and Relief” against “Foreign Sugar Colonies.” The language is protectionist and commercial, not a declaration of enslaved status.

Principal duty clause

The operative clause imposed duties, beginning on 25 December 1733, on foreign colonial products brought into British colonies. It provided that:

“there shall be raised, levied, collected, and paid, unto and for the Use of His Majesty, His Heirs, and Successors, upon all Rum or spirits of the Produce or Manufacture of any of the Colonies or Plantations in America, not in the Possession or under the Dominion of His Majesty, His Heirs, and Successors, which, at any Time or Times within or during the Continuance of this Act, shall be imported or brought into any of the Colonies or Plantations in America, which now are or hereafter may be in the Possession or under the Dominion of His Majesty … the sum of nine pence, money of Great Britain … for every gallon thereof…”

It then imposed:

“upon all molasses or syrups of such foreign produce or manufacture as aforesaid … the sum of six pence of like money for every gallon thereof…”

And:

“upon all sugars and paneles of such foreign growth, produce or manufacture as aforesaid … a duty after the rate of five shillings of like money, for every hundred weight Avoirdupois.”

The quoted text is reproduced at https://www.originalsources.com/Document.aspx?DocID=IAFKKB9RUXAN3CV and in the fuller Statutes Project text at https://statutes.org.uk/site/the-statutes/eighteenth-century/1733-6-george-2-c-13-the-molasses-act/

Quantitative meaning of the statutory rates

Using the contemporary monetary relationships of 12 pence to one shilling and 20 shillings to one pound:

- Foreign rum: 9d per gallon  
  9 ÷ 12 = 0.75 shillings per gallon  
  0.75 ÷ 20 = £0.0375 per gallon

- Foreign molasses or syrup: 6d per gallon  
  6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 shillings per gallon  
  0.5 ÷ 20 = £0.025 per gallon

- Foreign sugar and paneles: 5s per hundredweight  
  5 ÷ 20 = £0.25 per hundredweight

These calculations translate the denominations; they do not by themselves establish the duties as percentages of market value. Establishing an ad valorem burden would require reliable contemporary prices by port and year, which the sources assembled here do not provide.

What the Molasses Act does not say

The Act contains no language declaring Africans, “Negroes,” or enslaved people to be:

- slaves;
- goods;
- chattels;
- real estate;
- personal estate; or
- property.

It does not prescribe passes, curfews, searches of enslaved people, whipping, branding, mutilation, execution, slave courts, runaway patrols, or owner compensation for an executed enslaved person. For a novel, it would therefore be historically misleading to have a lawyer cite the Molasses Act as the legal source of an enslaved person’s chattel status.

The indirect connection is nonetheless substantial. The law expressly aimed to assist British sugar planters and British sugar colonies in competition with foreign sugar colonies. Sugar plantation production in the British Caribbean rested on enslaved labor. The statute consequently protected a slave-based commercial system without itself defining or policing slave status.

II. JAMAICA

A. The explicit property classification underlying the 1730s system

The clearest Jamaican statutory wording comes from “An Act for the Better Ordering of Slaves,” enacted in 1683 and incorporated into the island’s continuing body of slave law. It declared:

“no slave shall be free by becoming a Christian but as to payment of debts shall be deemed & taken as all other goods and chattels and where other goods and chattels are not sufficient to satisfie the said debts then so many slaves only as are necessary as well proportionably out of the slaves assigned for dowry as those that belong to ye heir or executor shall be sold for payment of debts and all negroes or slaves shall be accounted as freehold in all other cases whatsoever and descend accordingly.”

Full transcription: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1683

This is a legally hybrid property rule:

- For payment of debts, enslaved people were “all other goods and chattels.”
- If other assets were inadequate, the necessary number of enslaved people could be sold.
- For other purposes, they were “accounted as freehold” and descended with the inheritance.

The rule therefore did not make enslaved people simple personal chattels for every purpose. It adjusted their property classification according to the legal problem—especially creditor claims, dower, and descent—while treating human beings as alienable assets in all relevant senses.

The same 1683 act also imposed direct controls characteristic of a plantation code. It prohibited an enslaved person from leaving a plantation without a ticket or accompanying white servant, except for certain personal attendants, and required persons encountering unauthorized enslaved people to apprehend and punish them. It also addressed clothing, runaways, Christianity, ownership, and debts. Full text: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1683

Why an older law matters to a 1730s setting

A character living in Jamaica in 1733 did not inhabit a legal system recreated from scratch that year. The operative legal order included older enactments, later amendments, customary property practices, court decisions, and new legislation. Jamaica’s official printed compilation, Acts of Assembly, passed in the island of Jamaica; from 1681, to 1737, inclusive, was published in London by John Baskett in 1738. The Wellcome Collection identifies and provides access to that volume: https://wellcomecollection.org/works/cy7u7rbj

The Penn catalogue describes it as a government publication containing the laws from 1681 to 1737, with a separately dated 1739 abridgment; it notes that the text’s pagination is continuous despite an irregular sequence: https://find.library.upenn.edu/catalog/9979986332103681

Thus the 1683 classification was not merely irrelevant seventeenth-century background. It appeared within the body of Jamaican statutes compiled and printed for eighteenth-century use.

B. Jamaican enactment of 1730: weapons, rebellion, and collective security

The 1730 law, “An Act to prevent the selling of Powder to rebellious, or any other Negroes whatsoever,” did not reclassify enslaved people as property. Instead, it addressed armed resistance and the circulation of gunpowder. Its preamble stated:

“WHEREAS it may reasonably be conjectured that the great Number of Places where Powder is at present vended in all Parts of this Island contributes very much to the supplying of rebellious Negroes therewith, which tends to the increasing their Numbers, being a Means not only of supplying themselves with Provisions, but likewise of robbing and plundering the remote Parts of this Island, to the great Discouragement of new Settlements…”

It then required a gubernatorial license for retail sales of gunpowder in quantities under fifty pounds, supported by a certificate from the parish justices and vestry that the seller was qualified and trustworthy. Transcription: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1730

The measure illustrates a crucial difference between property classification and police control. It does not call enslaved people chattels, but its legal and racial premises are evident:

- “rebellious Negroes” were treated as a collective internal-security threat;
- commercial access to gunpowder was restricted to keep weapons from them;
- parish and gubernatorial licensing mechanisms mobilized the white civil government against resistance and marronage;
- the law linked armed Black autonomy to robbery, plunder, and discouragement of settlement.

C. Jamaican legislation of 1739

The 1739 statute was titled:

“An Act for confirming the Articles executed by Colonel John Guthrie, Lieutenant Francis Sadler, and Cudjoe the Commander of the Rebels; for paying Rewards for taking up and restoring runaway Slaves, and making Provision for four white Persons, residing…”

The title itself reveals the law’s principal subjects: confirmation of treaty articles with Cudjoe and the Maroons, rewards for recovering runaways, and provisioning white persons connected to implementation. The University of New Brunswick database lists it among Jamaica’s 1739 laws: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/locations/caribbean/jamaica

Again, this is slave control rather than a foundational property definition. The phrase “taking up and restoring runaway Slaves” assumes both that the runaways belonged to owners and that restoration of possession was a public objective. It treats escape as wrongful displacement of an owner’s labor and property interest, while also responding to the military and political reality that the Jamaican government had been unable simply to eliminate the Maroon communities.

D. Practical legal language for a Jamaican scene

Historically appropriate Jamaican legal expressions include:

- an enslaved person “belonging to” an owner;
- sale for payment of debts;
- slaves assigned for dower;
- slaves belonging to an heir or executor;
- slaves “accounted as freehold” for descent;
- a runaway being “taken up” and “restored”;
- a ticket authorizing travel;
- “rebellious Negroes” and restrictions on powder.

A lawyer, executor, creditor, planter, or provost marshal might speak of enslaved people as an estate asset while magistrates and militia officers spoke of the same people as punishable subjects or security threats. That simultaneous treatment—as property in civil law and as responsible or punishable persons in criminal-police law—is central to the dehumanizing legal structure.

III. BARBADOS

A. The explicit Barbadian property classification

Barbados presents an important technical warning against using “chattel” as an undifferentiated synonym for enslaved property. The island’s 1668 law was expressly titled:

“An Act declaring the Negro Slaves of this Island to be Real Estate.”

Its preamble stated:

“Whereas a very considerable part of the Wealth of this Island consists in our Negro slaves, without whose Labour and Service we should be utterly unable to manage our Plantations here, thereby relieving our own Wants, and bringing that considerable increase of Revenue, which this Place affords unto his Majesty’s Coffers, as well here as in England.”

It explained that intestacy disputes had arisen between heirs, executors, and administrators, and that the law sought to ensure that an heir and widow claiming dower would not receive “bare Land without Negroes to Manure the same.”

The operative clause declared:

“all Negro Slaves in all Courts of Judicature and other Places within this Island, shall be held, taken, and adjudged to be Estate real, and not Chattels…”

Full text: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1668

For precise historical narration:

- Enslaved Barbadians were property.
- They were bought, sold, mortgaged, inherited, and valued.
- But the statute classified them as “Estate real, and not Chattels” for the legal purposes it addressed.
- A Barbadian lawyer discussing descent or dower could therefore object to describing them simply as personal chattels.

The reason was not humanitarian recognition of personhood. It was estate planning and plantation continuity: land without a coerced labor force was economically impaired, so the law attached the labor force to the inheritance pattern of the plantation.

Jerome S. Handler’s peer-reviewed analysis emphasizes that chattel-property status, lifetime servitude, and inheritance of status from an enslaved mother were established in Barbadian custom before comprehensive statutory definition. He notes that enslaved people were bequeathed by wills, conveyed by deeds, given as gifts, mortgaged, pledged as loan security, and listed in inventories alongside movable property and livestock. Handler also stresses that, apart from the 1668 real-estate enactment, Barbados did not pass a general statute comprehensively defining slave status; the property premises were usually implicit whenever statutes mentioned slaves. Article text: https://www.jeromehandler.com/wp-content/uploads/Custom_Law-SA.pdf ; journal record and DOI page: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0144039X.2015.1123436

B. Barbados’s 1731 runaway act

The 1731 law was titled:

“An Act for the punishment of Run-away Slaves, and of Slaves who shall willfully entertain, harbour and conceal any Run-away Slaves.”

Its preamble stated:

“Whereas divers Negroes and other Slaves do often run away and absent themselves from the service of their Owners, and are wilfully entertained, harboured and concealed by other Slaves, to the great detriment of the Owners of such run-away Slaves, and to the grievous mischief of the Inhabitants of this Island in general…”

This expressly frames escape in terms of:

- absence from an owner’s “service”;
- “detriment” to the owners;
- a generalized threat to the white inhabitants.

The first-offense provision stated that an enslaved person found guilty of harboring a runaway, and the runaway who was harbored, should each:

“receive one and twenty lashes on their bare backs…”

For a second offense, each was to receive:

“thirty and nine lashes on the bare back…”

For a third offense, the law again prescribed thirty-nine lashes and branding “in the right cheek,” according to the surviving transcription. Full text: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1731

This statute is especially useful for a novel because it shows the ordinary machinery of coercion without relying on generalizations:

- jurisdiction was exercised by a justice of the peace;
- guilt could be established by confession or proof;
- punishment was corporal and graduated;
- branding made legal punishment permanently visible;
- an enslaved person could be punished both for personal flight and for solidarity with another fugitive;
- the owner’s economic loss was treated as a public legal wrong.

C. Barbados’s 1733 market and trading act

The 1733 act was titled:

“An Act for the better governing of Negroes; and the more effectual preventing the inhabitants of this island, from employing their Negroes or other Slaves, in selling or bartering.”

Its preamble said that earlier laws for governing enslaved people and preventing their employment in selling or bartering, if properly enforced, would:

“redound to the great advantage and benefit of the People of this Island, and prevent many felonies, and other crimes and abuses, daily committed by Negroes and other Slaves, to the great impoverishment, loss and damage of the Inhabitants…”

The Act required justices of the peace to enforce the earlier laws, particularly the statute of 8 August 1688 prohibiting inhabitants from using enslaved people in selling or bartering. It also empowered constables and market clerks or their deputies to enforce the restrictions. Transcription: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1733

The Act did not contain a new “chattel” declaration. Its structure nevertheless shows how law restricted enslaved economic agency:

- the legal responsibility was partly directed at inhabitants who deployed enslaved people as traders;
- Black market activity was associated in the preamble with felony, abuse, impoverishment, and damage;
- enforcement was decentralized among justices, constables, and market officials;
- older laws remained active components of the 1733 regime.

D. Barbados’s 1739 amendment: punishment, execution, compensation, and manumission

The 1739 statute was titled:

“An Act for amending an Act of this Island, entitled an Act for the Governing of Negroes, and for providing a proper Maintenance and Support for such Negroes, Indians, or Mulattoes as shall be hereafter manumitted or set free, and also for preventing certain Inconveniences from them arising to the Inhabitants of this Island.”

Its preamble provides unusually revealing evidence of the collision between human life, criminal punishment, and ownership:

“WHEREAS the sentence of death passed by the justices and freeholders in pursuance of an Act of this island bearing the date the eighth day of August, one thousand six hundred and eighty-eight, entitled ‘An Act for the Governing of Negroes,’ against any Negro or other Slave tried before them is immediately put into execution, without any stay or respite, whereby the owner or possessor of such Negro or other Slave is prevented from bringing a writ of error to reverse the judgment or sentence…”

It continued that, because of malice by a prosecutor or obstinacy by an owner or possessor:

“the pains of death” had sometimes been inflicted when “more proper and effectual methods” could have been used. It then gave an explicitly fiscal reason for restraint:

“the large sums of money that have been paid out of the treasury for such executed Slave might and ought to have been saved, as well as the life of such Slave preserved.”

Transcription: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1739

This language does not use the noun “chattel,” but it makes property treatment explicit in substance:

- the condemned person had an “owner or possessor”;
- the owner’s ability to challenge the conviction was protected;
- execution produced a treasury payment for the “executed Slave”;
- preservation of the enslaved person’s life and conservation of public funds appeared together;
- criminal procedure was shaped by the economic consequences of destroying someone’s property.

The statute also addressed manumission. Its title and preamble indicate that persons freeing enslaved “Negroes, Indians, or Mulattoes” were expected to provide for their maintenance and support, while lawmakers characterized unsupported free people as a source of “Inconveniences” to the island’s inhabitants. Freedom was therefore regulated as a possible fiscal and social burden.

E. The contemporary Barbadian statute book

Acts of Assembly, passed in the island of Barbadoes, from 1648, to 1718 was published in 1732, and the surviving digitized item includes a second part covering 1717/18 through 1738, printed in London in 1739. It is available through the Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_acts-of-assembly-passed_barbados_1732

That compilation is a better period-authentic source for spelling, capitalization, layout, marginal notes, and clause numbering than a modern paraphrase. The University of New Brunswick Laws of Enslavement and Freedom database supplies searchable modern transcriptions and a Barbados index: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/locations/caribbean/barbados

IV. SOUTH CAROLINA

A. The 1735 act and the limits of the available evidence

South Carolina enacted “An Act for the better ordering and governing Negroes and other Slaves” in 1735, numbered 586 in the later Statutes at Large of South Carolina. The statutes-at-large text identifies the act and places it at page 385: https://archive.org/stream/statutesatlargeo07edit/statutesatlargeo07edit_djvu.txt

The 1735 act included, among other controls, a tightened rule concerning private manumission. The prior 1722 enactment required a newly manumitted person to leave South Carolina within twelve months unless both houses of the Assembly approved the manumission. A historical account quoting the 1722 clause gives:

“all owners of slaves, who, at any time hereafter, shall manumit or set free any slave, for any particular service, shall make provision for his departure out of this province; and such slave who shall not depart this province, by the space of twelve months next after such manumission, (being at liberty so to do,) shall lose the benefit of such manumission, and continue to be a slave, to all intents and purposes whatsoever, unless such manumission shall be approved of and confirmed by an order of both Houses of Assembly.”

The same account reports that the 1735 revision shortened the departure period from twelve months to six and provided that a privately manumitted person who left and then returned would lose the benefit of freedom. Source: https://www.ccpl.org/charleston-time-machine/private-manumission-intimate-path-freedom?language=en

The important source-critical point is that the evidence gathered here does not establish that the 1735 act used the later formula “chattels personal.” That wording should not be silently backdated.

B. The 1740 act: the famous express chattel declaration

Following the Stono Rebellion of 1739, South Carolina enacted its comprehensive Negro Act in 1740. Because 1740 is immediately outside the requested 1730–1739 range, it is useful as context and contrast, but it should be dated accurately.

The preamble said:

“WHEREAS in his majesty’s plantations in America, slavery has been introduced and allowed; and the people commonly called negroes, Indians, mulatoes and mestizos, have [been] deemed absolute slaves, and the subjects of property in the hands of particular persons; the extent of whose power over such slaves, ought to be settled and limited by positive laws, so that the slaves may be kept in due subjection and obedience, and the owners and other persons having the care and government of slaves, may be restrained from exercising too great rigour and cruelty over them; and that the public peace and order of this Province may be preserved…”

Its first substantive declaration provided:

“all negroes, Indians, (free Indians in amity with this government, and negroes, mulatos and mestizos who are now free excepted) mulatos or mestizos, who now are or shall hereafter be in this Province, and all their issue and offspring born or to be born, shall be and they are hereby declared to be and remain for ever hereafter absolute slaves, and shall follow the condition of the mother; and shall be deemed, held, taken, reputed and adjudged in law to be chattles personal in the hands of their owners and possessors and their executors, administrators and assigns, to all intents, constructions and purposes whatsoever…”

Transcription: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/south-carolina-1740

A facsimile-style modern PDF also reproduces the language: https://www.scpronet.com/modjeskaschool/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/9-an-act-for-better-ordering-slavecodes1740.pdf

This formula accomplished several things:

- declared the covered population “absolute slaves”;
- made status hereditary;
- specified partus sequitur ventrem—the child followed the mother’s condition;
- classified enslaved people as personal chattels;
- vested property interests not just in owners and possessors but in executors, administrators, and assigns;
- simultaneously claimed to limit owners’ “too great rigour and cruelty” and to keep enslaved people in “due subjection and obedience.”

The Act therefore embodies the legal contradiction of plantation slavery: positive law purported to limit private cruelty while creating a comprehensive public regime for hereditary ownership, racial subordination, and coercion.

C. How to handle South Carolina’s date in fiction

For a scene set no later than 31 December 1739:

- Do not quote the 1740 “chattels personal” clause as already enacted law.
- A planter could certainly treat enslaved people as saleable and inheritable property under established law and practice.
- A lawyer could cite the 1735 governing act and earlier property and slave-law rules.
- After the Stono uprising in September 1739, legislators and officials could plausibly discuss tightening the law, but the comprehensive 1740 act should remain prospective.

For a scene in 1740 or later, the express “absolute slaves” and “chattels personal” formula is appropriate.

V. PARLIAMENTARY LAW VERSUS COLONIAL PLANTATION CODES

A. Parliamentary commercial regulation

The Molasses Act was enacted by the King in Parliament for an imperial commercial purpose. Its legal machinery concerned:

- origin of goods;
- importation into British possessions;
- customs duties;
- collection and enforcement;
- foreign versus British colonial production;
- navigation and imperial trade.

Its subjects were merchants, shipmasters, importers, customs officials, and taxable cargoes. Even where its economic purpose favored slave-owning planters, its immediate legal object was trade.

B. Colonial slave control

The Jamaican and Barbadian enactments operated directly on enslaved and free people within plantation societies. Their characteristic mechanisms included:

- passes or “tickets” for movement;
- recovery and restoration of runaways;
- punishment for harboring a runaway;
- restrictions on weapons and gunpowder;
- restrictions on trading, selling, and bartering;
- special or summary adjudication by justices and freeholders;
- whipping and branding;
- immediate execution;
- owner appeals or writs of error;
- treasury compensation for an executed enslaved person;
- controls on manumission and the residence of freed people.

The plantation codes also deputized much of white society. Owners, overseers, justices, freeholders, constables, market clerks, vestries, militia officers, and ordinary inhabitants could all participate in surveillance or enforcement.

C. Different sources of authority

Colonial assemblies enacted local statutes with the governor and council rather than exercising the sovereignty of the Westminster Parliament. Their laws were embedded in an imperial constitution in which Crown officials and metropolitan institutions could review, disallow, influence, or confirm colonial legislation.

A. B. Graham’s study of Jamaican legislation argues that the volume of Jamaican legislation grew enormously between 1664 and 1838 as the Assembly acquired greater legislative capacity and political power. He places Jamaica within a wider “transatlantic constitution,” rather than treating its Assembly either as a mere municipal body or as a fully sovereign parliament. A. B. Graham, “Jamaican legislation and the transatlantic constitution, 1664–1838,” The Historical Journal 61, no. 2 (2018), pp. 327–355, DOI 10.1017/S0018246X1700022X: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/1549583/

D. The distinction should not be overstated

A simple narrative in which England supplied neutral commerce law while colonial assemblies independently invented racial slavery is no longer adequate.

“Creating a Common Law of Slavery for England and its New World Empire” argues that English high-court judges and Crown policy helped create an imperial common law under which people could be deemed absolute property. It emphasizes debt recovery as crucial: allowing enslaved people to be recovered as assets helped make a market in human beings legally workable. The article challenges the conventional picture of a consistently “free” England wholly separate from colonial slave law. Law and History Review (2022): https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-history-review/article/creating-a-common-law-of-slavery-for-england-and-its-new-world-empire/8D27552070D9A6CD478BA9912DEFB26B

The better distinction is therefore functional, not moral or absolute:

- Westminster’s Molasses Act primarily regulated imperial commerce.
- Colonial assemblies supplied the dense, local police and punishment codes.
- English property doctrines, imperial courts, Crown policy, debt law, and metropolitan trade legislation helped make the plantation system economically and legally sustainable.
- Colonial law in turn influenced other colonies: Barbados supplied terminology and institutional models later adapted in Jamaica and South Carolina.

VI. RECENT PEER-REVIEWED SCHOLARSHIP, 2015–2025

The following are the strongest directly relevant journal articles identified. Not every one is in the three journals named in the request, but all address the legal production of slave status, property, or colonial legislative power. The limited number in Journal of British Studies, Slavery & Abolition, and William and Mary Quarterly devoted specifically to 1730s property classification is itself worth noting; much of the most direct recent work has appeared in Law and History Review and The Historical Journal.

1. Jerome S. Handler, “Custom and Law: The Status of Enslaved Africans in Seventeenth-Century Barbados,” Slavery & Abolition 37, no. 2 (2016), pp. 233–255.

Journal page: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0144039X.2015.1123436  
Accessible article text: https://www.jeromehandler.com/wp-content/uploads/Custom_Law-SA.pdf

Principal argument: Barbados is a case in which slave status was established substantially through custom before statutes comprehensively articulated it. Handler identifies three central features of status:

- chattel property;
- lifetime or permanent servitude;
- inheritance of the enslaved condition from an enslaved mother.

He argues that none of these characteristics was comprehensively defined by a general Barbadian statute; instead they were implicit in laws and legal documents mentioning slaves. The major exception was the 1668 act classifying enslaved people as real estate for specified inheritance purposes. This article is particularly important for avoiding the assumption that absence of a definition from a 1730s statute meant absence of legally recognized property status.

2. “A ‘Manifest Violation’ of the Rights of Englishmen: Rights Talk and the Law of Property in Early Eighteenth-Century Jamaica,” Law and History Review (2015).

Journal page: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-history-review/article/abs/manifest-violation-of-the-rights-of-englishmen-rights-talk-and-the-law-of-property-in-early-eighteenthcentury-jamaica/05CB34BAA228CCA4D699C64054DD25E8

Principal argument and example: the article reconstructs a 1706 Jamaican escheat dispute over an enslaved woman called Catalina and her “Seaven Pickaninny.” Jamaica’s provost marshal was ordered to empanel a jury to determine whether they belonged to merchant James Whitchurch or should escheat to Queen Anne because a previous owner had died without an heir. Whitchurch petitioned the Queen to return the enslaved people and quiet his title. The dispute made human beings the subject of Crown prerogative, title, inheritance, jury adjudication, and constitutional argument. It also shows Jamaican colonists using the “rights of Englishmen” primarily to defend their own property security during the island’s transition into a mature slave society.

3. A. B. Graham, “Jamaican Legislation and the Transatlantic Constitution, 1664–1838,” The Historical Journal 61, no. 2 (2018), pp. 327–355.

Repository and bibliographical record: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/1549583/  
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0018246X1700022X

Principal argument: Jamaica’s rapidly expanding legislative output reflected increasing local legislative capacity, political power, and demand from colonial interest groups. The Assembly belonged to a larger British and Atlantic pattern of legislative development. For slave law, the implication is that coercive plantation governance was not static: it was repeatedly legislated, revised, and institutionalized through an increasingly capable colonial state.

4. “Creating a Common Law of Slavery for England and its New World Empire,” Law and History Review (published online 2022).

Article page: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-history-review/article/creating-a-common-law-of-slavery-for-england-and-its-new-world-empire/8D27552070D9A6CD478BA9912DEFB26B

Principal argument: the article disputes the neat conventional separation between a free English common law and slave law created only “beyond the line” in the colonies. It argues that English judges and Crown policy participated in developing legal foundations for treating people as absolute property, especially by allowing their recovery as assets for debts. It connects the master’s claimed absolute power over an enslaved person with contemporary ideas about absolutism and the Crown’s effort to use courts and revenue without parliamentary consent.

5. Matthew Wyman-McCarthy, “Perceptions of French and Spanish Slave Law in Late Eighteenth-Century Britain,” Journal of British Studies 57, no. 1 (2018), pp. 29–52.

The article is cited in the Journal of British Studies literature here: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-british-studies/article/abs/slaves-and-peasants-in-the-era-of-emancipation/FC53CFA94CF3E369852AAD844E862F5D

Although its principal chronology is later than the 1730s, it is useful for understanding how Britons compared their slave system with French and Spanish legal systems. It helps place British claims about law, liberty, and supposedly foreign forms of despotism against the reality of British colonial property and punishment regimes.

6. “Slaves and Peasants in the Era of Emancipation,” Journal of British Studies (2020).

Article page: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-british-studies/article/abs/slaves-and-peasants-in-the-era-of-emancipation/FC53CFA94CF3E369852AAD844E862F5D

This later-period article traces another form of legal and ideological dehumanization: enslaved plantation laborers were redescribed as supposedly contented “peasants,” and even abolitionist visions could preserve plantation discipline and subordinated labor after slavery. It is less directly about 1730s chattel classification but useful for understanding the changing rhetorical disguises placed over coercion.

7. Relevant synthetic assessment: Ruma Chopra, review of Edward B. Rugemer, Slave Law and the Politics of Resistance in the Early Atlantic World, Journal of American History 106, no. 4 (2020), p. 1049.

Review page: https://academic.oup.com/jah/article-abstract/106/4/1049/5741441

The review highlights Rugemer’s argument that slave laws in Jamaica and South Carolina adapted to resistance, war, and later abolitionist pressure. It stresses the transmission of Barbadian legal terminology to Jamaica and South Carolina and argues that this borrowing was not mechanical: lawmakers adapted a shared logic to local threats and political circumstances. Because this item is a scholarly book review rather than an original research article, it should supplement rather than replace the journal articles above.

8. “Beyond Property: Uncovering Enslaved People in Women’s Wills in Colonial Jamaica, 1661–1771,” Journal of Slavery and Data Preservation 6, no. 3 (2025), pp. 83 ff.

Article page: https://scholarlypublishingcollective.org/msup/jsdp/article/6/3/83/403160/Beyond-Property-Uncovering-Enslaved-People-in

The article is based on a dataset of 741 wills from thirty-eight manuscript volumes dated between 1661 and 1771. It uses wills to recover both women’s economic and legal participation in slavery and information about enslaved people obscured by property records. Its evidence is valuable for fiction because wills reveal named individuals, family conflict, bequests, and household arrangements that abstract slave statutes omit.

Quantitative note on the wills dataset:

- 741 wills across 38 volumes gives an arithmetic mean of 741 ÷ 38 = 19.5 wills sampled per volume.
- The date range 1661–1771 spans 110 elapsed years, or 111 calendar years if both endpoints are counted.
- Neither calculation means that the source evenly samples every volume or year; the article should be consulted for its actual selection and coding methods.

VII. WAS THE MOLASSES ACT ABOUT TRADE REGULATION OR SLAVE CONTROL?

A. What the statutory language supports

The direct textual evidence strongly supports “trade regulation”:

- The title speaks of “securing and encouraging” sugar-colony trade.
- The preamble identifies British sugar planters’ competitive disadvantage.
- The operative provisions tax foreign rum, molasses, syrup, sugar, and paneles.
- Enforcement is customs-oriented.
- No provision defines enslaved status or prescribes slave discipline.

On a narrow legal classification, therefore, the Molasses Act is a customs and protection statute, not a slave-control act.

B. The traditional economic interpretation

The Journal of Economic History article “The Molasses Act and the Market Strategy of the British Sugar Planters” situates the controversy in:

- Anglo-French commercial rivalry;
- conflict between British colonial regions;
- West Indian planters’ attempt to obtain advantage over North American merchants trading with foreign sugar islands;
- conflict with Irish merchants;
- the British market for sugar and rum;
- adaptation of the Navigation Acts to changing market realities.

The article explains that an earlier proposed bill would have prohibited imports of foreign sugar, molasses, and rum into Great Britain, Ireland, and British dominions and barred exports of horses and lumber to foreign sugar colonies. After that proposal failed, the eventual Act represented a compromise. Article page: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-economic-history/article/abs/molasses-act-and-the-market-strategy-of-the-british-sugar-planters/F9DBE80ABEB2FFC7EE03EDC1BDF59428

This interpretation treats the Act as part of British sugar planters’ wider market strategy rather than as an isolated tax or a statute for governing enslaved people.

C. The recent imperial-political interpretation

Eva Brooks Landsberg’s recent dissertation, “The Politics of Sugar: Caribbean Roots of the American Revolution,” places the Molasses Act at the beginning of a longer political conflict between northern mainland merchants and Caribbean sugar planters. It argues that competing trade policies expressed competing visions of empire:

- commercial and settler-colonial development versus extractive plantation monoculture;
- colonies valued for their resemblance to Britain versus colonies valued for complementary tropical production;
- northern merchants’ interests versus British Caribbean planters’ claims to imperial priority.

Dissertation abstract and record: https://elischolar.library.yale.edu/gsas_dissertations/1884/

A dissertation is scholarly research but is not the same publication category as a peer-reviewed journal article. Its value here is in showing the direction of recent interpretation: the Molasses Act is analyzed as a political-economic choice about what kind of empire Britain would support.

D. Where slavery enters the interpretation

The protectionist and slavery-centered readings are compatible if kept at the right analytical levels.

At the level of immediate legal operation:

- the Act controlled goods and trade;
- it did not control enslaved people’s movement, weapons, family status, testimony, punishment, or manumission.

At the level of political economy:

- the favored British sugar colonies were plantation slave societies;
- the protected planters’ productive assets included enslaved laborers;
- the contested commerce in sugar, molasses, and rum was generated by plantation labor;
- restrictions on foreign sugar-island trade attempted to redirect commerce toward British plantation production;
- the law therefore helped reproduce the profitability and imperial importance of British slavery.

At the level of direct policing:

- Jamaican powder laws, Barbadian runaway laws, and local slave courts—not the Molasses Act—supplied the coercive controls.

The most accurate formulation is:

“The Molasses Act was a protectionist imperial trade law serving British West Indian sugar interests within a slave economy. It was structurally pro-slavery, but it was not a slave code or a direct statute of slave control.”

E. Why “slave control” can mislead

Calling every law that benefited a slave economy a “slave-control law” erases important legal distinctions. A customs duty and a statute authorizing thirty-nine lashes did different things, acted upon different legal subjects, and were enforced by different officials. For historical fiction, those distinctions matter:

- A customs officer would invoke the Molasses Act against an illicit cargo or an improperly documented import.
- A Barbadian justice would invoke slave laws against a runaway or a person harboring one.
- A Jamaican official might invoke powder restrictions against an unlicensed seller connected to rebellious or Maroon communities.
- An executor or creditor would invoke property, debt, dower, or inheritance law to sell or retain enslaved people.
- A planter whose enslaved person was condemned might contest the procedure or claim statutory compensation.

VIII. SOURCE AND ARCHIVAL GUIDE

The statutory material is not confined to the UK National Archives. For the texts discussed here, printed statute compilations and modern scholarly transcriptions are more immediately useful.

1. British parliamentary statute

- Molasses Act 1733, 6 Geo. II, c. 13, Statutes Project:  
  https://statutes.org.uk/site/the-statutes/eighteenth-century/1733-6-george-2-c-13-the-molasses-act/

- Statutes at Large, volume covering 1733–1747, HathiTrust:  
  https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nyp.33433035265135

- Transcription referencing Pickering, vol. XVI, pp. 374–379:  
  https://www.originalsources.com/Document.aspx?DocID=IAFKKB9RUXAN3CV

2. Jamaica

- Acts of Assembly, passed in the island of Jamaica; from 1681, to 1737, inclusive, London, 1738, Wellcome Collection:  
  https://wellcomecollection.org/works/cy7u7rbj

- Penn catalogue record, including publication and pagination information:  
  https://find.library.upenn.edu/catalog/9979986332103681

- University of New Brunswick Jamaica index:  
  https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/locations/caribbean/jamaica

- Jamaica 1683 act:  
  https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1683

- Jamaica 1730 powder act:  
  https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1730

3. Barbados

- Acts of Assembly compilation, Internet Archive:  
  https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_acts-of-assembly-passed_barbados_1732

- University of New Brunswick Barbados index:  
  https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/locations/caribbean/barbados

- Barbados 1668 real-estate act:  
  https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1668

- Barbados 1731 runaway act:  
  https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1731

- Barbados 1733 trading act:  
  https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1733

- Barbados 1739 amendment:  
  https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1739

4. South Carolina

- Statutes at Large of South Carolina, including the listing of the 1735 Act No. 586 at p. 385:  
  https://archive.org/stream/statutesatlargeo07edit/statutesatlargeo07edit_djvu.txt

- South Carolina 1740 act transcription:  
  https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/south-carolina-1740

- Modern PDF of the 1740 text:  
  https://www.scpronet.com/modjeskaschool/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/9-an-act-for-better-ordering-slavecodes1740.pdf

IX. FINAL GUIDANCE FOR HISTORICAL ACCURACY

For a novel set in the 1730s, the legally safest formulations are:

- The Molasses Act regulated foreign colonial sugar products and assisted British sugar planters; it did not declare enslaved people to be chattels.
- Jamaican law expressly treated enslaved people as “goods and chattels” for debt payment while treating them as freehold for other inheritance purposes.
- Barbados expressly classified enslaved people as “Estate real, and not Chattels,” while allowing them to be sold and otherwise treated as property.
- Barbadian laws of 1731, 1733, and 1739 controlled running away, harboring, market activity, punishment, execution, owner remedies, compensation, and manumission.
- Jamaica’s 1730 powder law addressed armed resistance and “rebellious Negroes”; its 1739 settlement legislation addressed Maroons and rewards for restoring runaways.
- South Carolina had a governing-slaves act in 1735, but the celebrated language declaring enslaved people “absolute slaves” and “chattels personal” dates to 1740 and should not appear as enacted statutory language in a scene set in 1739.
- “Property” is the broadly correct description throughout these slave societies, but the technical category varied by jurisdiction and legal purpose: goods and chattels, personal chattels, or real estate/freehold treatment.
- Colonial slave law did not simply deny all personhood. More precisely—and more disturbingly—it assigned enslaved people selective legal personhood when they could be tried and punished, while treating them as property when owners, creditors, heirs, and the treasury asserted economic interests.
