7. Power consumption and five-year electricity cost

Method

The specified electricity rate is $0.13/kWh and operation is 16 hours per day. Because the center is described as processing patients daily, the primary calculation assumes 365 operating days per year.

Annual operating hours:

16 hours/day × 365 days/year = 5,840 hours/year.

Annual cost for a workstation with average operating draw P watts:

P ÷ 1,000 × 5,840 × $0.13  
= P × $0.7592 per year.

Five-year cost for one workstation:

P × $0.7592 × 5  
= P × $3.796.

Five-year cost for 12 workstations:

P × $3.796 × 12  
= P × $45.552.

Average-draw scenarios

Average draw | Annual kWh/workstation | Annual cost/workstation | Five-year cost/workstation | Five-year cost, 12 units
---|---:|---:|---:|---:
100 W | 584 kWh | $75.92 | $379.60 | $4,555.20
150 W | 876 kWh | $113.88 | $569.40 | $6,832.80
200 W | 1,168 kWh | $151.84 | $759.20 | $9,110.40
250 W | 1,460 kWh | $189.80 | $949.00 | $11,388.00
300 W | 1,752 kWh | $227.76 | $1,138.80 | $13,665.60
400 W | 2,336 kWh | $303.68 | $1,518.40 | $18,220.80

These are workstation-only figures. They exclude diagnostic displays, navigation monitors, UPS losses, switches, shared PACS infrastructure and the building cooling needed to remove the heat.

Measured review data

An HP Z4 G5 review measured 66 W at Windows idle and 347 W under a combined CPU/GPU extreme load (https://3dvf.com/en/redaction/hp-z-g5-workstations-put-to-the-test/).

A Lenovo ThinkStation P5 review measured 89 W idle and approximately 600 W under load, using a 1,000 W Platinum PSU (https://www.servethehome.com/lenovo-thinkstation-p5-review-a-fast-intel-xeon-workstation-nvidia/3/).

These measurements are not directly comparable because the component configurations and test methods differ. They demonstrate the size of the range between idle and full CPU/GPU load; the PSU’s 750 W or 1,000 W rating is capacity, not continuous consumption.

Illustrative 25%-heavy-load/75%-idle duty model

If “heavy load” occupies 25% of the 16-hour operating period and idle/light use occupies 75%:

HP Z4 G5 review configuration:

Average power  
= 0.75 × 66 W + 0.25 × 347 W  
= 49.5 + 86.75  
= 136.25 W.

Annual energy  
= 0.13625 kW × 5,840 h  
= 795.7 kWh.

Annual cost  
= 795.7 × $0.13  
= $103.44 per station.

Five-year cost for 12  
= $103.44 × 5 × 12  
= approximately $6,206.

Lenovo P5 review configuration:

Average power  
= 0.75 × 89 W + 0.25 × 600 W  
= 66.75 + 150  
= 216.75 W.

Annual energy  
= 0.21675 kW × 5,840 h  
= 1,265.82 kWh.

Annual cost  
= 1,265.82 × $0.13  
= $164.56 per station.

Five-year cost for 12  
= $164.56 × 5 × 12  
= approximately $9,874.

The roughly $3,668 fleet difference is illustrative only; it must not be treated as an HP-versus-Lenovo forecast because the test systems were differently configured. A procurement pilot should meter each exact candidate at the wall for at least one normal clinical week.

Power-management opportunity

For each 100 W reduction in average fleet draw:

100 W × $45.552 = $4,555.20 saved over five years for 12 machines.

Therefore, selecting a right-sized CPU/GPU, using a 750 W high-efficiency PSU where appropriate, and enforcing sleep after clinical hours can matter more than small differences in purchase price. HP documentation for an ENERGY STAR Z4 G5 configuration reports approximately 74–76 W idle and 8.5 W sleep, illustrating why sleep policy matters (secondary compilation of certification data: https://manualharbor.com/computers/hp/z4-g5-workstation).

Arizona cooling effect

Nearly all electricity consumed by the workstation, displays and UPS ultimately becomes heat in the reading room. Phoenix’s long cooling season makes HVAC energy and comfort material TCO items. The center should have facilities staff measure actual HVAC efficiency and apply a cooling multiplier to workstation, monitor and UPS electricity. High-core CPUs and large GPUs also create localized heat and fan noise that can affect radiologist comfort even where the nominal room cooling capacity is adequate.

The specified $0.13/kWh assumption is reasonable relative to recent statewide commercial pricing: EIA-derived 2025 data report about 12.47 cents/kWh for Arizona commercial customers (primary EIA table: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_5_6_a). Actual Phoenix utility bills may include demand charges, time-of-use periods, taxes and fixed charges that are not captured by the simple energy calculation.

- OEM: motherboard, RAM, CPU, GPU, SSD, NIC and firmware

- Display vendor: calibration, luminance and display-QC system

9. Five-year TCO factors for 12 workstations

Acquisition cost

Include:

- Base workstations
- CPU upgrades
- 64–128 GB ECC memory
- Professional GPUs
- Enterprise NVMe and any 8 TB Hologic local-storage requirement
- 10GbE adapters and optics/transceivers
- Windows Enterprise/LTSC licensing where needed
- Diagnostic displays and navigation monitors
- Display controllers, calibration sensors and QC software
- UPS units
- Five-year support and media retention
- One hot spare
- Imaging-software licenses, AI/CAD licenses and interface fees

The diagnostic displays and application licenses may exceed the price of the tower and should not be treated as incidental accessories.

Deployment and validation

Budget for:

- Standard operating-system image
- Philips and Hologic installation
- DICOM node configuration
- Hanging protocols and user profiles
- GPU and display-driver validation
- DICOM grayscale and mammography display acceptance testing
- Network and firewall configuration
- Endpoint security exceptions approved by security and vendors
- User acceptance testing
- Data migration and cutover
- Staff training
- Documentation and asset tagging

If both applications share a machine, vendor co-residency validation is a direct TCO item. An unsupported combination can create far greater downtime cost than the saving from consolidating two workstations into one.

Electricity, cooling and UPS losses

At 200 W average, the workstation-only five-year electricity cost is approximately $9,110 for 12 units. At 300 W it is approximately $13,666. Add:

- diagnostic-display power;
- navigation monitors;
- UPS conversion losses and battery charging;
- network-switch power attributable to 10GbE ports; and
- Phoenix HVAC energy.

Power should be measured using the final clinical software load, not estimated from PSU wattage.

Storage architecture

Hologic’s 8 TB SSD recommendation can materially alter acquisition and replacement cost. Determine whether each client truly needs that local capacity or whether the site’s approved Manager/client architecture changes the requirement. Other storage TCO considerations are:

- write endurance;
- enterprise versus consumer SSD warranty;
- RAID requirements;
- time to rebuild or reload a failed local cache;
- encryption;
- secure disposal;
- retention of prior studies;
- growth in tomosynthesis resolution and AI outputs.

Network infrastructure

A 10GbE NIC provides little value without:

- sufficient switch ports;
- nonblocking switching capacity;
- 10Gb or faster server/archive uplinks;
- Cat6A or appropriate SFP+ cabling;
- adequate PACS storage throughput;
- network monitoring; and
- redundant core connectivity where clinically necessary.

Include switch licenses, optics, cabling labor and any cooling or UPS capacity for upgraded switches.

Downtime and clinical productivity

At 200 patients per day, the economic impact of slow retrieval or failed workstations can dominate electricity cost. TCO should assign values to:

- radiologist idle time;
- technologist delays;
- rescheduling;
- overtime;
- delayed reports;
- service-level failures;
- lost patient capacity; and
- the clinical risk of unavailable priors.

A one-second saving on a single study is trivial, but repeated delays while loading images, opening priors and navigating tomosynthesis stacks accumulate across thousands of interactions. Conversely, buying the maximum CPU is wasteful if PACS storage or the network remains the bottleneck.

Support and spare strategy

Include:

- five-year support uplift;
- media retention;
- any four-hour response premium;
- internal IT labor for diagnostics and case management;
- one standardized spare;
- spare GPU/NIC/display cables if vendors permit local replacement;
- shipping and secure storage of spares; and
- expected out-of-warranty repairs late in year five.

Standardizing one or two configurations reduces image maintenance, spare-parts diversity and troubleshooting time.

Security and compliance

Include:

- TPM, Secure Boot and full-disk encryption
- EDR/antivirus licensing
- vulnerability management
- patch testing against Philips/Hologic compatibility matrices
- audit logging
- privileged-access controls
- secure media retention and destruction
- HIPAA risk-management processes
- backup of local configuration and user profiles
- BIOS and firmware lifecycle management

Security software can affect DICOM cache and retrieval performance. It must remain enabled during acceptance testing so benchmark results reflect the production environment.

Display lifecycle and quality assurance

Primary mammography interpretation requires FDA-cleared 5 MP displays, not ordinary 4K office monitors. Five-year TCO must include:

- display purchase;
- calibration sensor;
- luminance and uniformity testing;
- scheduled QC;
- replacement for luminance degradation or failure;
- compatible 10-bit GPU outputs; and
- support for the full display chain.

Philips specifically warns that using unapproved monitors or video cards can cause incorrect measurements, inadequate image quality, or missing critical data (https://www.documents.philips.com/assets/Instruction%20for%20Use/20250725/a5a1d9b13cf34189b69ab32500763e29.pdf).

Residual value and refresh risk

Workstation resale value should be treated conservatively because drives containing protected health information may require destruction and medical application certification can limit reuse. Also consider:

- Windows support dates;
- Philips/Hologic support for the OS;
- availability of certified GPU drivers;
- SSD wear;
- display aging;
- OEM parts availability; and
- whether adding RAM or storage in year three can defer full replacement.

10. Final selection framework

Issue a request for quotation for all three vendors with one normalized configuration:

- CPU: 12–18 workstation cores, turbo at least 4.7–4.8 GHz
- RAM: 64 GB ECC, priced alternative for 128 GB
- GPU: certified professional 10-bit card with at least 8 GB VRAM
- Storage: 2 TB enterprise NVMe plus separately priced 8 TB SSD option
- Network: dual-port or single-port 10GbE matching the site switch
- PSU: highest-efficiency right-sized option
- OS: vendor-approved Windows edition and release
- Warranty: five years, next-business-day onsite, media retention
- Displays: quoted separately as FDA-cleared dual 5 MP mammography displays
- One additional hot-spare tower

Score the proposals approximately as follows:

- 30% application and display certification
- 20% measured Philips/Hologic workflow performance
- 15% five-year acquisition and support cost
- 10% local service and parts commitment
- 10% power and cooling
- 10% expansion, storage and 10GbE architecture
- 5% manageability and security

Run a two- to four-week pilot with at least one radiologist and one technologist. Capture wall power, network throughput, study-open latency, prior-study retrieval, scrolling responsiveness, application stability and support responsiveness.

Bottom line

The HP Z4 G6i is the best forward-looking hardware choice, provided Philips and Hologic certify the exact build. A Xeon 654, 64–128 GB ECC, approved 8–16 GB professional GPU, enterprise NVMe and 10GbE should provide a strong balance of clock speed, core count and five-year headroom.

The Lenovo ThinkStation P5 is the safest mature alternative: use a Xeon W5-2545 or W5-2565X, 64–128 GB ECC and an Intel X550-T2/X710-DA2 10GbE adapter. It has clear ECC, expansion and enterprise-support credentials.

The Dell Precision 5860 produced the strongest gathered official SPECworkstation CPU and storage scores among directly comparable systems and includes 10GbE, but its current US unavailability makes fleet procurement and five-year lifecycle consistency the central concern. Buy it only with confirmed inventory, identical configurations and full support coverage.

For 12 systems, workstation electricity is likely to be roughly $6,800–$13,700 over five years at 150–300 W average draw, before monitors, UPS and Phoenix cooling. That cost is meaningful but smaller than diagnostic-display, software, support and downtime costs. The decisive TCO factors are vendor certification, radiologist productivity, local storage design, end-to-end 10GbE performance, display QA, five-year onsite support and avoidance of unsupported Philips/Hologic software combinations.

final.content:
# Memristor-Based Neuromorphic Computing: Physics, Crossbar Engineering, and Benchmark Evidence

## Executive assessment

The debate contains two questions that are often conflated:

1. **Are commercial resistive-switching devices physical realizations of Leon Chua’s 1971 ideal fourth circuit element?**
2. **Are those devices nevertheless useful as nonvolatile, analog or stochastic synapses and in-memory multiply–accumulate elements?**

The evidence supports different answers.

* On the strict first question, the Hewlett-Packard claim remains disputed. Stanley Williams and colleagues argued in 2008 that coupled ionic and electronic transport in nanoscale TiO₂ devices realizes the charge-dependent memristance predicted by Chua. Vongehr and Meng argued in 2015 that such devices are material-memory resistors or, at most, members of Chua and Kang’s broader 1976 class of “memristive systems,” not the electromagnetic fourth element implied by the 1971 symmetry argument. Commercial devices such as Knowm’s self-directed-channel devices exhibit thresholds, stochastic switching, bounded states, device-to-device variation, and dependencies beyond total transported charge. Those characteristics make them technologically useful but generally prevent an unqualified identification with the ideal relation \(d\phi=M(q)dq\).

* On the second question, resistive memories clearly can act as compact physical synapses. Their conductance can encode a weight, currents through crossbars naturally sum, and conductance can be updated locally by pulses. The best-supported system advantage, however, is **nonvolatile in-memory analog computation and reduced data movement**, not a uniquely “memristive” plasticity law unavailable in CMOS. CMOS/SRAM alternatives can implement learning and stochasticity too, often with greater precision, maturity, endurance, and reproducibility.

* Crossbar implementations solve sneak paths and variability through ordinary engineering rather than through the ideal memristor relation:
  * **Knowm AHaH systems** partition arrays into small, multiplexed “unit crossbars,” use differential-pair synapses, and explicitly accommodate stochastic devices.
  * **University of Michigan Ag/amorphous-Si systems** use high ON/OFF ratio and intrinsic rectification to suppress crosstalk, with related one-selector/one-resistor analysis establishing selector requirements.
  * **KAIST-associated RRAM work** emphasizes selectors, self-rectifying cells, variability-aware sizing, and two-port sneak-current cancellation, including extensions to three-dimensional arrays.

* Benchmarks reported from 2020 through 2024 show that analog resistive hardware can achieve useful accuracy—more than 96% on MNIST in a 2020 fully hardware-implemented memristor CNN, 93.7% mapped accuracy and over 93.5% one-day retained accuracy on CIFAR-10 using phase-change memory, and 100% on a limited 1,500-example MNIST hardware experiment in 2024. These results do not establish universal superiority over CMOS. A cited SRAM implementation reached 98.3% MNIST and 85.7% CIFAR-10 at 139 TOPS/W, while another reached 98.6% MNIST at 658 TOPS/W. Differences in networks, precision, training, peripheral accounting, and test-set scope prevent direct technology rankings.

The current practical consensus is therefore: **memristive device physics provides an unusually compact and potentially efficient substrate for storing and updating synaptic weights, but neither the “fourth fundamental element” label nor intrinsic superiority in synaptic plasticity is necessary—or presently sufficient—to explain its value.**

---

## 1. The original theoretical claim

### 1.1 Chua’s 1971 relation

Chua’s construction completed a symmetry table involving four circuit variables:

* voltage \(v\),
* current \(i\),
* charge \(q=\int i\,dt\),
* flux linkage \(\phi=\int v\,dt\).

A charge-controlled ideal memristor is described by a single-valued constitutive relation

\[
\phi=\phi(q),
\]

with differential memristance

\[
M(q)=\frac{d\phi}{dq}.
\]

Differentiating with respect to time gives

\[
v(t)=M(q)i(t).
\]

The crucial restriction is that the instantaneous resistance is a function of accumulated charge alone. If two histories deliver the same \(q\), an ideal charge-controlled memristor should have the same state and resistance. Chua’s original paper is identified in the HP article as “Memristor—the missing circuit element,” IEEE Transactions on Circuit Theory 18, 507–519 (1971), DOI 10.1109/TCT.1971.1083337 (reference information reproduced at https://bishtref.com/articles/10.1038/nature06932).

In 1976, Chua and Kang generalized the concept to “memristive systems,” which may have one or more internal state variables:

\[
v=R(\mathbf{w},i,t)i,
\]

\[
\frac{d\mathbf{w}}{dt}=f(\mathbf{w},i,t).
\]

For that broader class, flux need not be a unique function of charge. The HP paper itself expressly distinguishes the ideal memristor from this wider class and notes that thermistors, neon bulbs, Josephson junctions, and even the Hodgkin–Huxley neuron model can be represented with memristive-system equations (https://web.ece.ucsb.edu/~strukov/papers/2008/Nature2008.pdf).

That distinction is central: a device can show pinched hysteresis and resistance memory without satisfying the strict one-state-variable, charge-only constitutive law.

---

## 2. Williams and the HP Labs position

### 2.1 What the 2008 Nature paper claimed

Dmitri Strukov, Gregory Snider, Duncan Stewart, and R. Stanley Williams titled their 2008 Nature article “The missing memristor found.” They claimed that memristance arises naturally when solid-state ionic and electronic transport are coupled under an applied voltage, and presented titanium-oxide cross-point switches as a physical example (https://web.ece.ucsb.edu/~strukov/papers/2008/Nature2008.pdf).

Their simplified device consisted of a semiconductor film of thickness \(D\), divided into:

* a low-resistance doped region of width \(w\), with full-length resistance \(R_{\mathrm{ON}}\), and
* a high-resistance undoped region of width \(D-w\), with full-length resistance \(R_{\mathrm{OFF}}\).

The terminal equation was

\[
v(t)=
\left[
R_{\mathrm{ON}}\frac{w(t)}{D}
+
R_{\mathrm{OFF}}\left(1-\frac{w(t)}{D}\right)
\right]i(t).
\]

Under linear ionic drift,

\[
\frac{dw}{dt}=\mu_v\frac{R_{\mathrm{ON}}}{D}i(t),
\]

so, before a physical boundary is reached,

\[
w(t)=\mu_v\frac{R_{\mathrm{ON}}}{D}q(t).
\]

Substitution produces a resistance that depends on transported charge. In the approximation \(R_{\mathrm{ON}}\ll R_{\mathrm{OFF}}\),

\[
M(q)\approx R_{\mathrm{OFF}}
\left(
1-\frac{\mu_vR_{\mathrm{ON}}}{D^2}q
\right).
\]

The factor \(1/D^2\) was the basis for HP’s scaling argument: the paper stated that this contribution is one million times larger at nanometre dimensions than at micrometre dimensions (https://web.ece.ucsb.edu/~strukov/papers/2008/Nature2008.pdf).

The paper identified familiar memristive signatures:

* a pinched, double-loop current–voltage hysteresis;
* collapse of hysteresis toward a straight line as excitation frequency increases;
* continuous intermediate conductance states;
* bipolar switching under opposite voltage polarities;
* history-dependent apparent negative differential resistance.

The paper also recognized an important limitation: the physical state \(w\) is bounded between zero and \(D\). Once a boundary is reached, the simple proportionality \(w\propto q\) no longer holds without boundary conditions. The authors consequently described the model as behaving like a “perfect memristor” over a restricted state range and as a more general memristive system over a wider, bounded range (https://web.ece.ucsb.edu/~strukov/papers/2008/Nature2008.pdf).

### 2.2 HP’s interpretation of flux and magnetism

HP’s response to the magnetic objection is already implicit in the 2008 paper. The authors argued that the mathematics requires a nonlinear relationship between the time integrals of voltage and current; it does not require the device’s memory mechanism to be magnetic. The paper states that the magnetic field’s lack of an explicit role may explain why the phenomenon had been overlooked: researchers were searching for a magnetic realization when ionic redistribution could generate the required terminal relation (https://web.ece.ucsb.edu/~strukov/papers/2008/Nature2008.pdf).

Thus, in the HP interpretation, \(\phi\) is the circuit-theory flux linkage defined by

\[
\phi(t)=\int v(t)\,dt,
\]

not necessarily a locally stored magnetic flux responsible for the memory state. Ionic motion can make \(\phi\) a nonlinear function of \(q\), satisfying the terminal equations over the applicable operating region.

HP’s public announcement went further, saying that the team had “proven the existence” of the fourth fundamental element and that it possessed properties not reproducible by combinations of resistor, capacitor, and inductor alone (https://www.hp.com/hpinfo/newsroom/press/2008/080430a.html).

### 2.3 From memory resistor to artificial synapse

The formal 2008 Nature letter chiefly established the device model; the synapse analogy was developed most explicitly in Williams’s accompanying exposition. An IEEE Spectrum article described the memristor as “the functional equivalent of a synapse” and proposed that it could enable systems that emulate networks of neurons and synapses rather than digitally simulate all their equations (https://spectrum.ieee.org/how-we-found-the-missing-memristor).

The analogy rests on three physical similarities:

1. synaptic efficacy can be represented by conductance;
2. activity pulses can alter that conductance;
3. the altered conductance can persist without continuous refresh.

This analogy is useful but does not itself prove that a device is Chua’s ideal fourth element. A phase-change cell, floating-gate transistor, magnetic memory, electrochemical transistor, or CMOS-plus-memory circuit can also store an adjustable synaptic weight.

---

## 3. Vongehr and Meng’s 2015 critique

Sascha Vongehr and Xiangkang Meng challenged the historical and physical interpretation in “The Missing Memristor has Not been Found,” Scientific Reports 5, 11657 (2015) (https://doi.org/10.1038/srep11657; abstract at https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26108376/).

Their argument has several components.

### 3.1 The ideal mathematical element already existed by definition

They distinguish among:

* the **ideal memristor**, a mathematical basic circuit element satisfying \(M=d\phi/dq\);
* a hypothetical **real device** corresponding to that element;
* a “perfect” charge-only memory resistor;
* the much broader category of **memristive systems**.

On this view, HP could not “discover” the mathematical element, which existed by definition after 1971. The empirical question was whether HP found the particular missing physical counterpart suggested by Chua’s symmetry construction.

### 3.2 Resistive switching was not new in 2008

Vongehr and Meng observed that thin-film resistive switching and hysteretic conduction were known before 1971 and that comparable devices had been reported well before HP’s announcement. They therefore contended that the novelty lay principally in relabeling known resistive-memory phenomena as the missing memristor, not in discovering the phenomena themselves (https://www.nature.com/articles/srep11657).

The HP paper itself partly supports the historical premise: it said that switching, hysteretic conductance, multiple states, and apparent negative differential resistance had appeared in the thin-film literature for nearly 50 years (https://web.ece.ucsb.edu/~strukov/papers/2008/Nature2008.pdf).

### 3.3 The 1971 symmetry argument was electromagnetic

Vongehr and Meng’s strongest objection is that Chua’s original table paired charge with flux in an electromagnetic framework. They argue that the real missing counterpart should involve magnetic induction in an essential manner, just as a physical inductor does. HP’s oxide device instead stores memory through matter redistribution—oxygen vacancies, ions, defects, or filaments—and would continue to exhibit resistance memory in a hypothetical world without magnetism. They therefore regard it as a material memory resistor rather than the electromagnetic fourth element implied by the original symmetry (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26108376/).

They use a mechanical analogy to make the distinction: it is possible to write a formal memory relation involving displacement and momentum and to construct dissipative systems with state-dependent drag, but that does not mean every mechanical memory resistor realizes the missing mass- or inertia-based counterpart suggested by the symmetry. Their related mechanical formulation defines \(M=dp/dx\) and distinguishes a realizable massless memory resistor from the hypothesized mass-involving element (https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.00300).

### 3.4 Real devices have extra state variables

A commercial resistive-memory device generally depends on more than total charge:

* pulse amplitude and duration;
* voltage thresholds;
* polarity;
* temperature;
* stochastic nucleation or filament rupture;
* prior state;
* relaxation time;
* compliance current;
* cycle count;
* boundary saturation.

Such a device is naturally described by

\[
v=R(\mathbf{w},i,T,\ldots)i
\]

and

\[
\dot{\mathbf{w}}=f(\mathbf{w},i,T,\ldots),
\]

rather than by the single-valued relation \(M=M(q)\).

Vongehr and Meng therefore classify the available devices as memristive systems under the 1976 generalization, not strict realizations of the 1971 ideal element. Their abstract concludes that the originally hypothesized real device remains missing and is likely impossible (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26108376/).

---

## 4. Strukov’s position and what the disagreement actually establishes

The evidence gathered here does not identify a separately published, point-by-point formal reply by Strukov to Vongehr and Meng. It does, however, establish the substantive defense associated with Strukov and the HP team:

1. **Circuit flux need not imply magnetic storage.**  
   Since \(\phi=\int vdt\), a terminal charge–flux relationship can arise from ionic-state evolution even when the microscopic memory is not magnetic.

2. **The simple drift model reaches the ideal equations within a restricted regime.**  
   Before saturation, \(w\propto q\), so terminal resistance can be written as \(M(q)\).

3. **Outside that regime, “memristive system” remains an appropriate description.**  
   The 2008 paper itself acknowledges the bounded state and describes the device as a perfect memristor in one range and a memristive system in another (https://web.ece.ucsb.edu/~strukov/papers/2008/Nature2008.pdf).

4. **Practical utility does not depend on metaphysical fundamentality.**  
   Whether called an ideal memristor, non-ideal memristor, RRAM, CBRAM, PCM, or memristive system, a two-terminal nonvolatile conductance can still perform memory and analog computation.

The deepest disagreement is therefore semantic and ontological rather than empirical:

* HP uses a **terminal-equation definition**: if the device realizes the required \(\phi(q)\) relationship over its operative range, it is a memristor.
* Vongehr and Meng use a **physical-correspondence definition**: the real fourth element should embody the electromagnetic symmetry that motivated Chua’s 1971 construction, not merely imitate its terminal behavior through matter rearrangement.

Later literature did not eliminate the dispute. A 2018 Nature Electronics retrospective adopted the HP historical narrative, saying that Williams’s group connected experimental observations to Chua’s prediction and that “the fourth fundamental circuit element was found” (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41928-018-0083-3). Conversely, a 2018 Scientific Reports paper argued that the HP device was not the 1971 postulate and that only three fundamental passive elements should be recognized (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-29394-7).

### Practical verdict on commercial devices

Under a broad modern engineering convention, commercial products marketed as memristors are legitimately called **memristive devices** because they possess resistance states affected by electrical history. Under Chua’s strict charge-controlled law, the available evidence does not establish that a commercial device is an ideal fourth element over its complete operating range.

Knowm’s devices illustrate the distinction. Their observed switching thresholds are probabilistic enough that a 2023 IEEE Latin America Transactions study modeled set/reset thresholds with skewed, heavy-tailed \(\alpha\)-stable random variables (https://latamt.ieeer9.org/index.php/transactions/article/view/8308). Knowm itself states that most practical memristors show stochastic behavior and promotes a generalized metastable-switch model that spans stochastic binary and incremental analog operation (https://knowm.org/the-generalized-metastable-switch-memristor-model/). A device whose state transition probabilities depend on threshold distributions and applied voltage is more naturally a stochastic memristive system than a unique \(M(q)\) element.

---

## 5. Crossbar challenges common to all three implementations

A passive crossbar places a programmable conductance at each row–column intersection. Ideally, applied row voltages generate column currents

\[
I_j=\sum_i G_{ij}V_i,
\]

which is an analog vector–matrix multiplication.

Two non-idealities dominate.

### 5.1 Sneak paths

When unselected rows or columns float or receive partial bias, current can travel through combinations of unselected cells and re-enter the sensed line. This:

* corrupts the selected-cell current;
* reduces read margin;
* increases power;
* causes unintended writes;
* worsens rapidly with array dimension and low-resistance-cell population.

Large arrays also suffer line resistance or IR drop, causing position-dependent voltages and effective weights.

### 5.2 Device variability

Relevant variation includes:

* device-to-device conductance range;
* cycle-to-cycle set/reset threshold;
* nonlinear pulse response;
* asymmetric potentiation and depression;
* limited endurance;
* retention drift;
* random telegraph noise;
* stuck or failed cells;
* stochastic filament formation;
* selector variation.

These effects are especially serious in analog learning because a requested weight increment does not produce the same conductance increment in every cell.

---

## 6. Knowm’s AHaH-node approach

### 6.1 Architecture

An AHaH—“anti-Hebbian and Hebbian”—node represents a synapse as a differential pair of memristive conductances. The node’s output is based on the difference between the two branches, allowing positive and negative effective weights. Knowm describes an AHaH node as \(n\) synapses sharing a common output electrode and says the device need only provide incremental, voltage-dependent state change (https://knowm.org/the-generalized-metastable-switch-memristor-model/).

Knowm’s stated desirable device characteristics include:

* adaptation thresholds below approximately 0.2 V;
* on-state resistance around 10 kΩ or more;
* high dynamic range;
* incremental response to very short pulses;
* retention of a week or longer for general use.

Knowm also notes that shorter retention can be useful for specific tasks such as combinatorial optimization (https://knowm.org/the-generalized-metastable-switch-memristor-model/).

### 6.2 Sneak-path strategy: small unit crossbars and explicit multiplexing

Knowm acknowledges that sparse input patterns can be especially problematic in a conventional large passive crossbar because floating rows and columns create unwanted paths, and that the problem worsens with array size (https://knowm.org/memristor-crossbars-as-easy-as-raspberry-pi/).

Rather than relying exclusively on a selector in series with every device, Knowm proposes a hierarchical architecture:

1. Build a small \(N\times M\) **unit crossbar**.
2. Place bidirectional analog multiplexers on its rows and columns.
3. Select one local crosspoint—or none—at a time.
4. Use many unit crossbars as the effective elements of a larger “meta-crossbar.”
5. Activate only the required synapses using digital address and enable signals.

Because the multiplexed unit crossbar acts as a selection structure, inactive local devices can be disconnected from the active large-scale row and column. Knowm argues that this allows a larger meta-array to perform computation without the same sneak-current exposure as a monolithic passive array (https://knowm.org/memristor-crossbars-as-easy-as-raspberry-pi/).

The cost is architectural overhead:

* analog multiplexers;
* row and column decoders;
* enable logic;
* reduced simultaneous access within each unit;
* additional capacitance and routing;
* hybrid digital/analog control.

This is therefore not a selector-free physical solution. It moves selection from a device at every crosspoint into a coarser multiplexed hierarchy.

### 6.3 Variability strategy: differential encoding and stochastic learning

Knowm uses differential pairs for three stated purposes:

* representing positive and negative weights;
* reducing common-mode noise;
* reducing the effect of common memristor decay (https://knowm.org/memristor-crossbars-as-easy-as-raspberry-pi/).

Its modeling philosophy explicitly treats stochasticity as part of the device rather than as a small perturbation. The generalized metastable-switch model is intended to describe transitions from stochastic binary behavior to incremental analog behavior (https://knowm.org/the-generalized-metastable-switch-memristor-model/). The 2023 threshold study reinforces that need by reporting probabilistic set/reset behavior with potentially skewed, heavy-tailed distributions (https://latamt.ieeer9.org/index.php/transactions/article/view/8308).

Sparse spike coding reduces the number of simultaneously active synapses and eliminates multiplications for binary active inputs: only the addressed weights are summed. There is a numerical error in Knowm’s worked example: two active inputs out of 64 equal

\[
\frac{2}{64}=0.03125=3.125\%,
\]

not 0.03125% as written on the page (https://knowm.org/memristor-crossbars-as-easy-as-raspberry-pi/). The architectural point—sparse activity reduces active devices and communication—remains valid, but the displayed percentage is off by a factor of 100.

### 6.4 Evidentiary qualification

The foundational AHaH computing article is a 2014 PLOS ONE paper, not an IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices article. The commercial-device variability source found here is in IEEE Latin America Transactions, also not IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (https://latamt.ieeer9.org/index.php/transactions/article/view/8308). Therefore, any premise that all three named implementations were individually documented in “their respective IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices publications” is bibliographically inaccurate. The comparison remains technically valid, but the venues should not be homogenized.

---

## 7. University of Michigan Ag/Si memristive crossbars

### 7.1 Device and demonstrated array

Sung Hyun Jo, Kuk-Hwan Kim, and Wei Lu reported a 1-kbit high-density Si-based memristive crossbar in Nano Letters in 2009. A two-terminal hysteretic resistive switch was formed at each crosspoint, with high addressing yield and a high ON/OFF ratio. Depending on configuration, the array could act as RRAM or write-once memory (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/nl8037689).

The University of Michigan technology description identifies an Ag/a-Si/p-Si or Ag/a-Si:H/c-Si structure and reports:

* cell dimensions at or below 100 nm × 100 nm;
* programming below 50 ns;
* endurance exceeding \(10^5\) operations;
* ON/OFF ratio above \(10^4\);
* years-long retention;
* storage density above \(10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm^{-2}}\);
* adjustable on-state resistance for multibit storage;
* rectifying or non-rectifying behavior depending on configuration (https://available-inventions.umich.edu/product/a-si-based-crossbar-memory).

These figures come from a university technology-transfer description rather than an independently normalized head-to-head benchmark, so they should be treated as reported device characteristics.

### 7.2 Sneak-path strategy: intrinsic rectification and selector behavior

The Michigan design’s principal device-level answer to sneak currents is **asymmetric or rectifying I–V behavior**. A symmetric resistor conducts unwanted current in both directions under half-select bias; a rectifying cell strongly suppresses current in the unfavorable direction. The Michigan description explicitly says that intrinsic rectification reduces crosstalk in dense arrays (https://available-inventions.umich.edu/product/nanoscale-amorphous-silicon-based-ultra-high-density-resistance-switching-memory-and-logic-devices).

The large ON/OFF ratio also improves separation between selected high- and low-resistance states. But a high ON/OFF ratio alone does not eliminate sneak current: nonlinear or rectifying behavior under partial bias is critical.

A related paper by Jiantao Zhou, Kuk-Hwan Kim, and Wei Lu, “Crossbar RRAM Arrays: Selector Device Requirements During Read Operation,” appeared in IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices in 2014. It analyzed a one-selector/one-resistor configuration and concluded that:

* passive RRAM crossbars require a nonlinear selector to address sneak paths;
* high selector current density is especially critical;
* selector nonlinearity requirements may be relaxed relative to current-drive requirements;
* read scheme, sensing resistance, and storage-element parameters should be jointly optimized (https://doi.org/10.1109/ted.2014.2310200).

Thus, Michigan’s approach combines material-level rectification with circuit-aware selector design rather than assuming that the memory element’s hysteresis alone solves array leakage.

### 7.3 Variability strategy

The 1-kbit demonstration emphasized reproducibility, reliability, yield, and high ON/OFF ratio (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/nl8037689). Rectification also narrows the contribution of unselected cells to the sensed current, making the array less sensitive to their exact conductances.

Nevertheless, Ag-based conductive-bridge devices operate through filament formation and dissolution. Their useful analog programmability is also a source of randomness. Conductance depends on filament geometry, compliance, and pulse history, so multilevel operation requires write verification, pulse adaptation, redundancy, or variability-aware training.

The Michigan group’s broader neuromorphic program demonstrated that analog memristive devices could implement spike-timing-dependent plasticity and short-term-to-long-term memory transitions, according to its research summary (https://lugroup.engin.umich.edu/memristor-based-logic-circuits/). This establishes physical emulation of biological learning rules, but it does not establish that the rule is unattainable or less efficient in CMOS.

### 7.4 Venue qualification

The primary “High-Density Crossbar Arrays Based on a Si Memristive System” report was published in Nano Letters, not IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/nl8037689). The selector-requirement study involving Michigan authors was the relevant IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices paper (https://doi.org/10.1109/ted.2014.2310200).

---

## 8. KAIST-associated RRAM crossbar approaches

The RRAM literature associated with Korean groups, including KAIST researchers, treats sneak paths and variability as coupled device/circuit problems. Three approaches represented in the IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices evidence are selectors, variability-aware sizing, and current cancellation.

### 8.1 One-selector/one-resistor arrays

In a 1S1R array, a nonlinear selector is placed in series with each resistive storage element. Ideally:

* the selected cell receives sufficient voltage for a large read current;
* half-selected cells receive a voltage at which the selector is highly resistive;
* aggregate leakage remains below the sensing margin.

A 2015 IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices study, “Cell Variability Impact on the One-Selector One-Resistor Cross-Point Array Performance,” considered three independent sources:

1. stored-data-pattern randomness;
2. selector variability;
3. resistive switching element variability.

It found that random data patterns were not the principal source of read-margin degradation. Narrowing of the resistive element’s ON/OFF window reduced margin, while selector variability caused further loss, particularly by affecting ON-state current. For a projected 1-Mbit array, the study reported that—with typical selector variability—a minimum resistive-state window of 5 and half-bias selector nonlinearity of approximately 8,000 were required to maintain at least a 10% read margin (https://doi.org/10.1109/ted.2015.2439958).

Those figures quantify why a nominally excellent selector is insufficient: its distribution, not just its mean I–V curve, determines scalable yield.

### 8.2 Self-rectifying and three-dimensional vertical RRAM

A 2018 IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices study examined cell variability in three-dimensional vertical RRAM using self-rectifying cells. It found:

* a broad cell-current distribution reduces read margin;
* the same distribution has little effect on total write power;
* a large HRS/LRS resistance ratio improves read margin and reduces variability sensitivity when the stack has relatively few word-line layers;
* with many word-line layers, increasing ON/OFF ratio produces little further margin benefit because leakage from half-selected cells in the selected vertical pillar dominates (https://doi.org/10.1109/ted.2018.2878440).

This is an important systems result: improving the memory window cannot indefinitely compensate for geometric accumulation of half-select leakage. Selector or rectifier quality, array partitioning, and sensing architecture become decisive.

### 8.3 Two-port sneak-current cancellation

Another strategy is not to prevent every leakage path physically but to measure and cancel its contribution.

The 2017 IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices paper “Extension of Two-Port Sneak Current Cancellation Scheme to 3-D Vertical RRAM Crossbar Array” extended a two-port current-mode readout method from two-dimensional arrays to vertical RRAM. HSPICE simulations of a \(32\times32\times8\) array, including practical circuit parameters, were used to verify feasibility (https://doi.org/10.1109/ted.2017.2664863).

The simulated cell count was

\[
32\times32\times8=8{,}192\ \text{cells}.
\]

Two-port sensing estimates or cancels the common sneak-current component so the remaining signal better represents the selected cell. It reduces read-margin loss without requiring ideal isolation at each junction, but adds sensing circuitry, calibration requirements, and sensitivity to mismatch.

### 8.4 Comparison with Knowm and Michigan

The three implementation philosophies are distinct:

| Platform | Principal sneak-path measure | Principal variability measure | Main cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Knowm AHaH | Small multiplexed unit crossbars; inactive devices disconnected; sparse addressed activation | Differential pairs; common-mode rejection; stochastic device models and learning | Multiplexer/decoder overhead and reduced local parallelism |
| Michigan Ag/Si | Intrinsic rectification, high ON/OFF ratio, and nonlinear selectors | High-yield fabrication, large read window, pulse/write control | Filament variability and need for selector-aware design |
| KAIST-associated RRAM | 1S1R selectors, self-rectifying cells, two-port cancellation, 3-D-aware sensing | Statistical array sizing; explicit selector/RRAM distributions; circuit cancellation | Selector area/voltage overhead, peripheral complexity, and reduced margins at scale |

None relies on an ideal \(M(q)\) law. All depend on selectors, nonlinear I–V characteristics, differential sensing, multiplexers, training compensation, or statistical margins.

---

## 9. Does memristor physics provide superior synaptic plasticity?

### 9.1 What the physics genuinely offers

Resistive memories can provide several functions directly in a two-terminal device:

* **nonvolatile weight storage** in conductance;
* **incremental potentiation and depression** through pulses;
* **local update rules**, because programming depends on waveforms applied at the two terminals;
* **conductance summation** through Kirchhoff’s current law;
* **stochastic switching**, which can be used for probabilistic learning;
* in some devices, **short-term and long-term dynamics** from relaxation and filament stabilization.

The University of Michigan group’s summary reports demonstrations of spike-timing-dependent plasticity and short-term-to-long-term transitions in physical memristive devices (https://lugroup.engin.umich.edu/memristor-based-logic-circuits/). A 2020 Scientific Reports study deliberately exploited stochastic switching in CMOS-integrated binary RRAM to emulate stochastic plasticity and evaluate stochastic neural networks on MNIST, rather than treating switching randomness purely as an error (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-71334-x).

These are legitimate device-level advantages: what would require several transistors, capacitors, or digital state bits in conventional circuitry may be condensed into one resistive device plus access circuitry.

### 9.2 Why “superior plasticity” is too strong

The same physics introduces limitations:

* highly nonlinear and asymmetric weight updates;
* large cycle-to-cycle and device-to-device variation;
* finite conductance states and precision;
* drift and retention loss;
* write noise;
* limited endurance;
* threshold variation;
* difficult isolation in passive arrays;
* energy and area consumed by DACs, ADCs, selectors, write verification, and control.

Furthermore, CMOS can implement all of the relevant learning functions:

* STDP with timing circuits;
* stochastic updates with pseudo-random or noisy circuits;
* metaplasticity with digital or analog state;
* short- and long-term memory with capacitors, SRAM, floating gates, or mixed-signal circuits;
* arbitrary update laws through programmable digital logic.

Memristor physics therefore offers **physical compactness and co-location**, not an exclusive plasticity mechanism.

A 2024 review describes the leading benefit as nonvolatile in-memory computation, which eliminates repeated shuttling of weights between separate processing and memory units. The same review stresses that practical accelerators remain hybrid systems with CMOS peripheral circuits for programming and analog–digital conversion (https://www.nature.com/articles/s44287-024-00037-6).

---

## 10. Benchmark evidence from 2020–2024

### 10.1 2020 fully hardware-implemented memristor CNN on MNIST

A 2020 Nature paper integrated eight 2,048-cell memristor arrays into a five-layer convolutional neural network and reported more than 96% MNIST accuracy (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-1942-4).

Total physical cells:

\[
8\times2{,}048=16{,}384.
\]

The work used hybrid training to adapt to poor yield, variation, and other nonideal device characteristics. It reported energy efficiency more than two orders of magnitude above state-of-the-art GPUs. “More than two orders” implies a factor greater than

\[
10^2=100.
\]

This is strong evidence for efficient parallel inference in a tailored demonstrator. It is not evidence that raw device plasticity alone produced the result: hybrid training and explicit adaptation to imperfections were required.

Accuracy also remained below the high-98% to 99% range obtainable on MNIST with mature digital implementations. The significance was full physical execution and energy efficiency, not a new accuracy record.

### 10.2 2020 phase-change-memory inference on CIFAR-10

A 2020 Nature Communications paper mapped ResNet-32 weights to phase-change memory and reported:

* 93.7% CIFAR-10 classification accuracy after mapping;
* over 93.5% accuracy retained for one day in hardware;
* 361,722 synaptic weights;
* two PCM devices per differential weight (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-16108-9).

The number of programmed PCM devices was therefore

\[
361{,}722\times2=723{,}444.
\]

The drop from initial mapped accuracy to the reported one-day lower bound was at most approximately

\[
93.7\%-93.5\%=0.2\ \text{percentage points}.
\]

The result depended on noise-aware training and batch-normalization-based compensation. It demonstrates that algorithm–hardware co-design can absorb analog noise and drift. PCM is a memristive nonvolatile memory in the broad engineering sense, but it is not evidence for the ideal Chua memristor.

### 10.3 2024 self-rectifying passive array on MNIST

A 2024 Nature Communications report used a 1-kbit self-rectifying memristor passive crossbar and achieved 100% classification on 1,500 tested MNIST examples in a fully hardware-based single-layer task (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-44620-1).

A 1-kbit array contains nominally

\[
1{,}024\ \text{cells}.
\]

The reported test produced zero observed errors in \(n=1{,}500\). The approximate “rule of three” 95% upper confidence bound on the underlying error probability after zero observed failures is

\[
p_{\text{error}}<\frac{3}{1{,}500}=0.002=0.2\%.
\]

Equivalently, this particular sample supports an approximate lower confidence bound near 99.8% accuracy, assuming independent, representative trials.

The result should not be compared directly with full-test-set, ten-class deep-network MNIST figures without checking task scope. The paper describes a single-layer classification task and a 1,500-example test, whereas standard MNIST evaluations commonly use more extensive architectures and test protocols. Its main contribution is evidence that self-rectifying passive arrays can perform reliable physical computation without per-cell transistors.

### 10.4 Crossbar-mapping results on CIFAR-10

A 2023 study of convolution mapping reported that partitioning 2-D plus 1-D kernels across smaller crossbars could reduce the number of required unit arrays by:

* almost 90% for \(128\times128\) crossbars;
* almost 95% for \(256\times256\) crossbars;

while keeping CIFAR-10 recognition-rate loss below 2% in the reported simulations (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9959389/).

This is primarily an architectural mapping result. It also reinforces why real accelerators partition large matrices: smaller arrays reduce line-resistance and analog-accuracy problems.

### 10.5 CMOS/SRAM comparison

A review of edge-intelligence implementations cited a 16-kbit, 65-nm SRAM-based chip with:

* 139 TOPS/W;
* 98.3% MNIST accuracy;
* 85.7% CIFAR-10 accuracy.

It also cited another SRAM result with:

* 658 TOPS/W;
* 98.6% MNIST accuracy.

These figures are summarized at https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/aisy.202000114.

The comparison illustrates both sides of the case:

* Against the 2020 hardware memristor CNN’s “more than 96%” MNIST result, 98.3% is at least approximately

\[
98.3-96.0=2.3
\]

percentage points higher, although the memristor result is stated only as “more than 96%,” so the exact gap is smaller than 2.3 points if its actual accuracy exceeded 96.0%.

* The PCM CIFAR-10 result of 93.7% exceeds the cited SRAM CIFAR-10 figure of 85.7% by

\[
93.7-85.7=8.0
\]

percentage points.

Neither arithmetic difference establishes a device winner. The compared systems used different networks, memory technologies, precisions, training methods, technology nodes, and accounting conventions. In particular, ResNet-32 is not necessarily the network used by the 65-nm SRAM chip.

TOPS/W can also be misleading if one paper counts only array operations while another includes ADCs, DACs, buffers, control, and data movement. The 2024 review specifically notes that CMOS conversion and programming peripherals are essential components of memristive accelerators (https://www.nature.com/articles/s44287-024-00037-6).

---

## 11. What the benchmark record does and does not prove

### It does prove:

1. Resistive-memory arrays can carry out useful neural computation in physical hardware.
2. Variability-aware or noise-aware training can recover software-like accuracy.
3. Differential encoding can mitigate drift and common-mode error.
4. Self-rectifying devices can make passive arrays more practical.
5. In-memory current summation can provide large energy and throughput advantages over architectures dominated by memory transfers.

### It does not prove:

1. That the device is Chua’s strict ideal fourth circuit element.
2. That memristive physics inherently learns better than CMOS.
3. That a passive array remains accurate at arbitrary scale.
4. That array-only TOPS/W survives inclusion of all peripheral circuitry.
5. That analog online training is more reliable than digital or SRAM-based training.
6. That MNIST performance predicts competitive performance on modern large-scale models.
7. That the reported systems have commercial-grade endurance, yield, lifetime, calibration stability, and manufacturability.

The 2020 memristor CNN explicitly framed poor yield and large device variation as central obstacles and required hybrid training (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-1942-4). The PCM result required noise injection and drift compensation (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-16108-9). These are successful remedies, but they show that accuracy arises from co-design rather than ideal device behavior.

---

## 12. Overall consensus

### 12.1 Physics and terminology

There is no universal consensus that commercial “memristors” are literal realizations of the unique, fundamental fourth passive element suggested in 1971.

A defensible terminology is:

* **Ideal memristor:** strict, single-valued \(\phi(q)\) element.
* **Memristive system:** state-dependent resistor governed by additional internal dynamics.
* **Resistive switching memory/RRAM/CBRAM/PCM:** a physical technology whose state is stored by defects, filaments, phase, ions, or interfaces.
* **Commercial memristor:** accepted engineering shorthand for a marketed resistive-switching device, not proof that the strict ideal law holds.

Under this terminology, most commercial devices are clearly memristive systems, while their status as ideal fundamental memristors remains unproven and, under Vongehr and Meng’s interpretation, categorically mistaken.

### 12.2 Neuromorphic value

The field’s practical center of gravity has moved away from proving an ideal fourth element. Contemporary work focuses on:

* analog in-memory vector–matrix multiplication;
* nonvolatile synaptic weight storage;
* selector and rectifier integration;
* differential cells;
* smaller tiled arrays;
* variability-aware training;
* hardware–software co-design;
* CMOS peripheral optimization.

The 2024 hardware-accelerator review describes a transition from proof-of-concept arrays toward products, but also highlights scale-up, peripheral circuitry, and commercialization as continuing issues (https://www.nature.com/articles/s44287-024-00037-6).

### 12.3 Final judgment on synaptic plasticity

Memristive device physics genuinely enables compact, local, persistent, and sometimes stochastic conductance adaptation. Those properties are valuable for synaptic hardware. But current evidence does not support the stronger proposition that memristors possess a categorically superior plasticity mechanism compared with CMOS alternatives.

The better-supported conclusion is narrower:

> Memristive devices can implement certain forms of synaptic state and update with fewer physical elements and less weight movement than conventional separated memory-and-logic systems. Their advantage is architectural density and in-memory operation, offset by variability, nonlinear updates, retention, endurance, sneak paths, and peripheral overhead.

CMOS remains necessary around nearly every demonstrated array, and SRAM-based systems remain highly competitive in accuracy and energy efficiency. Memristive accelerators are therefore best understood as **hybrid CMOS–resistive systems**, not replacements for CMOS and not applications whose success depends on resolving whether the device is Chua’s fundamental fourth element.

---

## Conclusion

Williams and the HP team made a consequential connection in 2008: nanoscale ionic motion can couple stored material state to electronic conduction in a way that approximates a charge-dependent memory resistance and is highly useful for dense memory and neuromorphic computation. Their work revived Chua’s terminology and supplied a compact model for many resistive-switching devices.

Vongehr and Meng correctly identified that this engineering achievement is not identical to demonstrating a unique electromagnetic fourth element. The HP model is ideal only in a restricted unsaturated regime; practical devices have bounded, stochastic, thresholded, multidimensional internal states. Calling them memristive systems is technically safer than claiming that every commercial device satisfies the strict 1971 constitutive law.

The crossbar evidence reinforces this conclusion. Knowm relies on multiplexed unit arrays, differential pairs, and stochastic modeling; Michigan relies on rectifying Ag/Si devices, high ON/OFF ratio, and selectors; KAIST-associated RRAM studies rely on 1S1R cells, statistical margins, self-rectification, and two-port cancellation. These are effective solutions precisely because real devices are non-ideal.

Finally, MNIST and CIFAR-10 results from 2020–2024 show genuine progress, including a 16,384-cell hardware CNN with more than 96% MNIST accuracy, a 723,444-device differential PCM mapping with 93.7% CIFAR-10 accuracy, and a self-rectifying 1-kbit array with zero errors in a 1,500-example MNIST experiment. Yet CMOS/SRAM systems report equally strong or stronger MNIST accuracy and very high TOPS/W. The evidence therefore supports memristors as promising, potentially superior **in-memory synaptic storage and computation devices in selected workloads**, but not as universally superior learning elements—and not conclusively as the literal fourth fundamental circuit element.

Compare how three specific crossbar array implementations—Knowm's AHaH nodes, the University of Michigan's Ag/Si memristive system, and RRAM-based approaches from KAIST—address the sneak path problem and device variability issues documented in their respective IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices publications.
